item.description: Potato wedges roasted hard with cumin, coriander and garlic until the edges blacken, finished with lemon and chilli.
item.content:encoded:
Ground cumin burns long before a potato is properly roasted, so half of it goes on at the start to perfume the oil and the rest goes on when the tray comes out. Coating potatoes in all the spice up front gives you a bitter, scorched crust and a bland interior. Parboiling first and then roughing the edges in the colander creates the broken surface that catches the oil and turns almost black — the same trick as a British roast potato, to a completely different end.

  • Rough the edges in the colander. That is where the crust comes from.
  • Half the cumin at the start, half at the end — it burns.
  • Lemon while they are still hot.

item.title: Fabada Asturiana
item.description: Fabada asturiana — Asturian bean stew with fabes, chorizo, morcilla and pork in a rich paprika broth.
item.content:encoded:
The beans are never stirred with a spoon — the pot is shaken instead — because stirring breaks their delicate skins and clouds the broth. Adding a splash of cold water twice during cooking, the technique called asustar, shocks the beans and helps them cook evenly without bursting.

  • Shake, never stir. Broken beans give a cloudy fabada and Asturians will notice.
  • Salt only at the very end, once you know how much the cured meats have contributed.
  • It is significantly better the next day, which is how it is traditionally eaten.

item.title: Dukkah
item.description: Toasted hazelnuts, sesame, coriander and cumin pounded to a dry, uneven rubble for dipping bread and oil into.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is toasted separately, because a hazelnut needs eight minutes and a sesame seed needs ninety seconds, and toasting them together guarantees that something is either raw or burnt. The texture is the other half: dukkah is pounded, not blended, and it must stay dry and uneven. A food processor run for more than a few pulses releases the oil in the nuts and turns the whole thing into a paste, which is a different and much worse condiment.

  • Toast each thing separately. The timings are not close.
  • Pound, do not blend. Blending makes nut butter.
  • Keep it dry — no oil in the mix itself.

item.title: Pastéis de Nata
item.description: Pastéis de nata — Portuguese custard tarts with laminated pastry and blistered, caramelised cinnamon custard.
item.content:encoded:
The oven must be as hot as it will go, because the pastry needs to set and laminate before the custard overcooks — a moderate oven gives a pale tart with a set, rubbery filling instead of a blistered one with a loose centre. The custard is deliberately underbaked at the centre and continues setting as it cools.

  • Maximum heat, top shelf. Without real heat you will never get the scorched tops.
  • Cold custard into room-temperature pastry cases. This buys the pastry time to laminate.
  • They are best within an hour of baking, which is why Lisbon bakeries sell them all day long.

item.title: Torly
item.description: Aubergine, courgette, potato and carrot roasted together in a garlic tomato sauce until soft enough to eat with a spoon.
item.content:encoded:
The vegetables are roasted before the sauce goes anywhere near them, which is the difference between torly and a wet vegetable stew. Twenty-five minutes in a hot oven drives off water and browns the cut faces; only then does the tomato go in, and it coats rather than boils. Cut everything large — 4 cm — because the point is soft, yielding pieces that keep their identity, and small dice simply dissolves into a mush.

  • Roast first, sauce second. Otherwise it is a boiled stew.
  • Cut everything large so the pieces survive.
  • Two trays for the roasting — crowding steams them.

item.title: Roz Mermah
item.description: Short-grain Egyptian rice cooked with vermicelli browned in butter first, giving a nutty base under every other dish.
item.content:encoded:
The vermicelli has to be browned properly in the butter — to the colour of strong tea, not pale gold — because that toasting is the entire flavour contribution and undercooked noodles just add texture. It takes about four minutes of constant attention and goes from perfect to burnt in roughly twenty seconds, so it cannot be left. Egyptian rice is short-grain and is rinsed rather than soaked; the small amount of surface starch that survives is what gives the dish its slight stickiness.

  • Brown the vermicelli to a real colour. Pale means no flavour.
  • Stir once after the liquid goes in, then never again.
  • Ten minutes covered off the heat is part of the cooking, not a rest.

item.title: Kishk Masri
item.description: A thick sour soup of yogurt cooked out with flour and garlic, poured over fried bread and crisp onions.
item.content:encoded:
The flour has to be cooked out for a good five minutes in the butter before any yogurt goes in, or the finished soup tastes raw and pasty — this is a roux, and it behaves like one. Once the yogurt is in, the same rule applies as to every yogurt sauce in this book: constant stirring in one direction until it simmers, at which point it is stable. Take the pan off the heat the moment it thickens; kishk left bubbling turns grainy.

  • Cook the flour out for a full 5 minutes or the soup tastes raw.
  • One direction, constant stirring, until it simmers.
  • Off the heat the moment it thickens.

item.title: Caldo Verde
item.description: Caldo verde — Portuguese potato soup with finely shredded greens and chouriço, ready in 50 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
The greens go in for only two or three minutes at the very end, which keeps them bright green and slightly firm — cooked into the soup they turn khaki and bitter. Blending the potato base rather than adding cream gives body from starch alone.

  • Shred the greens as finely as you can manage. Coarse pieces make it a different, lesser soup.
  • Three minutes for the greens, no more. Any longer and the colour goes.
  • Good olive oil, added off the heat, does more here than any amount of cream would.

item.title: Hawawshi
item.description: Flatbread stuffed with raw spiced minced beef and baked hard, so the rendering fat crisps the bread from the inside.
item.content:encoded:
Like arayes, the meat goes in raw so its fat renders into the bread rather than being lost in a pan first — but hawawshi is baked rather than griddled, and that means the oven has to be genuinely hot. At 240°C the bread crisps in the same fifteen minutes the thin layer of beef needs; any cooler and the bread goes leathery while it waits. Pricking the top lets steam out, without which the whole thing puffs and separates from its filling.

  • Raw meat, hot oven. Both, or it does not work.
  • A thin layer — 8 mm at most, or the middle stays raw.
  • Prick the top or it balloons away from the filling.

item.title: Macarona Bechamel
item.description: Penne bound in thick béchamel over spiced minced beef, baked until the top sets firm enough to cut into squares.
item.content:encoded:
The béchamel is made deliberately thicker than a sauce has any right to be, because it has to set firm enough to cut into squares rather than run across the plate. That means a full sixty grams of flour to a litre of milk, and cooking it out until it drops from the spoon in a heavy sheet. The pasta is also cooked several minutes short of al dente, since it keeps absorbing milk in the oven — cooked properly first it turns to porridge by the time the top has browned.

  • A very thick béchamel. It has to set, not pour.
  • Undercook the pasta by 4 minutes.
  • Cool the sauce before the eggs go in, or they scramble.

item.title: Bacalhau à Brás
item.description: Bacalhau à Brás — salt cod with straw potatoes and softly scrambled egg, finished with olives and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
The eggs are added off the heat and folded only until they just thicken, using the residual warmth of the potatoes and cod — a fully cooked egg turns the dish dry and granular. Frying the potatoes to complete crispness first means they hold some crunch even after the egg goes in.

  • Soak the cod for at least 24 hours with several water changes, and taste a flake before you commit.
  • Off the heat for the eggs. This is the difference between à Brás and a cod omelette.
  • Shop-bought batata palha is what most Portuguese cooks use and is entirely acceptable.

item.title: Fattah
item.description: Fried bread layered with rice and slow-cooked lamb under a sharp garlic, vinegar and tomato sauce poured on at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The vinegar in the sauce is what makes fattah taste Egyptian rather than merely rich, and it goes in off the heat so it stays sharp. Cooked into the tomato it mellows to nothing, and the dish becomes a heavy plate of meat and starch with no relief. The assembly order matters too: bread on the bottom, then rice, then meat, with the sauce poured over at the last second so the bread is softened by it rather than dissolved in it.

  • Vinegar off the heat. Cooked in, it disappears.
  • Moisten the bread with broth, not sauce, or it collapses.
  • Assemble at the last moment.

item.title: Kofta Masreya
item.description: Minced beef and lamb worked with onion, parsley and black pepper, shaped onto skewers and grilled hard and fast.
item.content:encoded:
Kofta falls off the skewer for one of two reasons: the meat was too lean, or it was not worked enough. Twenty per cent fat is the minimum, and the mixture has to be kneaded for a good three minutes until it turns tacky and starts clinging to the bowl — that is myosin developing, and it is the only binder in the recipe. Chilling the shaped skewers for half an hour firms them further. Grated onion must be squeezed bone dry, since its water is the other thing that loosens the mix.

  • Knead until it goes tacky. That is the only thing holding it together.
  • Squeeze the onion completely dry.
  • Flat skewers, not round ones — round ones let the meat spin.

item.title: Piri Piri Chicken
item.description: Piri piri chicken — spatchcocked and marinated in bird's eye chilli, garlic and lemon, then grilled and basted.
item.content:encoded:
Spatchcocking flattens the bird so the thighs and breast finish at the same time, which is otherwise impossible with a whole chicken. Half the marinade is cooked into a basting sauce so it thickens and clings, while the raw half does the marinating — never using the same batch for both.

  • Never baste with the marinade that touched raw chicken. Cook a separate batch for that.
  • Adjust the chillies to taste — ten is properly hot, five is approachable, twenty is a statement.
  • Finish under a hot grill for 3 minutes if you want more char on the skin.

item.title: Kebda Eskandarani
item.description: Beef liver cut into thin strips and seared in seconds with garlic, chilli and cumin, finished with lemon off the heat.
item.content:encoded:
Liver goes from tender to grey and grainy in under a minute, so the pan has to be extremely hot and the liver has to go in dry and in batches. A crowded pan drops in temperature, the liver releases water, and it stews in it — which is exactly how most people ruin this dish. Salt at the end for the same reason: salted liver weeps in the pan before it ever sees the heat.

  • Dry liver, smoking pan, two batches. All three or it stews.
  • Salt at the end. Early salt draws out water.
  • Still pink when it leaves the pan — it finishes on the way to the table.

item.title: Sayadeya Masreya
item.description: Fish fried and set aside while its stock and frying oil cook cumin-heavy rice under deeply browned onions.
item.content:encoded:
Frying the fish first rather than poaching it is the Egyptian difference, and the oil it leaves behind is not waste — it carries the flavour into the rice and is the reason this tastes markedly more of fish than its Lebanese cousin. Strain it, because the fried crumbs will burn in the twenty minutes the rice needs. Cumin goes in at a quantity that seems heavy-handed and is correct for the dish.

  • Strain the frying oil before the rice goes in, or the crumbs burn.
  • Take the onions genuinely dark.
  • More cumin than feels right. That is the dish.

item.title: Khao Soi
item.description: Khao soi — northern Thai coconut curry noodle soup with soft and crisp egg noodles, pickled greens and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Cracking the coconut cream over high heat until the oil separates and then frying the curry paste in that oil is the foundational Thai technique — it blooms the fat-soluble aromatics in a way that simmering never does. The two noodle textures are not decoration: the crisp nest keeps its crunch above the surface while the soft noodles absorb the broth.

  • Do not shake the coconut milk tin. You need the thick cream separately to crack the oil.
  • Fry the paste properly — four minutes, until it darkens and the kitchen smells of it.
  • The pickled mustard greens are essential. Their sourness is what balances the richness.

item.title: Hamam Mahshi
item.description: Pigeon stuffed with green freekeh, simmered in aromatics and then roasted hard so the skin crisps over the grain.
item.content:encoded:
Pigeon is small, lean and unforgiving, and roasting it from raw gives you either raw legs or a dry breast. Simmering first in the aromatics cooks the bird and the stuffing through gently and gives you the stock the freekeh needs; the oven then does nothing but crisp the skin, which takes fifteen minutes. Stuff loosely — freekeh swells, and a tightly packed bird splits along the breastbone.

  • Poach first, roast second. Roasting from raw dries the breast.
  • Two-thirds full — freekeh swells and will split the bird.
  • Dry the skin before it goes in the oven.

item.title: Ferakh Mashwi
item.description: Spatchcocked chicken grilled under a thin cumin, garlic and lemon paste until the skin chars in patches.
item.content:encoded:
The marinade contains no yogurt and very little oil, which is deliberate: a thick coating insulates the skin and steams it, where a thin one burns in patches and gives the char this dish depends on. Spatchcocking is the other half — flattening the bird means the thighs and breast finally sit at the same height and cook in the same time, which a whole roasting chicken never manages under a grill.

  • A thin marinade. A thick one steams the skin.
  • Slash to the bone or the thighs will not be done with the breast.
  • Char in patches is correct. Uniform gold means the heat was too low.

item.title: Mombar
item.description: Sausage casings filled loosely with spiced rice and mince, boiled until the rice swells, then fried until blistered.
item.content:encoded:
Fill them a third full and no more. The rice inside is raw and triples as it boils, and a casing packed even half full will burst along its length and empty into the water — which is the single failure mode of this dish and the reason it has a reputation for being difficult. It is not difficult, it is just counterintuitive. Prick each one before boiling as well, so steam has a route out that is not the seam.

  • A third full. This is the whole trick.
  • Prick them before boiling.
  • Bare simmer, never a rolling boil.

item.title: Larb Gai
item.description: Larb gai — Thai minced chicken salad with toasted rice powder, lime, fish sauce, mint and shallot.
item.content:encoded:
Khao khua — raw sticky rice toasted and ground — is the ingredient that makes larb larb: it adds a nutty aroma and a faint grittiness that also thickens the dressing so it clings to the meat. The chicken is poached in a splash of water rather than fried, keeping it moist and leaving a small amount of liquid that becomes part of the dressing.

  • Toast the rice until it is genuinely dark. Pale rice powder tastes of nothing.
  • Taste and adjust the dressing before it goes on. Larb should be sharper than seems sensible.
  • Add the herbs last and serve immediately, or they wilt in the residual heat.

item.title: Renga
item.description: Smoked herring flaked and dressed with lemon, oil, onion and cumin, eaten with bread and spring onions at Sham el-Nessim.
item.content:encoded:
Soaking is not optional. Renga is cured hard and comes out of the packet far too salty to eat; twenty minutes in milk or water pulls enough of it out to leave something seasoned rather than punishing, and rinsing afterwards takes the surface salt with it. Everything else is raw and sharp on purpose — this is a dish designed to stand up to a very strong fish, and a gentle dressing would simply vanish underneath it.

  • Soak it. Straight from the packet it is inedible.
  • Large flakes, folded gently — do not shred it.
  • Soak the onion too, briefly.

item.title: Goulash Masri
item.description: Layers of filo over spiced minced beef, brushed with butter and baked in a tray until shatteringly crisp, then cut into squares.
item.content:encoded:
Every single sheet gets brushed, and there is no shortcut. Filo layers that are not individually greased fuse into a pale leathery slab instead of separating into leaves, and the whole appeal of this dish is the shattering top. The other rule is cutting it before it bakes: filo that has crisped cannot be cut cleanly, and attempting it shatters the top into the filling. Score right through to the base while it is still soft.

  • Butter every sheet. Skipping any fuses the layers.
  • Score before baking. You cannot cut it cleanly afterwards.
  • The filling must be cool and dry, or the base goes soggy.

item.title: Thai Red Curry
item.description: Thai red curry with chicken, bamboo and Thai basil in a coconut sauce built by cracking the cream properly.
item.content:encoded:
Cracking the coconut cream — heating it until it splits into oil and solids — creates a frying medium for the curry paste, which dissolves its fat-soluble aromatics and transforms raw paste into a deep, rounded base. Adding the remaining coconut milk afterwards, and never boiling it hard, keeps the finished sauce smooth.

  • Do not shake the tin. Cracking the cream is the step that separates a real Thai curry from coconut milk with paste stirred in.
  • Thai basil, not Italian. The aniseed note is central and sweet basil is not a substitute.
  • Taste and adjust at the end, every time. Curry pastes vary enormously in salt and heat.

item.title: Feteer Meshaltet
item.description: Dough stretched paper-thin and folded repeatedly with ghee, baked into a layered pastry between a pancake and a croissant.
item.content:encoded:
The dough must be stretched until you can read through it, and the only way to get there is a very soft dough and a well-greased surface — flour is never used for this, because it would dry the sheet and stop the layers separating. Ghee rather than butter matters too: butter contains water, which turns to steam and blows the layers apart unevenly, where clarified ghee simply lubricates them so they slide and stay distinct.

  • Ghee on the surface, never flour.
  • Stretch until it is translucent. Thick means no layers.
  • Rest the ghee-coated balls before stretching or the dough tears.

item.title: Pad See Ew
item.description: Pad see ew — wide rice noodles charred in a hot wok with dark soy, egg and Chinese broccoli.
item.content:encoded:
Wok hei comes from noodles sitting undisturbed against searingly hot metal for thirty seconds at a time — constant stirring cools the pan and steams instead of chars. Fresh wide rice noodles must be separated by hand at room temperature, because cold ones shatter and hot ones tear.

  • Leave the noodles alone between tosses. That stillness is where the char comes from.
  • Cook one or two portions at a time. A crowded wok cannot get hot enough.
  • Never refrigerate fresh rice noodles. They go brittle and break into fragments.

item.title: Gebna Domiati Salad
item.description: Soft brined Damietta cheese cubed with tomato, cucumber and green pepper, dressed with oil, lemon and dried mint.
item.content:encoded:
Domiati is packed in a strong brine and its saltiness varies enormously between producers, so it is tasted before anything else is decided — a mild block wants a pinch of salt in the dressing and a fierce one wants a soak in cold water first. Adding salt blind is how this ends up inedible. Cutting the cheese in large cubes rather than crumbling it also matters: it holds its shape against the tomato instead of dissolving into a paste.

  • Taste the cheese before you season anything.
  • Cubes, not crumbles — they hold up.
  • Turn it once. Repeated tossing breaks the cheese down.

item.title: Batarekh
item.description: Cured and pressed grey mullet roe sliced paper-thin, served with olive oil, lemon and bread as a mezze.
item.content:encoded:
Batarekh is intense enough that the entire preparation is about restraint — the wax coating comes off, the block is sliced as thin as the knife will allow, and nothing is added but oil and lemon. Slicing it thick makes it overwhelmingly salty and slightly waxy on the tongue; at a millimetre it turns translucent and tastes of the sea rather than of salt. Chilling the block firms it enough to cut cleanly, which a room-temperature one will not do.

  • Slice it paper-thin. Thick slices are just salt.
  • Chill before slicing or it crumbles.
  • Oil and lemon only. It needs nothing else.

item.title: Thai Iced Tea
item.description: Thai iced tea (cha yen) — strong spiced black tea with condensed milk over ice and an evaporated milk float.
item.content:encoded:
The tea is brewed at roughly four times normal strength because it is about to be diluted by ice and milk — an ordinary brew tastes of nothing by the time it reaches the glass. Pouring the evaporated milk over the back of a spoon lets it float as a distinct layer, which is the drink's signature look.

  • Brew it much stronger than seems reasonable. Dilution is coming from every direction.
  • Chill the tea fully before it meets the ice, or the ice melts instantly and the drink is watery.
  • Genuine Thai tea mix is worth buying — the blend includes the spices and the colouring that make it recognisable.

item.title: Balah el Sham
item.description: Ridged choux fingers deep-fried rather than baked and dropped straight from the oil into cold sugar syrup.
item.content:encoded:
The oil starts cold, or nearly so, and comes up to temperature with the pastry already in it — which is the opposite of every other frying instruction in this book and is what gives balah el sham its hollow inside. Dropped into hot oil the outside sets instantly and the centre stays raw and dense. And as with every syrup-soaked pastry here: hot into cold, so it takes a coating and stops rather than drinking until it collapses.

  • Into cold oil, then heat it. This is what makes them hollow.
  • A star nozzle, not a plain one.
  • Hot pastry, cold syrup, forty seconds.

item.title: Om Ali
item.description: Torn puff pastry baked in sweetened milk with nuts, raisins and coconut until the top blisters and the base sets to custard.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry is baked dry and crisp before any milk goes near it, which is the step that decides whether this is a pudding or a bowl of wet paper. Twelve minutes in a hot oven drives the moisture out and sets the layers, so they can absorb the milk without disintegrating. Pour the milk hot as well — cold milk over crisp pastry soaks unevenly, leaving dry patches on top and sludge underneath.

  • Bake the pastry crisp first. Raw pastry turns to paste.
  • Hot milk, poured evenly, then pressed down.
  • The blistered top is the point — do not pull it out pale.

item.title: Roz bel Laban
item.description: Egyptian rice pudding cooked on the hob without eggs until the starch alone thickens it, served cold with cinnamon.
item.content:encoded:
The rice is boiled in water first and only then finished in the milk, which is what stops the milk catching and scorching over the forty minutes the grain needs. It also lets the starch out into the water where it can be kept — that starchy liquid goes into the pan with the milk and is the only thickener in the recipe. Short-grain rice is essential; long-grain simply does not release enough starch and the result stays thin however long it cooks.

  • Boil in water first, then finish in milk. It stops the milk catching.
  • Short-grain rice only.
  • It thickens hugely as it cools — take it off looser than you want it.

item.title: Bún Bò Huế
item.description: Bún bò Huế — spicy Vietnamese lemongrass beef noodle soup with thick rice noodles and a plate of herbs.
item.content:encoded:
Fermented shrimp paste dissolved into the broth supplies the savoury depth that defines this soup, and it must be simmered in rather than added at the end so its sharpness mellows. The annatto and chilli oil floated on top is both colour and aroma, and it separates from the broth by design.

  • Let the shrimp paste settle and use only the clear liquid. The sediment is gritty and bitter.
  • The herb plate is not garnish. Tearing herbs in as you eat is how the dish is meant to work.
  • Thick round noodles, not flat pho noodles. The texture is central to bún bò Huế.

item.title: Qatayef Mahshi
item.description: One-sided pancakes stuffed with walnuts and cinnamon, sealed, fried until crisp and dropped into cold syrup.
item.content:encoded:
The pancake is cooked on one side only, and the wet holed surface that leaves is what makes the seam stick — this is the same principle as the Lebanese atayef, but here the parcel is sealed completely and fried, so the seal has to be genuinely airtight. Pinch from the point of the fold all the way round and press hard. Any gap lets oil in and the nuts out, and a leaked qatayef will ruin the whole pan of oil.

  • One side only. A turned pancake will not seal.
  • Pinch the whole seam and check it. Leaks ruin the oil.
  • Hot from the fryer into cold syrup.

item.title: Zalabya
item.description: A wet yeasted batter dropped into hot oil in spoonfuls, fried into irregular golden balls and soaked in syrup.
item.content:encoded:
The batter is far wetter than a dough — closer to a thick pancake batter — and that is what gives the interior its open, almost hollow crumb. Anything stiff enough to roll gives you a dense fried ball. Handle it with two wet spoons and accept that the shapes will be irregular; that is what they look like. The oil at 170°C is deliberately moderate, because these need six minutes to cook through and would burn at frying temperature proper.

  • A loose batter, not a dough. Stiff means dense.
  • Two wet spoons, and accept irregular shapes.
  • Moderate oil — they need six minutes and would burn hotter.

item.title: Cơm Tấm
item.description: Cơm tấm — Saigon broken rice with lemongrass grilled pork chop, shredded pork skin and nước chấm.
item.content:encoded:
Broken rice grains absorb sauce far faster than whole ones because their exposed starchy interiors have nowhere to hide — it was originally a cheap by-product and turned out to be better for this dish. The pork is marinated with sugar and honey, which caramelises under the grill into the lacquered crust the dish is known for.

  • Stop basting with the raw marinade in the final minutes so the surface can char rather than steam.
  • Broken rice is sold in Vietnamese shops and is worth seeking out; jasmine rice works but is not the same.
  • Make more nước chấm than you think you need. It goes on everything on the plate.

item.title: Kunafa bil Manga
item.description: Shredded kunafa pastry baked crisp in butter, then layered with thick cream and fresh mango instead of syrup.
item.content:encoded:
This is the one kunafa that is not drowned in syrup, and the reason is the mango: fresh fruit brings its own sugar and acid, and syrup on top of it is simply too much. So the pastry is baked in butter until genuinely crisp and stays that way, assembled at the last minute. Rub the butter through the shredded pastry with your fingers rather than pouring it over — poured butter soaks the bottom layer and leaves the top dry.

  • Rub the butter through by hand. Pouring it soaks the base.
  • No syrup. The mango is the sweetness.
  • Assemble at the last minute or the pastry softens.

item.title: Karkade
item.description: Dried hibiscus steeped rather than boiled into a deep red, sour infusion, served either scalding hot or over ice.
item.content:encoded:
Hibiscus is steeped, never boiled. Boiling extracts the tannins that make it harshly astringent and dulls the colour from clear crimson to brown, so the water comes off the heat before the flowers go in. Fifteen minutes is enough for a full extraction. Sweeten while it is hot regardless of how you plan to serve it, because sugar will not dissolve properly in a cold infusion and you will end up with a gritty layer at the bottom of the jug.

  • Steep off the heat. Boiling makes it bitter and brown.
  • Fifteen minutes is plenty. Longer is not stronger, only harsher.
  • Sweeten hot, even if serving cold.

item.title: Sobia
item.description: Soaked rice and coconut blended with milk and sugar into a cloudy white Ramadan drink served very cold.
item.content:encoded:
The rice is soaked raw and never cooked, which is what gives sobia its particular cloudy body — cooked rice blends to a thin porridge instead. Soak it long enough that a grain crushes easily between finger and thumb, then blend hard and strain once through a coarse sieve rather than a fine one. Straining too finely removes the very slight grittiness that people who grew up with this drink expect and would notice missing.

  • Raw soaked rice. Cooking it gives a thin, sad drink.
  • A coarse sieve. Fine straining removes the texture.
  • It separates on standing — stir before every pour.

item.title: Chả Giò
item.description: Chả giò — Vietnamese fried spring rolls in rice paper with pork, prawn and glass noodles, wrapped in herbs.
item.content:encoded:
Rice paper fries into a bubbled, glassy shell quite unlike a wheat wrapper, but it burns fast, so the oil must sit around 170°C rather than the higher heat used for Chinese rolls. Squeezing the water from the vegetables and using dry glass noodles keeps the filling from steaming the wrapper open from inside.

  • The sugar in the dipping water helps the wrapper blister and brown. It is a traditional trick and it works.
  • Do not let the rolls touch while they rest or fry — rice paper glues itself to anything it meets.
  • Fry twice, once at 160°C and again at 180°C, if you want them to stay crisp for longer at a party.

item.title: Asab
item.description: Fresh-pressed sugarcane juice served immediately over ice with lime, since it browns within about twenty minutes of pressing.
item.content:encoded:
Sugarcane juice oxidises visibly within twenty minutes of pressing — it goes from pale green to grey-brown and loses its fresh grassy note entirely — which is why every asab stall in Egypt presses to order in front of you and why bottled versions taste nothing like it. A squeeze of lime slows the browning by acidifying the juice, and serving it over plenty of ice slows it further. There is no way to make this ahead, and no point trying.

  • Lime straight away. It buys you time against oxidation.
  • Press three times — most of the yield is in the later passes.
  • There is no making this in advance.

item.title: Harissa
item.description: Dried chillies rehydrated and pounded with garlic, caraway and coriander seed into a coarse, deeply red Tunisian paste.
item.content:encoded:
Caraway is what makes harissa Tunisian rather than merely hot, and it has to be toasted whole and ground fresh — pre-ground caraway loses the anise note within weeks and leaves you with heat and not much else. The chillies matter almost as much: use a mild, meaty dried chilli for the body and a small number of hot ones for the heat, rather than a single fierce variety, or you get a paste that burns without tasting of anything. Squeeze them properly dry after soaking, since water in the jar shortens the keeping time drastically.

  • Toast and grind the caraway yourself. This is the whole flavour.
  • Two kinds of chilli — mild for body, hot for heat.
  • Squeeze the chillies genuinely dry or it will not keep.

item.title: Kimbap
item.description: Korean kimbap — sesame rice rolled in seaweed with spinach, carrot, egg and beef, sliced into coins.
item.content:encoded:
Sesame oil rather than vinegar in the rice is the defining difference from sushi, and it also coats the grains so they stay soft rather than drying out at room temperature. Each filling is cooked and seasoned separately so it keeps its own identity in the finished slice rather than blurring into one flavour.

  • Less rice than you think. Overfilled kimbap will not close and bursts when sliced.
  • Wipe the knife constantly. Sticky rice on the blade tears the seaweed.
  • Kimbap is meant to be eaten at room temperature, not chilled, so it is ideal made a few hours ahead.

item.title: Lablabi
item.description: Chickpeas in cumin and garlic broth poured over torn stale bread with an egg stirred in, plus harissa, capers and olive oil.
item.content:encoded:
The bread goes in the bowl and the broth is poured over it, never the other way round — bread simmered in the pot dissolves into paste, where bread hit with boiling broth at the table softens but keeps its shape for the ten minutes it takes to eat. Stale bread is not a thrift measure but a requirement, since fresh bread collapses instantly. The egg is cracked into the hot bowl and stirred, so it sets in threads rather than poaching whole.

  • Stale bread only. Fresh bread turns to paste.
  • Broth over bread in the bowl, never bread into the pot.
  • The broth must be boiling when it hits the egg.

item.title: Slata Tounsia
item.description: Tomato, cucumber, pepper and onion cut to a very fine dice and dressed simply with olive oil, lemon and dried mint.
item.content:encoded:
The dice is smaller than any other salad in this book — five millimetres, not fifteen — and that is not fussiness. At this size the vegetables stop behaving like separate things on a fork and become a single dressed mass you eat with bread, which is how it is served. It also means the salad must be assembled immediately before eating: cut this fine, tomato gives up its water within about ten minutes.

  • Five millimetres. Larger and it becomes a different salad.
  • Deseed everything or it floods.
  • Salt last, serve immediately.

item.title: Omek Houria
item.description: Carrots boiled soft and crushed with harissa, garlic and caraway into a warm-spiced cold salad eaten with bread.
item.content:encoded:
The carrots are crushed with a fork, never blended — a food processor turns them into baby food and loses the uneven texture that lets the harissa sit in pockets rather than being evenly distributed. Boil them until genuinely soft, well past the point you would want for a side dish, so they crush without resistance. Dress them while hot, because warm carrot absorbs the oil and harissa in a way cold carrot simply will not.

  • Crush with a fork. Blending ruins the texture.
  • Dress while hot so the carrot drinks the oil.
  • Boil them properly soft — this is not a crunchy salad.

item.title: Sundubu Jjigae
item.description: Sundubu jjigae — Korean silken tofu stew with gochugaru chilli oil, seafood or pork, and an egg cracked in.
item.content:encoded:
Frying the gochugaru in oil with the pork before any liquid goes in creates a red chilli oil that carries the flavour throughout the stew — adding chilli flakes to the broth later leaves them gritty and dull. The stone pot retains enough heat to keep the stew boiling at the table, which is what cooks the egg.

  • Bloom the chilli flakes in oil. Every good Korean stew starts this way.
  • Do not stir the tofu apart. Large soft curds are the point of sundubu.
  • A stone ttukbaegi is worth owning — it holds heat for a remarkably long time.

item.title: Kafteji
item.description: Peppers, tomato, courgette and potato fried separately then chopped together on a board with fried eggs and harissa.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is fried separately, and skipping that is the one way to get this wrong. A courgette needs three minutes and a potato needs twelve; thrown into one pan you get burnt courgette and raw potato. Fry each in the same oil in sequence, building flavour as you go, then combine only on the board. The chopping itself is part of the dish — the vegetables are cut together with two knives until everything is roughly the same small size and the juices have mingled.

  • Fry each vegetable separately. The timings are not close.
  • Chop on a board, not in a pan.
  • The eggs get chopped in with everything else.

item.title: Salata Blankit
item.description: Warm potato salad dressed with harissa, capers, olives and lemon while the potatoes are still hot, with no mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
Hot potato absorbs dressing and cold potato repels it, which is why this is dressed the moment it comes out of the pan and left to cool afterwards rather than the reverse. The harissa also needs the heat to bloom — stirred into a cold salad it sits on the surface as red streaks, where on hot potato it disperses and colours the whole bowl. Use a waxy variety so the cubes survive being turned in the dressing.

  • Dress the potatoes hot. Cold potato takes up nothing.
  • Waxy potatoes, so the cubes survive turning.
  • No mayonnaise. It is not that kind of salad.

item.title: Galbi (Korean Short Ribs)
item.description: Galbi — Korean marinated beef short ribs with soy, Asian pear and sesame, grilled until charred at the edges.
item.content:encoded:
Asian pear contains calpain, a protease that breaks down muscle proteins, which is why traditional galbi marinades tenderise so effectively without turning the meat to mush. The sugar in the marinade caramelises fast over fire, so the ribs are cooked hot and briefly rather than slowly.

  • Do not marinate for more than 24 hours. The pear will turn the surface of the meat soft and pasty.
  • Wipe off surplus marinade before grilling. Excess sugar burns black before the meat is done.
  • Ask a butcher for flanken-cut short ribs, sliced across the bones. It is worth the request.

item.title: Doigts de Fatma
item.description: Malsouka or filo pastry rolled around cheese, parsley and minced meat and fried into crisp golden cigars.
item.content:encoded:
Malsouka is thinner and more brittle than filo and dries out within minutes of leaving its packet, so the sheets stay under a damp cloth and are worked one at a time. Egg wash rather than flour paste seals these — it sets hard in the oil and holds where a starch paste can soften. The filling must be cool and dry for the same reason as every fried parcel in this book: steam inside a sealed pastry finds the seam and opens it.

  • Keep the pastry under a damp cloth. Malsouka dries out in minutes.
  • Egg wash to seal — it sets harder than flour paste.
  • Cold, dry filling. Warm filling bursts the seam.

item.title: Chorba Frik
item.description: Lamb and green freekeh soup thickened by the grain itself, sharpened with harissa and finished with parsley and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Freekeh releases starch as it cooks and is the only thickener here — no flour, no blending — so it needs the full forty minutes and cannot be rushed. It also has to be rinsed and picked over first, because it is a fire-roasted field grain and genuinely arrives with grit in it. The harissa goes in early, fried into the tomato base, which is where it belongs in a soup: added at the end it tastes raw and sits on top.

  • Fry the harissa into the base. Added late it tastes raw.
  • Rinse the freekeh properly — it carries grit.
  • The grain is the thickener. Give it the full 40 minutes.

item.title: Hlelem
item.description: Hand-broken noodles cooked with chickpeas, white beans and greens in a harissa broth until thick enough to stand a spoon in.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles go in for the last twelve minutes only. Hlelem is meant to be thick but the pasta must still have some resistance, and noodles added with the beans will have dissolved into the broth long before the pulses are ready. The greens go in last of all — two minutes, no more, so they stay green. Everything before that point is about building a broth deep enough to carry three fairly bland pulses.

  • Noodles for the last ten minutes only.
  • Greens for two minutes, so they stay green.
  • It thickens as it stands — serve it looser than you want it.

item.title: Haemul Pajeon
item.description: Haemul pajeon — Korean seafood and spring onion pancake fried crisp at the edges, with a soy dipping sauce.
item.content:encoded:
A proportion of potato starch or rice flour in the batter is what makes the pancake crisp rather than bready, because those starches fry into a brittle sheet where wheat flour alone goes soft. Ice-cold batter hitting hot oil produces a violent reaction that sets the surface immediately.

  • Plenty of oil, and add more around the edges when you flip. This pancake is shallow-fried, not dry-cooked.
  • Keep the batter ice cold and use it immediately.
  • Press it flat with a spatula while it cooks so the whole surface makes contact with the pan.

item.title: Bsissa
item.description: Roasted barley and chickpea flour ground with fennel and coriander seed, stirred with olive oil into a breakfast paste or drink.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is roasted before grinding and that is where the entire flavour lives — raw flours give a pasty, faintly bitter mix that no amount of oil or honey will rescue. Roast the grains and seeds separately, since they colour at different rates, and take the barley to a proper nut brown rather than pale gold. Once mixed with liquid it thickens for several minutes, so it is made looser than it should end up.

  • Roast everything separately and take the barley properly dark.
  • Cool before grinding, or the flour steams and clumps.
  • It thickens for several minutes after mixing.

item.title: Mhalbiya
item.description: A rice-flour milk pudding scented with geranium water instead of rose, set in glasses under crushed pistachios.
item.content:encoded:
Geranium water is what distinguishes this from every other milk pudding in the region and it is worth seeking out — it is greener and less perfumed than rose, and rose water substituted straight across makes the dessert taste Levantine. It goes in off the heat, like every flower water, because the aromatics boil off within seconds. Rice flour rather than cornflour gives a softer, slightly grainy set that is characteristic and should not be smoothed out.

  • Geranium water, not rose, if you can find it.
  • It must boil for three minutes or it will not set.
  • Rice flour gives a slightly grainy set. That is correct.

item.title: Samgyetang
item.description: Samgyetang — Korean ginseng chicken soup with a whole stuffed bird, glutinous rice and jujubes in milky broth.
item.content:encoded:
The broth turns opaque and milky because collagen from the small bird's bones and skin emulsifies into the liquid during a long simmer — the same mechanism as tonkotsu ramen, at a gentler scale. The rice inside the cavity cooks in the chicken's own juices and thickens the broth as some of its starch escapes.

  • Do not overstuff. The rice roughly doubles and will split the bird open.
  • Never salt the broth in the pot. Seasoning at the table is the Korean way and lets everyone judge for themselves.
  • Skim well at the start for a clean-tasting broth, then leave it alone.

item.title: Ojja
item.description: Eggs broken into a thick harissa and tomato sauce with merguez sausage and cooked only until the whites just set.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce must be genuinely thick before the eggs go in — you should be able to draw a spoon through it and see the base of the pan for a second. A loose sauce means the eggs sink, poach unevenly and turn rubbery while the liquid reduces around them. Merguez releases a great deal of red fat as it fries and that fat is a seasoning, not something to drain off: it carries the harissa through the whole dish.

  • Reduce the sauce properly before the eggs go in.
  • Keep the merguez fat. It is half the seasoning.
  • Whites just set, yolks running. Thirty seconds too long ruins it.

item.title: Marqa Hlouwa
item.description: Lamb stewed slowly with quince, prunes and cinnamon so the sweetness plays against harissa, made for Eid.
item.content:encoded:
The fruit goes in for the last twenty-five minutes only. Quince and prunes added at the start dissolve entirely and leave a stew that is uniformly sweet with nothing to bite on — the point is whole pieces of fruit sitting in a savoury, chilli-warm sauce. Quince also needs poaching separately if it is very hard, because it can take longer than the lamb; test a piece before deciding, since ripeness varies enormously.

  • Fruit in for the last 25 minutes only.
  • Test the quince first — hardness varies enormously.
  • The sweetness is the point. Do not cut the honey.

item.title: Dakgalbi
item.description: Dakgalbi — Chuncheon-style spicy stir-fried chicken with cabbage, rice cakes and a gochujang marinade.
item.content:encoded:
Marinating for at least four hours lets the gochujang's salt and sugar penetrate the meat rather than sitting on the surface as a sauce. Cooking everything in one wide pan without a lid drives off moisture so the sauce reduces and clings, rather than braising the chicken in its own liquid.

  • The fried rice at the end (bokkeumbap) is not an afterthought — it is why Koreans order dakgalbi.
  • Use the widest pan you own. Crowding steams the chicken instead of frying it.
  • Soak the rice cakes in warm water for 20 minutes first or they stay hard in the centre.

item.title: Kamounia
item.description: Beef or liver stewed slowly with a deliberately large quantity of cumin until the sauce turns dark, thick and earthy.
item.content:encoded:
Three tablespoons of ground cumin is not a typo. Kamounia is named for the spice and is one of the very few stews built on a single dominant flavour, so cutting it back produces something anonymous. Half goes in early to cook down into the sauce and lose its dustiness, half goes in at the end for the sharp top note. If using liver, it is added only for the final ten minutes — an hour of simmering turns liver to rubber.

  • Three tablespoons of cumin. That is the dish.
  • Half early, half at the end.
  • Liver goes in for ten minutes, never an hour.

item.title: Mermez
item.description: Lamb and chickpeas simmered in a thin red harissa broth heavy with onion, poured over bread or couscous.
item.content:encoded:
The broth stays deliberately thin. Mermez is meant to be ladled over bread or couscous which then absorbs it, so a thick, clinging sauce defeats the purpose — it should look almost like a soup in the pot. Sliced onions rather than chopped are the other characteristic: they melt into strands over an hour and give the broth its body without any need for reduction.

  • Keep it thin. The bread does the thickening.
  • Sliced onions, not chopped — they melt into the broth.
  • Chickpeas late so they stay whole.

item.title: Mul Naengmyeon
item.description: Mul naengmyeon — Korean cold buckwheat noodles in icy beef and radish broth with pear, cucumber and egg.
item.content:encoded:
The broth is chilled until ice crystals begin to form, which both makes it genuinely refreshing and slightly dulls the salt, so it is seasoned more aggressively than it would be warm. Rinsing and massaging the cooked noodles under cold water removes surface starch and firms them into the springy, almost rubbery texture the dish is known for.

  • The broth must be freezing, with visible ice. Merely cold broth makes a flat, disappointing bowl.
  • Serve scissors with the bowls. Naengmyeon noodles are famously hard to bite through.
  • Season the broth more heavily than tastes right at room temperature — cold mutes salt considerably.

item.title: Tajine Tunisien
item.description: A thick baked Tunisian omelette of chicken, cheese and parsley set firm in the oven and cut into squares.
item.content:encoded:
This has to be baked until it is genuinely firm all the way through, which feels like overcooking an omelette and is not — a Tunisian tajine is eaten cold in squares from the hand, and anything with a soft centre falls apart. Grated hard cheese does most of the setting alongside the eggs. Cook the chicken and dry it out thoroughly first, because any liquid it releases in the tin will leave a wet layer at the bottom that never sets.

  • Bake it properly firm. A soft centre will not cut.
  • Dry the chicken out completely first.
  • Cool before cutting — hot, it crumbles.

item.title: Felfel Mahchi
item.description: Long green peppers stuffed with spiced meat and rice, then braised in a harissa tomato sauce until the skins blister.
item.content:encoded:
The peppers are browned in oil before they are stuffed, which blisters the skins and means they slip off easily on the plate — an unblistered pepper skin is tough and spoils the texture of everything inside it. Fill them two-thirds full because the rice is raw and swells. And braise them lying down rather than standing, since these are long peppers and standing them up puts the filling under gravity it cannot resist.

  • Blister the skins before stuffing so they slip off later.
  • Two-thirds full. Raw rice doubles.
  • Braise them lying down, not standing.

item.title: Kabkabou
item.description: White fish braised briefly with preserved lemon, olives, tomato and saffron so the sauce reduces around it.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is built and reduced first, and the fish goes in for the last eight minutes only. Fish simmered from the beginning of a thirty-minute reduction disintegrates into shreds — this way it poaches gently in an already-finished sauce and arrives in whole pieces. Preserved lemon is used skin only: the flesh is mushy and aggressively salty, and rinsing the rind before slicing brings it back to something you can use generously.

  • Reduce the sauce before the fish goes in.
  • Preserved lemon rind only — discard the flesh and rinse it.
  • Eight minutes for the fish. It carries on cooking off the heat.

item.title: Nasi Goreng
item.description: Nasi goreng — Indonesian fried rice with kecap manis, shrimp paste and a fried egg on top.
item.content:encoded:
Day-old refrigerated rice has retrograded starch and a dry surface, so the grains separate and fry rather than clumping and steaming. Frying the spice paste until the oil splits from it is what turns raw shallot and chilli into the deep, savoury base the dish rests on.

  • Day-old rice, always. Fresh rice gives a soft, clumpy nasi goreng that will not brown.
  • Kecap manis is thick and sweet and there is no real substitute; dark soy with palm sugar is the nearest approximation.
  • Toast the terasi wrapped in foil in a dry pan for a minute first — it smells alarming and tastes essential.

item.title: Complet Poisson
item.description: Grilled fish served with fried potatoes, tastira, salad, olives and harissa all assembled on a single plate.
item.content:encoded:
Tastira — peppers and tomatoes fried hard and then chopped — is the component people leave out and it is the one that ties the plate together, bridging the plain grilled fish and the harissa. Everything is cooked separately and assembled at the end, and each element should be at its own right temperature: the fish hot, the potatoes hot, the salad cold and the tastira warm. Serving it all at one temperature flattens the whole thing.

  • Do not skip the tastira. It is what joins the plate together.
  • Everything at its own temperature — the salad cold, the rest hot.
  • Assemble at the last second.

item.title: Hout Mechoui
item.description: Whole fish grilled over coals with only oil and salt, served with charred pepper tastira and a great deal of lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Salting the fish twenty minutes before it goes on the grill draws moisture to the surface, which then dries and forms the tacky layer that keeps the skin from welding to the bars. It is the single most useful thing you can do for grilled fish and it takes no effort. Oil the grill bars rather than the fish as well: oil on the fish drips into the coals and flares, coating the skin in soot.

  • Salt 20 minutes ahead. It stops the skin sticking.
  • Oil the bars, not the fish, or it flares and sooty smoke coats the skin.
  • Do not move it on the first side. It releases when ready.

item.title: Beef Rendang
item.description: Beef rendang — Indonesian dry-braised beef cooked four hours in coconut milk and spice paste until dark.
item.content:encoded:
Rendang passes through three stages: simmering in liquid, then a wetter curry called kalio, then finally frying as the coconut milk breaks and its oil is released. That last hour, when the meat browns in coconut oil with toasted coconut, is where the colour and the keeping quality come from.

  • Kerisik — coconut toasted dark and ground to a paste — is what gives rendang its texture. Make it by dry-frying desiccated coconut until deep brown and blitzing it.
  • Stir constantly in the last hour. This is when it catches and burns.
  • It genuinely improves over two or three days, which is why it was originally made for long journeys.

item.title: Rouz Jerbi
item.description: Djerban rice steamed rather than boiled, mixed through with lamb, spinach and herbs until dense and deeply green.
item.content:encoded:
Steaming rather than boiling is what makes this Djerban, and it changes the texture entirely — the grains stay separate and slightly firm rather than swelling soft, which is what lets the rice carry that much herb and meat without turning to porridge. The rice is soaked, drained, mixed raw with everything else, and then steamed as one mass. It takes about an hour and cannot be hurried by adding water.

  • Steamed, not boiled. It is the whole character of the dish.
  • Tip it in loosely — packed rice steams unevenly.
  • Fork it through once halfway.

item.title: Osbane
item.description: Sausage casings filled with rice, offal, chard and herbs, simmered gently and then sliced into a harissa broth.
item.content:encoded:
Filled loosely, pricked, and simmered gently — the same three rules as every rice-stuffed casing, and for the same reason: the grain triples and steam has to escape somewhere other than the seam. What makes osbane distinct is the sheer volume of greens, which should be roughly equal in bulk to the rice. They collapse to almost nothing during cooking, so a filling that looks alarmingly green going in is correct.

  • A third full, pricked, bare simmer. All three or they burst.
  • The filling should look far too green. It collapses.
  • Slice after cooking, never before.

item.title: Berkoukes
item.description: Hand-rolled semolina pearls larger than couscous, simmered in a lamb, chickpea and harissa broth until tender.
item.content:encoded:
The pearls are rolled by sprinkling water onto semolina and agitating it in a wide bowl until it clumps into small balls — a gradual process, and adding water too fast produces lumps rather than pearls. They are then cooked directly in the broth rather than separately, so the starch they release thickens it, which is the point. Shop-bought berkoukes works and needs about four minutes less.

  • Water slowly, a sprinkle at a time. Too much makes lumps.
  • Cook the pearls in the broth so their starch thickens it.
  • Shop-bought pearls need about four minutes less.

item.title: Chicken Satay
item.description: Chicken satay — turmeric and lemongrass marinated skewers grilled over charcoal with rich peanut sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The marinade contains sugar and coconut milk, so the skewers must be cooked over hot but not flaming coals and turned constantly — sugar chars fast, and a burnt satay is bitter. The peanut sauce is built on a fried spice paste rather than just blended peanut butter, which is what gives it depth rather than sweetness.

  • Wrap the exposed ends of the skewers in foil so they do not burn through.
  • Turn often. Sugar in the marinade catches quickly and satay burns before it dries out.
  • Make the sauce a day ahead — it thickens and deepens, and just needs loosening with hot water.

item.title: Fricassé
item.description: Small fried bread rolls split and packed with tuna, potato, egg, olives and harissa, eaten hot and standing up.
item.content:encoded:
The rolls are fried, not baked, and they go into moderate oil rather than hot — at 165°C they cook through and puff hollow, where hotter oil browns the outside and leaves raw dough at the centre. They also need to be split while warm, since the crumb compresses once cool and the pocket closes. The filling is assembled cold into a hot roll, which is the correct order and the reason this works as street food.

  • Moderate oil. Hot oil leaves the middle raw.
  • Split them warm — cold rolls will not open.
  • Harissa on the bread first, so it does not all end up in one bite.

item.title: Mlawi
item.description: A square layered flatbread folded repeatedly with oil and cooked in a dry pan so it pulls apart into leaves.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is stretched almost to transparency on an oiled surface and then folded in from four sides, which is what creates the layers — and it can only be done if the dough has rested long enough to slacken. Twenty minutes is the minimum. Flour on the surface would dry the sheet and glue the layers together, so oil is used throughout. The pan goes on dry: any fat in it fries the outside before the inside has cooked.

  • Oil on the surface, never flour.
  • Rest before stretching or the sheet tears.
  • A dry pan. Fat in the pan fries the outside too fast.

item.title: Gado-Gado
item.description: Gado-gado — Indonesian vegetable salad with tofu, tempeh and egg under a warm peanut and tamarind sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Each vegetable is blanched for its own precise time and refreshed in cold water, which keeps colours bright and textures distinct rather than uniformly soft. The sauce is served warm and slightly loose so it coats rather than clings, which is how it reaches every component.

  • Blanch separately and refresh. Cooking everything in one pot gives a grey, uniform salad.
  • The sauce should be pourable, not stiff. Loosen with hot water right before serving.
  • It is meant to be eaten at room temperature with a warm sauce, not chilled.

item.title: Khobz Tabouna
item.description: A dense semolina country loaf, traditionally baked against a clay oven wall, made here on a fiercely preheated tray.
item.content:encoded:
Semolina absorbs water more slowly than wheat flour, so the dough must be given time to hydrate before kneading — twenty minutes of sitting, then knead, and it goes from gritty and unworkable to smooth. Rushing this is why home versions come out dense and dry. The seeds pressed into the top are not decoration either: they toast against the hot surface and are most of what you smell when it comes out.

  • Let the semolina hydrate for 20 minutes before kneading.
  • Press the seeds in hard or they fall off.
  • Cool under a cloth for a soft crust, on a rack for a crisp one.

item.title: Curry Laksa
item.description: Curry laksa — Malaysian coconut noodle soup with prawns, tofu puffs and rice noodles in spiced broth.
item.content:encoded:
The rempah — the pounded spice paste — is fried until its oil separates and floats, which is both the flavour foundation and the source of the orange slick on the broth's surface. Tofu puffs are used rather than plain tofu because their honeycomb interiors soak up broth like sponges.

  • Fry the rempah longer than feels necessary. Fifteen minutes is not too long and it is where all the flavour lives.
  • Never boil the coconut milk. A split laksa looks and tastes wrong.
  • Both noodles together is traditional — the springy egg noodle and the soft vermicelli give different mouthfuls.

item.title: Makroudh
item.description: Semolina pastry rolled around an orange-scented date paste, cut into diamonds, fried and dipped in warm honey.
item.content:encoded:
The semolina dough is bound with oil rather than water, which is what gives makroudh its short, sandy crumb — a water-bound dough turns chewy and tastes like pasta. Work the oil in thoroughly with your fingers and let the mixture stand so the grains absorb it before adding the small amount of water needed to bring it together. Unusually, the honey here is warmed and the pastries go in hot: both hot, so the honey penetrates rather than sitting on the surface as a shell.

  • Oil into the semolina first, and let it stand. That is the crumb.
  • Barely work the dough — kneading makes it tough.
  • Hot pastries into warm honey, both hot.

item.title: Bambalouni
item.description: A large, light ring doughnut fried to order from a very wet dough and handed over hot under a heavy dusting of sugar.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is far wetter than a doughnut dough has any right to be — closer to a thick batter — and that is what produces the light, open, almost stringy interior. It cannot be rolled or cut; it is stretched with wet hands straight into the oil. Resist adding flour to make it manageable, because that is exactly what turns a bambalouni into an ordinary heavy doughnut.

  • A wet dough. Adding flour ruins the texture.
  • Wet hands for every single one.
  • They are stale in ten minutes. Fry to order.

item.title: Char Kway Teow
item.description: Char kway teow — flat rice noodles wok-fried at high heat with prawns, lap cheong, egg and chives.
item.content:encoded:
Wok hei is the aroma produced when oil and food vapour ignite at the wok's surface above about 200°C, and it needs both fierce heat and a pan left undisturbed long enough for the noodles to sear. Rendering pork fat first gives a higher smoke point and a flavour that neutral oil cannot match.

  • One portion at a time. Two portions in a domestic wok halves the heat and you lose the char entirely.
  • Leave the noodles alone between tosses. Constant stirring is the single most common mistake.
  • Pork lard is traditional and makes a real difference. It is worth rendering some.

item.title: Samsa
item.description: Pastry triangles filled with ground almond and sesame, fried until crisp and soaked in a lemon and rose syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Toasting the sesame and almonds before grinding is what stops this tasting flat, and they must be toasted separately because sesame colours in ninety seconds and almonds take six minutes. The syrup is cold and the pastries go in hot, as with everything fried and syruped in these volumes. Fold the triangles like a flag, corner over corner, so the layers overlap three deep and the parcel cannot open in the oil.

  • Toast the almonds and sesame separately — the timings are nowhere near each other.
  • Fold like a flag so the layers overlap three deep.
  • Hot pastry, cold syrup, forty-five seconds.

item.title: Zlabia
item.description: A fermented batter piped into hot oil in loops, fried crisp and soaked in a saffron and rose syrup.
item.content:encoded:
The batter is fermented rather than merely mixed, and the hour it takes gives zlabia its faint sourness — without it you have a sweet fried batter with nothing behind it. It also has to be thin enough to pipe in a continuous stream but thick enough to hold a loop, which is a narrower window than it sounds; test one before committing the batch. Saffron goes into the syrup rather than the batter, where its colour and scent survive the frying.

  • Ferment the batter a full hour. That sourness is the point.
  • Test one loop before committing the batch.
  • Fry them properly dark, or they go soggy in the syrup.

item.title: Assidat Zgougou
item.description: A dark Aleppo pine seed pudding layered with thick cream and nuts, made for Mouled and unlike any other dessert.
item.content:encoded:
The zgougou has to be washed repeatedly and then strained through muslin, and this is the whole difficulty of the dish: the seed carries grit and fine debris that no amount of blending removes, and one gritty mouthful ruins a dessert that took two hours. Wash until the water runs clear, blend with water, then strain twice — once through a sieve and once through muslin. The dark grey-brown colour is correct and cannot be improved.

  • Wash the seed until the water runs clear. Grit is the failure mode.
  • Strain twice, the second time through muslin.
  • The colour is meant to be dark grey-brown.

item.title: Hainanese Chicken Rice
item.description: Hainanese chicken rice — gently poached chicken with fat-rich stock rice, ginger-scallion oil and chilli sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is poached below a simmer and then shocked in ice water, which halts cooking instantly and contracts the skin into the gelatinous layer the dish is prized for. The rice is fried in rendered chicken fat before being cooked in the poaching stock, so every grain carries the flavour of the bird.

  • Never let the poaching water simmer. A thermometer is the only reliable way to hold 90°C.
  • The ice bath is what gives the skin its texture. Do not skip it.
  • Season the poaching stock only lightly — you will drink it as soup at the end.

item.title: Masfouf
item.description: Steamed couscous worked with oil, sugar, raisins and nuts into a sweet dish eaten at breakfast or with cold buttermilk.
item.content:encoded:
Masfouf is steamed twice rather than three times, because a slightly softer grain suits a sweet dish, but the raking between steamings is exactly as important — it is what keeps the grains separate rather than letting them clump into a sweet cake. The raisins go into the second steaming so they plump in the vapour instead of staying hard, and the nuts go on at the very end so they stay crisp against the soft grain.

  • Rake between steamings or it clumps into a cake.
  • Raisins into the second steaming, so they plump.
  • Nuts at the end, for the contrast.

item.title: Thé aux Pignons
item.description: Green tea boiled hard with mint and sugar, poured from a height over pine nuts left to soften in the bottom of the glass.
item.content:encoded:
Tunisian tea is boiled rather than steeped, and boiled hard — which would ruin a delicate green tea and is exactly right here, because the resulting bitterness is what the very large amount of sugar is balanced against. The pouring from a height is not showmanship: it aerates the tea and puts a head of foam on the glass, which Tunisians judge the pour by. The pine nuts go in dry and soften in the hot tea as you drink.

  • Boil it, do not steep it. The bitterness is deliberate.
  • Rinse the leaves first and discard that water.
  • Pour from a height for the foam — it is how the pour is judged.

item.title: Chicken Adobo
item.description: Filipino chicken adobo — braised in vinegar, soy, garlic and bay until the sauce reduces to a dark glaze.
item.content:encoded:
The vinegar is brought to the boil without stirring for the first few minutes, a Filipino rule that lets the harsh acetic edge cook off before it is incorporated. Finishing by reducing the sauce hard and frying the chicken in it is what turns a braise into the glossy, lacquered dish adobo should be.

  • Do not stir during the first few minutes of boiling. It is a small superstition with a real basis in letting the acid volatilise.
  • Cane vinegar or coconut vinegar are the authentic choices; cider vinegar is the best supermarket substitute.
  • Adobo is famously better the next day, and better again the day after.

item.title: Céleri Rémoulade
item.description: Raw celeriac cut into fine matchsticks and bound in a sharp, mustard-heavy mayonnaise with lemon and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Celeriac browns within about two minutes of being cut, so it goes into acidulated water as you work or into the lemon juice directly — and the lemon is doing double duty, because it also begins to soften the matchsticks before the mayonnaise goes anywhere near them. The mayonnaise itself needs far more mustard than seems reasonable, a full two tablespoons, since raw celeriac is bland and slightly waxy and a gentle dressing simply disappears against it.

  • Lemon on the celeriac immediately. It browns in about two minutes.
  • Two full tablespoons of mustard. Less and it tastes of nothing.
  • Let it sit half an hour before serving.

item.title: Poireaux Vinaigrette
item.description: Whole leeks poached until completely soft, pressed under a weight and dressed warm with a sharp mustard vinaigrette.
item.content:encoded:
Pressing the poached leeks under a weight for twenty minutes squeezes out the water they are full of, which does two things: it concentrates the flavour and, more importantly, it means the vinaigrette is not immediately diluted into a puddle at the bottom of the plate. Dress them while still warm, because warm leek absorbs the dressing and cold leek repels it. They must also be genuinely soft — squeaky, undercooked leek is unpleasant here.

  • Press them. Unpressed leeks water down the dressing.
  • Cook them properly soft — no squeak.
  • Dress warm, serve cool.

item.title: Œufs Mayonnaise
item.description: Halved soft-boiled eggs under a thick homemade mayonnaise, the yolks left barely set at the centre.
item.content:encoded:
Nine minutes, not twelve. The yolk should be set at the edge and still faintly waxy at the centre — a fully hard yolk goes chalky and grey-rimmed and the whole dish becomes an English picnic egg. Straight into iced water afterwards, both to stop the cooking dead and because the temperature shock is what makes the shell come away cleanly. The mayonnaise wants to be thick enough to coat and stay put rather than run off onto the plate.

  • Nine minutes. Twelve gives you a grey, chalky yolk.
  • Iced water straight away, for the shell as much as the cooking.
  • Thick mayonnaise — it has to sit on the egg, not run off.

item.title: Arepas
item.description: Venezuelan arepas — griddled corn cakes from masarepa, split and stuffed with cheese, beef or beans.
item.content:encoded:
Masarepa is pre-cooked and dehydrated maize, so it hydrates in minutes into a workable dough — ordinary cornmeal or masa harina will not do the same thing and gives a gritty, crumbling cake. Griddling first and then finishing in the oven sets a crust while the centre steams through and hollows enough to split.

  • Masarepa, not masa harina and not polenta. The brands to look for are P.A.N. or Goya.
  • Smooth the edges with wet fingers before cooking, or the arepas crack open on the griddle.
  • They should sound hollow when tapped. That is how you know the centre has cooked and can be split.

item.title: Carottes Râpées
item.description: Coarsely grated carrot in a lemon and Dijon dressing with parsley, dressed while the shreds are still dry.
item.content:encoded:
Grate on the coarse side of a box grater, or with the coarse disc of a processor — never the fine one. Finely grated carrot collapses into a wet mass within ten minutes and the salad turns to orange sludge; coarse shreds hold their shape and their bite for an hour. Dress at the last moment for the same reason, and always with lemon rather than vinegar, which is sharper than the carrot needs and flattens its sweetness.

  • Coarse grate only. Fine grating gives you sludge.
  • Lemon, not vinegar.
  • Dress at the last minute.

item.title: Salade de Lentilles
item.description: Green lentils simmered until just tender and dressed while hot with mustard vinaigrette, shallot and plenty of parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Dressed hot, always. Lentils absorb vinaigrette as they cool and the difference between hot-dressed and cold-dressed is enormous — cold lentils sit in the dressing rather than taking it up. Salt goes in only at the end of the cooking as well, since salted water firms the skins and gives you lentils that stay hard in the middle no matter how long they simmer. Puy or Castelluccio lentils hold their shape; brown lentils collapse into mush.

  • Salt at the end, or the skins stay tough.
  • Dress them hot. This is the whole difference.
  • Puy lentils, which hold; brown ones turn to mush.

item.title: Pupusas
item.description: Salvadoran pupusas — thick stuffed corn cakes with cheese and beans, griddled and served with curtido.
item.content:encoded:
Sealing the filling completely inside the masa is the whole technique: any breach and the cheese escapes onto the griddle and burns instead of melting inside. Keeping a bowl of oiled water beside you stops the masa sticking to your hands, which is what makes patting them out possible at all.

  • Wet hands, constantly. Dry hands and masa dough are incompatible.
  • Seal completely before flattening. A leak is unrecoverable once it hits the griddle.
  • Curtido needs at least three hours and is better after a day, so make it first.

item.title: Gougères
item.description: Savoury choux buns with Comté beaten through the paste, baked until hollow, dry and deep gold, and eaten warm.
item.content:encoded:
The paste has to be dried out properly on the hob before the eggs go in — two full minutes of beating over the heat, until a film forms on the base of the pan. Skipping it leaves too much water in the mixture and the buns collapse as they cool. The other rule is not opening the oven: gougères set their structure in the last third of the bake, and a draught at eight minutes will flatten a whole tray irretrievably.

  • Dry the paste on the hob for two full minutes.
  • Do not open the oven. They collapse.
  • Deep gold, not pale — undercooked gougères sink.

item.title: Rillettes de Porc
item.description: Pork shoulder cooked slowly in its own fat until it shreds to threads, packed into pots and sealed under a fat layer.
item.content:encoded:
The meat is shredded with two forks rather than blended, because rillettes should be threads held loosely in fat and not a paste — a processor emulsifies it into something closer to pâté. It also needs to be seasoned when cold and then tasted again, since fat mutes salt considerably and a mixture that tastes right hot will be flat once set. The fat cap on top is a seal: as long as it is unbroken, the pot keeps for weeks.

  • Two forks, never a processor. Threads, not paste.
  • Season cold, then taste again. Fat hides salt.
  • The fat cap is the seal — keep it unbroken.

item.title: Terrine de Campagne
item.description: A coarse country pâté of pork, liver and fat baked in a bain-marie, pressed under weights and rested before slicing.
item.content:encoded:
Pressing it overnight is what turns a crumbly baked meatloaf into something that slices cleanly, and it cannot be skipped or shortened — the weights compact the meat as the fat sets around it. The mixture must also be fatty enough, a third fat to two-thirds lean, because a terrine made with lean pork is dry and grainy however carefully it is cooked. Test the seasoning by frying a spoonful before it goes in the tin.

  • A third fat. Lean terrine is dry terrine.
  • Fry a spoonful and taste before committing.
  • Press it overnight or it will not slice.

item.title: Chimichurri Steak
item.description: Argentinian chimichurri steak — fire-grilled beef under a hand-chopped parsley, oregano and garlic sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Chopping the herbs by hand rather than blending keeps the parsley in distinct pieces suspended in oil, which is why it reads as a sauce with texture rather than a green purée. Resting it for at least an hour lets the garlic and oregano infuse the oil, and the vinegar softens the raw garlic edge.

  • Chop by hand. A blender turns chimichurri into a bitter green paste in about four seconds.
  • Make it at least an hour ahead. It is noticeably better after that time.
  • Rest the steak for half as long as you cooked it. Slicing early loses the juices onto the board.

item.title: Jambon Persillé
item.description: Chunks of ham set in a wine and parsley jelly made from the cooking stock, chilled and turned out to slice.
item.content:encoded:
The parsley goes into the cooled jelly, never the hot one — chopped parsley stirred into boiling stock goes khaki within seconds and the whole point of this dish is the green. Let the stock cool to the point where it is beginning to thicken but still pourable, then fold the parsley through. The ham is torn rather than diced, too, so the finished slice shows irregular pieces rather than neat cubes.

  • Parsley into cooled stock. Hot stock turns it khaki.
  • Tear the ham, do not dice it.
  • Reduce the stock properly or the jelly will be weak.

item.title: Escargots à la Bourguignonne
item.description: Snails packed into shells under a garlic, parsley and shallot butter and baked until the butter bubbles over.
item.content:encoded:
The butter has to be properly soft but not melted when it is packed in, so it holds around the snail rather than running straight out of the shell in the first minute of heat. Work it with a spatula rather than warming it. Get the oven genuinely hot as well — 220°C — because the butter should bubble and brown at the mouth of the shell within eight minutes, and a slower bake simply melts it out into the dish.

  • Soft butter, never melted, or it runs straight out.
  • Butter under the snail as well as over it.
  • A hot oven so it bubbles rather than merely melting.

item.title: Lomo Saltado
item.description: Lomo saltado — Peruvian beef stir-fry with onion, tomato, soy and ají amarillo, served with chips and rice.
item.content:encoded:
The dish is a chifa creation — Chinese wok cooking applied to Peruvian produce — so it needs genuine wok heat and cooking in batches, or the beef stews in tomato juice. The chips go in at the very last second so they absorb some sauce while keeping their structure.

  • Fry the chips fresh. Oven chips go limp the moment they meet the sauce.
  • Cook the beef in two batches. Crowding is what turns lomo saltado grey and watery.
  • The onion and tomato should still have bite. This is a stir-fry, not a stew.

item.title: Anchoïade
item.description: Anchovies melted into olive oil with garlic and a little vinegar, served warm as a dip for raw vegetables.
item.content:encoded:
The anchovies are melted rather than blended, over the gentlest possible heat, and the difference matters: warmed slowly in oil they dissolve completely and lose their fishy edge, where blitzed raw they stay grainy and aggressive. Keep the heat low enough that the oil never sizzles — if the garlic colours at all, the whole thing turns bitter. Serve it warm, since it sets and dulls as it cools.

  • The lowest heat you have. Coloured garlic ruins it.
  • Melt the anchovies rather than blending them.
  • Serve warm — it dulls as it sets.

item.title: Ají de Gallina
item.description: Ají de gallina — Peruvian shredded chicken in a creamy ají amarillo, walnut and bread sauce over potatoes.
item.content:encoded:
Bread soaked in evaporated milk is the traditional thickener, and it gives a body that flour cannot: the starch and the milk emulsify into something smooth and rich without any floury taste. Frying the ají amarillo paste in oil before liquid goes in blooms its colour and takes the raw edge off.

  • Ají amarillo paste is essential and widely sold frozen or jarred. There is no close substitute.
  • Fry the paste properly before adding liquid — four minutes, until the oil colours.
  • Shred the chicken by hand rather than chopping it; the texture matters.
