item.title: Brandade de Morue
item.description: Salt cod soaked, poached and beaten with potato, garlic, warm oil and milk into a smooth, savoury purée.
item.content:encoded:
The salt cod must be soaked for a day and a half in several changes of cold water, and this is not negotiable — under-soaked cod is inedibly salty and no amount of potato will rescue it. Taste a flake before you commit. The oil and milk both go in warm, alternately, exactly as for a mayonnaise: cold liquid into hot fish makes the mixture seize and turn grainy rather than emulsifying into a smooth purée.

  • Soak for a day and a half and taste before proceeding.
  • Warm oil, warm milk, added alternately.
  • Poach the cod, never boil it.

item.title: Œufs en Meurette
item.description: Eggs poached directly in red wine and served on fried bread under a reduced sauce of the same wine with bacon and mushrooms.
item.content:encoded:
The eggs are poached in the wine itself, which stains the whites a startling purple and is the whole visual identity of the dish — poached in water and sauced afterwards, it is simply eggs with gravy. Wine is far less viscous than water, so drop each egg into a whirlpool and keep the heat at a bare shiver, or the whites shred. Very fresh eggs hold together; older ones spread however careful you are.

  • Poach in the wine, not water. That is the dish.
  • A bare shiver — wine is thinner than water and shreds whites.
  • Very fresh eggs only.

item.title: Moqueca Baiana
item.description: Moqueca baiana — Brazilian fish stew with coconut milk, peppers and dendê palm oil, cooked in a clay pot.
item.content:encoded:
The vegetables and fish cook in their own liquid plus coconut milk, with no stock at all — layering them so the vegetables sit underneath means they release moisture upward and steam the fish rather than boiling it. Dendê oil is added near the end because heat destroys both its colour and its distinctive flavour.

  • Do not stir. Moqueca is layered and left alone; stirring breaks the fish into flakes.
  • Dendê oil is what makes it Bahian. Without it you have a perfectly good coconut fish stew but not a moqueca.
  • A clay pot holds heat evenly and is traditional, but any heavy lidded casserole works.

item.title: Vichyssoise
item.description: A chilled leek and potato soup finished with cream, blended completely smooth and seasoned again once cold.
item.content:encoded:
Cold blunts salt dramatically, so a vichyssoise seasoned to taste while hot will be flat by the time it reaches the table — season it again after chilling, and expect to add noticeably more than felt right. It also thickens considerably in the fridge, so it comes off the heat looser than the finished consistency. Sweat the leeks without letting them colour: any browning shows as grey flecks in what should be an ivory-white soup.

  • Do not colour the leeks. Grey flecks in a white soup.
  • Sieve it after blending.
  • Season again when cold. Cold hides salt.

item.title: Potage Parmentier
item.description: A hot leek and potato soup of four ingredients, roughly mashed rather than blended and finished with butter.
item.content:encoded:
Water rather than stock, which sounds like an economy and is a decision — stock muddies a soup that is meant to taste precisely of leek and potato and nothing else. The texture is the other thing: this is crushed with a masher or passed through a mouli, never blended. A blender bursts the potato starch cells and turns the soup gluey, which is the single most common way people ruin it.

  • Water, not stock. The point is to taste the vegetables.
  • Masher or mouli. A blender makes it gluey.
  • Cold butter beaten in off the heat.

item.title: Garbure
item.description: A thick Gascon soup of cabbage, white beans and confit duck, cooked long enough that a spoon stands up in it.
item.content:encoded:
The confit goes in for the last twenty minutes only. It is already cooked, and an hour in the pot shreds it into the broth and leaves nothing to eat; twenty minutes warms it through and lets it give up some fat without disintegrating. The cabbage goes in in two stages for the same reason — half early to melt into the soup and thicken it, half late so there is something with texture left in the bowl.

  • Confit in for the last twenty minutes only.
  • Cabbage in two stages — half to thicken, half for texture.
  • Taste before salting. The bacon and duck do a lot of it.

item.title: Pão de Queijo
item.description: Pão de queijo — Brazilian tapioca cheese bread with a crisp shell and chewy hollow centre. Naturally gluten free.
item.content:encoded:
Scalding the tapioca starch with boiling milk and oil gelatinises it, which is what creates the elastic, stretchy structure — tapioca has no gluten, so this pre-cooked starch network is doing all the structural work. The steam it traps in the oven puffs the rolls and leaves them hollow.

  • The lumpy stage after scalding is normal. Keep going; the eggs bring it together.
  • Tapioca starch only. Cornflour or potato starch will not produce the same structure.
  • Rolled unbaked balls freeze perfectly and bake from frozen with 4 extra minutes.

item.title: Soupe de Poisson
item.description: Small whole fish cooked with fennel and saffron and forced through a mouli, served with rouille, croutons and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Everything goes through a mouli — bones, heads and all — and that is what gives this soup its body and its intensity. A blender will not do it, because the bones need to be crushed and then held back by the plate rather than pulverised into the liquid. Use small, cheap, bony rockfish rather than fillets: the gelatine in the heads and bones is the entire point, and a soup made from fillets is thin and disappointing.

  • Small bony fish, never fillets. The bones are the body.
  • A mouli, not a blender.
  • Serve the rouille and cheese separately so people build their own.

item.title: Hachis Parmentier
item.description: Slow-braised beef chopped by hand under a buttery potato purée and baked until the top is deeply browned.
item.content:encoded:
The meat is braised and then chopped, not fried from raw mince, and the difference is total: braised beef has already given up its collagen and tastes of the wine and stock it cooked in, where raw mince browned in a pan tastes of browned mince. This is the dish that leftover pot-au-feu was invented for. The purée wants an alarming amount of butter — a quarter of the potato weight — because it has to stay soft over an hour in the oven.

  • Braise then chop. Raw mince is a different, lesser dish.
  • A quarter of the potato weight in butter. It is not a misprint.
  • Fork ridges into the top — they are what browns.

item.title: Alfajores
item.description: Alfajores — melt-in-the-mouth cornflour biscuits sandwiched with dulce de leche and rolled in coconut.
item.content:encoded:
Roughly half the flour is replaced with cornflour, which has no gluten at all, so the biscuits have almost no structure and simply dissolve. That also makes the dough fragile, which is why it must be chilled hard before cutting and handled as little as possible.

  • Pale is correct. A browned alfajor has been overbaked and loses the melting texture.
  • Roll between paper, not on flour. Extra flour toughens an already delicate dough.
  • Use a thick dulce de leche (repostero grade) or the biscuits will slide apart.

item.title: Poulet Basquaise
item.description: Chicken braised with peppers, tomato and Espelette pepper until the peppers collapse entirely into the sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The peppers need forty minutes before the chicken joins them, and most recipes rush this. Peppers cooked only until soft stay watery and taste raw against the tomato; cooked right down they collapse into a jammy base that is the actual sauce. Piment d'Espelette is worth buying — it is fruity rather than merely hot, and paprika with cayenne is a poor substitute for the specific flavour this dish is built on.

  • Forty minutes on the peppers before anything else. They are the sauce.
  • Skin above the sauce so it stays crisp.
  • Real Espelette. Paprika and cayenne are not the same thing.

item.title: Poule au Pot
item.description: A whole chicken stuffed with a bread and ham forcemeat and poached with vegetables, broth served first and meat after.
item.content:encoded:
A bare shiver, never a boil. Boiling shreds the chicken and clouds the broth irretrievably, and the broth is half the dish — it comes to the table first, as a course in its own right, and should be clear enough to read a newspaper through. Skim relentlessly for the first fifteen minutes, and sew the cavity shut rather than trusting the stuffing to stay put; it swells considerably and will otherwise cloud the pot.

  • A bare shiver. Boiling ruins both the meat and the broth.
  • Skim hard for the first fifteen minutes.
  • Sew the cavity shut — the stuffing swells.

item.title: Navarin d'Agneau
item.description: Lamb braised until tender with spring vegetables added in sequence so each arrives at the table properly cooked.
item.content:encoded:
Everything goes in at a different moment and the sequence is the recipe: turnips and carrots need twenty-five minutes, new potatoes fifteen, peas and beans four. Cooked together from the start, half of them are grey mush by the time the lamb is ready. Dusting the browned lamb with sugar before the flour is the small step people skip — it caramelises in the pan and gives the sauce its colour and a rounder flavour.

  • The sugar before the flour. It is what colours the sauce.
  • Vegetables in sequence, not all at once.
  • Peas and beans for four minutes only.

item.title: Chicken Kiev
item.description: Chicken Kiev — breadcrumbed chicken breast filled with garlic herb butter that floods out when cut.
item.content:encoded:
The butter is frozen solid before it goes in, which buys enough time for the chicken to cook through before the butter melts and finds a way out. Double breadcrumbing seals every seam, and chilling the finished parcels for an hour sets that coating so it does not split in the fryer.

  • Frozen butter, double breadcrumbs, and a proper chill. Skip any one and the butter escapes.
  • Fry then finish in the oven. Frying alone either burns the crumb or leaves the chicken raw.
  • Warn people to cut into it over the plate. The butter comes out with some enthusiasm.

item.title: Daube Provençale
item.description: Beef marinated overnight in red wine with orange peel and cooked slowly with olives until it falls apart.
item.content:encoded:
Dried orange peel is the ingredient that makes a daube a daube rather than a bourguignon, and it goes in with the marinade so it has time to give up its oils. The marinating is not optional either — overnight in the wine both flavours the meat and, more usefully, means the wine has already lost its raw edge before the long cook begins. Do not brown the meat too hard after marinating: wet meat will not colour, so pat it genuinely dry first.

  • Dried orange peel. It is what separates this from a bourguignon.
  • Pat the meat properly dry or it will not brown.
  • Olives at the end — an hour in the pot makes them bitter.

item.title: Carbonade Flamande
item.description: Beef braised in dark Belgian beer with mustard-spread bread laid on top to dissolve and thicken the sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The bread is the thickener and it must be laid on top rather than stirred in — it dissolves gradually from below over the two and a half hours, and the mustard on it disperses through the sauce as it goes. Stirred in at the start it simply becomes sludge. Use a genuinely dark beer and add the vinegar and sugar together at the end: the sweet-sour balance is the whole character of the dish and it is far easier to adjust once you can taste the reduced sauce.

  • Bread on top, mustard down, never stirred in.
  • A properly dark beer — a lager gives you nothing.
  • Balance the vinegar and sugar at the end, by taste.

item.title: Blini with Soured Cream
item.description: Russian blini — small yeasted buckwheat pancakes served warm with soured cream, dill and smoked fish.
item.content:encoded:
Yeast rather than baking powder gives blini their faint sourness and their open, spongy crumb — chemical leavening produces a flat, cakey pancake with none of the character. A proportion of buckwheat brings the earthy flavour, but too much and there is no gluten left to hold the rise.

  • Fold the whites in last and treat the batter gently from then on. That air is your rise.
  • Serve them warm, not hot from the pan and not cold. Under a cloth is the traditional holding method.
  • For a milder pancake, shift the ratio towards plain flour; for a more assertive one, go the other way.

item.title: Choucroute Garnie
item.description: Sauerkraut rinsed and braised in riesling with juniper and a collection of smoked pork cuts and sausages.
item.content:encoded:
Rinsing the sauerkraut is what makes this palatable rather than punishing. Jarred kraut is packed in a brine far too sour to eat in quantity, and a rinse and a squeeze brings it back to something that can absorb the wine and fat over two hours. The meats go in by cooking time — smoked hock early, sausages in the last twenty minutes — because boiled sausage is a poor thing and they only need heating through.

  • Rinse and squeeze the kraut. Straight from the jar it is inedible in quantity.
  • Meats by cooking time. Boiled sausage is a sad thing.
  • A muslin bag for the spices, or you eat juniper berries whole.

item.title: Magret de Canard
item.description: Duck breast started skin-down in a cold dry pan so the fat renders slowly and the skin crisps to glass before resting.
item.content:encoded:
A cold pan is the entire technique. Duck skin carries a thick layer of fat that needs eight or nine minutes to render out, and a hot pan seizes the skin shut before that can happen, leaving a flabby fat layer under a browned surface. Starting cold and bringing the heat up slowly lets the fat run out and the skin dry and crisp in what it leaves behind. Score the skin but never cut into the meat, or the juices escape into the pan.

  • Cold pan, no oil. This is the whole method.
  • Pour the fat off as it renders and keep it for potatoes.
  • Rest it eight minutes, which is longer than feels necessary.

item.title: Poulet Rôti
item.description: Roast chicken with butter worked under the skin, roasted on one side then the other before finishing breast up.
item.content:encoded:
Roasting the bird on each side before finishing it breast-up is what keeps the breast from drying: for the first two-thirds of the cook the breast is not facing the heat at all, and the leg above it bastes it as its fat renders. Butter under the skin rather than on it does the same job from the other direction. The bird also comes out at 70°C and rises to 74°C while resting, so pulling it at the target temperature overcooks it.

  • Butter under the skin, not on it.
  • Turn it twice. The breast should face the heat last.
  • Out at 70°C — it carries on cooking while it rests.

item.title: Olivier Salad
item.description: Olivier salad — Russian potato salad with carrot, egg, peas, pickles and ham in mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is cut to the same small dice, roughly the size of the peas, so no single ingredient dominates a forkful — this is the one rule that separates a good Olivier from a lumpy potato salad. The vegetables are cooked whole in their skins so they do not waterlog before dicing.

  • Uniform dice is the whole technique. Take the time.
  • Cool the vegetables completely before dicing and dressing.
  • It needs more salt than you expect once cold. Always taste again before serving.

item.title: Gigot d'Agneau
item.description: Leg of lamb studded with garlic and anchovy and roasted over sliced potatoes that catch every drop of the juices.
item.content:encoded:
The anchovy dissolves completely during roasting and what it leaves is not fishiness but depth — it is doing the job salt does, with glutamates on top. Slit the meat and push a sliver of garlic and a scrap of anchovy right into each cut rather than laying them on the surface, where they simply burn. The potatoes underneath are half the reason to make it, so use a tray that fits them in one dense layer.

  • Push the garlic and anchovy right in. On the surface they burn.
  • A rack over the potatoes so they catch everything.
  • Twenty-five minutes of rest, minimum.

item.title: Épaule d'Agneau de 7 Heures
item.description: Lamb shoulder cooked for seven hours at a low temperature until it can be pulled apart and served with a spoon.
item.content:encoded:
Seven hours at 130°C is not an exaggeration for effect. Shoulder is full of connective tissue that only converts to gelatine after a very long time below simmering point, and at four hours it is merely well-done lamb — the transformation into something spoonable happens in the last two. Keep the dish tightly sealed so nothing evaporates; the small amount of liquid at the bottom is meant to steam the meat, not reduce.

  • The full seven hours. At four it is merely well-done.
  • Seal it tightly — the liquid should steam, not reduce.
  • Twelve minutes at high heat at the end for colour.

item.title: Gołąbki
item.description: Gołąbki — Polish cabbage rolls stuffed with pork, beef and rice, braised in a tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Freezing the whole cabbage overnight and thawing it collapses the cell walls, so the leaves peel away limp and pliable without any blanching — a far easier route than wrestling with boiling water. The rice goes in only half-cooked because it finishes in the braise, absorbing meat juices as it swells.

  • The freezer trick is far easier than blanching and gives more pliable leaves. Plan a day ahead.
  • Line the pot with spare leaves. Rolls that catch on the base fall apart when you serve them.
  • Half-cook the rice. Raw rice stays hard and fully cooked rice turns to paste.

item.title: Steak Tartare
item.description: Raw beef chopped by hand and seasoned with capers, shallot, mustard, Tabasco and an egg yolk folded through.
item.content:encoded:
Chopped by hand with a heavy knife, never minced. A mincer crushes the fibres and presses out the juices, giving a wet paste; a knife leaves clean-cut pieces that stay distinct and hold their texture. Everything must be cold, including the board and the knife, and the beef should go back into the fridge if it starts to warm. Buy fillet or rump from a butcher you trust and use it the day you buy it.

  • Hand-chopped. A mincer gives you paste.
  • Everything cold — beef, board and knife.
  • Buy the beef the day you eat it.

item.title: Entrecôte Marchand de Vin
item.description: Sirloin steak rested while a red wine and shallot sauce is built in the pan, finished with cold butter off the heat.
item.content:encoded:
The butter goes in off the heat and cold, in pieces, and this is the difference between a glossy sauce and a greasy one. Cold butter whisked into a warm reduction emulsifies; butter melted into a hot pan simply splits into fat and liquid. The wine also has to be reduced almost to nothing — au sec, until the pan is nearly dry — before the stock goes in, or the sauce keeps a raw alcoholic edge.

  • Reduce the wine until the pan is nearly dry.
  • Cold butter, off the heat, in pieces.
  • Add the resting juices to the sauce — they are the best of it.

item.title: Cordon Bleu
item.description: Chicken breast beaten thin, rolled around ham and Gruyère, double-breaded and fried until the cheese just runs.
item.content:encoded:
Double breading is what holds the cheese in. One coat of crumb cracks as the chicken swells in the pan and the cheese finds the gap; flour, egg, crumb, then egg and crumb again gives a shell that survives. Chilling the breaded rolls for half an hour firms everything and is the other half of the seal. Beat the breast thin enough to roll without cracking — 5 mm — and overlap the ham so no cheese touches the edge.

  • Double breading. A single coat cracks and leaks.
  • Keep the filling 2 cm from every edge.
  • Chill before frying so the crust sets.

item.title: Käsespätzle
item.description: Käsespätzle — Swabian egg noodles layered with melted cheese and topped with crisp fried onions.
item.content:encoded:
The batter must be beaten hard until it blisters and pulls away in strings, which develops enough gluten for the noodles to hold together in the water without a firm dough. They are cooked by the two-minute rule: they float when done, and anything longer makes them mushy.

  • Beat the batter until it blisters. Undeveloped batter falls apart in the water.
  • A spätzle press is cheap and makes this trivial, but a colander and a spatula work fine.
  • Layer the cheese between batches rather than dumping it on top, so it melts throughout.

item.title: Rognons à la Moutarde
item.description: Lamb kidneys seared hard and finished in a mustard and cream sauce, returned to the pan only at the last moment.
item.content:encoded:
Kidneys go from tender to rubber in about ninety seconds, so they are seared, removed, and returned only to warm through at the very end. Any liquid they release into the pan gets discarded rather than added to the sauce, because it is bitter — this is the step people skip and then wonder why the dish tastes of ammonia. The mustard goes in off the heat as well, since boiling destroys its pungency entirely.

  • Sixty seconds a side. They toughen almost instantly.
  • Throw away the liquid they release. It is bitter.
  • Mustard off the heat, or it loses everything.

item.title: Foie de Veau Lyonnaise
item.description: Calf liver seared briefly over onions cooked slowly to sweetness, sharpened with a splash of vinegar off the heat.
item.content:encoded:
The onions take twenty-five minutes and the liver takes ninety seconds, so they cannot share a pan for long. Cook the onions right down to a sweet golden tangle first, set them aside, then sear the liver in a screaming pan. Liver must go in dry and unfloured for a real crust, and come out while the centre is still rosy — grey liver is grainy and slightly metallic, and no sauce will bring it back.

  • Onions first and slowly, liver second and fast.
  • Dry liver, smoking pan, no flour.
  • Rosy in the middle. Grey liver is ruined liver.

item.title: Sauerbraten
item.description: German sauerbraten — beef marinated three days in vinegar and wine, braised with a gingerbread gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Three days in an acidic marinade denatures the surface proteins and tenderises what is otherwise a tough cut, while also driving the sour flavour deep into the meat. Lebkuchen or gingerbread thickens the gravy and supplies spice and sweetness at once, which is why no flour or sugar is needed.

  • Three days is the minimum for a proper sauerbraten. Two gives you a pleasant pot roast.
  • Dry the beef very thoroughly before browning or it will not colour at all.
  • Taste the gravy carefully at the end. The sweet-sour balance is the whole character of the dish.

item.title: Boudin Noir aux Pommes
item.description: Black pudding fried until crisp and served with apples cooked down in butter and a splash of cider vinegar.
item.content:encoded:
The boudin is cooked whole in its skin and split only at the table, because the filling is loose and will collapse into the pan if the skin is broken while it is hot. It also needs a gentle heat: high heat bursts the casing and the interior spits out. The apples want to keep some shape, so they go in cut into thick wedges rather than slices and are turned rarely — the flat faces should caramelise while the pieces stay whole.

  • Cook the sausages whole and split at the table.
  • Gentle heat, or the casing bursts.
  • Turn the apples twice, not constantly.

item.title: Endives au Jambon
item.description: Chicory braised in butter and lemon, wrapped in ham, covered in béchamel and baked until browned and bubbling.
item.content:encoded:
The chicory has to be braised and then squeezed dry before it is wrapped, and skipping either step gives you a watery gratin swimming in liquid. Chicory holds a great deal of water and releases all of it in the oven. A pinch of sugar and a squeeze of lemon in the braising liquid tempers the bitterness without removing it — the aim is to make it pleasant, not to hide it, since bitterness is the reason the dish works against the ham and cream.

  • Cut the cone out of the base — that is where the bitterness concentrates.
  • Press the braised chicory dry or the dish floods.
  • Sugar and lemon temper the bitterness rather than removing it.

item.title: Quenelles de Brochet
item.description: Pike beaten with choux paste and cream into light dumplings, poached gently and baked under a crayfish nantua sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is beaten cold over ice, because the mixture is an emulsion of fish protein, butter and cream and it will split the moment it warms. Bowl over ice, ingredients from the fridge, and stop the moment it comes together. The poaching water must not boil either — a shiver, no more — or the quenelles disintegrate. They double in size in the oven, so leave real space between them in the dish.

  • Everything cold, and the bowl over ice. Warmth splits it.
  • A shiver, not a simmer, for the poaching.
  • They double in the oven. Leave space.

item.title: Gravlax
item.description: Gravlax — Nordic dill-cured salmon with salt and sugar, sliced thin and served with mustard sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Salt and sugar draw water out of the fish by osmosis and replace it with a saline, sugary solution that firms the flesh and makes it safe to eat raw — the ratio matters, and a salt-only cure gives something closer to salt fish than gravlax. Weighting the fillets presses out the liquid faster and gives an even, dense texture.

  • Equal weights of salt and sugar. Shifting the ratio either way changes the character completely.
  • Weight it properly and drain the liquid, or the fish sits in brine and cures unevenly.
  • Use very fresh salmon from a fishmonger you trust, or previously frozen fish, since it is never cooked.

item.title: Bouchée à la Reine
item.description: Puff pastry cases filled with chicken, mushrooms and sweetbreads in a white wine and cream sauce, baked briefly to serve.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry cases are baked blind and empty, and filled only at the last minute — filling raises the steam that keeps puff pastry crisp, and a case that sits full for even ten minutes goes soft at the base. The filling must also be thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon, because a loose sauce goes straight through the pastry. Reduce it further than looks necessary; it loosens again as it warms in the oven.

  • Bake the cases empty. Filling them early softens the base.
  • Reduce the filling further than feels right — it loosens in the oven.
  • Fill at the last second.

item.title: Moules Frites
item.description: Mussels steamed open in white wine with shallots and parsley, served with chips fried twice for a proper crust.
item.content:encoded:
Chips are fried twice and the first fry is at a low temperature — 140°C — which cooks the potato through without colouring it. The second, at 190°C, does nothing but crisp the outside. One fry gives you either raw centres or burnt exteriors, and there is no way around it. For the mussels, the pan must be big enough that they are no more than three deep, or the ones at the bottom overcook while the top layer is still shut.

  • Two fries: 140°C to cook, 190°C to crisp.
  • A pan big enough that the mussels are three deep at most.
  • Do not thicken the liquor. It is the sauce as it is.

item.title: Kanelbullar
item.description: Kanelbullar — Swedish cardamom and cinnamon buns twisted into knots and topped with pearl sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Freshly ground cardamom is the defining flavour and it must be ground from pods rather than bought pre-ground, because the volatile oils that carry the aroma dissipate within weeks of grinding. Pearl sugar rather than icing keeps the bun on the right side of sweet, which is the Swedish preference.

  • Grind the cardamom yourself. Pre-ground cardamom has lost most of what makes these buns worth making.
  • The letter fold and twist gives more layers of filling than a simple spiral roll.
  • Cool them under a tea towel, which keeps the crumb soft.

item.title: Sole Normande
item.description: Sole fillets poached in cider and finished in a cream sauce with mussels and prawns, glazed under the grill.
item.content:encoded:
The sole poaches in the cider for four minutes and comes out; the sauce is finished afterwards. Fish left in a sauce while it reduces goes from delicate to woolly, and sole is the most delicate flat fish there is. The final glaze under a hot grill is what makes the dish look like itself — a spoonful of whipped cream folded into the sauce browns in ninety seconds and gives the glossy blistered top the classic version is known for.

  • Fish out of the pan before the sauce is reduced.
  • Strain the poaching liquid — it is the base of everything.
  • Whipped cream folded in at the end is what lets it glaze.

item.title: Bar en Croûte de Sel
item.description: A whole sea bass buried in egg-white-bound salt and baked, so it steams inside a sealed crust that is cracked at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The fish is not gutted through the belly for this — or if it is, the cavity is packed with herbs and closed — because any opening lets salt into the flesh and the whole thing becomes inedible. Leave the scales on as well: they are a second barrier between the salt and the flesh, and they lift away with the skin when the crust comes off. Egg white is what makes the salt set into a solid shell rather than a heap.

  • Scales on. They are a second barrier against the salt.
  • Seal completely — any gap and the flesh goes salty.
  • Crack it at the table. It is the best part of serving it.

item.title: Jollof Rice
item.description: Nigerian jollof rice — long-grain rice cooked in a reduced pepper and tomato base with a smoky bottom crust.
item.content:encoded:
The pepper base must be fried down until it visibly darkens and the oil separates — this drives off the raw tomato water that would otherwise make the rice mushy, and concentrates the flavour. The smoky note comes from letting the bottom layer catch deliberately in the last few minutes, which is the whole point of party jollof.

  • Reduce the pepper base properly. Watery base makes soggy jollof, and there is no recovering from it.
  • Parboiled long-grain rice holds its shape through the long cook; basmati collapses.
  • The bottom crust is not a mistake. Deliberately letting it catch for a few minutes is what gives party jollof its flavour.

item.title: Fondue Savoyarde
item.description: Three Alpine cheeses melted into white wine with garlic and kirsch, stabilised with cornflour and kept barely simmering.
item.content:encoded:
Cheese and wine want to separate, and cornflour is the only thing holding them together — tossed through the grated cheese it coats every strand and keeps the fat emulsified as it melts. Add the cheese in handfuls over a low heat, waiting for each to melt before the next, and stir in a figure of eight rather than circles, which keeps the mixture moving without whipping air into it. Never let it boil.

  • Cornflour through the cheese, not into the wine.
  • A handful at a time, waiting for each to melt.
  • Figure of eight, and never let it boil.

item.title: Aligot
item.description: Potato purée beaten hard with young tomme cheese until it turns elastic enough to lift in long ropes from the pan.
item.content:encoded:
Only young, unripened tomme fraîche stretches — a mature cheese has broken down proteins that will not form the long strands aligot is made of, and Cheddar or Gruyère simply give you cheesy mash. The potatoes must also be riced rather than mashed and kept genuinely hot, because the beating has to be vigorous and sustained for several minutes and a cooling mixture will never come together.

  • Young tomme fraîche only. Mature cheese will not stretch.
  • A ricer, never a processor.
  • Beat hard for several minutes. It changes suddenly.

item.title: Egusi Soup
item.description: Nigerian egusi soup — ground melon seeds in palm oil with spinach, beef and stockfish. Rich and thick.
item.content:encoded:
The ground egusi is added to the hot oil in lumps and left undisturbed for several minutes so it sets into curds rather than dissolving into a uniform paste — that lumpy texture is the defining characteristic. Palm oil is essential for both the colour and the particular flavour that no other fat reproduces.

  • Leave the egusi lumps alone while they fry. Stirring turns the whole soup into a smooth paste, which is not what you want.
  • Red palm oil is not interchangeable with any other oil. It is the colour and the flavour.
  • Add the greens last and briefly, so they stay green and retain some texture.

item.title: Truffade
item.description: Sliced potatoes fried slowly in duck fat and folded with fresh tomme until they set into a single browned cake.
item.content:encoded:
The potatoes are sliced rather than diced and cooked slowly in a covered pan so they soften and stick together into a cake before the cheese goes in — this is not a fry-up. Once the cheese is added it should be folded through only two or three times and then left to set and brown on the bottom, undisturbed. Stirring after that point breaks the cake up and gives you cheesy potato pieces instead of a truffade.

  • Sliced, not diced, and cooked covered so they soften.
  • Fold the cheese through two or three times, then stop.
  • Leave the base alone at the end so it crusts.

item.title: Pipérade
item.description: Peppers, tomato and onion cooked to a jam with Espelette pepper, with eggs stirred through at the last moment.
item.content:encoded:
The vegetables are cooked down for a full forty minutes until there is no liquid left at all, and the eggs are stirred in off the heat. A wet pepper base plus eggs gives you scrambled eggs in a puddle; a properly reduced one binds with the egg into something closer to a loose omelette. The residual heat of the pan is enough to set the eggs — put it back on the flame and they curdle in seconds.

  • Cook the vegetables until the pan is dry.
  • Eggs off the heat. Back on the flame and they curdle.
  • Serve it slightly looser than looks right — it keeps setting.

item.title: Gratin de Courgettes
item.description: Courgettes cooked down with rice that absorbs their liquid, bound with egg and cheese and baked until browned.
item.content:encoded:
Courgettes are more than ninety per cent water and the rice is there to absorb it — added raw to the pan with the salted courgettes, it cooks in the liquid they release rather than in added stock. That is what stops the finished gratin being watery, which is the usual fate of this dish. Salt the courgettes first and give them ten minutes to weep before anything else happens.

  • Do not squeeze the courgettes. The rice needs their liquid.
  • Raw rice into the pan — it cooks in what they release.
  • Cool before the eggs go in, or they scramble.

item.title: Beef Suya
item.description: Beef suya — thin skewers rubbed in peanut and chilli yaji spice, grilled over coals and dusted again.
item.content:encoded:
Yaji is built on defatted ground peanut, which sticks to the meat and toasts on the grill into a crust — using peanut butter instead leaves an oily coating that burns. The spice goes on twice, once before and once after grilling, because the raw dusting at the end carries an aroma that heat would destroy.

  • Blot the peanut oil out. Oily yaji burns black on the grill instead of toasting.
  • Slice the beef very thin, which is far easier after half an hour in the freezer.
  • The second dusting of raw spice at the end is not optional — it is where the aroma comes from.

item.title: Gratin de Macaronis
item.description: Macaroni bound in a nutmeg-scented béchamel under Gruyère and breadcrumbs, baked until browned and still creamy inside.
item.content:encoded:
The béchamel is deliberately looser than an English macaroni cheese, because the pasta goes in undercooked and continues to absorb it in the oven — sauced to the right consistency at the point of assembly, it comes out dry. Nutmeg is not optional in a French béchamel and should be grated fresh; the pre-ground kind is flat and slightly musty, which is very noticeable in a sauce this plain.

  • Undercook the pasta by three minutes.
  • A loose sauce. It tightens considerably in the oven.
  • Grate the nutmeg fresh.

item.title: Frisée aux Lardons
item.description: Curly endive dressed with hot bacon fat deglazed with vinegar, topped with croutons and a soft poached egg.
item.content:encoded:
The dressing is poured over the leaves boiling hot, straight from the pan, which half-wilts the frisée — that is the dish, and a cold vinaigrette makes it a completely different and much duller salad. Use only the pale inner leaves; the dark outer ones are tough and unpleasantly bitter. The egg should be poached to a completely liquid yolk, because the yolk is the second half of the dressing once it is broken.

  • The dressing goes on boiling hot. That is the dish.
  • Pale inner leaves only.
  • A liquid yolk — it becomes part of the dressing.

item.title: Doro Wat
item.description: Doro wat — Ethiopian chicken stew with berbere, niter kibbeh and a mountain of dry-cooked onions.
item.content:encoded:
The onions are cooked dry, with no oil at all, for close to an hour before any fat is added — they release their own moisture and collapse into a sweet purée that becomes the body of the sauce, a job no amount of frying would do. Niter kibbeh, butter clarified with spices, then carries the berbere's fat-soluble aromatics through the stew.

  • No oil during the onion stage. This is the single most important instruction in the recipe.
  • Berbere varies enormously in heat. Start with four tablespoons and taste before adding more.
  • Score the boiled eggs lightly so the sauce penetrates the whites.

item.title: Omelette aux Fines Herbes
item.description: A pale rolled French omelette with chervil, chives, parsley and tarragon, taken from the pan while still soft inside.
item.content:encoded:
A French omelette is not browned. The pan is at medium heat, not high, and the eggs are stirred constantly with the flat of a fork for the first thirty seconds so they set in tiny curds rather than a sheet. It comes off the heat while the centre is still visibly wet, because it keeps cooking on the plate — baveuse is the term and it is the whole standard. Fines herbes means four herbs specifically: chervil, chives, parsley and tarragon.

  • Medium heat. A browned omelette is the wrong dish.
  • Stir constantly for the first thirty seconds.
  • Out of the pan while the middle is still wet.

item.title: Pain de Campagne
item.description: A country sourdough of white and wholemeal flour raised on a levain, proved slowly and baked dark in a covered pot.
item.content:encoded:
The loaf is baked in a covered pot for the first two-thirds, which traps the steam the dough releases and keeps the crust soft enough to expand — take the lid off too early and the crust sets before the loaf has finished rising, giving a dense crumb and a torn side. The autolyse before the salt goes in matters too: forty minutes of flour and water alone lets the gluten begin forming without any work, which is most of the kneading done for free.

  • Lid on for the first twenty minutes. It is the steam that lets it rise.
  • Bake it darker than feels right — pale crust means flat flavour.
  • Cool completely. Cutting it warm ruins the crumb.

item.title: Fougasse
item.description: Provençal flatbread slashed into a leaf and stretched so the cuts open wide, giving far more crust than crumb.
item.content:encoded:
The cuts must go all the way through the dough to the tray and then be pulled open with your fingers — a slash that is not opened simply closes again as the bread proves and bakes, and you get an ordinary flatbread with lines on it. Pull them wider than looks right, because they shrink by roughly half. The dough is also wetter than most bread doughs, which is what gives the thin sections their crispness.

  • Cut all the way through and pull the holes wide open.
  • A wet dough. It gives the thin parts their crispness.
  • Brush with oil the moment it leaves the oven.

item.title: Bobotie
item.description: Bobotie — South African curried mince with dried fruit under a baked egg custard topping with bay leaves.
item.content:encoded:
Bread soaked in milk and squeezed keeps the mince moist and gives the filling a soft, almost pâté-like texture rather than a granular one. The custard must go onto a cooled filling or it curdles from below before it has a chance to set into a smooth layer.

  • Cool the filling before the custard goes on, or it will curdle rather than set.
  • Mild curry powder is correct. Bobotie is aromatic and fruity, not fiery.
  • The bay leaves are traditional and perfume the custard as it bakes; remove them before eating.

item.title: Pain aux Noix
item.description: A dense walnut bread that stains faintly purple around the nuts, made with wholemeal flour and a little honey.
item.content:encoded:
The walnuts go in at the very end of the kneading, after the gluten has developed, because their sharp edges cut the strands and a dough kneaded with nuts in it never builds proper structure. The purple staining around them is a reaction between walnut tannins and the alkaline dough — it is harmless, characteristic, and a sign you used enough nuts. Toast them first: raw walnuts in bread taste faintly of nothing.

  • Nuts in last, after the gluten has developed.
  • Toast them first or they taste of nothing.
  • The purple staining is normal and means you used enough.

item.title: Tarte Flambée
item.description: A paper-thin Alsatian flatbread topped with fromage blanc, raw onion and bacon and baked in minutes at maximum heat.
item.content:encoded:
The dough has no yeast, which is what lets it be rolled to the thickness of paper without springing back — a yeasted dough fights you and puffs in the oven, and this is meant to be flat and cracker-crisp at the edges. Everything on top goes on raw, because the whole bake is under twelve minutes at maximum heat. Fromage blanc thinned with cream gives the right tang; crème fraîche alone is too rich and too heavy.

  • No yeast. That is what lets it roll paper-thin.
  • Maximum heat, preheated properly.
  • Everything raw on top. It cooks in the twelve minutes.

item.title: Jamaican Curry Goat
item.description: Jamaican curry goat — slow-stewed goat with Jamaican curry powder, thyme, allspice and scotch bonnet.
item.content:encoded:
Jamaican curry powder is heavier on turmeric and allspice than Indian blends, and burning it into hot oil — a step called "burning the curry" — is what develops its depth and turns the oil a deep yellow. Goat is almost pure working muscle, so it needs two and a half hours of gentle stewing before the connective tissue gives way.

  • Burn the curry powder in oil first. It is the step that separates Jamaican curry from every other kind.
  • Leave one scotch bonnet whole so it perfumes the pot without releasing all its heat. Do not burst it.
  • If goat is unavailable, mutton or lamb shoulder works with about 90 minutes of stewing.

item.title: Pan Bagnat
item.description: Salade niçoise packed into a round loaf and pressed for hours so the bread absorbs the oil and tomato juices.
item.content:encoded:
Pressing it for at least two hours is the entire dish. The bread has to absorb the oil, vinegar and tomato juices and compress into something dense — an unpressed pan bagnat is just a tuna roll. Rub the cut faces with raw garlic and a halved tomato first, which seasons the crumb before anything else touches it. And no lettuce, ever: it collapses to slime under the weight.

  • Press it. Two hours minimum, and longer is better.
  • Rub the bread with garlic and tomato before anything else.
  • No lettuce. It turns to slime.

item.title: Galettes Bretonnes
item.description: Dark buckwheat crêpes filled with ham, Gruyère and an egg, the edges folded square around a still-runny yolk.
item.content:encoded:
The batter needs to rest for a couple of hours, because buckwheat has no gluten and the starch needs time to hydrate — an unrested batter tears in the pan and tastes chalky. It is also made with water rather than milk, which is what makes the galette crisp rather than soft. The egg goes onto the galette in the pan and the white sets while the yolk stays liquid, so the folding has to happen fast.

  • Rest the batter two hours. Buckwheat needs it.
  • Water, not milk, or it will not crisp.
  • Fold fast, while the yolk is still liquid.

item.title: Saucisson en Brioche
item.description: A Lyon poaching sausage cooked, cooled and wrapped in enriched brioche dough, then baked until dark and glossy.
item.content:encoded:
The sausage is poached first and then cooled completely, for two reasons: a raw sausage releases fat and water into the dough and gives you a soggy grey layer around it, and a warm one starts the dough proving unevenly before it goes in the oven. The brioche also needs an overnight cold prove — the butter content makes it impossible to handle at room temperature, and cold dough is the only way to wrap it neatly.

  • Cook and cool the sausage completely first.
  • Cold dough, straight from the fridge, or it cannot be handled.
  • Cool 20 minutes before slicing or it tears.

item.title: Ackee and Saltfish
item.description: Ackee and saltfish — Jamaica's national dish, with ackee, soaked salt cod, peppers, onion and thyme.
item.content:encoded:
Ackee has the texture of soft scrambled egg and disintegrates if stirred, so it goes in at the very end and is folded through rather than mixed. The salt cod must be soaked and then boiled and drained, because the salt concentration is high enough to ruin the dish if you take a shortcut.

  • Fold the ackee, do not stir it. It breaks down into a paste within seconds of vigorous mixing.
  • Taste the cod after boiling. Salt levels vary hugely between brands and soaking times.
  • Only ever use tinned ackee or fruit prepared by someone who knows what they are doing; unripe ackee is genuinely toxic.

item.title: Tarte au Citron
item.description: A blind-baked pastry case filled with a sharp lemon cream set with butter and eggs, baked only until it just wobbles.
item.content:encoded:
The filling is baked at a low temperature and pulled while the centre still wobbles, because it sets considerably as it cools — a tart baked until firm in the oven will be rubbery and weeping by the time it is cut. The pastry case must also be sealed with beaten egg after blind baking and returned to the oven for two minutes, which varnishes the surface and stops the wet filling soaking into it.

  • Seal the case with egg wash. It is what keeps the base crisp.
  • Pull it while the middle wobbles. It sets as it cools.
  • Trim the overhang after baking, not before.

item.title: Fried Sweet Plantain
item.description: Fried sweet plantain — very ripe plantain fried until caramelised at the edges and soft in the middle.
item.content:encoded:
Plantains only develop enough sugar to caramelise once the skin is black — a yellow plantain is starchy and will fry to something closer to a chip. Moderate rather than screaming heat gives the sugars time to brown before the interior overcooks and disintegrates.

  • Black skins. This is the entire recipe and the mistake everyone makes the first time.
  • Do not crowd the pan. Overlapping slices steam instead of frying.
  • A rack, never paper, or the underside goes soggy in the trapped steam.

item.title: Tarte aux Pommes
item.description: Thin apple slices fanned over a compote base in a pastry case, baked until the edges catch and glazed with apricot.
item.content:encoded:
Two kinds of apple do two jobs. A cooking apple collapses into the compote that lines the base and keeps everything moist; a firm eating apple holds its shape in the fanned slices on top. Using one variety for both gives you either a dry tart or a soupy one. The apricot glaze is not decoration either — it seals the cut surfaces and stops them browning within the hour.

  • Two apple varieties: one to collapse, one to hold.
  • Pack the slices tightly — they shrink considerably.
  • Glaze while hot so it soaks in rather than sitting on top.

item.title: Tarte Normande
item.description: Apples baked into an almond and Calvados custard in a pastry case, until puffed, set and deeply browned on top.
item.content:encoded:
The custard is poured over raw apples and they cook in it, which means they have to be cut thick — 1 cm wedges, not slices — or they disintegrate and turn the filling to mush. Ground almonds in the custard absorb the liquid the apples release, which is what stops the tart weeping. It is baked hotter than a plain custard tart because the almond protects it from curdling.

  • Thick apple wedges. Thin slices dissolve into the custard.
  • Ground almonds absorb the apple juice — do not reduce them.
  • Cool before cutting or it runs.

item.title: Flan Parisien
item.description: A deep pastry case filled with thick vanilla custard, baked hot so the surface scorches while the inside stays soft.
item.content:encoded:
The custard is cooked on the hob to a thick pastry cream before it goes into the case, not poured in raw — that is what gives the flan its dense, sliceable set rather than a loose baked custard. The oven is then hot, 200°C, purely to scorch the surface: dark brown almost to black in patches is correct and is what a French bakery aims for. A pale flan is an underbaked one.

  • Cook the custard thick on the hob first. That is the set.
  • A dark, scorched top. Pale means underbaked.
  • Chill it properly — four hours minimum — or it will not slice.

item.title: Ahi Poke Bowl
item.description: Ahi poke bowl — cubed raw tuna in soy, sesame and sweet onion over seasoned rice with avocado and cucumber.
item.content:encoded:
The tuna is dressed no more than fifteen minutes before serving, because soy sauce is salty enough to start curing the surface and turning it opaque and firm. Cutting against the grain into even cubes gives a clean bite; ragged pieces read as mushy however good the fish is.

  • Buy tuna from a fishmonger you trust and tell them it is for eating raw. Previously frozen fish is safer and often better.
  • Dress it late. Fifteen minutes is the ceiling before the soy starts curing the surface.
  • Keep the fish very cold right up to the moment of cutting.

item.title: Far Breton
item.description: A dense Breton batter pudding baked with prunes soaked in tea and rum, set firm with a browned skin on top.
item.content:encoded:
The prunes are soaked in hot tea rather than water, which sounds like an affectation and is not — tannin cuts the sweetness of the prune and stops the whole pudding being cloying. Rest the batter for an hour as well: it allows the flour to hydrate and gives the far its characteristic dense, almost rubbery set rather than a light spongy one, which would be a clafoutis.

  • Tea, not water, for the prunes. The tannin cuts the sweetness.
  • Rest the batter an hour for the dense set.
  • It sinks as it cools. That is not a failure.

item.title: Kouign-Amann
item.description: Laminated dough with sugar folded into the butter layers, baked so the sugar caramelises against the tin into a glass shell.
item.content:encoded:
Sugar is folded in with the butter during lamination, not sprinkled on, and it melts during baking and runs to the bottom of the tin where it caramelises into a hard shell. That means the tins must be well buttered and heavily sugared, and the pastries turned out within a minute of leaving the oven — leave them any longer and the caramel sets like cement and they will never come out. Work fast and keep the dough cold.

  • Sugar folded into the layers, not sprinkled on top.
  • Turn them out within a minute or the caramel welds them in.
  • Keep the dough cold between every turn.

item.title: Açaí Bowl
item.description: Açaí bowl — frozen açaí blended thick as soft-serve, topped with granola, banana, berries and honey.
item.content:encoded:
The ratio of frozen fruit to liquid is what separates a bowl from a smoothie: roughly six parts frozen to one part liquid, added a tablespoon at a time. A tamper or a stop-and-scrape approach is essential, because adding more liquid to get the blender moving is how every thin açaí bowl happens.

  • Frozen bananas are the trick. They thicken the base and sweeten it without any added liquid.
  • A tamper or repeated scraping beats adding liquid every time.
  • Unsweetened açaí is quite tart on its own. Taste and adjust the honey before you pour.

item.title: Paris-Brest
item.description: A ring of choux pastry split and filled with hazelnut praline mousseline cream, topped with flaked almonds.
item.content:encoded:
Mousseline is pastry cream beaten with butter, and it splits if the two are at different temperatures — both must be at exactly room temperature before they meet, and if it does curdle, warming a third of the mixture gently and beating it back in will bring it round. The choux ring is baked until genuinely dry and dark; a pale ring collapses under the weight of the filling within minutes of being cut.

  • Butter and pastry cream both at room temperature or the mousseline splits.
  • Bake the choux dark and dry. Pale rings collapse.
  • If it splits, warm a third of it and beat it back in.

item.title: Religieuse
item.description: Choux buns in two sizes filled with chocolate crème pâtissière, glazed in fondant and joined with a piped buttercream collar.
item.content:encoded:
The buns are filled before they are glazed, never after — a glazed bun cannot be pierced without cracking the fondant, and the hole would show. The fondant needs to be warmed only to about 35°C: any hotter and it loses its shine and sets dull and streaky. Dip rather than spoon, and let the excess run off for a few seconds before turning the bun upright.

  • Fill before glazing, always.
  • Fondant at 35°C. Hotter and it sets dull.
  • Bake the buns dry or they collapse when filled.

item.title: Chia Pudding
item.description: Overnight chia pudding — chia seeds set in milk with vanilla and maple, topped with fruit and nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Chia seeds absorb roughly ten times their weight in liquid, forming a gel around each seed — the ratio of about one part seed to five parts liquid is what gives a spoonable set rather than a soup or a solid block. Stirring twice in the first half hour prevents the seeds clumping into lumps that never hydrate.

  • Stir at least twice in the first half hour, or you will find clumps of dry seed in the middle.
  • One part seeds to five parts liquid by volume is the reliable ratio to remember.
  • Make five jars on Sunday and breakfast is settled for the week.

item.title: Opéra
item.description: Layers of coffee-soaked almond joconde sponge, coffee buttercream and chocolate ganache under a poured mirror glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Everything depends on each layer being genuinely flat and each one being set before the next goes on, so this is a dessert made over two days and chilled between every stage. The joconde sponge is baked thin and fast — seven minutes — so it stays flexible enough to layer without cracking. Trim the edges with a hot knife at the end, which is what gives the clean striped section the cake is judged on.

  • Chill between every single layer. This is a two-day cake.
  • Seven minutes for the sponge — it must stay flexible.
  • Trim the edges with a hot knife for the stripes.

item.title: Fraisier
item.description: Génoise layered with mousseline cream and strawberries stood cut-side out around the edge, topped with marzipan.
item.content:encoded:
The strawberries around the edge are halved and pressed cut-side against the ring so the cross-section shows, and they need to be roughly the same height or the top layer sits crooked. Sort them by size before you start. The mousseline must be stiff enough to hold them in place, which means properly cooled pastry cream and butter beaten until it is genuinely aerated — a slack cream lets the fruit slide as it chills.

  • Sort the strawberries by size before you start.
  • Cut faces against the ring, or the sides look wrong.
  • Both mousseline components at room temperature.

item.title: Maple Pecan Granola
item.description: Maple pecan granola baked into proper clusters — oats, nuts and seeds with maple syrup and cinnamon.
item.content:encoded:
Clusters form when the sugars melt and then recrystallise as the granola cools, gluing the oats together — stirring during cooling breaks that bond and gives you loose muesli. A lightly beaten egg white is the professional trick, adding protein that sets into a scaffold around the clusters.

  • Do not stir during baking or cooling. That is the entire secret to clusters.
  • Press the mixture down hard before it goes in. Compaction is what lets it set as a slab.
  • Add dried fruit only after baking — it burns and turns bitter in the oven.

item.title: Dacquoise
item.description: Discs of hazelnut and almond meringue layered with praline buttercream, baked soft so they stay chewy rather than crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Ground nuts folded into the meringue keep it from drying out completely, so a dacquoise is baked at a moderate temperature for an hour rather than dried overnight like a pavlova — it should still give slightly under a finger when it comes out. Fold the nuts in with a light hand and stop the moment they are incorporated; over-folding knocks the air out and gives a flat, dense disc that never rises.

  • Stop folding the moment the nuts are in.
  • It should still give under a finger. Crisp means overbaked.
  • Cool on the paper — peeling them warm tears them.

item.title: Lemon Herb Quinoa Salad
item.description: Lemon herb quinoa salad with cucumber, tomato, feta and a sharp dressing added while the grains are warm.
item.content:encoded:
Rinsing quinoa removes saponin, a bitter natural coating that makes unwashed grains taste soapy. Dressing the quinoa while it is still warm lets the grains absorb the vinaigrette as they cool and set, seasoning them from within rather than just coating the outside.

  • Rinse thoroughly. Unwashed quinoa tastes bitter and soapy, and people blame the quinoa.
  • Dress it warm. This is the step that makes the difference.
  • Spread it on a tray to cool rather than leaving it in the pan, where it steams and clumps.

item.title: Crème Caramel
item.description: A baked vanilla custard set over hard caramel, chilled overnight so the caramel dissolves into a sauce, then turned out.
item.content:encoded:
It has to chill overnight, and not for convenience — the hard caramel in the base only dissolves into a pourable sauce after several hours in contact with the cold custard. Turned out after two hours you get set custard and a layer of toffee stuck to the dish. The bain-marie water must also be no more than a bare tremble; a simmering water bath boils the custard and gives it a bubbled, curdled texture.

  • Overnight in the fridge. That is when the caramel becomes a sauce.
  • Skim the bubbles before baking.
  • A bare tremble in the water bath, never a simmer.

item.title: Spiced Red Lentil Soup
item.description: Spiced red lentil soup with cumin and turmeric, finished with lemon and a sizzling chilli butter.
item.content:encoded:
Red lentils have no skins, so they disintegrate completely within twenty minutes and thicken the soup themselves — no blending or cream required. Blooming the ground spices in fat before the liquid goes in dissolves their fat-soluble compounds, which is why the same quantity of spice tastes far stronger this way.

  • Salt at the end. Salting lentils early slows their breakdown considerably.
  • The lemon is not a garnish. Without acid the soup tastes muddy and heavy.
  • The spiced butter takes ninety seconds and transforms the bowl. Do not skip it.

item.title: Île Flottante
item.description: Meringue quenelles poached briefly in milk and floated on vanilla crème anglaise under a thread of hard caramel.
item.content:encoded:
Crème anglaise curdles above 85°C, so it is cooked over gentle heat and stirred constantly until it coats the back of a spoon and holds a line drawn through it. Keep a bowl of cold cream nearby to stop it fast if it starts to grain. The meringues poach in barely trembling milk for two minutes a side; boiling milk makes them swell and then collapse into shreds.

  • Take the anglaise off at 82°C. Above 85°C it scrambles.
  • Poach in a bare tremble. Boiling milk shreds the meringue.
  • Thread the caramel from a height for fine lines.

item.title: Riz au Lait
item.description: Round rice cooked slowly in vanilla milk until creamy but still distinct, enriched with egg yolk and a little cream.
item.content:encoded:
Round or pudding rice, never long-grain: the whole texture depends on the starch that short grains release, and a long-grain version stays thin and separate. It is stirred often but not constantly, and taken off the heat while still looser than you want it, because it thickens a great deal in the first ten minutes off the stove. The yolks go in off the heat as well, or they scramble in the hot rice.

  • Round rice only. Long-grain gives a thin pudding.
  • Blanch it first to wash off the raw starch.
  • Off the heat looser than you want — it thickens fast.

item.title: Financiers
item.description: Small almond cakes made with beurre noisette and egg whites, baked hot so the edges crisp against a soft middle.
item.content:encoded:
Beurre noisette is the entire flavour, so the butter must be taken past melted to genuinely nutty and brown — it should smell of hazelnuts and the solids at the bottom should be the colour of dark toast. Pull it off the heat a shade before it looks right, because it keeps cooking in the pan. Resting the batter overnight is the other thing professionals do and amateurs skip: it hydrates the almonds and improves the texture noticeably.

  • Take the butter properly brown. It is the whole flavour.
  • Egg whites unwhipped, straight in.
  • Rest the batter. Overnight is better than two hours.

item.title: Negroni
item.description: The Negroni — equal parts gin, Campari and sweet vermouth, stirred over ice with an orange twist.
item.content:encoded:
It is stirred rather than shaken because every ingredient is clear and spirit-based: shaking would aerate it, cloud it and over-dilute it. The stir is not just chilling — it adds around 25% water by volume, and that dilution is a deliberate part of the recipe rather than an accident.

  • Stir, never shake. A shaken Negroni is cloudy, foamy and wrong.
  • One large cube in the glass melts far more slowly than several small ones.
  • Vermouth is a wine and oxidises. Refrigerate the bottle after opening and use it within a month.

item.title: Palmiers
item.description: Puff pastry rolled in sugar rather than flour, folded into hearts and baked until the sugar caramelises on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry is rolled out in sugar instead of flour, which is what makes this work — the sugar gets pressed into the surface of the dough and caramelises against the tray. Flouring the bench and sprinkling sugar on afterwards gives you a much paler, less crisp biscuit. They are also turned halfway through baking so both faces caramelise, and they burn from perfectly bronzed to black in under a minute.

  • Roll in sugar, never flour.
  • Turn them halfway so both faces caramelise.
  • They go from bronze to burnt in under a minute.

item.title: Chouquettes
item.description: Small empty choux buns scattered with pearl sugar and baked until hollow, dry and deep gold.
item.content:encoded:
Pearl sugar is not the same as any other sugar and there is no real substitute — it is compressed enough not to melt in the oven, so it stays as visible white nuggets. Granulated sugar dissolves into the surface and caramelises, giving something entirely different. The buns are also baked with the oven door propped open for the last five minutes, which lets the steam out and stops them going soft as they cool.

  • Pearl sugar only. Granulated melts away.
  • Prop the door open at the end to dry them.
  • They are meant to be empty. Do not fill them.

item.title: Piña Colada
item.description: Piña colada — white rum, coconut cream and pineapple blended thick, with a pineapple wedge and cherry.
item.content:encoded:
Cream of coconut is sweetened and emulsified, quite different from tinned coconut milk, and swapping one for the other gives a thin, watery drink that separates. Frozen pineapple in place of some of the ice thickens the drink without diluting the flavour, which is what stops the last third tasting of melted water.

  • Cream of coconut, not coconut milk or coconut cream from a carton. It is the sweetened, emulsified kind in a tin.
  • Frozen pineapple instead of extra ice keeps the flavour concentrated as the drink softens.
  • Freeze the glasses. It buys you ten minutes before it starts to melt.

item.title: Gâteau au Yaourt
item.description: The classic French yogurt cake measured in the empty yogurt pot rather than by weight, plain and reliably moist.
item.content:encoded:
The proportions are traditionally measured with the empty yogurt pot — one of yogurt, two of sugar, three of flour, half of oil — and they are given both ways here because the ratio is the recipe. Oil rather than butter is what keeps it moist for days, and the yogurt provides both the acid for the raising agent and enough fat that the crumb stays tender without creaming anything.

  • The pot is the measure. That is the recipe.
  • Oil, not butter — it stays moist for days.
  • Fold the flour in; do not beat it.

item.title: Bagna Cauda
item.description: A warm Piedmontese dip of anchovy, garlic and olive oil melted slowly together and kept hot at the table for raw vegetables.
item.content:encoded:
The garlic is poached in milk before it goes anywhere near the oil, which sounds fussy and is the difference between a sauce you can eat a bowl of and one that repeats on you all evening. Milk draws out the harsh sulphur compounds and leaves the sweetness. After that the whole thing is a matter of very low heat: the anchovies must dissolve rather than fry, and oil hot enough to sizzle turns the garlic bitter within seconds.

  • Poach the garlic in milk first. It is what makes it digestible.
  • The lowest heat you have. Sizzling oil turns it bitter.
  • Keep it warm at the table, not hot.

item.title: Carpaccio di Manzo
item.description: Raw beef fillet frozen briefly, sliced and beaten paper-thin, dressed with a thinned mustard mayonnaise and parmesan.
item.content:encoded:
Freeze the fillet for forty minutes before slicing — not solid, just firm enough that a knife goes through cleanly. Room-temperature beef drags, tears and can never be cut thin enough. After slicing, each piece is beaten between oiled cling film until it is genuinely translucent; that thinness is the dish, and a thick carpaccio is just raw steak. Oil the film rather than the beef, or the meat sticks and shreds as you lift it.

  • Forty minutes in the freezer. Room-temperature beef cannot be cut thin.
  • Oil the film, not the meat.
  • Assemble on cold plates at the last moment.

item.title: Bloody Mary
item.description: Bloody Mary — vodka and tomato juice with horseradish, Worcestershire and celery salt, rolled not shaken.
item.content:encoded:
Rolling — pouring the drink between two vessels — mixes it thoroughly without shaking, which would aerate the tomato juice into a pale, frothy mess. Building the seasonings into the glass before the juice ensures they dissolve rather than sitting on top, and the horseradish needs that contact to bloom.

  • Roll, do not shake. Shaking turns tomato juice pale, frothy and thin.
  • Rim the outside of the glass so the salt does not collapse into the drink and over-season it.
  • Taste before you pour. Tomato juices vary enormously in salt and acidity.

item.title: Baccalà Mantecato
item.description: Salt cod poached and then beaten with olive oil until it emulsifies into a pale fluffy cream, served on grilled polenta.
item.content:encoded:
Mantecato means beaten to a cream, and the emulsion is between the fish's own gelatine and the oil — which is why the cod must still be warm when the beating starts and why the oil goes in a drop at a time exactly as for mayonnaise. Cold fish will not take it up. The Venetian version contains no potato and no garlic, both of which are added elsewhere to make a smaller amount of expensive fish go further.

  • The fish must be warm when you start beating.
  • Oil drop by drop at first. It is an emulsion.
  • No potato and no garlic. That is a different dish.

item.title: Sarde in Saor
item.description: Fried sardines layered with sweet-sour vinegar onions, pine nuts and raisins, then left two days before eating.
item.content:encoded:
This is not a dish you eat on the day you make it. The vinegar needs forty-eight hours to move through the fish and mellow, and the onions need the same to give up their sweetness into it — eaten fresh it is sharp and disjointed, and on day two it becomes one thing. The onions are also cooked in a great deal more oil than looks reasonable, because that oil ends up as the dressing rather than being drained away.

  • Two days, minimum. On day one it is not the dish.
  • Do not colour the onions — they should stay pale.
  • Finish with onions on top so nothing is exposed.

item.title: Brown Sugar Bubble Tea
item.description: Brown sugar bubble tea — chewy tapioca pearls steeped in syrup under strong black milk tea over ice.
item.content:encoded:
Tapioca pearls are boiled and then rested off the heat in the covered pan, which lets the heat travel to the centre without the outside disintegrating — boiling them the whole time gives a mushy exterior and a chalky core. They are then steeped in syrup, which both sweetens them and keeps them from hardening as they cool.

  • Boil, then rest covered. Skipping the rest gives you pearls with hard white centres.
  • Eat them within about four hours. Refrigerated tapioca goes hard and cannot be revived.
  • Brew the tea much stronger than you would drink it — ice and milk are about to dilute it heavily.

item.title: Insalata di Mare
item.description: Squid, prawns and mussels each cooked separately for their own time and dressed simply with lemon, oil and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Squid has two states — under two minutes or over forty — and everything between is rubber. Prawns need ninety seconds, mussels four. Cooked together in one pot, at least two of the three will be wrong, so each goes into the same pan of water in turn and comes out on its own schedule. Dress the seafood while it is still warm: it absorbs the lemon and oil then, and refuses to once cold.

  • Ninety seconds for the squid. Anything more needs forty minutes to recover.
  • Each thing cooked separately, in turn.
  • Dress it warm, serve it cool.

item.title: Fritto Misto
item.description: Mixed seafood dusted in fine semolina and fried very briefly, so the coating stays thin and almost invisible.
item.content:encoded:
Semolina flour rather than plain, and a dusting rather than a batter — the coating exists to dry the surface and crisp, not to form a shell. Shake every piece hard in a sieve before it goes in the oil, because loose flour burns and clouds the oil within two batches. Fry in small batches at 180°C: crowding drops the temperature and everything absorbs oil instead of sealing.

  • Shake off every scrap of loose flour or it burns in the oil.
  • Small batches. Crowding is what makes it greasy.
  • Drain on a rack and salt while hot.

item.title: Carciofi alla Romana
item.description: Whole artichokes stuffed with mint and garlic and braised upside down in oil and water until spoon-tender.
item.content:encoded:
They cook stem-up, packed tightly into a pan just big enough to hold them, so the leaves stay submerged in the oil and water while the stems steam above it. Turned the other way the outer leaves dry out and toughen. Lemon water is not optional while you trim: a cut artichoke goes brown and slightly bitter within a minute or two of meeting the air.

  • Lemon water from the first cut. They brown in a minute.
  • Stem-up and packed tight, so the leaves stay submerged.
  • Cook them soft enough to eat with a spoon.

item.title: Mulled Wine
item.description: Mulled wine gently warmed with orange, cinnamon, star anise and cloves — never boiled, so the alcohol stays.
item.content:encoded:
Alcohol boils off at 78°C, so mulled wine is held at around 70°C — hot enough to extract the spice oils, cool enough to keep the wine intact. Making a spiced sugar syrup first with a small amount of wine, then adding the rest, means the sugar dissolves without ever putting the whole batch near a boil.

  • Never let it boil. You lose the alcohol and the wine turns harsh and stewed.
  • Zest strips rather than grated zest, and remove them; the white pith turns the wine bitter over time.
  • A cheap but drinkable fruity red is ideal. Nothing tannic or oaked, and nothing you would rather drink cold.

item.title: Carciofi alla Giudia
item.description: Whole artichokes fried gently to cook through, pressed flat into a flower and fried hot again until the leaves shatter.
item.content:encoded:
Two fryings at two temperatures, and the reason is that the heart and the leaves need opposite things. The first fry at 130°C cooks the dense heart through without colouring; the second at 180°C, after the artichoke has been pressed flat, blasts the thin outer leaves into something like glass. One fry gives you either a raw heart or burnt leaves. Press it flat while it is still warm from the first fry, when the leaves are pliable.

  • Two fryings at two temperatures. There is no shortcut.
  • Press them flat while warm, when the leaves still bend.
  • The outer leaves should shatter, not bend.

item.title: Ragù Napoletano
item.description: Ragù napoletano — whole cuts of beef and pork simmered four hours in tomato until the sauce turns brick red.
item.content:encoded:
Whole cuts rather than mince is the defining difference: large pieces render their collagen slowly into the sauce over hours, which is what gives Neapolitan ragù its glossy body without any reduction trickery. The tomato is cooked long past the point where it tastes of tomato, into something darker and sweeter.

  • Four hours is the recipe, not a suggestion. At two hours you have a decent tomato sauce; at four you have ragù.
  • Never let it boil. A bare simmer, uncovered, is what reduces it without turning the meat stringy.
  • It is better the next day, which is why Neapolitan families start it on Saturday.

item.title: Supplì
item.description: Roman risotto croquettes with a core of mozzarella that stretches into a thread, breadcrumbed and fried until dark.
item.content:encoded:
The risotto has to be made the day before and refrigerated until it is genuinely cold and stiff. Warm rice will not hold a shape, and a supplì that loses its form in the fryer bursts and empties. The mozzarella must be drained and dried too — fresh mozzarella carries a great deal of water, and any of it inside the croquette turns to steam and blows a hole in the crumb.

  • The rice must be cold and stiff. Warm rice bursts.
  • Dry the mozzarella or the steam blows a hole in the crumb.
  • Seal every seam.

item.title: Panelle
item.description: Chickpea flour cooked to a thick paste, set flat, cut into squares and fried until blistered, eaten in a bread roll.
item.content:encoded:
The paste must be cooked far longer than it looks like it needs — a full fifteen minutes of hard stirring after it thickens, because raw chickpea flour tastes bitter and chalky and only long cooking drives that off. It also has to be spread while genuinely hot, since it sets within a minute or two and cannot be moved afterwards. Oil the surface you spread it on rather than flouring it.

  • Fifteen minutes of stirring after it thickens. Less and it tastes raw.
  • Spread it hot and fast — it sets in about a minute.
  • Oil the surface, never flour it.

item.title: Giardiniera
item.description: Hard vegetables blanched briefly in vinegar and packed under oil with garlic and chilli, ready after a week.
item.content:encoded:
Each vegetable is blanched for its own time in the vinegar rather than all together — carrot needs three minutes and celery ninety seconds, and a uniform blanch gives you either raw carrot or dissolved celery. Blanching in vinegar rather than water matters too: it acidifies the vegetable right through, which is what preserves it, where water-blanched vegetables dilute the pickle and can spoil.

  • Blanch each vegetable for its own time.
  • In vinegar, not water — that is what preserves them.
  • Dry them completely before they go in the jar.

item.title: Pasta e Fagioli
item.description: Pasta e fagioli — pasta and borlotti beans cooked together into a thick soup with rosemary and Parmesan rind.
item.content:encoded:
Cooking the pasta directly in the bean broth rather than separately is the whole point: the starch it sheds is what thickens the liquid, and draining it away leaves a thin, disappointing soup. Blending a ladleful of beans adds body without cream.

  • Keep the Parmesan rind in a bag in the freezer. It is the single best thing you can add to a bean soup.
  • The soup should be thick enough that a spoon stands up briefly. Loosen with hot water if it goes past that.
  • Cook the pasta in the soup, not in a separate pan. That starch is the recipe.

item.title: Tagliatelle al Ragù
item.description: The authentic Bolognese ragù, built on milk and wine with barely any tomato, cooked three hours and served on egg tagliatelle.
item.content:encoded:
Milk goes in before the wine and is cooked away completely, which is the step that separates a Bolognese ragù from every other meat sauce. The lactose tenderises the meat and rounds off the acidity that follows. Tomato is a seasoning here, not a base — two spoonfuls of purée, not a tin — and the sauce should end up the colour of terracotta rather than red. Three hours at a bare blip; anything faster gives you mince in gravy.

  • Milk first, cooked away completely. It is the whole difference.
  • Two spoons of purée, not a tin of tomatoes.
  • Three hours at a blip. There is no fast version.

item.title: Tortellini in Brodo
item.description: Tiny meat-filled tortellini served in a clarified capon broth, with nothing added but a little parmesan.
item.content:encoded:
The broth must be clear, which means starting the meat in cold water and never letting it boil — a rolling boil emulsifies the fat into the liquid and clouds it permanently. Skim for the first twenty minutes and then leave it alone at a bare shiver. The tortellini are rolled thin enough to see your hand through, because in a broth there is nothing to hide a thick edge behind.

  • Start in cold water and never boil, or the broth clouds.
  • Roll the pasta until you can see your hand through it.
