  • A pea of filling. Overfilled tortellini burst in the broth.

item.title: Vitello Tonnato
item.description: Vitello tonnato — cold poached veal sliced thin under a tuna, anchovy and caper sauce. Piedmontese classic.
item.content:encoded:
The veal is poached gently and then cooled in its own broth, which keeps it moist where roasting would dry a lean cut out. Slicing it fridge-cold is what allows the paper-thin cuts the dish needs — warm veal tears.

  • Cool the veal in its broth. Lifting it out hot loses you both moisture and flavour.
  • Slice it straight from the fridge. Room-temperature veal will not cut thinly.
  • Assemble at least an hour ahead so the sauce settles into the meat.

item.title: Agnolotti del Plin
item.description: Piedmontese pasta filled with roast meat and pinched along a single strip, then cut into a row of small parcels.
item.content:encoded:
The filling is made from meat that has already been roasted and is traditionally the leftovers of a Sunday joint — braised or roasted meat has lost its water and its collagen has set, so it minces into something dry enough to pipe, where raw meat would leak and steam the pasta open. The plin, the pinch between each mound, is what seals them; done properly you cut a whole row apart with a wheel in one pass.

  • Cooked meat only. Raw filling leaks and steams the seal open.
  • Pinch hard between each mound — that is the seal.
  • Butter and sage. Anything heavier buries them.

item.title: Culurgiones
item.description: Sardinian pasta filled with potato, mint and pecorino and closed with a wheat-ear pleat, served in simple tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The potatoes are baked rather than boiled, because boiled potato carries water that turns the filling slack and bursts the pleat. Bake them in their skins, scoop the flesh and rice it while hot. Mint rather than basil is what makes this Sardinian, and it goes in at a quantity that seems excessive — a whole large bunch to a kilo of potato — because the pecorino is assertive and mint is the only thing that stands up to it.

  • Bake the potatoes. Boiled ones make a wet filling.
  • A whole bunch of mint. It has to stand up to the pecorino.
  • Pleat alternately, side to side, up the seam.

item.title: Malloreddus alla Campidanese
item.description: Ridged Sardinian semolina gnocchetti in a sausage, saffron and tomato sauce finished with aged pecorino.
item.content:encoded:
Saffron goes into the sauce rather than the pasta in the Campidanese version, and it needs to be bloomed in a little warm stock for ten minutes first — thrown in dry it stays as red threads and gives colour to almost nothing. The sausage is skinned and crumbled rather than sliced, so it disperses through the sauce and seasons all of it; sliced sausage stays as separate lumps and leaves the tomato bland.

  • Bloom the saffron in warm liquid first.
  • Crumble the sausage, never slice it.
  • The ridges hold the sauce — do not substitute a smooth shape.

item.title: Focaccia Genovese
item.description: Focaccia Genovese — high-hydration dough dimpled and flooded with olive oil and brine, baked blistered and golden.
item.content:encoded:
The salamoia — a brine of water, oil and salt poured into the dimples before baking — steams the surface as it bakes, which is what gives Genoese focaccia its soft, faintly wet top rather than a crisp crust. High hydration and a long cold prove build the open crumb.

  • Press to the bottom of the tin. Timid dimples spring back and the brine has nowhere to sit.
  • The salamoia looks like a mistake. Pour all of it in — it is absorbed during the bake.
  • The cold overnight prove is what separates good focaccia from bread with oil on it.

item.title: Strozzapreti alla Boscaiola
item.description: Hand-rolled Romagnol pasta twists in a woodsman sauce of mushrooms, sausage and a little cream.
item.content:encoded:
The mushrooms go into a dry pan first with no fat at all and are left alone until they squeak and then brown. Mushrooms are mostly water, and adding oil at the start means they stew in it and never colour — dry-frying drives the water off first, and the oil goes in once they have already browned. The cream is a small amount stirred in at the very end, not a base: boscaiola is a woodsman's sauce, not a cream sauce.

  • Dry pan for the mushrooms. Oil first means they stew.
  • A splash of cream at the end, not a base.
  • Roll the twists loosely — tight ones stay raw in the middle.

item.title: Pici all'Aglione
item.description: Fat hand-rolled Tuscan pici in a sauce of slowly softened garlic and tomato, with no cheese and nothing else.
item.content:encoded:
The garlic is softened in oil over very low heat for a full fifteen minutes before the tomato goes in, until it collapses to a sweet paste — this is a sauce with three ingredients and garlic browned even slightly turns the whole thing acrid. Aglione, the Tuscan giant garlic, is mild enough to use in the quantities the dish calls for; with ordinary garlic use half as much and poach it in milk first if you have the time.

  • Fifteen minutes of very low heat on the garlic. No colour at all.
  • Roll them uneven. Machine-perfect pici are not pici.
  • No cheese. The sauce is three things and that is the point.

item.title: Gnocchi alla Sorrentina
item.description: Gnocchi alla Sorrentina — potato gnocchi baked in tomato sauce under mozzarella until blistered and molten.
item.content:encoded:
Baking floury potatoes rather than boiling them keeps water out of the dough, which means less flour is needed and the gnocchi stay light — waterlogged potato is the reason most homemade gnocchi turn to rubber. The mozzarella is torn and drained so it melts rather than releasing a pool of whey.

  • Bake the potatoes, never boil them. It is the single biggest factor in light gnocchi.
  • Use as little flour as will hold the dough together. More flour is more certainty and less pleasure.
  • Test one gnocco before rolling the rest — if it disintegrates, work in another spoonful of flour.

item.title: Pappardelle al Cinghiale
item.description: Wild boar marinated overnight in red wine and juniper, stewed three hours and served on wide pappardelle ribbons.
item.content:encoded:
Boar is strongly flavoured and can be muddy, and the overnight marinade in red wine with juniper and bay is what draws that off — the marinade is then discarded rather than used, which surprises people but is the point of it. Juniper goes back in fresh for the cooking. If using farmed boar or pork shoulder instead, keep the juniper and shorten the marinade, since the muddiness is not there to remove.

  • Throw the marinade away. Its job was to draw the muddiness out.
  • Fresh juniper for the cooking.
  • Dry the meat properly or it will not brown.

item.title: Trofie al Pesto
item.description: Ligurian trofie boiled with potato and green beans and dressed in pesto loosened with the starchy cooking water.
item.content:encoded:
Everything cooks in one pot and the starch from the potato is what lets the pesto cling — a pesto tossed through plain pasta slides off, where the same pesto loosened with potato-starchy water becomes a coating. The pesto itself is never heated. Take the pan off the heat, let it stop steaming for thirty seconds, then stir the pesto in; heat turns basil khaki and makes the cheese stringy.

  • One pot. The potato starch is what makes the pesto cling.
  • Pesto off the heat, always. Basil goes khaki in seconds.
  • Keep back plenty of the cooking water.

item.title: Pizzoccheri della Valtellina
item.description: Buckwheat pasta ribbons boiled with cabbage and potato, layered with valtellina cheese and finished with sage butter.
item.content:encoded:
The cheese is layered in rather than stirred through, and the dish is assembled in a warm bowl in alternating layers so it melts from the residual heat rather than in the pan. Stirred into hot pasta it goes stringy and gathers into a single lump. Buckwheat has no gluten, so the pasta is fragile and must be lifted with a slotted spoon rather than poured into a colander, which breaks it.

  • Layer the cheese, never stir it in.
  • Lift the pasta out with a spoon. Buckwheat breaks in a colander.
  • Brown the butter properly — pale butter leaves it flat.

item.title: Pasta alla Gricia
item.description: Pasta alla gricia — guanciale, pecorino and black pepper emulsified into a glossy sauce with pasta water.
item.content:encoded:
There is no cream, no egg and no tomato, so the sauce is nothing but rendered pork fat, starchy pasta water and cheese forced into an emulsion. That happens off the heat: pecorino added to a hot pan seizes into strings, and the whole dish depends on keeping the temperature below that point.

  • Off the heat for the cheese. Pecorino in a hot pan turns to rubber strings and there is no recovering it.
  • Guanciale, not pancetta. The cured jowl renders differently and its fat is the sauce.
  • Keep more pasta water than you think you need. The sauce tightens as it sits and needs loosening.

item.title: Pasta alla Genovese
item.description: A Neapolitan ragù of onions cooked down for four hours with beef until they collapse into a sweet brown sauce, with no tomato.
item.content:encoded:
The onions are cooked with the lid on for the first two hours, which sounds wrong for something meant to brown and is exactly right: they need to collapse and release all their water before any colouring can happen. Take the lid off too early and they catch. The quantity also looks absurd — a kilo of onions per two people — and reduces to about a fifth of its volume, so it is not absurd at all.

  • Lid on for the first two hours. They have to collapse before they can brown.
  • The quantity of onions is not a mistake.
  • No tomato. This is the point of the dish.

item.title: Pasta e Ceci
item.description: Chickpeas and broken pasta cooked together into a thick soup with rosemary, part of it blended for body.
item.content:encoded:
A third of the chickpeas is blended and returned to the pot, which is what gives the dish its body — otherwise it is chickpeas and pasta sitting in water. The pasta also cooks in the soup rather than separately, so its starch thickens things further; drained pasta added at the end leaves a thin broth. Rosemary goes in as a whole sprig and comes out, since chopped rosemary in a soup is unpleasantly woody.

  • Blend a third of it. That is the body.
  • Cook the pasta in the soup, not separately.
  • Whole rosemary sprigs, removed before serving.

item.title: Sicilian Caponata
item.description: Sicilian caponata — sweet-and-sour aubergine with celery, olives and capers. Served at room temperature.
item.content:encoded:
Frying each vegetable separately keeps their textures distinct — cooked together they collapse into one soft mass. The agrodolce goes in at the end and is boiled hard for a minute so the vinegar's harshness cooks off and only the sweet-sour balance remains.

  • Fry the vegetables separately. Every shortcut here costs you the texture the dish is about.
  • It is meant to be eaten at room temperature, never hot and never fridge-cold.
  • Make it a day ahead. The agrodolce needs time to settle into the aubergine.

item.title: Pasta con le Sarde
item.description: Sardines cooked with wild fennel, saffron, raisins and pine nuts, finished with toasted breadcrumbs instead of cheese.
item.content:encoded:
The fennel is boiled first and its cooking water is then used for the pasta, which carries the flavour through the whole dish rather than leaving it in the sauce — this is the step that makes it taste Sicilian rather than merely fishy. Breadcrumbs stand in for cheese, as they do in most Sicilian fish pastas, and they must be toasted dry and added at the table so they stay crisp.

  • Cook the pasta in the fennel water. That is the whole flavour.
  • Half the sardines dissolve, half stay whole.
  • Breadcrumbs instead of cheese, added at the table.

item.title: Busiate al Pesto Trapanese
item.description: A raw Trapanese pesto of almonds, tomato, basil and garlic pounded in a mortar and tossed through spiral busiate.
item.content:encoded:
The tomatoes are peeled and deseeded before they go in, and skipping that gives you a watery pink sauce rather than a pesto — the seeds and their jelly carry most of the liquid and none of the flavour. Almonds are blanched and raw, not toasted, which keeps the sauce pale and sweet. Everything is pounded rather than blitzed, because a processor emulsifies the tomato into a smoothie.

  • Deseed the tomatoes completely or the sauce is watery.
  • Raw almonds, not toasted — it should stay pale.
  • Never heat it. This is a raw sauce.

item.title: Anelletti al Forno
item.description: Small pasta rings baked with ragù, peas, aubergine and cheese into a firm timballo that can be cut into slices.
item.content:encoded:
The tin is lined with toasted breadcrumbs rather than greased, which does two things: it stops the timballo sticking, and it forms a crust that lets you turn it out whole and cut it in slices. Undercook the pasta by four minutes as well — it keeps absorbing sauce in the oven, and pasta boiled to al dente first will be soft and shapeless by the time the top has browned.

  • Breadcrumb the tin, not grease it. That is the crust.
  • Undercook the pasta by four minutes.
  • Rest twenty minutes before turning out or it collapses.

item.title: Zeppole
item.description: Zeppole di San Giuseppe — fried choux buns filled with pastry cream and topped with an amarena cherry.
item.content:encoded:
Frying choux instead of baking it puffs the paste from the outside in, which gives a crisper shell and a more open, hollow centre than an oven can. The oil must sit at 170°C: hotter and the outside sets before the steam has finished inflating it, leaving a raw core.

  • A thermometer matters here. Below 165°C they soak up oil; above 180°C they brown before the middle sets.
  • The paper-square trick means you never have to handle a piped ring.
  • Fill them within a couple of hours of frying, and eat them the same day.

item.title: Panettone
item.description: Panettone — the Milanese Christmas bread, proved over two days and cooled upside down to keep its height.
item.content:encoded:
Hanging the loaf upside down as it cools is not a flourish: the crumb is so open and the dough so rich that a warm panettone left upright compresses under its own weight into a dense band at the base. The staged proves build enough gluten to carry that much butter, sugar and fruit.

  • This is a two-day bake and a stand mixer is essential. Do not attempt the butter stage by hand.
  • Hang it upside down. A panettone left to cool the right way up collapses, every time.
  • It keeps far longer than an ordinary bread — a week wrapped is normal.

item.title: Risotto al Nero di Seppia
item.description: Risotto blackened with cuttlefish ink and cooked with the cuttlefish itself, finished with oil rather than butter and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
The ink goes in in two stages — most of it early so it cooks into the rice, and a spoonful at the very end for the colour, which dulls with heat. And this risotto is finished with olive oil rather than butter and parmesan, because in Venice cheese does not go near fish; the creaminess comes from beating the rice hard off the heat with oil and a little of the cooking liquid instead.

  • Ink in two stages. The last spoonful is the colour.
  • No cheese with fish. Olive oil does the mantecatura.
  • Cuttlefish is either two minutes or forty. Aim for the short end.

item.title: Risi e Bisi
item.description: A loose Venetian rice and pea dish, wetter than a risotto, built on a stock made from the empty pea pods.
item.content:encoded:
The stock is made from the pea pods, which are otherwise thrown away and carry more pea flavour than the peas do. Simmer them for twenty minutes and strain. The dish is also deliberately looser than a risotto — all'onda, wavy, and eaten with a spoon rather than a fork — so it takes more liquid and is served the moment it is ready, before it tightens.

  • Make the stock from the pods. That is where the flavour is.
  • Looser than a risotto. It is eaten with a spoon.
  • Peas in for the last four minutes only.

item.title: Canederli
item.description: Tyrolean bread dumplings with speck and parsley, bound with milk and egg and simmered gently in broth.
item.content:encoded:
Genuinely stale bread — three or four days, dry all the way through — is the only kind that works. Fresh bread turns to paste when the milk hits it and the dumplings dissolve in the pot. Test one dumpling before committing the batch: if it falls apart, work a little flour into the mix; if it is heavy, add a splash more milk. The pot must never boil, only shiver.

  • Properly stale bread, dry all the way through.
  • Test one dumpling before committing the batch.
  • A shiver, never a boil.

item.title: Duck Confit
item.description: Duck confit — legs salt-cured overnight then poached in duck fat until meltingly tender, crisped to serve.
item.content:encoded:
Fat is not a cooking liquid in the way water is: it carries no moisture, so the duck poaches at a steady low temperature without ever boiling or drying. The overnight salt cure draws out water and seasons the meat right through, which is what makes confit keep for months under its own fat.

  • Rinse the cure off properly. Leave it on and the finished confit is inedibly salty.
  • The fat must never boil. A bubbling confit fries the duck rather than poaching it.
  • Strain and keep the fat afterwards. It will do this job several more times and makes the best roast potatoes there are.

item.title: Testaroli al Pesto
item.description: Thin batter pancakes cooked on a hot pan, cut into diamonds and softened in boiling water before dressing with pesto.
item.content:encoded:
Testaroli are cooked twice and the second cooking is barely a cooking at all — the cut diamonds go into water that has been brought to the boil and then taken off the heat, for about a minute. Water still boiling will disintegrate them completely. The pancake itself is cooked on one side only and should stay pale and slightly spongy, since it needs to absorb the water and then the pesto.

  • One side only. A turned testarolo goes tough.
  • Water off the heat for the second cooking, or they dissolve.
  • Sixty seconds, no more.

item.title: Brasato al Barolo
item.description: A Piedmontese braise of beef marinated overnight in Barolo with root vegetables and spices, then cooked slowly until the sauce is dark and glossy.
item.content:encoded:
The marinade is not for flavour so much as for colour and acidity — a night in the wine takes the beef a deep purple and starts breaking down the connective tissue before any heat gets to it. Boil the marinade separately before it goes back in the pot: raw wine reduced under a lid tastes harsh and thin, while wine boiled hard for ten minutes throws its scum, loses its edge and turns sweet. And use a wine you would drink. Barolo is expensive, so a good Nebbiolo is the honest substitute; cooking wine is not.

  • Boil the marinade separately for 10 minutes before it goes back in.
  • Dry the meat properly after the marinade or it will not brown.
  • Slice across the grain, and only after resting.

item.title: Soupe au Pistou
item.description: Soupe au pistou — Provençal summer vegetable and bean soup finished with a basil and garlic pistou.
item.content:encoded:
Pistou is not pesto with the pine nuts left out — it is a raw condiment that must never see heat, because basil turns black and bitter above about 60C. Stirring it into each bowl rather than the pot keeps the soup tasting of the garden rather than of stewed herbs.

  • Pistou off the heat, in the bowl. In the pot it turns black within minutes.
  • A mortar beats a blender here — the texture and the colour are both better.
  • Cut every vegetable to the same dice so a spoonful gets a little of everything.

item.title: Bollito Misto
item.description: A northern Italian dish of beef, tongue, chicken and cotechino simmered in one broth and served with salsa verde and mostarda.
item.content:encoded:
Everything goes in at a different time and it matters, because the cuts want between one and three hours and a chicken boiled for three hours is a wet rag. The other rule is that the water must never boil once the meat is in — a bare tremble at the surface. A rolling boil drives the albumin out of the meat into the broth, which clouds the stock and leaves the beef dry and stringy. Cotechino is cooked in its own separate pan of water, always, because its fat would grease the whole broth.

  • A tremble, never a boil. Boiling ruins both the meat and the broth.
  • Cotechino cooks in its own water. It would grease everything else.
  • Peel the tongue while it is still hot or the skin will not come away.

item.title: Coda alla Vaccinara
item.description: Roman oxtail braised slowly in tomato and wine with a whole head of celery, finished with pine nuts, raisins and bitter chocolate.
item.content:encoded:
Four hours is the minimum and there is no shortcut, because oxtail is almost entirely connective tissue and only long wet heat turns that into gelatine. Under four hours it is chewy; at four it slides off the bone. The celery is not a background aromatic here — a whole head goes in near the end, cut into finger lengths, and it should still have some bite when it reaches the table. And the finish of pine nuts, raisins and a square of bitter chocolate is not a modern flourish: it is the old Roman sweet-sour, and it is what stops four hours of oxtail from tasting heavy.

  • Four hours. Anything less and the oxtail will be chewy.
  • Blanch the celery separately so it keeps some bite.
  • Skim the fat at the end — oxtail throws a lot of it.

item.title: Trippa alla Romana
item.description: Roman tripe simmered in tomato and white wine, finished with fresh mint and grated pecorino romano.
item.content:encoded:
Buy tripe already blanched — almost all of it is — and then boil it again yourself for an hour in fresh water with a lemon before it goes anywhere near the sauce. That second boil is what removes the last of the barnyard smell, and skipping it is why most people think they dislike tripe. Cut it into strips no wider than a finger after that boil, never before: hot tripe cuts cleanly and cold tripe rubbers away from the knife. The mint goes in off the heat, at the end.

  • Boil it once in fresh water with lemon before the sauce, even if it came blanched.
  • Cut the tripe hot. Cold tripe will not cut cleanly.
  • Mint off the heat, or it goes dull and grassy.

item.title: Coquilles Saint-Jacques
item.description: Coquilles Saint-Jacques — scallops in a mushroom velouté, piped into shells under Gruyère and grilled golden.
item.content:encoded:
The scallops are poached for barely a minute and then removed while the sauce is built from their poaching liquor — a scallop cooked twice, once in the pan and once under the grill, turns to rubber. Piping duchess potato around the rim is not decoration: it dams the sauce so it browns rather than running out.

  • Ninety seconds in the wine, no more. The grill finishes them and a twice-cooked scallop is ruined.
  • The sauce should be thicker than seems right — it loosens under the grill.
  • Assemble ahead and refrigerate, then grill from cold for 8 minutes. It is the ideal dinner-party starter.

item.title: Porchetta
item.description: A whole rolled and tied roast of pork belly around loin, stuffed with fennel, garlic and rosemary, slow-roasted then blasted for crackling.
item.content:encoded:
Dry skin or no crackling — there is no third option. The scored belly is salted and left uncovered in the fridge for a full day, which draws water out of the skin and is the single thing that separates shattering crackling from leather. The cooking is then in two parts: four hours low so the meat and fat render and the roll sets, then a short blast at maximum heat at the very end. Doing the blast first seals the skin before the fat under it has rendered, and you get a hard shell over a greasy layer.

  • A full day uncovered in the fridge. Wet skin will never crackle.
  • Low first, hot last. The other way round gives a greasy layer under a shell.
  • A serrated knife for slicing, or the crackling shatters off the meat.

item.title: Polpette al Sugo
item.description: Italian meatballs of beef and pork bound with a milk-soaked bread panade, browned then simmered through a long tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The panade is the whole thing. Stale bread soaked in milk and squeezed out, worked into the meat, holds moisture through an hour in the sauce in a way that breadcrumbs cannot — dry crumbs absorb the meat's own juice instead of adding any. And the meatballs finish cooking in the sauce, not in the pan: browning is only for colour and should take four minutes, after which they go into the tomato raw in the middle and poach there. Cooking them through in the pan first is why so many meatballs come out like gravel.

  • Bread soaked in milk, not dry breadcrumbs. It is the difference.
  • Brown for colour only, 4 minutes. They cook through in the sauce.
  • Handle the mixture as little as possible.

item.title: Salade Lyonnaise
item.description: Salade Lyonnaise — bitter frisée with lardons, croutons and a poached egg under a hot bacon vinaigrette.
item.content:encoded:
The dressing is made in the bacon pan and poured over while it is still spitting, which wilts the frisée just enough to take its edge off without collapsing it. Bitter leaves are essential — a soft lettuce turns to slime the moment hot fat hits it.

  • Pour the dressing hot. A cold vinaigrette on frisée gives you a completely different, lesser salad.
  • Bitter leaves only. Frisée, chicory or escarole — never anything soft.
  • Taste before salting. The lardons usually bring enough.

item.title: Scaloppine al Limone
item.description: Thin veal escalopes floured and fried fast, with a pan sauce of lemon, stock and cold butter whisked in off the heat.
item.content:encoded:
Two failures account for nearly every bad scaloppine. The first is a pan that is not hot enough, so the flour goes pasty and the veal stews in its own liquid instead of taking colour in ninety seconds a side. The second is boiling the butter into the sauce: the emulsion only holds if the pan is off the heat and the butter goes in cold, in pieces, swirled rather than stirred. A sauce that has boiled after the butter went in will be a greasy slick, and it cannot be brought back.

  • The pan must be properly hot. A cool pan makes the flour pasty.
  • Butter in off the heat, cold and in pieces, or the sauce splits.
  • Shake off every bit of loose flour before frying.

item.title: Cotoletta alla Milanese
item.description: A bone-in veal chop beaten flat, breaded and shallow-fried in clarified butter until golden, served with nothing but lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Clarified butter, not whole butter. The milk solids in whole butter burn well below the temperature the crust needs and turn the breadcrumbs black and bitter in about two minutes; clarified butter takes the heat and still tastes of butter. The chop is beaten out to a centimetre with the bone left in, which sounds like showmanship but keeps the meat juicy through a crust that has to fry long enough to colour. And there is no egg wash step before the flour here — the chop goes straight from egg to crumb, so the coating stays thin and stuck rather than puffing away from the meat.

  • Clarified butter only. Whole butter burns before the crust colours.
  • Beat the meat, never the bone.
  • Drain on a rack. Paper steams the underside soft.

item.title: Canelés de Bordeaux
item.description: Canelés de Bordeaux — dark caramelised shells with soft rum and vanilla custard centres. Batter rests two days.
item.content:encoded:
The two-day rest lets the gluten relax completely, which stops the batter puffing up and pushing the custard out of the mould — a rested canelé sets rather than rises. The near-black shell is caramelised sugar, not burning, and it needs a very hot oven and a heavily greased mould to form.

  • Forty-eight hours in the fridge. At twelve the batter rises and pushes the custard out.
  • Darker than you think. A canelé that looks right in the oven is undercooked and will be pale and soft.
  • Copper moulds are traditional and expensive; silicone works but gives a slightly softer shell.

item.title: Cacciucco
item.description: A Tuscan seafood stew of several fish and shellfish built on a fish stock made from the heads and bones, spooned over garlic toast.
item.content:encoded:
The stock is made from the fish you are about to cook — heads, bones and prawn shells simmered for twenty-five minutes and no longer, because fish bones turn bitter past about half an hour. Then the fish go into the finished broth in order of toughness, from the octopus that needs forty minutes down to the mussels that need three, and the pot is not stirred once anything delicate is in it. Shaking the pan is fine; a spoon breaks the fish into shreds. The bread is rubbed with raw garlic and sits under the stew, never in it.

  • Twenty-five minutes on the stock. Fish bones go bitter after half an hour.
  • In order of toughness, and never stir once the fish is in.
  • Garlic toast under the stew, not soaked into it.

item.title: Brodetto all'Anconetana
item.description: An Adriatic fish stew from Ancona built on a mixture of fish, tomato and a splash of white wine vinegar that lifts the whole pot.
item.content:encoded:
Vinegar, not wine, and it goes in early enough to boil off its sharpness while leaving the acidity behind. That single difference is what separates the Ancona version from every other Italian fish stew — it cuts through oily fish like mackerel and sardine in a way white wine cannot. The fish is laid in the pot in a single layer and never turned or stirred; anything that needs moving is moved by tilting the pan. Ancona also uses no stock at all: the fish releases enough liquid on its own, and adding stock makes a soup rather than a brodetto.

  • Vinegar, and boil it hard for 2 minutes before the tomatoes go in.
  • No stock. The fish makes its own liquid.
  • Tilt the pan instead of stirring.

item.title: Gâteau Basque
item.description: Gâteau Basque — thick almond shortcrust around vanilla pastry cream, scored and baked golden.
item.content:encoded:
The dough carries enough butter and egg to behave like a biscuit rather than a pastry, so it does not need blind baking — it sets around the filling as it bakes. Chilling the assembled cake before it goes in stops the top layer sinking into the cream.

  • The dough is sticky by design. Chill it rather than adding flour.
  • Cool it fully. Cut warm, the pastry cream runs and the whole thing collapses.
  • For the cherry version, swap the cream for 300 g of black cherry jam — the Basque original.

item.title: Bagnùn di Acciughe
item.description: A light Ligurian soup of fresh anchovies in tomato and white wine, poured over dry biscuit or toasted bread.
item.content:encoded:
Fresh anchovies, not salted — this is not a sauce, it is a soup of whole small fish, and salted anchovies would make it inedible. They go in for the last five minutes only. Anchovy flesh is so thin that it cooks through almost the moment it hits hot liquid, and anything past five minutes turns it to fibres. The bread is the other half: Liguria uses gallette del marinaio, hard ship's biscuit, and if you use fresh bread it must be dried out in the oven first or it dissolves into paste.

  • Fresh anchovies only. Salted ones would wreck it.
  • Five minutes for the fish, no more.
  • Dry the bread out in the oven or it turns to paste.

item.title: Sarde a Beccafico
item.description: Sicilian sardines butterflied, filled with a sweet-sour breadcrumb stuffing and rolled, baked upright between bay leaves with orange juice.
item.content:encoded:
Toast the breadcrumbs in oil before they go into the filling. Raw crumbs inside a rolled sardine steam and turn to wet paste in the oven, while toasted crumbs keep their texture through twenty minutes of heat and stay separate. The rolls are then packed upright and tight against each other with a bay leaf between every pair — they hold each other closed, so no sticks are needed, and the bay perfumes the fish from both sides. The orange juice goes over at the end and should not be replaced with lemon; it is sweeter, and the dish is built around that.

  • Toast the crumbs first or the filling turns to paste.
  • Pack them tight. They hold each other shut without sticks.
  • Orange, not lemon. The dish is meant to be sweet-sour.

item.title: Katsu Curry
item.description: Katsu curry — panko-crumbed cutlet over rice with thick, dark Japanese curry sauce made from a scratch roux.
item.content:encoded:
Japanese curry gets its body from a browned flour-and-butter roux rather than from reduction, which is why it coats rice like gravy instead of running off. Cooking that roux to the colour of peanut butter before the curry powder goes in removes the raw flour taste that shop-bought blocks disguise with sugar.

  • Cook the roux to peanut-butter brown. Pale roux tastes of raw flour and no amount of curry powder hides it.
  • The grated apple is standard in Japan and does more for the balance than extra sugar would.
  • Rest the fried cutlet on a rack before slicing so the crumb stays crisp under the sauce.

item.title: Peperonata
item.description: Sweet peppers and onions stewed slowly with tomato and a little vinegar until soft and jammy, good hot or cold.
item.content:encoded:
The heat stays low and the lid stays on for the first half hour, because the peppers have to sweat out their own water before anything else can happen. On high heat they brown at the edges and stay squeaky in the middle. Once they have collapsed the lid comes off and the liquid boils away, which is when the sugars concentrate and it turns jammy. The splash of vinegar goes in at the very end, off the heat — cooked into the pot it just disappears, added at the end it makes the sweetness legible.

  • Lid on and low heat for the first half hour. They must sweat, not brown.
  • Lid off at the end so the liquid goes and the sugars concentrate.
  • Vinegar off the heat, or you will not taste it.

item.title: Farinata
item.description: A Ligurian baked pancake of chickpea flour, water and olive oil, rested for hours then baked at maximum heat until blistered.
item.content:encoded:
The batter has to rest at least four hours and better overnight, which does two things: the chickpea flour hydrates fully, so the finished farinata is creamy rather than gritty, and a grey foam rises that must be skimmed off — it is what makes badly made farinata taste bitter and sit heavily. The pan then goes into the oven empty until it is properly hot, and the batter should hiss on contact. A cold pan gives a pale, dense disc with no blistering at all.

  • Four hours minimum on the batter, and skim the foam.
  • Heat the pan empty first. The batter must hiss when it hits.
  • Thin — 6 mm. A thick farinata is a different and worse thing.

item.title: Miso Ramen
item.description: Miso ramen — Sapporo-style bowl with miso tare, rich broth, stir-fried pork and a slick of aroma oil.
item.content:encoded:
Miso is never boiled: its aromatics are volatile and a rolling boil flattens them, so the tare is whisked into the bowl and the hot broth poured over. The layer of aroma oil on the surface is functional — it traps heat, which is why a good ramen stays scalding to the last mouthful.

  • Never boil the miso. Whisk it into the bowl and pour the broth over.
  • Warm the bowls. A cold bowl drops the soup below serving temperature before it reaches the table.
  • Drain the noodles hard. Water clinging to them dilutes the broth you spent hours on.

item.title: Torta Pasqualina
item.description: A Ligurian layered pie of chard, ricotta and whole eggs baked inside a stack of hand-stretched pastry sheets, served warm or cold.
item.content:encoded:
The chard must be squeezed until it is genuinely dry — wrung out in a tea towel, not just drained — because any water left in it will soak through the base pastry and the whole pie goes soggy from underneath. The eggs are cracked into hollows pressed into the ricotta layer, and each hollow needs a knob of butter and a wall of filling around it or the whites spread flat and you lose the round yolk in the slice. Oil goes between every pastry sheet; that is what separates them into flakes instead of gluing them into one thick pad.

  • Wring the chard out in a towel. Draining is not enough.
  • Oil between every sheet or they fuse into one pad.
  • Prick between the eggs, never over them.

item.title: Sfogliatella Riccia
item.description: The Neapolitan shell pastry: dough stretched translucent, spread with fat, rolled into a log, chilled and cut into cones filled with semolina and ricotta.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is stretched until you can read through it and then coated with soft fat before it is rolled into a log — that fat is what keeps the layers from welding together, and the leaves in the finished pastry are simply the coils of that log pushed outwards. Skimp on the stretching and you get a bread roll. The log then has to chill hard for twelve hours: cutting a soft log squashes the coils flat, and cold discs are what let you push the centre out into a cone without tearing.

  • Thin enough to read through, or there are no leaves.
  • Twelve hours in the fridge. A soft log cannot be cut into clean discs.
  • Push the cone out with your thumbs from the centre, not the edge.

item.title: Unagi Don
item.description: Unagi don — grilled eel lacquered in sweet soy tare over steamed rice, with sansho pepper.
item.content:encoded:
The tare is brushed on in several thin coats with the eel returning to the heat between each, which builds a lacquer — one thick coat simply slides off and burns. Sansho pepper is not optional: its numbing citrus edge is what cuts the richness of the eel.

  • Rinse the packet sauce off. It is far sweeter than a proper tare and masks the eel.
  • Thin coats, repeated. One heavy brushing runs off and scorches.
  • Sansho, not black pepper. The numbing quality is the point.

item.title: Pastiera Napoletana
item.description: The Neapolitan Easter tart of cooked wheat berries, ricotta and orange flower water in a sweet pastry case under a lattice.
item.content:encoded:
Orange flower water is the whole character of the tart and it is the one thing people leave out, usually because they have only met it in cheap sweets. Use a real one and use it sparingly — two teaspoons in a twelve-portion tart, no more, or it turns soapy. The wheat is cooked with milk before it goes in, which softens the grains and stops them staying gritty in the set filling. And it must cool completely in its tin, four hours at least: cut warm, a pastiera runs.

  • Two teaspoons of orange flower water. More is soapy.
  • Cook the wheat in milk first or it stays gritty.
  • Cool it completely in the tin. A warm pastiera runs.

item.title: Cassata Siciliana
item.description: The Sicilian cassata: a sponge and sweet ricotta dome lined with green marzipan, glazed white and covered with candied fruit.
item.content:encoded:
Sheep's ricotta drained for hours and then pushed through a sieve is what makes the filling: whipped ricotta stays grainy no matter how long you beat it, and undrained ricotta weeps into the sponge overnight and turns the whole thing to a puddle. The marzipan lining must be rolled thin enough to bend around the tin without cracking — about four millimetres — and the glaze goes on only when the assembled cassata is cold from the fridge, or it slides straight off.

  • Drain the ricotta, then sieve it. Beating alone leaves it grainy.
  • Marzipan at 4 mm — thinner cracks, thicker will not bend.
  • Glaze it cold, straight from the fridge.

item.title: Nikujaga
item.description: Nikujaga — Japanese beef and potato simmer in sweet dashi and soy, with onions and snow peas.
item.content:encoded:
An otoshibuta — a lid resting directly on the food rather than on the pan — keeps everything submerged and circulates the broth over the top without needing much liquid, so the seasoning concentrates rather than dilutes. Cooling in the broth is when the potatoes actually absorb it, which is why nikujaga tastes better reheated.

  • The paper drop lid is the whole technique. It keeps everything submerged in half the liquid you would otherwise need.
  • Let it cool in the broth before serving. Straight from the heat it tastes thin.
  • Waxy potatoes hold together; floury ones dissolve into the broth.

item.title: Cuccidati
item.description: Sicilian Christmas biscuits of a spiced fig, date, nut and citrus filling wrapped in short pastry, baked and iced with sprinkles.
item.content:encoded:
The filling is minced, not blended. A food processor run to smoothness turns figs and dates into a gluey black paste that oozes out of every seam in the oven; minced coarsely, or pulsed in short bursts, it stays granular and holds its shape. The pastry has to be chilled hard before cutting because it carries a lot of butter and a lot of sugar, and warm dough tears rather than sealing around the filling. Roll the log seam side down and cut on the diagonal.

  • Mince the filling, never blend it smooth.
  • Chill the pastry hard or it will tear rather than seal.
  • Pale gold only. Browned cuccidati go hard.

item.title: Struffoli
item.description: Neapolitan struffoli: small pieces of citrus-scented dough deep-fried, coated in warm honey and piled into a ring.
item.content:encoded:
The honey is warmed only until it runs, never boiled. Boiled honey sets hard as it cools and welds the whole ring into a single inedible lump; warm honey stays tacky and lets the pieces separate under a spoon. Fry in small batches at 170C — a crowded pan drops the oil temperature and the dough absorbs rather than puffs — and drain them properly before they meet the honey, because any oil left on the surface stops it sticking.

  • Warm the honey, never boil it. Boiled honey sets like cement.
  • Small batches at 170C, or they soak up oil.
  • Drain on a rack. Honey will not stick to an oily surface.

item.title: Zuppa Inglese
item.description: An Emilian layered dessert of savoiardi soaked in alchermes with alternating vanilla and chocolate custard, chilled until sliceable.
item.content:encoded:
Dip the savoiardi, do not soak them — one second a side in the alchermes is enough. They keep absorbing for another minute after they leave the liquid, and a biscuit that felt right in the bowl will be mush by the time the dish is assembled. The custards are cooked separately and cooled with cling film pressed directly onto the surface, because a skin broken back into the custard leaves lumps that no amount of whisking will clear.

  • One second a side. They keep drinking after they leave the liquid.
  • Cling film onto the custard surface, not over the bowl.
  • Alchermes is the colour and the scent. Rum works but it is a different dish.

item.title: Gyudon
item.description: Gyudon — thin beef and onion simmered in sweet dashi and soy, served over rice with pickled ginger.
item.content:encoded:
The beef is sliced paper-thin so it cooks in about ninety seconds, which means the onions can be softened first and the meat added at the very end — cooked together, the beef would be tough long before the onion gave in. Simmering uncovered lets the broth reduce and cling rather than pooling under the rice.

  • Paper-thin beef, separated before it goes in. A clump of slices steams instead of simmering.
  • Season the broth harder than tastes right on its own. Rice absorbs a lot.
  • The raw yolk is traditional — use pasteurised eggs if that is a concern, or leave it off.

item.title: Crostata di Marmellata
item.description: The Italian jam tart: a lemon-scented pasta frolla pressed into a tin, filled with thick jam and finished with a lattice top.
item.content:encoded:
Pasta frolla is not shortcrust. It carries egg yolk and sugar, which means it is worked briefly and then chilled hard, and any attempt to knead it smooth develops gluten and gives you a tough, shrinking case. Use a thick jam or reduce a loose one first — a runny jam boils, climbs over the lattice and welds the tart to the tin. And the tin goes in the bottom third of the oven, so the base sets before the lattice colours.

  • Bring it together, do not knead it. Frolla goes tough fast.
  • Thick jam only, or it will boil over the lattice.
  • Bottom third of the oven so the base cooks through.

item.title: Yakisoba
item.description: Yakisoba — griddled wheat noodles with pork, cabbage and a fruity brown sauce, topped with bonito and aonori.
item.content:encoded:
Rinsing and loosening the pre-cooked noodles before they hit the pan stops them frying as a solid brick, and a splash of water added under a lid steams them apart in seconds. The sauce goes in at the very end and over high heat so it caramelises onto the noodles rather than boiling and turning them soggy.

  • Loosen the noodles before they go in. A brick of noodles never separates once it is frying.
  • Sauce last, heat highest. Added early it steams the noodles into mush.
  • The bonito flakes should move in the heat — that is how you know the dish is hot enough to serve.

item.title: Ciambellone
item.description: A simple Italian ring cake of eggs, oil, milk and citrus zest, baked in a bundt tin and dusted with icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Oil rather than butter, and that is deliberate: an oil crumb stays soft for four or five days where a butter cake goes dry by the second, and this is a cake meant to last the week. Whisk the eggs and sugar until genuinely pale and tripled — five minutes, not one — because there is no other aeration in the recipe. And butter and flour the tin thoroughly, right into the central funnel, since a ring cake that sticks cannot be rescued.

  • Oil, not butter. It is what keeps it soft all week.
  • Five minutes of whisking. It is the only aeration there is.
  • Flour the funnel as well as the sides.

item.title: Colomba Pasquale
item.description: The Italian Easter dove cake — a long-fermented enriched dough with candied orange, baked under an almond and pearl sugar crust.
item.content:encoded:
The cold overnight fermentation is not optional. Twelve hours in the fridge is what develops the flavour and, more importantly, what strengthens the gluten enough to carry all that butter and fruit — a colomba proved warm in one go collapses under its own crust. Butter goes in only after the dough has already come together and can pass a windowpane test, a piece at a time; added early it coats the flour and the gluten never forms. And it hangs upside down to cool, like panettone, or the crumb compresses under its own weight.

  • Twelve hours cold. It is where the flavour and the strength come from.
  • Butter only after the windowpane test, a piece at a time.
  • Hang it upside down or the crumb compresses.

item.title: Pandoro
item.description: The Veronese Christmas cake — a slowly fermented butter and egg dough baked in a star mould and dusted heavily with vanilla icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Pandoro has no fruit and no crust to hide behind, so everything depends on the dough — which means the butter has to be worked in cold and slowly, in three stages, keeping the dough below about 24C throughout. Warm dough breaks the emulsion and the butter leaks out in the oven into a greasy pool. The mould is buttered and dusted with sugar rather than flour, which gives the ridged crust its thin crisp shell, and the cake is cooled in the mould for half an hour before turning out or the points snap off.

  • Cold butter, in three stages, and keep the dough below 24C.
  • Sugar the mould, not flour. It is where the crisp shell comes from.
  • Half an hour in the mould before turning out, or the points break.

item.title: Castella Cake
item.description: Castella — Japanese honey sponge with a fine, moist crumb and dark top. Rests overnight before slicing.
item.content:encoded:
There is no butter and no baking powder: the entire rise comes from eggs whipped to the ribbon stage over gentle warmth, which holds far more air than cold eggs will. Wrapping the cake while still warm and resting it overnight redistributes moisture from the crust into the crumb, and that rest is what makes castella castella.

  • The overnight wrapped rest is not optional. Cut on the day it is dry; cut on day two it is dense and moist.
  • Warming the eggs before whisking roughly doubles the volume you can get into them.
  • Bread flour, not plain. The extra protein is what holds this much air.

item.title: Amaretti Morbidi
item.description: Soft Italian almond macaroons of ground almonds, sugar and egg white, dried before baking so the tops crack.
item.content:encoded:
Leave the piped mounds uncovered for an hour before they go in the oven. A skin forms on the surface, and when the biscuit rises against that skin it splits into the cracks that define an amaretto — bake them straight away and you get smooth domes. Bitter almond is what makes them taste of amaretti rather than of marzipan: a few drops of extract, or a handful of apricot kernels ground in with the almonds. Underbake slightly; they firm up as they cool and a browned amaretto is a hard one.

  • An hour uncovered. The dry skin is what makes them crack.
  • Bitter almond extract, not vanilla. It is the flavour.
  • Underbake. They set as they cool.

item.title: Pizzelle
item.description: Abruzzese pizzelle: a thin anise-scented batter pressed in a patterned iron into crisp snowflake wafers.
item.content:encoded:
A stiff batter, not a pourable one — it should drop from the spoon in a lump, because a loose batter spreads past the pattern and gives you a thick, floppy wafer with no impression on it. One heaped teaspoon slightly behind the centre of each mould, and the iron closed firmly rather than clamped. And they crisp only as they cool, so lift each one off flat onto a rack; stacked warm, they steam each other soft and bend.

  • A stiff batter. Loose batter spreads past the pattern.
  • Cool them flat and in one layer, or they bend and soften.
  • Shape cones within about ten seconds of lifting them out.

item.title: Mapo Eggplant
item.description: Mapo eggplant — aubergine in a fiery doubanjiang sauce with garlic, ginger and numbing Sichuan pepper.
item.content:encoded:
Aubergine is a sponge, so it is fried hard first to collapse its cell structure before the sauce goes near it — added raw to liquid it stays spongy and drinks the oil instead. Frying the doubanjiang until the oil runs red is what separates a Sichuan sauce from chilli paste stirred into stock.

  • Fry the aubergine properly first. Undercooked, it never stops tasting spongy.
  • Sichuan pepper goes in off the heat — its numbing compound breaks down over sustained heat.
  • Pixian doubanjiang is worth seeking out; generic chilli bean sauce is sweeter and thinner.

item.title: Maritozzo
item.description: The Roman maritozzo: a light enriched bun with orange zest, split and overfilled with barely sweetened whipped cream levelled flat.
item.content:encoded:
The cream is barely sweetened and whipped to a stiff peak, because a soft cream slumps out of the split within minutes and a sweet one buries the bun. Fill far more than looks reasonable — a proper maritozzo is more cream than bread — then draw a palette knife across the open face in one pass to cut it flush. And the buns must be completely cold before splitting: warm bread melts the cream on contact and the whole thing weeps.

  • Barely sweeten the cream and whip it stiff.
  • Cold buns only. Warm bread melts the cream.
  • One pass with the knife. Going back and forth smears it.

item.title: Granita di Caffè
item.description: Sicilian coffee granita: sweetened espresso frozen in a shallow tray and scraped with a fork every half hour into loose crystals.
item.content:encoded:
A shallow tray and a fork, and that is the entire method — the scraping every half hour is what breaks the ice into separate crystals instead of letting it set into a solid block you would have to chip. Metal freezes faster and more evenly than plastic. The coffee must also be sweeter than you would drink it, because cold suppresses sweetness sharply and a granita made to drinking strength tastes flat and bitter straight from the freezer.

  • A metal tray. Plastic freezes too slowly and too unevenly.
  • Every half hour with the fork, without fail.
  • Sweeter than you would drink it. Cold hides sugar.

item.title: Bellini
item.description: The Venetian Bellini: fresh white peach purée chilled hard and topped with cold prosecco, mixed only by pouring.
item.content:encoded:
White peaches, not yellow, and fresh ones — the drink is pale pink because white peach flesh oxidises to that colour, and a yellow peach gives you an orange drink that tastes of tinned fruit. Everything must be properly cold, the purée and the glasses as much as the wine, because a warm purée makes the prosecco foam over the rim the moment it lands. And it is never stirred with a spoon: pour the wine into the purée slowly and let the pouring do the mixing.

  • White peaches. Yellow ones give the wrong colour and the wrong taste.
  • Cold purée, cold glasses, cold wine, or it foams over.
  • Pour slowly and never stir.

item.title: Scallion Pancakes
item.description: Chinese scallion pancakes — hot-water dough rolled with oil and spring onion, coiled and fried into flaky layers.
item.content:encoded:
Boiling water gelatinises some of the flour's starch and denatures its gluten, which gives a dough that stays soft and rolls thin without springing back. The layers come from a roux of flour and hot oil painted between them — plain oil alone leaks out and the pancake fries as a single sheet.

  • Roll the dough as thin as you can before filling. Thin dough plus a tight coil is what makes the layers.
  • The flour-and-oil roux is what stops the layers merging. Plain oil leaks and gives a solid pancake.
  • Slap the cooked pancake between your hands or squash it in the pan to separate the layers before serving.

item.title: Potted Shrimps
item.description: Brown shrimps warmed in mace and cayenne butter, packed into pots and sealed under a layer of clarified butter.
item.content:encoded:
The butter is never allowed to boil. Shrimps this small cook in the residual heat alone, and butter hot enough to bubble turns them to rubber and splits the emulsion so the pots set greasy instead of smooth. Mace, not nutmeg — they come from the same fruit but mace is warmer and less sweet, and it is the flavour everyone recognises in a potted shrimp without being able to name it. Seal each pot with clarified butter: whole butter carries water and milk solids that will sour within days.

  • Never let the butter bubble. The shrimps only need warming.
  • Mace, not nutmeg. It is the flavour that makes it taste right.
  • Seal with clarified butter or they will not keep.

item.title: Devils on Horseback
item.description: Soft prunes stuffed with a whole almond, wrapped in streaky bacon and grilled until the bacon crisps and the fruit softens.
item.content:encoded:
Streaky bacon, stretched thin with the back of a knife before it is wrapped. Stretching does two things: it makes each rasher long enough to go round without overlapping into a thick band that never crisps, and it thins the fat so it renders in the ten minutes the prune needs. Back bacon is too lean and dries out. Soak the prunes in tea or wine first if they are at all leathery, because a hard prune stays hard and the bacon will be black before it gives.

  • Stretch the bacon thin with a knife or it will not crisp.
  • Streaky, never back. Back bacon has no fat to render.
  • Two minutes off the heat. The prunes are hot enough to burn.

item.title: Beef Chow Fun
item.description: Beef chow fun — wide rice noodles seared with velveted beef and beansprouts in a smoking wok.
item.content:encoded:
Velveting the beef in cornflour and bicarbonate raises its surface pH, which stops the proteins tightening in the wok and is why restaurant beef is silky where home beef is chewy. The noodles are tossed with tongs rather than a spatula and left still between tosses, because agitation is what breaks them.

  • Tongs, not a spatula, and stillness between tosses. Both protect the noodles.
  • Never refrigerate fresh ho fun — cold noodles shatter into fragments.
  • Cook one or two portions at a time. A crowded wok cannot reach the temperature this needs.

item.title: Scotch Broth
item.description: A thick Scottish soup of lamb neck, pearl barley, dried peas and root vegetables simmered until everything has collapsed together.
item.content:encoded:
The barley goes in at the start, with the meat, and that is what makes it broth rather than soup: two hours of simmering bursts the grains and releases enough starch to thicken the whole pot without a roux. Barley added late stays as separate pearls in a thin liquid. Skim properly in the first twenty minutes — lamb throws a grey scum that turns the broth muddy if it is stirred back in — and cook it the day before if you can, because the fat then lifts off in a solid sheet.

  • Barley in at the start. That is where the thickness comes from.
  • Skim hard for the first twenty minutes.
  • Better made a day ahead, when the fat lifts off in a sheet.

item.title: Lion's Head Meatballs
item.description: Lion's head meatballs — huge, tender pork meatballs braised in light broth with Chinese cabbage.
item.content:encoded:
The mince is stirred in one direction until it turns sticky, which develops the myosin that holds the meatball together despite having almost no binder — this is why they can be so loose and still survive braising. Water beaten in a spoonful at a time is what makes them tender rather than dense.

  • One direction only when stirring. Changing direction breaks the protein strands that hold these together.
  • They should feel almost too soft to shape. That is correct — firm mixture gives dense meatballs.
  • Do not stir the braise. Lift the pot and swirl it if you must move things.

item.title: Mulligatawny Soup
item.description: An Anglo-Indian soup of chicken and lentils with curry spices, apple and coconut milk, finished with rice and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the spices in the fat before any liquid goes in — thirty seconds is enough, and it is the difference between a soup that tastes of curry and one that tastes of curry powder. The apple is not a garnish either: it goes in early and cooks to nothing, and its acidity is what keeps a soup this rich from sitting flat. Coconut milk goes in at the end and must not boil, or it separates into oil and grit.

  • Fry the spices for thirty seconds before any liquid goes in.
  • A Bramley in early. Its acidity is what lifts the whole pot.
  • Coconut milk last, and never let it boil.

item.title: Hong Kong Egg Tarts
item.description: Hong Kong egg tarts — short biscuity pastry with a smooth, glassy custard baked just to a set.
item.content:encoded:
Straining the custard twice and skimming the foam is what gives the glassy surface — any bubble left in the mix bakes into a pockmark. The oven starts hot to set the pastry and then drops sharply, because a custard held above about 90°C curdles and weeps.

  • Strain twice and skim. That is the whole difference between a glassy top and a pitted one.
  • The syrup must be cold before it meets the eggs.
  • A puffed, domed custard has gone too far — pull them the moment the centre stops rippling.

item.title: Oxtail Soup
item.description: A deeply reduced British soup of browned oxtail and root vegetables simmered four hours, chilled to lift the fat, and sharpened with sherry.
item.content:encoded:
Brown the oxtail properly and brown it in batches — this is where every bit of the colour and most of the flavour comes from, and a crowded pan steams the meat grey. Then leave it alone for four hours, because oxtail is almost pure connective tissue and the gelatine that thickens the finished soup only appears in the last hour. Chill it overnight if you can: the fat sets in a solid disc you can lift off in one piece, and no amount of skimming a hot pot gets close.

  • Brown in batches. A crowded pan steams the meat grey.
  • Four hours. The gelatine only comes in the last one.
  • Chill it overnight and lift the fat off in a disc.

item.title: Scotch Woodcock
item.description: A Victorian savoury of soft scrambled eggs on anchovy-buttered toast, finished with anchovy fillets and cayenne.
item.content:encoded:
Scramble the eggs off the heat as much as on it — lift the pan away every twenty seconds and keep stirring, and they will stay in soft curds instead of setting into a solid mass. Take them off while they still look slightly underdone, because they carry on cooking in the pan for another half minute. The anchovy goes in two places, mashed into the butter under the eggs and laid across the top, which is what stops it reading as a garnish nobody asked for.

  • Lift the pan off the heat every twenty seconds.
  • Take the eggs off underdone. They finish in the pan.
  • Anchovy in the butter as well as on top.

item.title: Jellied Eels
item.description: Freshwater eel cut into rounds and poached in a spiced vinegar stock that sets to a natural jelly without any added gelatine.
item.content:encoded:
Eel skin and bone carry so much collagen that the stock sets on its own — no gelatine, no setting agent, nothing but cooling. What breaks that is boiling: a hard boil emulsifies the fat into the liquid and you get a cloudy, greasy jelly instead of a clear one. Keep it at a bare tremble for twenty-five minutes and no more. Cool the pieces in their own liquid rather than lifting them out, or the jelly sets around empty space and the eel dries at the edges.

  • A tremble, never a boil. Boiling gives a cloudy, greasy jelly.
  • No gelatine. The eel sets its own stock.
  • Cool them in the liquid, not on a plate.

item.title: Wonton Noodle Soup
item.description: Wonton noodle soup — prawn and pork wontons in clear Cantonese broth with springy thin egg noodles.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles are boiled separately and shocked in cold water before going into the bowl, because cooking them in the broth clouds it with starch and leaves them soft. Wontons are wrapped loosely with plenty of air around the filling so the wrapper ruffles into a tail rather than sitting tight and doughy.

  • Cook the noodles separately and shock them. Boiling them in the broth ruins both.
  • Wrap loosely. A tightly packed wonton is a dumpling; the ruffled tail is the point.
  • Dried flounder is the authentic Cantonese backbone of the broth and is worth hunting down.

item.title: Melton Mowbray Pork Pie
item.description: A Melton Mowbray style raised pie: hand-formed hot water crust around seasoned chopped pork shoulder, baked free-standing and filled with pork jelly.
item.content:encoded:
Hot water crust is worked warm and only warm. The lard and boiling water are what make it pliable enough to raise by hand, and once it cools past blood heat it cracks the moment you bend it — so shape it fast, within about ten minutes of mixing. The meat is chopped, never minced: minced pork packs solid and sets into a dense grey block, while hand-chopped shoulder stays in distinct pieces with gaps for the jelly. And the jelly goes in through the hole only after the pie is cold, or it soaks into hot pastry instead of setting in the gaps.

  • Shape the crust warm, within ten minutes. Cold hot water crust cracks.
  • Chop the pork by hand. Mincing gives a solid grey block.
  • Jelly into a cold pie only, and pour it in slowly.

item.title: Sausage Rolls
item.description: Homemade sausage rolls of seasoned pork sausagemeat with apple and sage, rolled in all-butter puff pastry and baked until deep gold.
item.content:encoded:
Chill the shaped rolls hard before they go in — twenty minutes in the freezer is enough. Puff pastry rises because the water in cold butter turns to steam and forces the layers apart, and if the butter has softened before the oven, it leaks out and the pastry fries flat instead of lifting. The other thing is a hot oven from the start: 200C, not 180C, so the layers set before the fat runs. Grated apple in the meat keeps it from drying, which is the second thing shop rolls get wrong.

  • Twenty minutes in the freezer before baking. Warm butter will not puff.
  • A hot oven from the start, 200C fan.
  • Grated apple keeps the meat from drying out.

item.title: Lamb Rogan Josh
item.description: Lamb rogan josh — Kashmiri lamb braised in yoghurt with Kashmiri chilli, fennel and dried ginger.
item.content:encoded:
A true Kashmiri rogan josh uses no onion, garlic or tomato — the body comes from yoghurt whisked in off the heat and the colour from Kashmiri chilli, which is mild and intensely red. Ground fennel and dried ginger stand in for the aromatics, which is why the dish tastes floral rather than savoury-sweet.

  • Kashmiri chilli, not ordinary chilli powder. It is mild and its whole job is colour.
  • Off the heat for the yoghurt, added slowly. This is the step where the dish usually goes wrong.
  • No onion, garlic or tomato. Adding them makes a decent curry but not a rogan josh.

item.title: Piccalilli
item.description: A British mustard pickle of brined cauliflower, onion, cucumber and beans in a turmeric and mustard sauce thickened with flour.
item.content:encoded:
The vegetables are brined dry — layered with salt overnight and then rinsed, not boiled in brine — because that draws water out while leaving the cell walls intact, which is the whole reason a good piccalilli crunches and a bad one is mush. The sauce is made separately and poured over the raw drained vegetables; cooking them in it is what turns commercial piccalilli into yellow sludge. Give it a month in the jar before opening: the mustard is raw and harsh at first and mellows completely.

  • Dry salt overnight, then rinse. Never boil the vegetables.
  • Two minutes in the sauce, no more.
  • A month in the jar. The mustard is harsh until it mellows.

item.title: Pickled Onions
item.description: British pub pickled onions: small onions dry-brined overnight and packed in spiced malt vinegar, left to mature for six weeks.
item.content:encoded:
Brine dry, in salt, overnight — not in a wet brine. Salt on its own pulls water out of the onion by osmosis and leaves the layers firm, while a wet brine soaks water back in and gives you soft pickled onions, which are a waste of six weeks. The vinegar must be cold when it goes over: hot vinegar cooks the outer layers and they go slippery. Peel them under water or in a bowl of iced water if you would rather not weep through the whole job.

  • Dry salt, never a wet brine. Wet brine gives soft onions.
  • Cold vinegar over. Hot vinegar makes them slippery.
  • Six weeks minimum. They are harsh before that.

item.title: Cumberland Sauce
item.description: A clear British sauce of redcurrant jelly melted with port, orange and lemon juice, mustard and ginger, with fine strips of citrus zest through it.
item.content:encoded:
Blanch the zest strips before they go in, twice, in changes of water. Citrus pith and raw zest carry a bitterness that concentrates as the sauce reduces, and two quick blanches take it out entirely while leaving the perfume. Cut the zest into hair-fine julienne with a knife rather than grating it, because grated zest disappears into the sauce and the whole point is that you can see and bite the strips. And it is served cold, always — warm Cumberland sauce is just gravy that has lost its way.

  • Blanch the zest twice. Otherwise it turns bitter as the sauce reduces.
  • Cut the zest by hand — grated zest vanishes.
  • Serve it cold. It is not a gravy.

item.title: Dal Makhani
item.description: Dal makhani — black urad lentils simmered for hours and finished with butter and cream until thick and dark.
item.content:encoded:
The long, slow simmer is not about cooking the lentils through — that happens in an hour — but about breaking their starch down until it thickens the dal on its own, which is why restaurant versions cook overnight. Butter added in stages emulsifies into the starch rather than sitting on top.

  • Two hours of slow simmering after the lentils are cooked. That is the whole difference from an ordinary dal.
  • Add the butter in stages. All at once and it floats rather than emulsifying.
  • Kasuri methi crushed between the palms at the end is what makes it taste like a restaurant.

item.title: Cockles and Laverbread
item.description: A Welsh breakfast of laverbread mixed with oatmeal and fried in bacon fat with cockles, served with bacon and toast.
item.content:encoded:
Laverbread is already cooked — it is boiled for hours before it is sold — so it only wants heating, and long frying dries it into a bitter black paste. Mix it with oatmeal before it goes anywhere near the pan: the oatmeal absorbs the water it carries, which is what lets the cakes hold together and take a crust instead of spreading into a puddle. Bacon fat, not oil. The whole dish is built on it and butter burns before the cakes have coloured.

  • Laverbread is already cooked. It only wants heating.
  • Oatmeal in the mix, not just on the outside.
  • Bacon fat. Butter burns before the cakes colour.

item.title: Lancashire Hotpot
item.description: A Lancashire braise of lamb neck and onions in a light stock, topped with overlapping sliced potatoes and baked until the top is crisp.
item.content:encoded:
The lid goes on for the first two hours and comes off for the last thirty minutes, which is the only complicated thing about the dish. Covered, the potatoes steam soft and the lamb braises; uncovered at the end with butter brushed over, the top browns and crisps. Do it the other way round and you get a hard brown crust over raw potato. Lamb neck, not leg — this is a two-and-a-half-hour braise and lean meat will be dry and stringy long before the time is up.

  • Lid on for two hours, off for the last thirty. That order, always.
  • Neck, not leg. Lean lamb dries out over this long.
  • Slice the potatoes 3 mm and overlap them tightly.

item.title: Hyderabadi Biryani
item.description: Hyderabadi kachchi biryani — raw marinated lamb layered under par-cooked rice and sealed for dum cooking.
item.content:encoded:
In the kachchi method the meat goes in raw, so everything depends on the seal: the dough lid traps steam and the lamb cooks in its own marinade while the rice absorbs the aromatics rising through it. The rice is boiled to exactly 70% so it finishes in that steam rather than turning to paste.

  • The seal is not decoration. Without it the steam escapes and the lamb will not cook through.
  • Rice at 70%. Fully cooked rice turns to mush in the dum.
  • Do not lift the lid to check. Trust the timing and rest it fully before opening.

item.title: Liver and Bacon with Onion Gravy
item.description: Lamb's liver dredged in seasoned flour and fried fast, served with crisp bacon and a deep onion gravy built in the same pan.
item.content:encoded:
Ninety seconds a side and no more. Liver is almost pure protein with no connective tissue and no fat, so there is nothing to break down and nothing to keep it moist — the moment it goes past pink in the centre it turns grainy and dry, and it cannot be rescued. Soak it in milk first for half an hour, which draws out the bitterness that puts most people off, and dry it thoroughly afterwards or the flour turns to paste. The onions want a full fifteen minutes to go properly sweet.

  • Ninety seconds a side. Past pink it is ruined.
  • Soak in milk for the bitterness, then dry it properly.
  • Give the onions the full fifteen minutes.

item.title: Faggots and Peas
item.description: Black Country faggots of pig's liver, belly pork and onion wrapped in caul fat, baked in onion gravy and served with mushy peas.
item.content:encoded:
Caul fat is what makes them faggots rather than meatballs. It is the lacy membrane from around a pig's stomach, it costs almost nothing, and it holds each faggot together while melting away entirely in the oven and basting the meat as it goes. Without it you need egg and a great many breadcrumbs, and the result is dense. Keep the mince coarse — one pass through the widest plate, or hand-chopped — because a fine mince turns to pâté in the gravy.

  • Caul fat holds them together and bastes them. Ask the butcher.
  • Coarse mince only. Fine mince gives you pâté.
  • Gravy around, not over. The tops need to brown.

item.title: Vada Pav
item.description: Vada pav — Mumbai potato fritter in a soft bun with garlic, tamarind and coriander chutneys.
item.content:encoded:
The gram flour batter is beaten until aerated and left slightly loose, so it puffs into a thin shell rather than a thick jacket — a heavy batter absorbs oil and dominates the potato. Dry garlic chutney is what makes it Mumbai rather than just a fritter in bread.

  • Beat the batter to aerate it. A flat batter gives a heavy, greasy shell.
  • The dry garlic chutney is the signature. Without it this is just a fritter sandwich.
  • Eat within minutes of frying, which is exactly how it is sold.

item.title: Devilled Kidneys
item.description: Lamb's kidneys fried fast and finished in a devilling sauce of mustard, cayenne, Worcestershire sauce and butter, served on toast.
item.content:encoded:
Core the kidneys properly with scissors, taking out every bit of the white central gristle — that core is where the ammoniac smell people associate with kidneys actually lives, and a well-cored kidney does not have it. Then fry them hard and fast, two minutes a side, and take them out before the sauce is made. Kidney is like liver: past pink it goes rubbery, and simmering them in the sauce is how most versions go wrong. The sauce is finished in the pan and the kidneys go back in for ten seconds.

  • Take out every scrap of the white core. That is where the smell is.
  • Two minutes a side, then out of the pan.
  • Ten seconds back in the sauce, no longer.

item.title: Beef Stew and Dumplings
item.description: A British beef braise with root vegetables and stout, finished with suet dumplings steamed on the surface under a lid.
item.content:encoded:
The dumplings go on top of the stew, not into the liquid, and the lid stays on for the whole twenty minutes. They cook in the steam rising off the surface, which is what makes them light — a dumpling submerged in stock boils, absorbs liquid and goes heavy and grey. Do not lift the lid to look, because the burst of cold air makes them sink. Mix the dumpling dough at the last moment too: self-raising flour starts working the moment the water goes in.

  • Dumplings on top, lid on, and do not peek.
  • Mix the dumpling dough at the last minute.
  • Brown the beef in batches, not all at once.

item.title: Masala Chai
item.description: Masala chai — black tea boiled with milk, ginger, cardamom and whole spices until strong and fragrant.
item.content:encoded:
Boiling rather than steeping is what extracts enough tannin to carry the milk and sugar — a gently steeped chai tastes thin and milky. Bruising the whole spices rather than using ground releases their oils gradually over the boil instead of clouding the cup with sediment.

  • Let it rise and fall three times. Rushed chai tastes like spiced milk.
  • Bruise the spices, do not grind them. Ground spice makes the cup gritty.
  • Strong tea leaves, not delicate ones. Assam or a CTC blend stands up to the milk.

item.title: Roast Lamb with Mint Sauce
item.description: A roast leg of lamb studded with garlic and rosemary, rested properly, with a traditional vinegar and sugar mint sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Rest it as long as you roast it is an exaggeration, but not by much: thirty minutes under loose foil for a leg this size. The muscle fibres contract under heat and squeeze moisture towards the centre, and carving straight from the oven dumps all of it on the board. The mint sauce needs the boiling water poured over the chopped mint and sugar before the vinegar goes in — it dissolves the sugar and sets the colour, and mint chopped straight into cold vinegar goes black and tastes of nothing.

  • Thirty minutes resting, loosely covered. Not optional.
  • Boiling water on the mint and sugar before the vinegar.
  • An hour out of the fridge first, or the outside overcooks.

item.title: Roast Pork with Crackling
item.description: A roast pork loin with scored, salted and dried skin blasted hot for crackling, served with a sharp Bramley apple sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Dry skin is the entire secret, and the way to get it is salt and time: score, salt heavily, and leave the joint uncovered in the fridge for a day. The salt draws water to the surface where it evaporates, and skin that is dry going into the oven crackles every time. Twenty minutes at maximum heat first to blister it, then down to moderate for the meat. And the apple sauce should be made with Bramleys and barely sweetened — its job is acidity against the fat, and a sweet apple sauce leaves the plate tasting heavy.

  • A day uncovered in the fridge. Wet skin never crackles.
  • Hot first, moderate after — and never the other way round.
  • Bramleys, barely sweetened. The sauce is there for acidity.

item.title: Misal Pav
item.description: Misal pav — Maharashtrian sprouted bean curry with crunchy farsan, raw onion and soft pav rolls.
item.content:encoded:
Misal is two things in one bowl: the usal, a mild sprouted-bean base, and the rassa, a thin spiced gravy poured over it. Keeping them separate until the moment of serving is what stops the farsan going soft, and the layer of red oil on top of the rassa is not a fault — it is rendered from the kanda lasun masala and carries most of the aroma.

  • Assemble at the table. Farsan added early turns to paste within two minutes.
  • The red oil on the rassa is the point, not a fault. Leave it.
  • Sprout the beans yourself — tinned or unsprouted moth beans give a flat, heavy misal.

item.title: Stargazy Pie
item.description: A Cornish pie of whole pilchards or sardines baked in a shortcrust case with egg and cream, heads emerging through the lid.
item.content:encoded:
The heads are outside the crust for a reason: they are full of oil, and left inside they would make the filling bitter, while sticking out they drain their oil down into the pie as it bakes. So the fish are laid tails to the centre with the heads propped on the rim, and the pastry is cut round them. Bone the fish along the backbone but leave them whole in outline — a filleted stargazy is just a fish pie in a hat. And custard rather than sauce: the egg and cream set around the fish and hold everything together.

  • Heads outside the crust. Inside, their oil turns the filling bitter.
  • Bone them but keep them whole. That is the dish.
  • Custard, not white sauce. It sets around the fish.

item.title: Garlic Naan
item.description: Garlic naan — yoghurt-enriched flatbread cooked in a screaming pan until charred and blistered, with garlic butter.
item.content:encoded:
