Yoghurt does two things: its acid tenderises the gluten so the bread stays soft, and its protein browns fast under high heat, which is where the char spots come from. The pan must be dry and near-smoking — oil in the pan fries the surface rather than blistering it.

  • The pan must be smoking and dry. Any oil and you get a fried flatbread instead of a naan.
  • Wetting one side makes it stick to the pan, which is how a tandoor works and how you get the char.
  • Stack the cooked naans under a cloth so the steam keeps them soft.

item.title: Grilled Kippers
item.description: Whole split kippers grilled skin side up with butter and pepper, served with lemon and brown bread.
item.content:encoded:
Grill them skin side up, not flesh side. The skin protects the flesh from the direct heat and holds the oil in, so the fish steams gently underneath while the skin blisters — and there is no need to turn them at all. Kippers are already cooked in the smoking, so this is heating, not cooking, and five to seven minutes is plenty. The butter goes on the flesh before they go under, and melts down through as they heat.

  • Skin side up under the grill, and no turning.
  • Six minutes. They are already cooked — this is heating.
  • Butter on the flesh before they go under.

item.title: Soused Herring
item.description: Herring fillets rolled around onion and baked slowly in spiced vinegar and water, cooled in the liquor and served cold.
item.content:encoded:
Low and slow, in the oven, not on the hob. At 150C the vinegar softens the fine pin bones until they disappear entirely, which is what makes a soused herring pleasant to eat rather than an obstacle course; boiled hard on the stove, the flesh shreds before the bones give. The vinegar is cut with water roughly half and half — neat vinegar cooks the fish to a rubbery grey and is unpleasantly sharp when cold, and you cannot correct it afterwards.

  • Low oven, not the hob. It is what softens the pin bones.
  • Half vinegar, half water. Neat vinegar is inedible cold.
  • Cool them in the liquor and give them a night.

item.title: Dressed Crab
item.description: A cooked crab picked clean, the brown meat bound with breadcrumbs and mustard, the white left loose, both returned to the cleaned shell.
item.content:encoded:
Keep the two meats completely separate and dress only the brown. Brown meat is soft, rich and strongly flavoured and wants breadcrumbs, mustard and lemon to give it body; white meat is delicate and needs nothing but a squeeze of lemon, and mixing them buries it. Discard the dead man's fingers — the grey feathery gills — without hesitation, and the stomach sac behind the eyes. Neither is dangerous, but both taste unpleasant and ruin the whole crab.

  • Brown and white kept separate. Mixing buries the white meat.
  • Gills and stomach sac go in the bin, every time.
  • Check the white meat twice for shell. There is always one more piece.

item.title: Enchiladas Verdes
item.description: Enchiladas verdes — corn tortillas rolled around chicken in a charred tomatillo salsa, baked with crema and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Charring the tomatillos under a grill rather than boiling them concentrates their sugars and takes the raw metallic edge off, so the salsa tastes round instead of sour. Dipping each tortilla in warm oil before the salsa is the step restaurants never skip — it waterproofs the corn so the enchiladas hold their shape instead of dissolving into a casserole.

  • Char the tomatillos, do not boil them. Boiled salsa verde tastes thin and sour.
  • The oil dip is not optional. Skip it and the tortillas turn to paste in the oven.
  • Assemble and bake immediately — enchiladas left sitting in salsa go soft.

item.title: Devilled Whitebait
item.description: Whole whitebait tossed in flour spiced with cayenne and deep-fried in two batches until crisp, served with lemon and cayenne salt.
item.content:encoded:
Fry them twice, briefly, in oil at 190C. One long fry cooks the inside to mush before the coating is properly hard, whereas a short fry, a rest, and a second short fry drives out the remaining moisture and makes them audibly crisp. Dry the fish thoroughly and flour them at the last second — flour that has sat on wet fish turns to a slick paste that slides off in the oil. And salt them the moment they come out, while the surface is still hot enough for it to stick.

  • Two short fries, not one long one.
  • Flour them at the last second, and sieve off the excess.
  • Salt the instant they leave the oil.

item.title: Chicken and Leek Pie
item.description: A British pie of poached chicken and softened leeks in a tarragon cream sauce built on the poaching stock, under a shortcrust lid.
item.content:encoded:
Poach the chicken rather than roasting it, and make the sauce with the poaching liquid. Roast chicken in a pie is dry by the time the pastry is done, because it cooks twice; poached and cut into large pieces, it stays succulent through the bake. Cool the filling completely before the pastry goes on — a hot filling melts the butter in the pastry before it reaches the oven, and you get a greasy, sunken lid instead of a crisp one.

  • Poach the chicken. Roast chicken in a pie comes out dry.
  • Make the sauce with the poaching stock.
  • The filling must be cold before the pastry goes on.

item.title: Aguachile
item.description: Aguachile — raw prawns cured in lime, green chilli and coriander with cucumber and red onion.
item.content:encoded:
Aguachile differs from ceviche in timing: the prawns go into the chilli water minutes before serving, not an hour, so they stay translucent and sweet rather than turning opaque and firm. Blending the lime with the chilli first means the acid and heat hit the prawn at the same moment.

  • Buy prawns you would happily eat raw, from a fishmonger you trust.
  • Five minutes, not fifty. Long curing turns aguachile into rubbery ceviche.
  • Chill the serving plate — the dish should be cold from first bite to last.

item.title: Rabbit Pie
item.description: Wild or farmed rabbit braised in cider with bacon and mustard, the meat picked from the bone and baked under a shortcrust lid.
item.content:encoded:
Braise the rabbit on the bone first and pick the meat afterwards. Rabbit is very lean and full of small bones, and jointing it raw into a pie leaves you either with dry meat or with bones in every mouthful; two hours in cider on the bone gives you meat that falls apart and a braising liquid worth building the sauce from. Bacon is not optional — rabbit carries almost no fat of its own, and the bacon supplies what the meat cannot.

  • Braise on the bone and pick afterwards.
  • Bacon is structural here — rabbit has no fat of its own.
  • Reduce the braising liquid before it becomes the sauce.

item.title: Stovies
item.description: A Scottish one-pot of potatoes slowly stewed in beef dripping with onions and leftover roast beef until they collapse and catch at the base.
item.content:encoded:
Barely any liquid, and the lid stays on. The potatoes cook mostly in steam and in the fat, which is what makes them collapse into a rough, buttery mass rather than boiling into soup — a splash of stock at the start is all it needs, and more than that makes a stew you could have made anywhere. And the base is meant to catch a little, so use a heavy pan, keep the heat low, and stir only two or three times in the whole hour. Those darkened bits are the point.

  • Almost no liquid. Any more and it is just stew.
  • Stir twice in the whole hour. The catching base is the flavour.
  • A heavy pan and the lowest heat you have.

item.title: Bubble and Squeak
item.description: Leftover mashed potato and cooked cabbage or sprouts pressed into a hot pan and fried undisturbed until a dark crust forms on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Cold leftovers, and leave it alone. Fresh mash carries too much moisture and will never crust; a day in the fridge dries it out and firms it. Once it is in the pan the whole method is patience — press it down, then do not touch it for eight full minutes, because every stir breaks the crust that is forming and you end up with hot mash instead. Turning it is the only difficult part, and the honest answer is to slide it onto a plate and invert the pan over it.

  • Cold leftovers only. Fresh mash will not crust.
  • Eight minutes untouched. Every stir destroys the crust.
  • Turn it with a plate, not a spatula.

item.title: Horchata
item.description: Horchata — Mexican rice and cinnamon drink soaked overnight, blended and strained, served over ice.
item.content:encoded:
The overnight soak softens the rice enough that a domestic blender can break it into particles fine enough to carry flavour and body through the strainer. Blending dry or briefly soaked rice gives a thin, gritty drink no amount of sugar rescues.

  • Blend for two full minutes. This is the whole difference between silky and gritty.
  • Strain twice through muslin if you want it restaurant smooth.
  • It separates in the fridge, which is normal. Stir before pouring.

item.title: Braised Red Cabbage
item.description: Red cabbage slowly braised with cooking apple, onion, vinegar, brown sugar and warm spices until soft and glossy.
item.content:encoded:
Vinegar at the start, not the end. Red cabbage owes its colour to anthocyanins, which turn a dull blue-grey in alkaline conditions and stay vivid purple in acid — so the acid goes in with everything else, and cabbage cooked without it comes out the colour of a bruise. Cook it low and long, at least an hour and a quarter, with the lid on for the first hour so it steams and then off so the liquid reduces to a glaze.

  • Vinegar in at the start. It is what keeps the colour.
  • Lid on for an hour, off for the last fifteen.
  • Make it two days ahead. It improves markedly.

item.title: Carolina Pulled Pork
item.description: Carolina pulled pork — pork shoulder rubbed and cooked low for six hours, dressed with a thin vinegar sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Pork shoulder is roughly a fifth collagen, and collagen only becomes gelatine above about 70C held for hours — which is why a hot, fast roast gives dry meat and a six-hour braise gives strands that stay moist. Carolina vinegar sauce is thin on purpose: it cuts the fat rather than coating it, so the pork tastes of pork.

  • Overnight in the fridge, uncovered. Dry surface, seasoned through, better bark.
  • Cook to feel, not to the clock. When the probe meets no resistance, it is done.
  • Toss the pulled meat with the juices in the tin — that is where the flavour collected.

item.title: Pease Pudding
item.description: Yellow split peas simmered in ham stock in a cloth or basin until collapsed, beaten smooth with butter and set firm.
item.content:encoded:
Cooked in ham stock, not water, and that is the whole flavour of the dish — pease pudding made in water is a bowl of plain split peas. If you are not boiling a ham, use a stock cube and a piece of bacon. Beat it hard when it comes off the heat, for a good two minutes, because that is what turns a pan of soft peas into something smooth enough to slice cold. And salt only at the end, since ham stock brings its own and the amount is unpredictable.

  • Ham stock, always. Water gives you nothing.
  • Beat it hard for two minutes off the heat.
  • Salt last. The stock decides how much it needs.

item.title: Texas Smoked Brisket
item.description: Texas smoked brisket — salt, pepper and ten hours of smoke, rested until the bark sets and the flat stays moist.
item.content:encoded:
Brisket has two muscles with different fat contents cooking as one piece, which is why the lean flat dries out before the fatty point is done. Wrapping at the stall — around 70C, where evaporative cooling halts the temperature climb — pushes it through without stripping the bark, and the long rest lets rendered fat redistribute into the flat.

  • Thin blue smoke, not white. White smoke is unburnt fuel and it tastes like an ashtray.
  • Wrap when the bark is set, not at a fixed clock time.
  • The two-hour rest is part of the cook, not an afterthought. Slicing early loses the juice.

item.title: Champ
item.description: Irish mashed potato beaten with milk in which spring onions have been steeped, served in a mound with a well of melted butter.
item.content:encoded:
Steep the spring onions in the milk rather than stirring them in raw. Two minutes in hot milk takes the raw allium bite off and pushes the flavour through the whole bowl instead of leaving it in green flecks, and it is what separates champ from mash with something scattered over it. The milk must be hot when it goes in as well — cold milk into hot potato makes it claggy — and the potatoes want to be steamed dry in the pan for a minute after draining.

  • Steep the onions in the hot milk. Raw ones stay as flecks.
  • Hot milk into hot potato, always.
  • Softer than ordinary mash, and the well of butter is the dish.

item.title: Pan Haggerty
item.description: A Northumbrian dish of thinly sliced potato and onion layered with cheddar in a heavy pan, cooked slowly on the hob and browned under the grill.
item.content:encoded:
Slice the potatoes on a mandolin at two millimetres and do not rinse them. The starch on the cut surfaces is the only thing binding the layers together — rinsed potatoes slide apart when you cut into it. It cooks on the hob under a lid for most of its time, which steams the layers soft while the base fries, and only goes under the grill for the last five minutes. Grilling it from the start browns the top over raw potato.

  • Do not rinse the potatoes. The starch is the glue.
  • Hob first under a lid, grill only at the end.
  • Press each layer down firmly as you build it.

item.title: Cioppino
item.description: Cioppino — San Francisco seafood stew with crab, clams, mussels and prawns in a tomato and wine broth.
item.content:encoded:
Cioppino is really a broth recipe with seafood added at the end, so the depth has to be built before anything shellfish goes in: shells and fennel simmered into the tomato, then twenty minutes of reduction. Adding the seafood in order of cooking time — clams and mussels first, prawns and fish last — means everything finishes in the same minute.

  • Build the broth first and taste it before any seafood goes near it.
  • Seafood in order: clams, mussels, then prawns and fish. Eleven minutes total, no more.
  • Shell-on prawns give the broth more flavour, and a bib solves the rest.

item.title: Laverbread with Bacon
item.description: Laverbread beaten with oatmeal and fried in bacon fat until crusted, served with streaky bacon on hot buttered toast.
item.content:encoded:
Laverbread comes ready cooked and carries a lot of water, so the oatmeal is not a filler — it absorbs that water and is the only reason the mixture holds together in the pan. Give it five minutes to swell before frying. Then fry it hot and briefly in bacon fat: laverbread held over heat for too long dries out and turns bitter and metallic, and the difference is about ninety seconds either way.

  • Give the oatmeal five minutes to swell before it goes in the pan.
  • Three minutes a side. Overcooked laverbread turns bitter.
  • Bacon fat, not butter or oil.

item.title: Stuffed Marrow
item.description: A marrow halved and hollowed, filled with beef mince cooked with tomato and herbs, topped with cheese and breadcrumbs and baked.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the hollowed halves and leave them upside down for half an hour. Marrow is almost entirely water and, unsalted, it floods the filling and you serve mince in a puddle — this one step is the whole difference between a good stuffed marrow and the soggy version everyone remembers. Cook the filling down until it is genuinely dry too, drier than you would want to eat on its own, because the marrow will give back plenty as it bakes.

  • Salt the cavities for half an hour. Everything depends on it.
  • Cook the filling until it is drier than seems right.
  • Dry the marrow properly before filling it.

item.title: Watercress Soup
item.description: A vivid British soup of potato and onion base with watercress added at the last moment and blended straight away to keep the colour.
item.content:encoded:
The watercress goes in for ninety seconds at the very end and the soup is blended immediately after. Green leaves lose their colour to heat and to acid over time, so every extra minute in the pan takes the soup a shade further towards khaki. Build the whole base first — onion, potato, stock, fully cooked — then wilt the cress into it and blend at once. Cooling it fast under a cold tap holds the colour if you are serving it later.

  • Ninety seconds for the cress, then blend at once.
  • Build the base completely before the leaves go anywhere near it.
  • Cool it fast if you are not serving straight away.

item.title: Sloppy Joes
item.description: Sloppy joes — beef mince in a sweet-sharp tomato sauce, spooned onto soft buns.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce needs both sugar and vinegar in balance — the sweetness alone reads as tinned spaghetti, the vinegar alone as a bad barbecue sauce. Cooking the mince until the water has gone and the meat is actually browning, rather than stewing grey, is what gives the sandwich savour instead of just sweetness.

  • Brown the mince properly. Grey mince makes a sweet sandwich with no depth.
  • Thick enough to sit on a spoon, or it runs straight out of the bun.
  • Toast and butter the buns — it waterproofs them for a minute or two longer.

item.title: Coronation Chicken
item.description: Poached chicken in a lightly curried mayonnaise with apricot purée, cream and lemon, finished with flaked almonds.
item.content:encoded:
The curry powder must be cooked before it goes anywhere near the mayonnaise — fried with the onion, then simmered with wine and apricot and blitzed. Raw curry powder stirred into mayonnaise is exactly what makes the sandwich-shop version taste dusty and flat. Poach the chicken and let it cool in its liquid rather than roasting it, so it stays moist when cold, and cut it into decent pieces: shredded chicken turns the whole thing to paste.

  • Cook the curry powder. Raw powder in mayonnaise tastes of dust.
  • Let the chicken cool in its liquid, then cut it in decent pieces.
  • Cool the curry base fully before it meets the mayonnaise.

item.title: Corn Dogs
item.description: Corn dogs — hot dogs dipped in sweet cornmeal batter and deep fried until crisp.
item.content:encoded:
The batter has to be thick enough to cling to a wet sausage, which means a tall narrow jar rather than a bowl: you dip and lift in one motion and gravity does the coating for you. Drying the sausages first is the difference between batter that stays on and batter that slides off in the oil.

  • A tall jar, not a bowl. It is the only way to get an even coat.
  • Dry sausages, dusted with flour. Wet ones shed their batter into the oil.
  • 180C exactly — cooler and the coating soaks up oil, hotter and it browns before it sets.

item.title: Cucumber Sandwiches
item.description: Afternoon tea cucumber sandwiches: cucumber salted and drained, laid on thin buttered white bread and cut into fingers with the crusts removed.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the cucumber and drain it for twenty minutes, then dry it. Cucumber is ninety-six per cent water and unsalted slices will soak through the bread within ten minutes, which is why the sandwiches at bad afternoon teas are always slightly damp. The butter is the second defence: spread right to the edges, it waterproofs the crumb. Slice the cucumber on a mandolin as thin as you can — the texture should be barely there, not a chunk of salad in bread.

  • Salt and dry the cucumber. It is the whole thing.
  • Butter to the very edges — it waterproofs the bread.
  • Cut the crusts after filling, not before.

item.title: Spotted Dick
item.description: A steamed British suet pudding with currants and lemon zest, cooked two hours in a basin and served with hot custard.
item.content:encoded:
A suet pudding is light because of steam, not because of raising agent, so the water must stay at a rolling boil for the whole two hours and be topped up with boiling water only — a splash of cold and the pudding sinks. Pleat the paper and foil cover, because the pudding rises and a flat cover holds it down. And the mixture should be soft enough to drop reluctantly off a spoon: a stiff suet mix steams into something you could stop a door with.

  • A rolling boil for the whole two hours, topped up with boiling water only.
  • Pleat the cover. A flat one stops it rising.
  • A soft mixture. Stiff suet steams heavy.

item.title: Treacle Sponge Pudding
item.description: A light steamed sponge pudding built over a layer of golden syrup and breadcrumbs, turned out so the syrup runs down the sides.
item.content:encoded:
The breadcrumbs in the syrup at the bottom of the basin are not a mistake — they stop the syrup from being absorbed straight into the sponge during the two hours of steaming, so it is still a distinct pool when you turn it out. Without them the pudding comes out uniformly sweet and there is no sauce. Cream the butter and sugar for a full five minutes: a steamed sponge gets no help from the oven and all of its lift comes from the air beaten in at that stage.

  • Breadcrumbs under the syrup, or there is no sauce at the end.
  • Five minutes of creaming. There is no oven to help it rise.
  • Top up with boiling water only.

item.title: Philadelphia Soft Pretzels
item.description: Philadelphia soft pretzels — oblong, chewy pretzels dipped in a soda bath and baked with coarse salt.
item.content:encoded:
The alkaline bath is what makes a pretzel a pretzel: it raises the surface pH so the Maillard reaction runs far faster than the crumb bakes, giving the mahogany skin and that distinct tang. Baking the soda on a tray first drives off carbon dioxide and turns it into a stronger alkali, closer to the food-grade lye bakeries use.

  • Bake the bicarbonate of soda. Raw, it gives a pale pretzel with no tang.
  • Chill before the bath so the shapes survive the dip.
  • Deep brown, not golden. A pale pretzel tastes like a bread roll.

item.title: Jam Roly-Poly
item.description: A rolled suet pastry pudding spread with raspberry jam, wrapped in pleated paper and foil and steamed until spiralled through.
item.content:encoded:
Leave a clear two-centimetre border of bare pastry all the way round the jam. Jam boils and expands enormously in the steam, and a roll spread to the edges will split along its seam and empty itself into the pan. Roll it loosely too, not tightly — the pastry needs room to expand — and seal the ends by pinching them properly closed. Warm the jam slightly first so it spreads without tearing the soft pastry.

  • A clear 2 cm border, or it splits and empties in the pan.
  • Roll it loosely and pleat the wrapping. It needs room.
  • Warm the jam first so it does not tear the pastry.

item.title: Treacle Tart
item.description: A British tart of golden syrup thickened with fresh breadcrumbs and sharpened with lemon zest and juice, in shortcrust under a lattice.
item.content:encoded:
Fresh breadcrumbs, not dried. Fresh crumbs swell and set the syrup into something sliceable, whereas dried crumbs stay gritty and the filling runs. Use plenty of lemon — the zest of two and the juice of one is not a garnish but the only thing standing between the tart and pure sugar. Bake it until the centre has only the faintest wobble; a treacle tart taken out too early will never set and one overbaked goes hard and chewy at the edges.

  • Fresh breadcrumbs. Dried ones stay gritty and the filling runs.
  • Two lemons' zest. It is structural, not decorative.
  • The faintest wobble at the centre, then cool it completely.

item.title: Boston Cream Pie
item.description: Boston cream pie — vanilla sponge layered with pastry cream and finished with a poured chocolate glaze.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry cream has to be cooked until it actually boils and thickens, then chilled solid, or it slumps out from between the layers under the weight of the glaze. A ganache glaze poured at around 35C is fluid enough to fall over the edge in a clean line and sets without going dull.

  • Boil the pastry cream for a full 45 seconds. Under-cooked, it will loosen in the fridge.
  • Cold cake, cool glaze. Warm glaze on warm sponge runs straight off onto the plate.
  • Level the sponges with a bread knife if they have domed, or the top layer slides.

item.title: Apple Crumble
item.description: Bramley apples baked under a coarse rubbed crumble of flour, butter, sugar and oats, until the fruit bubbles up at the edges.
item.content:encoded:
Rub the topping only until it looks like coarse gravel with lumps in it, and then stop. Rubbed to fine breadcrumbs it bakes into a solid sandy lid; left lumpy it stays open and rubbly and the fat pools into crisp nuggets. Do not pre-cook the apples: Bramleys collapse in the oven on their own and precooked fruit turns to a purée under the crumble. And a spoonful of cornflour tossed with the apples catches the juice that would otherwise turn the base of the topping to paste.

  • Coarse gravel, not breadcrumbs. Stop rubbing early.
  • Never press the topping down.
  • Do not pre-cook the apples. Bramleys collapse on their own.

item.title: Rhubarb Fool
item.description: Forced rhubarb roasted with sugar and orange, cooled, and folded loosely through whipped cream so it stays streaked.
item.content:encoded:
Roast the rhubarb rather than stewing it, in a single layer with sugar and no added liquid. Stewed rhubarb releases its water and collapses into a slack purée; roasted, it keeps its shape and its colour, and the juices reduce to a syrup. Then cool it completely — warm fruit deflates whipped cream instantly — and fold it through in three or four strokes only, so it stays in distinct ribbons. A fool folded to a uniform pink is a mousse that has lost its nerve.

  • Roast, do not stew. Roasted rhubarb keeps its shape and colour.
  • Everything cold before it meets the cream.
  • Three or four folds. A uniform pink fool is a failed one.

item.title: Summer Pudding
item.description: A basin lined with day-old white bread filled with lightly cooked summer berries and weighted overnight until saturated crimson.
item.content:encoded:
Day-old bread, crusts off, and no fresher. Fresh bread is too soft and turns to mush against the fruit; properly stale bread absorbs the juice and holds its structure so the pudding stands up when turned out. Cook the berries for three minutes and no longer — they only need to release their juice, and boiled fruit loses both texture and colour. Weight it overnight with something genuinely heavy: a tin of beans is not enough, and an under-pressed summer pudding collapses on the plate.

  • Day-old bread. Fresh bread turns to mush.
  • Three minutes of cooking, total. The fruit only needs to bleed.
  • Weight it properly. Something genuinely heavy, overnight.

item.title: Steak and Ale Pie
item.description: Steak and ale pie — beef shin braised in dark ale under a rough puff pastry lid, baked until glossy.
item.content:encoded:
The filling has to be cold and thick before the pastry goes on, or steam lifts the lid off and the base of it never cooks. Shin rather than braising steak is the choice worth making: it carries far more collagen, so two and a half hours turns it into something that thickens the gravy on its own.

  • Cold filling, always. Warm filling steams the pastry off the top.
  • Shin, not stewing steak. It is cheaper and it makes a better gravy.
  • Brown the beef in batches with real space around it. This is the step people rush.

item.title: Chelsea Buns
item.description: An enriched British bun dough rolled around butter, currants and mixed spice, cut into spirals, baked touching and glazed with sugar syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Bake them touching in a tin, not spread out on a tray. Buns baked apart brown on every side and go dry; packed in so their sides press together, only the tops colour and the sides stay pale, soft and pull-apart. The glaze goes on the moment they come out of the oven, while the surface is still hot enough to absorb it — brushed on cool buns it just sits there and sets tacky. And chill the rolled log for twenty minutes before slicing, or the spirals squash flat under the knife.

  • Bake them touching. Buns baked apart go dry.
  • Glaze them straight out of the oven while they are hot.
  • Twenty minutes in the fridge before slicing keeps the spirals round.

item.title: English Trifle
item.description: English trifle — sherry-soaked sponge, fruit, set custard and whipped cream, layered in a glass bowl.
item.content:encoded:
A trifle stands or falls on the custard being thick enough to hold a layer rather than soaking into the sponge, which means cooking it to a real nappe and then chilling it completely before it goes in. Each layer needs to be cold and set before the next goes on, so the whole thing is a series of waits.

  • Cold custard on cold fruit. Warm custard slides through the sponge and you lose the layers.
  • Soft peaks on the cream. Over-whipped cream looks grainy on top.
  • Make it the day before — the sponge and sherry need the time.

item.title: Baked Rice Pudding
item.description: Pudding rice baked slowly in milk and cream with nutmeg until thick and creamy under a browned skin.
item.content:encoded:
Baked, not simmered, and at a low temperature for two full hours. On the hob you have to stir it, and stirring breaks the grains and gives a gluey pudding; in a low oven the starch releases slowly and the rice stays whole in a thick creamy liquid. Do not stir it at all once it is in, because the skin forms from the first twenty minutes and every stir buries it. Butter dotted on the surface at the start is what browns that skin.

  • Baked, not simmered. Stirring makes it gluey.
  • Do not stir it at all once it is in the oven.
  • Butter on the surface is what browns the skin.

item.title: Syllabub
item.description: A traditional British dessert of cream whipped with lemon-steeped sweet wine and brandy until it holds soft peaks.
item.content:encoded:
Steep the lemon zest in the wine before anything is whipped, and give it at least an hour — the alcohol pulls the oils out of the zest and that is where nearly all the flavour comes from. Then add the liquid to the cream gradually while whisking, not all at once, or the cream will never thicken. Stop at soft peaks: syllabub over-whipped with alcohol in it splits into a grainy mess very suddenly and cannot be brought back.

  • Steep the zest an hour. That is where the flavour is.
  • Add the liquid gradually or the cream never thickens.
  • Stop at soft peaks. Over-whipped syllabub splits instantly.

item.title: Banoffee Pie
item.description: A British no-bake pie of digestive biscuit base, boiled condensed milk toffee, sliced banana and whipped cream, finished with chocolate.
item.content:encoded:
The tin must stay completely covered with water for the whole three hours of boiling. An exposed tin overheats and can burst, which is genuinely dangerous, so top it up from a kettle and set a timer. If you would rather not, tip the condensed milk into a pan with butter and sugar and cook it to a caramel on the hob. Either way it must be cold before it goes on the base, and the bananas go on at the last possible moment because they brown within the hour.

  • The tin must stay under water the entire time, and cool before opening.
  • Bananas at the last moment. They brown within the hour.
  • Press the base up the sides, not just across the bottom.

item.title: Crumpets
item.description: Crumpets — yeasted batter cooked in rings on a griddle until the tops are full of holes.
item.content:encoded:
The holes come from carbon dioxide escaping through a batter loose enough to let bubbles rise but set enough to keep the walls standing — which is why the batter needs both a yeast rise and a pinch of bicarbonate of soda stirred in at the end. Too thick and the top stays blank; too thin and the batter runs under the ring.

  • Low heat and patience. A hot pan burns the base before the holes ever form.
  • Butter the rings every batch or the crumpets will not release.
  • Crumpets are made to be toasted later, not eaten off the griddle.

item.title: Custard Tart
item.description: A deep shortcrust case blind baked and sealed with egg, filled with a nutmeg-scented egg custard and baked slowly until barely set.
item.content:encoded:
Seal the blind-baked case with beaten egg and give it two minutes back in the oven before the custard goes in. That thin cooked film waterproofs the pastry, and it is the only thing standing between you and a soggy base. Then bake it low — 140C — and take it out when the centre still has a distinct wobble, because custard carries on setting for a good twenty minutes out of the oven. A custard baked until firm in the tin will be rubbery and weeping by the time it is cold.

  • Seal the baked case with egg. It is what stops a soggy base.
  • Skim the bubbles off the custard before it goes in.
  • Take it out wobbly. It sets as it cools.

item.title: Lemon Posset
item.description: A three-ingredient British set cream: double cream boiled with sugar and set with lemon juice, chilled until firm.
item.content:encoded:
It sets because lemon acid denatures the milk proteins in cream that has been boiled and concentrated, which means two things are non-negotiable: the cream must have enough fat, so double cream only, and it must actually boil for three minutes to reduce. Single cream will not set at all. Add the lemon juice off the heat and give it two minutes before pouring, or the acid can curdle rather than set it. And do not exceed the lemon: too much juice makes it grainy.

  • Double cream only. Anything lighter will not set.
  • Three full minutes at a boil. That reduction is what sets it.
  • Lemon juice off the heat, then two minutes before pouring.

item.title: Ploughman's Lunch
item.description: Ploughman's lunch — sharp cheddar, crusty bread, pickled onions, chutney and apple on a board.
item.content:encoded:
The whole plate is built on contrast, so the components have to pull in different directions: sharp cheese against sweet chutney, sour pickle against soft butter, crisp apple against dense bread. Taking the cheese out of the fridge an hour ahead matters more than anything else — cold cheddar tastes of very little.

  • Room-temperature cheddar. Straight from the fridge it is waxy and mute.
  • Buy the best single thing on the board and let it carry the rest.
  • Keep the wet components in small dishes so the bread stays dry.

item.title: Welsh Cakes
item.description: Welsh griddle cakes of spiced currant dough cooked on a dry bakestone over low heat and dusted with caster sugar while warm.
item.content:encoded:
A low, steady heat and a dry griddle. Welsh cakes are about a centimetre thick and the outside will burn long before the middle is cooked if the pan is hot — medium-low, and three minutes a side. The griddle stays dry, or barely greased once at the start, because these carry enough butter of their own and added fat fries the surface rather than baking it. Sugar them the moment they come off, while the surface is still warm enough for it to stick.

  • Medium-low heat. Hot pans burn them before the middle cooks.
  • A dry griddle. They have butter enough of their own.
  • Sugar them straight off the heat so it sticks.

item.title: Eccles Cakes
item.description: Lancashire cakes of currants, butter, sugar and spice enclosed in flaky pastry, slashed three times, sugared and baked until caramelised.
item.content:encoded:
Three slashes across the top, and they matter — the filling produces a lot of steam and pastry without vents will burst at the seam underneath, emptying itself onto the tray. Chill the filled cakes hard before baking so the pastry layers stay distinct. And the egg white and caster sugar go on together: the white makes the sugar stick and it caramelises into a thin crackling glaze that is half the reason to make them.

  • Three slashes. Unvented cakes burst at the seam.
  • Chill them before baking so the layers stay separate.
  • Egg white first, then sugar. It is what gives the crackling glaze.

item.title: Yorkshire Parkin
item.description: A Yorkshire cake of medium oatmeal, black treacle and golden syrup with ginger, baked slowly and matured in a tin for a week.
item.content:encoded:
It has to be kept. Straight from the oven parkin is dry and the ginger is raw and aggressive; wrapped and left in a tin for five days to a week, the syrup migrates through the crumb and it turns sticky, dark and soft — this is not a nicety, it is when the cake becomes the thing it is supposed to be. Medium oatmeal, not flour or fine oatmeal: the slight grittiness is characteristic. And bake it low and slow, because treacle burns easily.

  • Five days in a tin, minimum. On day one it is not parkin.
  • Medium oatmeal, not flour. The texture is the point.
  • A low oven. Treacle burns fast.

item.title: Irish Stew
item.description: Irish stew — lamb neck, potatoes and onions simmered slowly with nothing else in the pot.
item.content:encoded:
A real Irish stew has no browning step and no flour: the body comes from two layers of potato, the lower one deliberately breaking down into the liquid. Lamb neck on the bone gives enough gelatine that the stew sets to a light jelly when it cools, which is the sign it is right.

  • No browning, no flour. Both belong to a different stew.
  • Two potato cuts, two jobs: one thickens, one stays whole.
  • Neck on the bone. Boneless leg makes a thin, disappointing pot.

item.title: Har Gow
item.description: Cantonese prawn dumplings in a wheat starch and tapioca wrapper made with boiling water, pleated and steamed until transparent.
item.content:encoded:
The wrapper is wheat starch, not wheat flour, and the water must be at a full rolling boil when it goes in. Wheat starch has had the gluten washed out of it, so it cannot form a dough at all until the starch gelatinises, and water even slightly below boiling gives you a crumbly mixture that will not hold together. Work it while it is almost too hot to handle. The other rule is that half the prawn is chopped and half left whole, so the filling has both a paste that binds and pieces you can bite.

  • Wheat starch, not flour, and water at a full rolling boil.
  • Work the dough hot and keep every piece covered.
  • Half the prawn chopped, half in pieces.

item.title: Irish Soda Bread
item.description: Irish soda bread — a no-yeast loaf of flour, buttermilk and bicarbonate of soda, mixed and baked in under an hour.
item.content:encoded:
The lift comes from acid meeting alkali the moment the buttermilk hits the bicarbonate of soda, and that reaction starts to run out within a few minutes — so the dough goes into a hot oven immediately, and anything that delays it costs you rise. Handling it more than a few seconds develops gluten and turns the crumb tough.

  • Oven hot before you start mixing. The reaction is already running.
  • Thirty seconds of handling, no more. This is not a bread you knead.
  • The deep cross is not decoration — it lets the middle cook through.

item.title: Siu Mai
item.description: Cantonese open-topped dumplings of pork, prawn and shiitake in thin yellow wrappers, steamed and topped with roe or diced carrot.
item.content:encoded:
Beat the pork mixture in one direction for a full two minutes until it turns sticky and pulls away from the bowl. That is not folklore — the mechanical action extracts myosin from the meat, which sets on steaming into the springy, bouncy texture that separates a good siu mai from a loose meatball in a wrapper. The wrapper is not pleated at all: it is gathered around the filling and squeezed at the waist, then the top is left open and pressed flat with a spoon.

  • Beat in one direction for two full minutes. That is the bounce.
  • No pleating — gather and squeeze at the waist.
  • Flatten the open top with a wet spoon.

item.title: Cheung Fun
item.description: Cantonese rice noodle rolls: a thin rice flour batter steamed in a flat tray, rolled while hot and served with sweetened soy sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The batter must be stirred immediately before every single pour, because rice flour settles to the bottom of the bowl within about a minute and an unstirred ladleful gives you a translucent, holey sheet at the top of the batch and a thick chalky one at the bottom. Pour it thin — barely two millimetres — and roll each sheet the moment it comes out of the steamer, while it is still hot and pliable. A cooled sheet cracks along the fold.

  • Stir the batter before every single ladleful.
  • Two millimetres. Any thicker and it is stodgy.
  • Roll it hot. A cool sheet cracks.

item.title: Lo Mai Gai
item.description: Glutinous rice soaked and steamed with chicken, lap cheong and shiitake, wrapped in lotus leaves and steamed again.
item.content:encoded:
Glutinous rice has to be soaked for at least four hours before it is steamed. Unlike ordinary rice it will not absorb enough water during cooking alone, and unsoaked grains come out with hard opaque centres however long you steam them. The lotus leaves also need soaking, in hot water, until pliable — a dry leaf splits as you fold it. And the rice is steamed once before it is wrapped and once after, which is what makes the grains distinct rather than a single paste.

  • Four hours of soaking for the rice, and there is no shortcut.
  • Soak the leaves in hot water or they split.
  • Steam the rice before wrapping as well as after.

item.title: Colcannon
item.description: Colcannon — Irish mashed potato with buttery kale, spring onions and a well of melted butter.
item.content:encoded:
Cooking the greens separately in butter, rather than boiling them with the potatoes, keeps them green and keeps their water out of the mash. Warming the milk before it goes in matters more than people expect: cold liquid makes potato starch seize and turns the mash gluey.

  • Steam the potatoes dry before mashing. Three minutes in the colander.
  • Hot milk, cold potato is the wrong way round — warm the liquid.
  • A ricer, if you have one. A food processor turns potato into wallpaper paste.

item.title: Chicken Feet in Black Bean Sauce
item.description: Phoenix claws: chicken feet blanched, fried, soaked until puffed, then braised and steamed in a black bean, garlic and chilli sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The frying-then-soaking is the entire technique and cannot be skipped. Deep-frying blisters the skin, and the long cold soak afterwards lets those blisters swell with water, which is what gives phoenix claws their characteristic puffed, wrinkled surface and lets them absorb sauce. Skip either step and you have chewy chicken feet in gravy. Dry them completely before they go in the oil — wet feet spit violently — and keep a lid to hand.

  • Fry, then soak in cold water. That is what makes them puff.
  • Bone dry before they go in the oil, and keep a lid to hand.
  • The final steam is what makes them fall off the bone.

item.title: Boxty
item.description: Boxty — Irish potato pancakes made from half grated raw potato and half mash, fried until crisp.
item.content:encoded:
The two potato states do different jobs: raw grated potato gives structure and a slight chew, mashed potato gives softness and stops the pancake tasting starchy. Squeezing the grated potato dry and then adding back the starch that settles out of the liquid is the traditional step, and it is what binds the batter without extra flour.

  • Wring the grated potato genuinely dry, then put the settled starch back.
  • Medium heat, four minutes a side. Too hot and the raw potato inside stays raw.
  • Cook the batter within 20 minutes; it discolours if it sits.

item.title: Sheng Jian Bao
item.description: Shanghai pan-fried pork buns with jellied stock in the filling, fried base down then steamed in the same covered pan until crisp beneath and soft above.
item.content:encoded:
The soup inside comes from aspic — stock set with gelatine, diced and mixed cold into the filling, which melts in the pan. There is no other way to get liquid inside a bun. The cooking is fried and steamed at once: the buns go base down into hot oil, water is poured in and the lid goes on, so the bottoms crisp while the tops steam. Do not lift the lid until the water has gone, and listen for the sound to change from bubbling to a dry sizzle.

  • Aspic in the filling is the only way to get soup inside.
  • Seam up, base down. The base is the crisp part.
  • Lid on until the sound goes from bubbling to sizzling.

item.title: Jianbing
item.description: A Beijing street crepe of mung bean and wheat batter spread thin, topped with egg, sauces, coriander and a crisp cracker, then folded.
item.content:encoded:
The batter must be genuinely thin — the consistency of single cream — and spread immediately with the back of a ladle in one continuous spiral. Thick batter gives a pancake rather than a crepe, and hesitating while you spread leaves ridges that tear. The egg goes on within about twenty seconds, while the surface is still tacky enough for it to bond; any later and it slides off when you fold. The cracker goes in last and is what the whole thing is for.

  • Batter the thickness of single cream, spread in one spiral.
  • Egg on within twenty seconds while the surface is still tacky.
  • The cracker is the point. Do not leave it out.

item.title: Rou Jia Mo
item.description: Xi'an chopped pork sandwich: pork belly braised in a spiced master stock, chopped with coriander and packed into a griddled flatbread.
item.content:encoded:
The meat is chopped, not shredded or sliced — a cleaver, a board, and enough chopping that the fat and the lean become one mixture held together by the braising jelly. Shredded pork falls out of the bread. The bread is a baijimo, cooked on a dry griddle and finished in the oven, so it has a crisp skin and a hollow inside; a soft bun collapses under the wet meat within a minute. Split it round the equator and keep the crust intact.

  • Chop the meat. Shredded pork falls straight out.
  • A crisp baijimo, not a soft bun.
  • Include some of the braising jelly — it is the binder.

item.title: Cullen Skink
item.description: Cullen skink — Scottish smoked haddock, potato and onion soup, thickened with the potato itself.
item.content:encoded:
Poaching the haddock in the milk first and then using that milk as the base is the whole recipe — the smoke and salt go into the liquid, and the fish comes back at the end still in flakes. Undyed smoked haddock matters: the bright yellow kind is dyed and usually more salt than smoke.

  • Undyed haddock. The yellow stuff makes a soup that tastes of dye and salt.
  • Poach the fish in the milk that becomes the soup. Nothing is wasted.
  • Never boil once the milk is back in — it will split.

item.title: Liangpi
item.description: Xi'an cold skin noodles: a wheat dough washed until the starch separates, the starch water steamed into sheets and cut, dressed with chilli oil, vinegar and…
item.content:encoded:
The washing separates the dough into two things you use separately: the starch water, which becomes the noodles, and the gluten ball left behind, which is steamed and torn into the bowl as a sponge. Wash until the water runs almost clear, six or seven changes, and then let the starch water settle for at least four hours — the starch sinks and the clear water on top is poured away. Skip the settling and the sheets will not set. Stir the settled starch thoroughly before every pour.

  • Wash until the water runs almost clear — six or seven changes.
  • Four hours of settling, then pour the clear water off.
  • Keep the gluten ball. It goes back in the bowl.

item.title: Smashed Cucumber Salad
item.description: Cucumber smashed rather than sliced so it holds dressing, salted and drained, then tossed with garlic, black vinegar, soy and chilli oil.
item.content:encoded:
Smashing rather than slicing is the whole idea. A cleaver blow splits the cucumber along its own irregular lines, creating rough torn faces and open seed channels that hold dressing, where a clean knife cut gives a smooth surface the dressing runs straight off. Then salt it and let it drain for ten minutes: cucumber is mostly water and, undrained, that water dilutes the dressing into a pale puddle within minutes of it reaching the table.

  • Smash it, do not slice it. The torn faces hold the dressing.
  • Salt and drain for ten minutes, and do not rinse.
  • Dress it at the last moment.

item.title: Haggis, Neeps and Tatties
item.description: Haggis, neeps and tatties — baked haggis with swede and potato mash and a whisky cream sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Haggis is already cooked when you buy it, so the job is reheating it through without drying it — which means wrapping it in foil with a splash of water and treating the oven as a steamer. The two mashes are kept separate on the plate on purpose: swede is sweet and wet, potato is starchy and dry, and combined they cancel each other out.

  • Wrap it in foil with water. A dry haggis is a sad thing.
  • Steam the swede dry properly — it holds more water than potato does.
  • Let the whisky bubble before the cream goes in or the sauce tastes raw.

item.title: Bang Bang Chicken
item.description: Poached chicken cooled in its liquid and hand-torn into shreds, dressed in a Sichuan sauce of sesame paste, chilli oil and black vinegar.
item.content:encoded:
Tear the chicken along the grain with your fingers rather than cutting it. Torn shreds have rough fibrous surfaces that trap a thick sesame sauce; knife-cut strips are smooth and the sauce slides off into the bottom of the bowl. And take the pan off the heat once the chicken is in, letting it cook through in the cooling water — actively simmering chicken breast for twenty minutes gives you dry meat, while residual heat leaves it juicy.

  • Tear the chicken, never slice it.
  • Off the heat and covered. Simmering dries the breast out.
  • Loosen the sesame paste with the poaching liquid, not water.

item.title: Century Egg with Cold Tofu
item.description: Chilled silken tofu topped with chopped century eggs, crisp fried shallots, soy dressing, chilli oil and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse the century eggs after peeling and cut them with a wet knife or a length of thread. The yolk is soft and sticky enough to drag a dry blade through the white and smear the whole slice grey, while thread cuts cleanly. The tofu must be properly cold and thoroughly drained: silken tofu carries a lot of water and, undrained, it releases it under the dressing within a few minutes and everything turns pale and dilute.

  • Cut the eggs with wet thread or a wet blade.
  • Drain the tofu properly and keep it cold.
  • Dress at the table, not in advance.

item.title: Drunken Chicken
item.description: Chicken poached and cooled in its own liquid, then steeped overnight in a Shaoxing wine and stock marinade and served cold in slices.
item.content:encoded:
Chill the poached chicken in iced water before it goes into the wine. The shock sets the skin into the springy, slightly gelatinous texture that is half the point of the dish, and it stops the residual heat carrying the meat past done. The wine marinade is never heated with the chicken in it either — heat drives off the alcohol and most of the aroma, and the whole character of drunken chicken is raw Shaoxing wine against cold set stock.

  • Iced water straight after poaching. It sets the skin.
  • Never heat the marinade. Heat takes the wine with it.
  • A full day in the fridge, and the jelly is part of the dish.

item.title: Cranachan
item.description: Cranachan — Scottish dessert of toasted oats, whisky, honey, cream and raspberries layered in a glass.
item.content:encoded:
Toasting the oats until they smell of biscuit is the difference between cranachan and cream with muesli in it, and they need to go in at the last minute or they soften. Crushing only half the raspberries gives you both a ribbon of sharp purée and whole berries to bite.

  • Cool the oats fully before they meet cream, or they go soft immediately.
  • Soft peaks. Over-whipped cream makes the whole glass heavy.
  • Build it just before serving — this is not a make-ahead pudding.

item.title: Red Oil Wontons
item.description: Sichuan red oil wontons: pork and ginger wontons boiled and served in a sauce of chilli oil, black vinegar, garlic and sweetened soy.
item.content:encoded:
Lift the wontons out with a slotted spoon and shake them properly dry before they go in the sauce. Water carried over from the pan dilutes chilli oil instantly, and a bowl of red oil wontons that arrives pink and watery has been drained badly. The sauce is also assembled in the bowl, not cooked — the garlic is raw, the vinegar has not been heated, and warming any of it flattens the whole thing.

  • Shake them properly dry. Water ruins chilli oil.
  • Assemble the sauce cold in the bowl.
  • Press the air out as you fold, or they burst.

item.title: Marbled Tea Eggs
item.description: Eggs boiled, cracked all over the shell, then simmered and steeped in a spiced black tea and soy brine until marbled.
item.content:encoded:
Crack the shells thoroughly but leave every piece attached — tap the whole surface with the back of a spoon rather than rolling the egg, so you get a dense web of fine cracks. Loose shell falls away and the marbling turns into a solid brown egg. And the colour comes from steeping, not simmering: twenty minutes in the pan and then a night in the cold brine, because eggs boiled for hours in soy turn rubbery and unpleasantly salty.

  • Tap the whole shell, and leave every piece attached.
  • Twenty minutes of simmering, then steeping. Long boiling makes them rubbery.
  • Peel at the last moment so the pattern is a surprise.

item.title: Welsh Cawl
item.description: Welsh cawl — lamb and root vegetable broth, served as broth first and then meat and vegetables.
item.content:encoded:
Cawl is built in two stages because the root vegetables need an hour and the leeks and cabbage need eight minutes — putting them all in at the start gives you grey vegetables in a thin broth. Cooking it the day before and lifting the set fat off the top is standard, and it makes the broth taste cleaner.

  • Start in cold water and skim properly. It is the only way to a clear broth.
  • Overnight in the fridge, fat lifted off. Worth the wait.
  • Leeks and cabbage last, eight minutes. They are the point of the dish.

item.title: Youtiao
item.description: Chinese fried dough sticks: a slack alkaline dough rested overnight, cut into strips, pressed in pairs and deep-fried until hollow and puffed.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is deliberately slack and is never kneaded hard — it is folded a few times over several hours and then left overnight, so the gluten relaxes completely. A tight dough cannot expand fast enough in the oil and gives a dense, solid stick instead of a hollow one. Two strips are pressed together with a chopstick before frying, and it is the seam between them, held shut, that forces the expansion outwards and sideways. The oil must be at 200C — cooler and they soak rather than leap.

  • Never knead it. Fold, rest, and leave it overnight.
  • Press two strips together with a chopstick — the seam is what makes it hollow.
  • Oil at 200C. Cooler oil gives a greasy solid stick.

item.title: Dongpo Rou
item.description: Hangzhou braised pork belly: squares of belly tied with string, braised slowly in Shaoxing wine, soy and rock sugar, then steamed.
item.content:encoded:
The string is not decoration. Three hours of braising turns the connective tissue to gelatine and the squares would collapse into the pot without it — tied, each piece keeps its shape and can be lifted out whole. The other difference from ordinary red-braised pork is that the liquid is almost entirely Shaoxing wine rather than water, which is expensive and is the reason it tastes as it does. Lay a bed of spring onion and ginger under the pork so it never touches the base and cannot catch.

  • Tie every square. Untied pork falls apart in the pot.
  • A raft of spring onion and ginger so nothing touches the base.
  • Mostly wine, not water. It is the whole flavour.

item.title: Yuxiang Rousi
item.description: Sichuan shredded pork stir-fried with wood ear and bamboo shoots in a pickled chilli sauce balanced sweet, sour and salty.
item.content:encoded:
Mix the sauce in a bowl before you light the wok. The whole dish takes about ninety seconds from the pork hitting the oil, and measuring soy, vinegar and sugar while it cooks guarantees an overcooked, unbalanced result. Pickled chillies — paojiao — are what makes it yuxiang rather than merely spicy; doubanjiang alone gives heat without the sourness. And velvet the pork in cornflour and water first, which is what keeps thin shreds tender through high heat.

  • Mix the sauce before you light the wok.
  • Pickled chillies, not just chilli paste. That is the yuxiang.
  • Velvet the pork in cornflour or the shreds go tough.

item.title: Bara Brith
item.description: Bara brith — Welsh tea loaf with dried fruit soaked overnight in tea, spiced and baked dark.
item.content:encoded:
Soaking the fruit overnight in hot tea does two things: it plumps the fruit so it does not steal moisture from the crumb, and the tannins in the tea give the loaf its characteristic slight bitterness against all that sugar. Skipping the soak gives a loaf that is dry by the next morning.

  • Overnight soak, no shortcuts. This is a one-bowl recipe that trades effort for time.
  • Do not drain the fruit. That tea is the liquid in the batter.
  • Low oven, long bake. A hot oven gives a burnt crust and a raw middle.

item.title: Zhajiangmian
item.description: Beijing noodles with a slow-fried sauce of pork belly and fermented bean pastes, served over thick wheat noodles with raw vegetable shreds.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is fried, hard, for a good twenty minutes — that is what zhajiang means. The bean pastes are raw and harsh out of the jar and only long frying in plenty of oil drives off the harshness and turns the sauce dark and glossy; ten minutes is not enough and you will taste the difference. Rinse the pastes with a little water first if they are very salty. The raw vegetables are not a garnish either: the sauce is deliberately too salty to eat alone and the cucumber and radish are its other half.

  • Twenty minutes of frying the paste. Anything less tastes raw.
  • The sauce is meant to be too salty alone. The vegetables fix it.
  • Rinse the noodles so they stay springy under the sauce.

item.title: La Zi Ji
item.description: Chongqing chicken: marinated chicken cubes double-fried until crisp, then tossed through a wok of toasted dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns.
item.content:encoded:
The chillies are toasted in oil below smoking point, and if they go black the whole wok turns acrid and cannot be saved — pull the pan off the heat the moment they darken a shade and smell fragrant. Fry the chicken twice: once at 160C to cook it through and once at 190C to crisp it, which keeps it crunchy under the tossing. And use whole dried chillies snipped in half rather than flakes, because the point is aroma released slowly, not raw heat.

  • Pull the pan the second the chillies darken. Burnt chillies are unfixable.
  • Fry twice — 160C then 190C.
  • Whole chillies, not flakes. It is aroma, not raw heat.

item.title: German Pork Schnitzel
item.description: German pork schnitzel — pork loin beaten thin, breadcrumbed and fried until the coating puffs and crisps.
item.content:encoded:
The souffléd coating that separates a good schnitzel from a breaded chop comes from frying in enough fat that the pan can be swirled — the moving fat lifts the crumb off the meat as steam escapes. Dry, well-pressed cutlets and a light hand with the crumbs are what let that happen.

  • Enough fat to swirl. A dry pan gives you a breaded chop, not a schnitzel.
  • Press the crumbs lightly. This is the step everyone gets wrong.
  • Fry to order and serve immediately — a schnitzel goes soft within minutes.

item.title: Duo Jiao Yu Tou
item.description: A Hunanese dish of split fish head steamed under chopped salted chillies with ginger, garlic and fermented black beans, finished with hot oil.
item.content:encoded:
Twelve minutes and not a minute more. Fish head has a great deal of collagen and very little muscle, and it goes from silky to dry with almost no warning; the cheek should slip off the bone under a chopstick. The chopped chillies are salted and fermented rather than fresh, which is the difference between Hunan heat and Sichuan heat — bright and sour rather than numbing. And the smoking oil poured over at the end is not a flourish: it blooms the aromatics on the surface in the last five seconds.

  • Twelve minutes. Fish head dries out with no warning.
  • Salted chopped chillies, not fresh. Bright and sour is the point.
  • Pour off the watery liquid before the hot oil goes on.

item.title: Beggar's Chicken
item.description: A whole stuffed chicken wrapped in lotus leaves and encased in salt dough, baked three hours and cracked open at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The clay casing has to be completely sealed with no cracks, because the whole method depends on the chicken cooking in trapped steam — one gap and the moisture escapes and you get a dry roast bird in an expensive shell. Patch any splits with more dough before it goes in. The lotus leaves are the layer that actually matters for flavour: they perfume the meat in a way nothing else does, and the clay is there to hold everything shut. Rest it thirty minutes in the shell before breaking it.

  • Seal every crack in the clay. A leak dries the bird out.
  • The lotus leaves are the flavour; the clay just holds it shut.
  • Rest it half an hour before breaking it open.

item.title: White Cut Chicken
item.description: A whole chicken poached gently and shocked in iced water so the skin sets, chopped on the bone and served with ginger and scallion oil.
item.content:encoded:
The ice bath is the technique. Straight from the poaching liquid into iced water, the skin contracts and sets into the taut, faintly gelatinous layer that defines the dish, and the temperature shock also stops the meat cooking on. Skip it and the skin is flabby. The water must also never actually boil — bubbles tear the skin and toughen the breast, so hold it at a bare tremble and let the residual heat do most of the work with the pan off the heat.

  • Never let it boil. A tremble, then off the heat.
  • Straight into iced water. That is what sets the skin.
  • Smoking oil over the raw ginger and scallion, not the other way round.

item.title: Bratwurst with Sauerkraut
item.description: Bratwurst with sauerkraut — sausages simmered in beer then browned, on apple and caraway sauerkraut.
item.content:encoded:
Simmering the sausages in beer before browning cooks them through gently so the skins do not split, and the browning afterwards is purely for colour and flavour. Rinsing the sauerkraut once takes the raw brine edge off without losing the sourness that makes the dish work.

  • A bare simmer, never a boil. Boiled bratwurst burst and leak.
  • Rinse the sauerkraut once, not three times, or it tastes of nothing.
  • Grated apple, not chopped — it melts into the kraut and sweetens it evenly.

item.title: Soy Sauce Chicken
item.description: A whole chicken simmered and steeped in a spiced dark soy master stock until deeply coloured, then chopped and served with the reduced sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is turned every ten minutes so it colours evenly, and the pot must be only just wide enough — in a large pan you need twice the stock to cover the bird, which is wasteful given how much soy sauce and rock sugar goes into it. Most of the cooking happens off the heat, steeping in the hot stock, which colours the skin deeply without overcooking the breast. Strain the stock, chill it, lift the fat off and keep it: a master stock genuinely gets better every time it is used.

  • A narrow pot. A wide one needs twice the soy sauce.
  • Turn it every ten minutes so the colour is even.
  • Keep the master stock. It improves each time you use it.

item.title: Three Cup Chicken
item.description: Taiwanese chicken simmered with sesame oil, soy sauce and rice wine in equal measure with ginger and garlic, finished with Thai basil.
item.content:encoded:
The ginger is fried in the sesame oil first, on its own, until the slices curl and go slightly crisp at the edges — that takes a few minutes and it is where most of the depth comes from. Black sesame oil is worth seeking out and it must not be allowed to smoke, because it burns bitter faster than any other oil. The basil goes in at the very end, off the heat, and it should still be bright green when the pot reaches the table; anything more than thirty seconds and it turns black.

  • Fry the ginger alone until it curls. That is the depth.
  • Sesame oil must never smoke — it goes bitter instantly.
  • Basil off the heat, thirty seconds, lid on.

item.title: Bavarian Brezel
item.description: Bavarian brezel — lye-dipped pretzels with a fat belly, thin arms and a dark, salted crust.
item.content:encoded:
The pretzel bakers of Bavaria use food-grade lye, which is a stronger alkali than any home substitute; baking bicarbonate of soda in a low oven for an hour drives off carbon dioxide and gets much closer than the raw powder. Chilling the shaped pretzels uncovered dries the surface, and a dry surface is what takes the bath evenly and splits cleanly in the oven.

  • Bake the bicarbonate of soda first, and handle it with gloves.
  • Chill uncovered until the surface is dry. Wet dough takes the bath badly.
  • Thin arms, fat belly. That contrast is the whole shape.

item.title: Salt Baked Chicken
item.description: A Hakka whole chicken wrapped in paper and buried in a pot of hot coarse salt, baked until cooked through and served hand-torn.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is wrapped in paper before it goes into the salt, so almost none of the salt actually reaches the meat — the salt is a heat medium, not a seasoning, and an unwrapped bird comes out inedible. Heat the salt in the empty pot until it is genuinely hot and moving freely before the chicken goes in, because cold salt takes far too long to come up and the bird stews. And the meat is torn by hand rather than carved, which is how it is served in Hakka restaurants and does keep it juicier.

  • Wrap it properly. The salt is heat, not seasoning.
  • Heat the salt until it pours freely before the chicken goes in.
  • Tear it by hand. It stays juicier than carving.

item.title: Da Pan Ji
item.description: A Xinjiang stew of chicken on the bone with potatoes, peppers and beer, spiced with dried chilli and Sichuan pepper, served over wide noodles.
item.content:encoded:
The potatoes are added halfway through and are meant to break down at the edges — they are the thickener, and there is no cornflour in this dish. Cut them in large chunks so they hold some shape while the outsides dissolve into the sauce. The noodles go in only at the very end, underneath the finished stew rather than cooked in it, because noodles simmered in the sauce swell, go soft and drink all the liquid. Beer rather than stock is standard in Xinjiang and it does make a difference.

  • The potatoes are the thickener. Let them break at the edges.
  • Noodles under the stew, never cooked in it.
  • Beer, not stock. It is what Xinjiang uses.

item.title: Braised Beef Brisket
item.description: Cantonese braised beef brisket and tendon with daikon in a chu hou paste and fermented bean curd sauce, cooked three hours.
item.content:encoded:
Buy brisket with the tendon and connective tissue still attached, or ask for a piece of shin alongside — the gelatine those release is what makes the sauce cling, and lean brisket gives a thin, watery braise however long it cooks. The daikon goes in for the last forty minutes only: added at the start it disintegrates completely and turns the sauce cloudy. And blanch the beef first and rinse the pot, because scum trapped in the sauce makes it grey.

  • Brisket with the tendon on. Lean brisket gives a watery sauce.
  • Daikon in for the last forty minutes only.
  • Blanch the beef and wash the pot, or the sauce goes grey.

item.title: Apple Strudel
item.description: Apple strudel — hand-stretched pastry rolled around spiced apples, raisins and buttered breadcrumbs.
item.content:encoded:
Strudel dough is stretched, not rolled, and it can be because it is made with a high-protein flour, a little oil and a long rest that relaxes the gluten completely. The buttered breadcrumb layer under the apples is structural: it absorbs the juice the fruit releases, which is what stops the base going soggy.

  • Rest the dough a full hour. Under-rested dough tears the moment you stretch it.
  • The breadcrumb layer is what keeps the base crisp. Do not skip it.
  • Drain the apples before they go on, or the juice will find its way out.

item.title: Sweet and Sour Spare Ribs
item.description: Shanghai spare ribs braised in black vinegar, Shaoxing wine and rock sugar, then reduced hard until the sauce coats them like lacquer.
item.content:encoded:
Two additions of vinegar, and the second is the whole point. Chinkiang vinegar loses most of its aroma to long cooking, so half goes in at the start for its acidity and half goes in during the final reduction for its smell. Reduce the sauce hard at the end over high heat, turning the ribs constantly — at that stage it goes from syrup to lacquer in about ninety seconds and from lacquer to burnt sugar not long after, so it needs watching rather than a timer.

  • Vinegar in two stages. The second is for the aroma.
  • The last ninety seconds needs watching, not a timer.
  • Just as good at room temperature the next day.

item.title: Steamed Ribs with Black Bean
item.description: Pork ribs cut small, marinated with rinsed fermented black beans, garlic and cornflour, and steamed on a plate until tender.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse the fermented black beans before you use them. They are packed in a great deal of salt and unrinsed they will make the whole plate inedible; a quick rinse leaves the funky, savoury flavour behind and takes the harshness away. The ribs also need to be soaked in cold water for half an hour and dried, which draws out blood and gives the pale, clean-tasting result you get in dim sum restaurants rather than a grey, slightly livery one.

  • Rinse the black beans. Unrinsed they are far too salty.
  • Soak the ribs first — it is what keeps them pale.
  • One layer only on the plate, or the top ones stay raw.

item.title: Sachertorte
item.description: Sachertorte — dense chocolate sponge with apricot jam under a poured chocolate glaze that sets hard.
item.content:encoded:
The glaze is a cooked sugar syrup with chocolate melted into it, not a ganache, which is why it sets to a shell rather than staying soft — and it has to be poured at once, in one pass, because it starts to skin within about a minute. The apricot glaze under it seals the crumb so no cake shows through.

  • One pour, few strokes. Working the glaze leaves streaks that never come out.
  • The apricot layer seals the crumb. Without it, the glaze picks up cake.
  • Set at room temperature, not in the fridge. Cold kills the shine.

item.title: Siu Yuk
item.description: Cantonese roast pork belly: skin pricked and salted, meat seasoned with five-spice, dried overnight and roasted hot until the skin blisters into crackling.
item.content:encoded:
Prick the skin until it is covered in holes — hundreds of them, with a meat pricker or a clean needle — because those holes are where the fat renders out and the steam escapes, and skin without them puffs unevenly into hard bubbles. Then a full day uncovered in the fridge, and salt only on the skin, never the meat side. The oven goes moderate first to cook the meat, then to maximum for the last twenty minutes to blister the skin; the reverse order gives leather over raw pork.

  • Hundreds of holes in the skin, and not one into the meat.
  • A full day uncovered. Damp skin cannot crackle.
  • Moderate first, maximum last.

item.title: Mei Cai Kou Rou
item.description: Hakka steamed pork belly: belly blanched, coloured, fried, sliced and packed skin down over rinsed preserved mustard greens, steamed two hours and inverted.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse and soak the mei cai in several changes of water. It is preserved in a great deal of salt and sand both, and unwashed it is inedible and gritty — thirty minutes and three changes is the minimum. The pork is fried after being coloured with dark soy, and it will spit violently, so use a lid. Packing the slices skin down and steaming for two hours is what lets the fat render into the greens below; the greens are arguably the better half of the dish by the end.

  • Three changes of water on the mei cai. It is salty and gritty.
  • A lid ready when the pork goes in the oil — it spits hard.
  • Skin down in the bowl. It comes out on top.

item.title: Ginger and Scallion Crab
item.description: Cantonese wok-fried crab: crab chopped through the shell, dusted and fried, then tossed with ginger, spring onion and a light wine sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Dust the cut faces of the crab in cornflour before frying. The exposed meat at each cut would otherwise leak straight into the wok and be lost, and the cornflour seals it in and browns into a light crust. Fry the ginger long enough to lose its raw edge — a full minute, until the shreds go pale and fragrant — and add the spring onion at the very end, because it only needs to wilt. The shells go into the wok too, since most of the flavour in the sauce comes from them.

  • Cornflour on every cut face or the meat leaks out.
  • Fry the ginger a full minute before anything else joins it.
  • The shells go in the wok. That is where the sauce comes from.

item.title: Kaiserschmarrn
item.description: Kaiserschmarrn — Austrian shredded pancake torn in the pan and caramelised in butter and sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Whipped egg whites folded in at the end make the batter thick enough to hold its own air, so the torn pieces stay light rather than dense. The sugar goes in only after the tearing: added earlier it burns before the middle sets, added later it caramelises on the torn edges, which is where all the flavour is.

  • Sugar after tearing, not before. Otherwise it burns in the pan.
  • Do not be careful with the flip. Ragged pieces are the point.
  • Serve immediately — it goes soft in about five minutes.

item.title: Steamed Whole Fish
item.description: A whole white fish steamed briefly on ginger and spring onion, dressed with sweetened soy and finished with smoking hot oil poured over raw aromatics.
item.content:encoded:
Everything about this dish is timing: roughly twelve minutes for a fish of about seven hundred grams, and the flesh should be opaque at the bone and no more. The other essential step is pouring off the liquid that collects on the plate before the sauce goes on. That liquid is fishy and slightly bitter, and leaving it in is the single most common reason a home-steamed fish tastes muddier than a restaurant one. Then smoking oil over raw ginger and scallion, which cooks them in place in about two seconds.

  • Twelve minutes for a 700 g fish. Check at the bone.
  • Pour off the collected liquid. It is the usual culprit.
  • Smoking oil over raw shreds, and sauce around the fish, not over it.

item.title: Dry-Fried Green Beans
item.description: Sichuan dry-fried green beans: beans fried until blistered and wrinkled, then wok-tossed with minced pork, ya cai and dried chillies.
item.content:encoded:
The beans must be bone dry before they meet the oil, and they need long enough in it — six or seven minutes — for the skins to shrivel and go leathery. That dehydration concentrates the flavour and is what "dry-frying" means; beans stir-fried for two minutes are simply green beans in a sauce. Ya cai, the Sichuan preserved mustard stem, is the other half and there is no real substitute: it supplies a salty, slightly sour depth that neither the pork nor the chilli can.

  • Bone dry beans, or they steam instead of blistering.
  • Seven minutes of frying. Two minutes is not dry-frying.
  • Ya cai is not optional. It is the savoury depth.

item.title: Cheese Fondue
item.description: Cheese fondue — Gruyère and Vacherin melted into white wine with kirsch, served with bread cubes.
item.content:encoded:
Cheese splits when the fat separates from the protein, and the two defences are acid and starch: an acidic dry wine keeps the proteins dispersed, and cornflour tossed through the grated cheese physically holds the emulsion. Adding the cheese in handfuls, each one melted before the next, is what stops the temperature spiking.

  • Grate the cheese and toss it with cornflour. Cubed cheese melts unevenly and splits.
  • Figure of eight, never circles. It is not superstition, it stops the strands winding up.
  • Day-old bread. Fresh bread falls off the fork.

item.title: Di San Xian
item.description: A north-eastern Chinese dish of potato, aubergine and green pepper fried separately, then combined in a garlic and soy sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the three vegetables separately and in that order. They cook at completely different rates — potato needs several minutes, aubergine drinks oil and collapses, pepper wants barely a minute — and thrown in together you get raw potato with disintegrated aubergine. Salting the aubergine first and pressing it dry also cuts the amount of oil it absorbs by roughly half, which is the difference between this dish being good and being greasy.

  • Fry them separately: potato, aubergine, pepper, in that order.
  • Salt and press the aubergine or it drinks twice the oil.
  • Pepper for forty-five seconds only.

item.title: Stir-Fried Water Spinach
item.description: Water spinach stir-fried very fast with garlic, chilli and fermented white bean curd so the stems stay crisp and the leaves just wilt.
item.content:encoded:
Stems in first, leaves thirty seconds later. Water spinach has hollow stalks that stay crunchy and thin leaves that wilt almost instantly, and adding them together gives you either raw stems or grey leaves. The wok must also be as hot as your hob will manage before anything goes in — this dish is ninety seconds from start to plate and a cool pan makes the greens release water and stew. Fermented white bean curd is the traditional seasoning and does the job of both salt and umami.

  • Stems first, leaves thirty seconds later.
  • A smoking wok. A cool one stews the greens.
  • Onto the plate immediately or it keeps cooking.

item.title: Rösti
item.description: Rösti — grated potato fried slowly in butter until a deep golden crust forms on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Par-boiling the potatoes the day before and chilling them makes the starch retrograde, so the strands stay separate when grated instead of turning to glue. Not pressing the cake down while it cooks is the other half: an untouched rösti steams internally and crisps externally, which is exactly what you want.

  • Par-boil the day before. Same-day potatoes give a gluey rösti.
  • Never press it flat. Pressing squeezes out the air that makes it light.
