  • Medium-low heat for twelve minutes a side. Rushing gives a pale crust and raw middle.

item.title: Home-Style Tofu
item.description: Firm tofu cut in triangles and shallow-fried until golden, then braised with pork belly, doubanjiang, peppers and black beans.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the tofu before it goes anywhere near the sauce. Frying gives it a skin that holds it together through braising and gives the sauce something to cling to, and unfried tofu simply breaks into curds when you stir. Press it dry first and cut it into thick triangles rather than cubes, which gives more surface. And doubanjiang needs frying in the oil until the oil turns red before any liquid arrives — thirty seconds of that is worth more than any amount of simmering.

  • Fry the tofu first. Unfried tofu falls apart in the sauce.
  • Fry the doubanjiang until the oil turns red.
  • Turn gently once the tofu is back in.

item.title: Yong Tau Foo
item.description: Hakka stuffed tofu and vegetables: a beaten fish and pork paste packed into tofu, peppers, aubergine and chillies, pan-fried and simmered in broth.
item.content:encoded:
The fish paste has to be thrown against the side of the bowl repeatedly — twenty or thirty times — until it is elastic enough to hold a shape. That slapping develops the proteins into the springy texture the dish depends on; a paste that is merely stirred stays soft and falls straight out of the pepper in the pan. Dust the inside of each cavity with cornflour before filling as well, which glues the paste to the vegetable at the seam.

  • Throw the paste against the bowl 25 times. That is the spring.
  • Cornflour inside every cavity so the filling grips.
  • Fry the filling side first to seal it.

item.title: Raclette
item.description: Raclette — cheese melted and scraped over boiled potatoes with pickles and cured meats.
item.content:encoded:
Raclette works because the cheese arrives at the plate at the moment it stops being solid and before it starts to split, which is a window of about thirty seconds — so it is served in rounds rather than all at once. Waxy potatoes hold their shape under all that fat where floury ones collapse into it.

  • Waxy potatoes, boiled whole in salty water and kept hot.
  • Melt in rounds, not all at once. Cheese that waits goes oily.
  • Crush the potato before the cheese lands so it soaks in.

item.title: Hot Dry Noodles
item.description: Wuhan re gan mian: alkaline noodles parboiled, oiled and cooled, then reheated and tossed with loosened sesame paste, pickled radish and chilli oil.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles are cooked, oiled and cooled well before they are eaten, which is not a shortcut but the definition of the dish — the cooling firms them so that the second, very brief dip in boiling water leaves them chewy rather than soft. Sesame paste must also be loosened before it goes near the noodles, with warm water or sesame oil, until it pours; straight from the jar it seizes into lumps that never coat anything.

  • Cook, oil and cool the noodles first. That is the dish.
  • Twenty seconds in the boiling water on the second dip.
  • Loosen the sesame paste until it pours, or it will lump.

item.title: Biang Biang Noodles
item.description: Xi'an hand-pulled wide noodles: a rested dough stretched and slapped into belts, boiled, and finished with chilli, garlic and smoking hot oil.
item.content:encoded:
The dough needs two rests, and the second one — oiled, covered, at least an hour — is what makes it stretchable. Gluten that has not relaxed springs back the moment you pull it, and no amount of force will give you a belt; a properly rested dough pulls to a metre with almost no effort. Slapping the strip on the counter as you pull is not showmanship, it uses the dough's own weight to do the stretching. And the oil at the end must genuinely smoke, or the raw garlic and chilli on top stay raw.

  • The second, oiled rest is what makes them pull. Do not skip it.
  • Slap as you pull — the weight does the work.
  • The oil must actually smoke.

item.title: Yangzhou Fried Rice
item.description: The classic Yangzhou fried rice with prawns, char siu, egg and peas, made with cold day-old rice over very high heat.
item.content:encoded:
Day-old refrigerated rice, and there is no way around it. Fresh rice carries too much surface moisture, clumps the moment it hits the wok and steams into a sticky mass; a night uncovered in the fridge dries the outside of each grain. The other technique worth learning is coating the rice in beaten egg before it goes in, so every grain is sealed in yolk — that is what gives the golden, separate grains of proper Yangzhou rice rather than egg in visible lumps.

  • Cold day-old rice, broken up by hand.
  • Coat the rice in beaten egg first. That is the golden grain.
  • Maximum heat and constant tossing once the rice is in.

item.title: Belgian Waffles
item.description: Belgian waffles — yeast-raised Brussels waffles, crisp outside and light inside, dusted with icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
A yeasted batter left to rise makes a waffle that is structurally different from a baking-powder one: the fermentation produces both lift and a slight sourness, and the resulting batter is thin enough to fill the deep pockets completely. Folding in whipped whites at the end gives the hollow, almost brittle interior.

  • Yeast, not baking powder. It is the whole difference in texture.
  • Onto a rack, not a plate. Trapped steam ruins the crust.
  • Wait for the steam to stop before opening the iron.

item.title: Claypot Rice
item.description: Cantonese bo zai fan: rice cooked in a clay pot with marinated chicken and lap cheong, finished over high heat to build a crisp base crust.
item.content:encoded:
The crust — the guo ba — comes from the last few minutes over high heat with oil drizzled down the inside of the pot, and it will not form on low heat however long you wait. Rotate the pot a quarter turn every minute during that stage so the crust builds evenly rather than in one scorched patch. Soak the rice for thirty minutes first, which lets it cook through in the small amount of water this method uses without needing a longer time that would burn the base.

  • Oil down the inside edge and high heat at the end. That is the crust.
  • Turn the pot a quarter turn every minute so it browns evenly.
  • Soak the rice, or the base burns before the grain is done.

item.title: Zongzi
item.description: Savoury zongzi: soaked glutinous rice and marinated pork belly with salted egg yolk, folded into bamboo leaf cones, tied and boiled four hours.
item.content:encoded:
The parcel has to be tied tightly enough to compress the rice but not so tightly that it cannot expand — a loose zongzi lets water in and comes out as porridge, and an over-tight one splits along a seam. Fold a proper cone with no gap at the point, which is where leaks always start. Four hours at a steady simmer is not negotiable either: glutinous rice needs that long to go fully translucent, and undercooked zongzi have a chalky core.

  • No gap at the point of the cone. That is where leaks start.
  • Tie tight enough to compress, loose enough to expand.
  • Four hours. Undercooked glutinous rice has a chalky core.

item.title: Carbonnade Flamande
item.description: Carbonnade flamande — beef braised in Belgian brown ale with onions, thickened by mustard bread.
item.content:encoded:
The slice of bread spread with mustard, laid on top and stirred in at the end, is the traditional thickener and it also carries the mustard through the whole pot without cooking its sharpness away. The brown sugar is not for sweetness so much as balance — Belgian brown ale is bitter, and long reduction concentrates that bitterness.

  • Twenty minutes on the onions. Rushing them leaves the stew bitter.
  • The mustard bread is the thickener. No flour slurry, no cornflour.
  • Taste at the end and adjust sugar against vinegar. That balance is the dish.

item.title: Wood Ear Salad
item.description: Dried wood ear mushrooms soaked, blanched and chilled, dressed with black vinegar, garlic, coriander and chilli oil.
item.content:encoded:
Blanch the soaked wood ear for a full minute and then plunge it into iced water. The blanching removes the faintly muddy taste that soaked-but-raw wood ear carries, and the ice bath is what makes it snap between the teeth rather than feeling rubbery. Soak in cold water rather than hot, over several hours if you can: hot water swells them fast but leaves them slack, and cold-soaked wood ear has noticeably better bite.

  • Cold soak, several hours. Hot water leaves them slack.
  • Blanch a minute, then straight into iced water.
  • Ten minutes in the dressing before it reaches the table.

item.title: Belgian Frites
item.description: Belgian frites — potatoes fried twice, low then hot, for a crisp shell and a fluffy middle.
item.content:encoded:
The first fry at 140C cooks the potato through and drives water out of the surface; the second at 180C sets a glassy shell before the inside can dry out. Doing it in one go at a single temperature gives you either a raw middle or a leathery outside — there is no temperature that does both.

  • Two fries, two temperatures. There is no one-step version of this.
  • Dry the potatoes completely. Wet chips are dangerous and soggy.
  • Salt the moment they come out, while the surface can still take it.

item.title: Hot and Sour Potato Slivers
item.description: Potato cut into fine slivers, rinsed of surface starch, then flash-fried with dried chilli, Sichuan pepper and black vinegar so it stays crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse the cut potato in several changes of cold water until it runs completely clear, then dry it. The surface starch is what makes potato go soft and sticky in a pan, and washed away the slivers stay separate and crunchy through the frying. Cut them as fine and even as you can, ideally on a mandolin then stacked and sliced, because uneven slivers cook unevenly and there is no time to correct it in ninety seconds.

  • Three changes of water until it runs clear.
  • Dry them, or the wok will not stay hot enough.
  • Ninety seconds. They should still crunch.

item.title: West Lake Beef Soup
item.description: A Hangzhou soup of finely minced beef and tofu thickened with cornflour, finished with egg white ribbons and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Blanch the minced beef in water and drain it before it goes in the soup. Beef added raw releases scum and grey particles that cloud the whole pot, and this soup is meant to be translucent — restaurant versions are always blanched first. Add the cornflour before the egg white, because the thickened liquid holds the egg in suspension as long ribbons; in thin broth the egg sinks and clumps. And pour the egg white in a thin stream while stirring in one direction only.

  • Blanch the beef first or the soup goes cloudy.
  • Thicken before the egg white goes in, not after.
  • Pour the egg in a thin stream and stir one way only.

item.title: Stroopwafels
item.description: Stroopwafels — thin waffle discs split while hot and filled with caramel syrup.
item.content:encoded:
The waffle has to be split within seconds of leaving the iron, while the crumb is still soft enough to part cleanly along its middle — let it cool and it shatters instead. The syrup is cooked to a soft caramel just below the hard-ball stage so it stays chewy at room temperature.

  • Split within seconds. A cooled waffle cannot be split, only broken.
  • Keep the syrup warm and pourable throughout, or the filling will not spread.
  • Trim before splitting. Neat edges make the split far easier.

item.title: Egg Drop Soup
item.description: A light Chinese soup of seasoned stock with sweetcorn, thickened with cornflour and finished with beaten egg poured in a thin stream.
item.content:encoded:
The soup must be barely simmering when the egg goes in — a rolling boil shreds it into fragments and a cold soup lets it sink and cloud. Take the pan almost off the heat, pour the beaten egg in the thinnest stream you can manage from a height, and then stop stirring completely for half a minute so the ribbons set. Thicken the soup slightly first with cornflour, which suspends the egg where it lands rather than letting it drift to the bottom.

  • Barely simmering, never boiling, when the egg goes in.
  • Thin stream, from a height, then stop stirring.
  • Thicken first — it holds the ribbons up.

item.title: Winter Melon Soup
item.description: A clear Cantonese soup of winter melon simmered with pork ribs, dried shrimp and dried scallop until the melon turns translucent.
item.content:encoded:
Blanch the pork ribs and then wash the pot before starting properly. Cantonese soups are judged on clarity and the scum released in the first few minutes will cloud the whole thing if it is simmered back in. Add the winter melon in the last twenty minutes only: it is more than ninety-five per cent water, cooks to translucency very quickly, and melon added at the start dissolves entirely and leaves nothing to eat.

  • Blanch the ribs and wash the pot. Clarity is the point.
  • Melon in for the last twenty minutes only.
  • Season at the end — the dried seafood brings its own salt.

item.title: Lotus Root and Pork Rib Soup
item.description: A Hubei soup of pork ribs and lotus root simmered two hours in a clay pot until the root softens and thickens the broth.
item.content:encoded:
Use the fat, starchy variety of lotus root — the one with a powdery cut face rather than a glassy one — because only that kind breaks down and gives the soup its body and the characteristic starchy threads. The crisp variety used for stir-frying stays crunchy however long you cook it, which is a different and much less interesting soup. Two hours at a bare simmer, never a boil, or the broth turns cloudy and the ribs go stringy.

  • The starchy variety of lotus root, not the crisp one.
  • A bare simmer for two hours. Boiling clouds it.
  • The threads when you lift a piece are how you know it is done.

item.title: Bitterballen
item.description: Bitterballen — Dutch beef ragout croquettes, crisp outside and molten inside, with mustard.
item.content:encoded:
The filling is a roux-based ragout taken far thicker than a sauce — thick enough to slice when cold — because it has to hold a shape at room temperature and then liquefy in the fryer. A double crumb is not optional: a single coat splits and the filling escapes into the oil.

  • Thicker than seems reasonable. If it is spreadable when cold, it will burst.
  • Double crumb, always, and chill after coating.
  • Rest two minutes before biting. The filling comes out of the fryer very hot.

item.title: Mantou
item.description: Northern Chinese steamed bread: a simple yeasted dough rolled and cut into buns, proved and steamed until white, smooth and springy.
item.content:encoded:
Roll the dough out and roll it up rather than shaping each bun by hand, because the tight spiral is what gives mantou their dense, layered, faintly chewy crumb rather than the open texture of a bread roll. Knead until the dough is genuinely smooth — ten minutes at least — since any pockmark on the surface will still be there after steaming. And when the time is up, turn the heat off and wait three minutes before lifting the lid: cold air on hot steamed dough makes it wrinkle and collapse.

  • Roll and cut, do not shape by hand. The spiral is the texture.
  • Knead until there are no pockmarks — they survive steaming.
  • Wait three minutes before lifting the lid.

item.title: Shao Bing
item.description: Northern Chinese sesame flatbreads made with a flour and oil roux spread inside the dough for layers, coated in sesame and baked until hollow.
item.content:encoded:
The layers come from you tang — a paste of flour cooked in hot oil — spread inside the rolled dough. Oil alone slides out during shaping and the layers fuse; flour thickens it into a paste that stays put and keeps the leaves separate. The maltose or syrup wash is what makes the sesame stick and gives the deep colour: plain water leaves seeds all over the tray and a pale bread.

  • Flour cooked into the oil, not oil alone. That is what holds the layers.
  • Maltose wash so the sesame sticks and the colour deepens.
  • They should sound hollow when tapped.

item.title: Poffertjes
item.description: Poffertjes — tiny Dutch yeasted buckwheat pancakes with melting butter and icing sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Buckwheat flour is what makes a poffertje taste different from a small pancake — it brings a nutty, slightly bitter note that stands up to all the butter and sugar. The yeast rise gives a spongy, open crumb that a batter raised with baking powder cannot match.

  • Buckwheat is not optional if you want them to taste like poffertjes.
  • Medium-low heat. They should puff rather than sear.
  • Cold butter on hot pancakes, then the sugar. In that order.

item.title: Sichuan Chilli Oil
item.description: Sichuan chilli oil: aromatics infused into oil, which is then poured over coarse chilli flakes in three stages at falling temperatures.
item.content:encoded:
The oil is poured over the chilli in three stages, at three temperatures, and that is the whole technique. The first pour at around 190C toasts and blooms the flakes; the second at 160C extracts the colour; the third at 130C keeps the aroma without cooking it away. One pour at high heat scorches the top layer and leaves the bottom raw, which is exactly what most disappointing homemade chilli oil is. Use coarse flakes, not powder, which burns instantly.

  • Three pours at three temperatures. One pour scorches the top.
  • Coarse flakes, never powder.
  • Keep the sediment. It is most of the flavour.

item.title: XO Sauce
item.description: A Hong Kong relish of dried scallops and shrimp soaked, shredded and slowly fried with chilli, garlic, shallot and cured ham in oil.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is fried separately and at a low temperature — this is a forty-minute job at a lazy sizzle, not a stir-fry. The dried seafood must dehydrate again and go crisp in the oil, which is where the texture comes from, and anything rushed at high heat browns outside while staying leathery inside. Shred the soaked scallops by hand along their natural grain rather than chopping, which gives the fine threads that define the sauce.

  • Low and slow. Forty minutes at a lazy sizzle, not a stir-fry.
  • Shred the scallops by hand along the grain.
  • Keep the solids under the oil in the jar.

item.title: Smørrebrød
item.description: Smørrebrød — Danish open sandwiches on buttered rye with herring, prawns, roast beef or egg.
item.content:encoded:
Butter spread right to the edges is structural rather than decorative — it waterproofs the rye against wet toppings, which is why a smørrebrød holds together for the twenty minutes it takes to eat. Each one is built around a single idea, and the garnishes are there to sharpen it, not to add a second idea.

  • Butter to the very edge. Nothing else keeps the rye from going soft.
  • One idea per slice. Two competing toppings make a mess, not a smørrebrød.
  • Build them within half an hour of eating.

item.title: Red Bean Soup
item.description: A Cantonese sweet soup of adzuki beans simmered until collapsed with rock sugar and dried tangerine peel, served warm or chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Sugar goes in at the end, never at the start. Sugar in the cooking water slows the beans down dramatically — it draws water out of them by osmosis — and beans cooked in sweetened liquid can simmer for hours and still be firm. Cook them in plain water until they collapse, then sweeten. Dried tangerine peel is the traditional aromatic and it does more than it looks like it should: soak it and scrape the bitter white pith off the inside first.

  • Sugar at the end. Early sugar stops the beans softening.
  • Scrape the pith from the tangerine peel or it turns bitter.
  • Crush some of the beans to thicken it.

item.title: Mango Pomelo Sago
item.description: A chilled Hong Kong dessert of mango purée and coconut milk with sago pearls and pomelo segments folded through.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the sago until the pearls are entirely translucent with no white dot at the centre, then rinse them under cold running water until the water runs clear. That rinse removes the loose surface starch that would otherwise make the whole dessert gluey within an hour. Pomelo, not grapefruit — pomelo segments separate into dry, firm beads that stay separate, while grapefruit collapses and releases juice that turns the purée bitter.

  • No white dot left in the sago pearls.
  • Rinse the sago until the water runs clear or it goes gluey.
  • Pomelo, not grapefruit. Grapefruit collapses and turns it bitter.

item.title: Danish Pastries
item.description: Danish pastries — laminated yeast dough folded three times, filled with custard and baked golden.
item.content:encoded:
Lamination is a temperature discipline before it is a technique: the butter must stay cold enough to remain a sheet but pliable enough to bend, which in practice means chilling between every single fold. Warm butter absorbs into the dough and you get a sweet bread instead of layers.

  • Chill between every fold, without exception.
  • If butter starts breaking through the dough, stop and refrigerate for 20 minutes.
  • Prove until they wobble when you shake the tray. Under-proved pastries leak butter.

item.title: Eight Treasure Rice
item.description: A Chinese celebration pudding of sweetened glutinous rice moulded around red bean paste in a bowl lined with dried and candied fruits, steamed and inverted.
item.content:encoded:
Oil the bowl heavily before the fruit goes in, and lay the fruit face down in the pattern you want to see — it comes out inverted, so what touches the bowl ends up on top. Glutinous rice sticks ferociously and a poorly oiled bowl will leave half your design behind. Press the rice firmly but do not compact it into a solid mass; it needs to hold together while still having some give when it is turned out.

  • Oil the bowl heavily and lay the fruit face down.
  • Press the rice firmly but do not compact it solid.
  • Run a knife round the edge before inverting.

item.title: Sesame Balls
item.description: Chinese fried glutinous rice balls filled with red bean paste, rolled in sesame seeds and fried slowly from cold oil so they expand hollow.
item.content:encoded:
Start them in oil that is only moderately warm and bring the heat up slowly, pressing each ball gently against the side of the pan with a slotted spoon as it fries. The gentle pressure and the slow temperature rise are what make them expand hollow; dropped into hot oil they set their skin immediately and stay small and dense. Roll them in sesame seeds over a damp hand so the seeds stick, and press the seeds in firmly or they detach in the oil.

  • Start in moderately warm oil and raise the heat slowly.
  • Press each ball against the pan as it fries. That is what hollows them.
  • Wet the surface before the sesame, and press the seeds in hard.

item.title: Frikadeller
item.description: Frikadeller — Danish pork and veal meatballs fried in butter, with potatoes and pickled cucumber.
item.content:encoded:
The mince is beaten rather than folded, for several minutes, until it becomes sticky and pale — that developed protein is what holds the meatball together without egg doing all the work, and what gives frikadeller their springy bite. Resting the mixture in the fridge lets the breadcrumbs finish absorbing the milk.

  • Beat the mixture until it changes colour. Gentle mixing gives crumbly meatballs.
  • Two wet spoons make the traditional oval shape and stop the mince sticking.
  • Medium heat and real butter. Rushed frikadeller are dark outside and pink inside.

item.title: Hong Kong Egg Waffle
item.description: Hong Kong gai daan jai: a custard-scented batter with custard powder and evaporated milk baked in a spherical waffle iron until crisp outside and soft inside.
item.content:encoded:
Rest the batter for at least an hour, which lets the flour hydrate and gives the smooth, custardy interior the bubbles are meant to have; unrested batter cooks up chewy. The iron has to be genuinely hot and generously oiled on both plates before the batter goes in, and it is flipped almost immediately and repeatedly, which is what forces the batter into the spheres. Tapioca starch in the mix is what keeps the outside crisp rather than going soft within a minute.

  • An hour of resting. Unrested batter cooks up chewy.
  • Oil both plates and flip immediately, then keep turning.
  • Cool on a rack for a minute — that is when it crisps.

item.title: Paneer Butter Masala
item.description: North Indian paneer in a smooth tomato, cashew and butter gravy, simmered and blended, finished with cream and crushed fenugreek leaf.
item.content:encoded:
The gravy is blended and then strained, and the straining is the step people skip. Cashew and tomato skin leave grit no amount of blending removes, and a restaurant gravy is smooth in a way a home one usually is not — passing it through a sieve is the whole difference. Add the cream off the heat: boiled cream splits in an acidic tomato base, and the sauce goes grainy in a way you cannot bring back.

  • Sieve the gravy — that is what makes it taste like the restaurant.
  • Cream goes in off the heat or it splits.
  • Soak shop-bought paneer in hot water for 10 minutes and it softens.

item.title: Norwegian Fish Soup
item.description: Norwegian fish soup — salmon and white fish poached in a creamy root vegetable and dill broth.
item.content:encoded:
Nordic fish soups almost always carry a little vinegar or lemon, because cream and fish together go flat very quickly without acid to lift them. The fish goes in off the heat and finishes in the residual warmth, which keeps salmon at the point where it flakes but has not gone chalky.

  • Fish off the heat. Simmering it turns salmon dry and breaks the white fish up.
  • Vinegar at the end. Without it the soup tastes heavy.
  • Cut all the root vegetables to the same small dice so they cook evenly.

item.title: Matar Paneer
item.description: Paneer cubes and green peas simmered in a north Indian onion, tomato and ginger gravy with garam masala.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the onion paste until the oil separates and pools at the edge of the pan. That is not a garnish, it is the signal that the water has gone and the sugars have caught — before it, the gravy tastes raw and sharp; after it, sweet and round. It takes about eight minutes and there is no shortcut. Frozen peas go in near the end: they need three minutes, and twelve turns them grey.

  • Wait for the oil to separate before you add water.
  • Peas at the end, not the beginning.
  • Slit the chillies rather than chopping them, and they season without burning.

item.title: Kadai Paneer
item.description: Paneer and peppers cooked in a kadai with a coarsely ground coriander seed and dried chilli masala, finished with ginger julienne.
item.content:encoded:
The masala is pounded, not powdered. Coriander seeds and dried chillies crushed coarsely in a mortar give bursts of flavour you bite into; the same spices bought ready-ground disappear into the sauce and taste flat. Grind them yourself and stop while the pieces are still visible. The peppers want high heat and about four minutes — they should still snap.

  • Pound the masala coarse. Powder tastes like a different dish.
  • Blister the peppers separately and add them back at the end.
  • Keep a third of the masala for the finish so it stays fragrant.

item.title: Paneer Bhurji
item.description: Crumbled paneer cooked with onion, tomato, turmeric and green chilli into a soft scramble, finished with coriander and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Crumble the paneer by hand rather than grating it. Grated paneer is uniform and turns pasty; hand-crumbled gives you pieces of three or four different sizes, which is what makes it read as a scramble rather than a paste. Add it at the very end and give it two minutes — paneer cooked longer than that squeaks and tightens.

  • Crumble by hand for uneven pieces.
  • Two minutes for the paneer, no more.
  • The lemon at the end is not optional — it lifts the whole thing.

item.title: Krumkake
item.description: Krumkake — thin patterned Norwegian waffle cookies rolled into cones while hot.
item.content:encoded:
The batter is deliberately high in butter and low in liquid so the cookie crisps as it cools rather than staying leathery. The window for rolling is about eight seconds — after that the sugar has set and the cookie will crack rather than curl — so the cone form has to be in your hand before you open the iron.

  • Roll within eight seconds or it will crack. Have the cone in your hand.
  • One tablespoon per cookie. Too much batter squeezes out and blurs the pattern.
  • Fill at the table. Cream softens them within minutes.

item.title: Chilli Paneer
item.description: Paneer in a cornflour batter, fried and tossed with peppers, onion and a soy, vinegar and chilli sauce thickened to a gloss.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is thickened with a cornflour slurry added at the very end, off a rolling boil, and it must go in while the pan is moving. Poured into a still pan it seizes into lumps that never disperse. The other rule is speed: once the fried paneer meets the sauce you have about ninety seconds before the crust softens, so have everything cut and measured before the wok goes on.

  • Slurry into a moving pan, never a still one.
  • Everything cut before the wok goes on.
  • Serve within a minute or the crust goes soft.

item.title: Gobi Manchurian
item.description: Cauliflower florets in a cornflour batter, deep fried and tossed in a garlic, ginger, soy and chilli sauce with spring onions.
item.content:encoded:
Blanch the florets for two minutes before battering. Raw cauliflower needs longer in the fryer than the batter can survive, so you end up with a dark crust around a hard centre; blanched, both are ready together. Drain them properly and dry them on a cloth, because a wet floret slides out of its batter in the oil.

  • Blanch first, then batter. It is the whole trick.
  • Dry the florets or the batter slides off.
  • A rack, not paper, so the underside stays crisp.

item.title: Karelian Pies
item.description: Karelian pies — thin rye shells filled with rice porridge, baked hot and topped with egg butter.
item.content:encoded:
The rye shell is rolled almost translucent and baked at a very high temperature so it blisters and cooks before it can dry out — a thicker shell or a cooler oven gives something closer to a biscuit. Brushing them with buttered milk the moment they come out softens the rye edge just enough to bite through.

  • The hottest oven you have, with the tray preheated.
  • Roll the shells thin enough to be translucent. This is the whole texture.
  • Cold filling on the dough. Warm porridge makes the shell soggy before it bakes.

item.title: Hakka Noodles
item.description: Boiled egg noodles stir-fried with shredded cabbage, carrot and pepper in soy and vinegar over a high heat.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the noodles a minute short, rinse them cold and toss them in a teaspoon of oil. Noodles that go into the wok hot and wet steam rather than fry, and they clump into a single mass. Cold, oiled and slightly under, they separate and take the heat. Shred everything the same thickness as the noodles so a forkful is one texture.

  • Cold, oiled noodles or they clump.
  • Shred the vegetables noodle-thin.
  • The highest heat your hob has, and keep everything moving.

item.title: Schezwan Fried Rice
item.description: Cold cooked rice stir-fried with vegetables and a garlic and dried chilli schezwan sauce over a high flame.
item.content:encoded:
The rice must be cold and at least a few hours old. Fresh rice is still full of surface moisture and steams into a sticky mass the moment it meets a hot wok; refrigerated overnight, the grains dry and firm and they fry into separate pieces. If you have only fresh rice, spread it on a tray and refrigerate it uncovered for an hour.

  • Day-old rice, or an hour uncovered in the fridge.
  • Fry the schezwan sauce for half a minute before the rice goes in.
  • Press and lift rather than stir, so the grains catch.

item.title: Lohikeitto
item.description: Lohikeitto — Finnish salmon soup with potatoes, leek, cream and a great deal of dill.
item.content:encoded:
Lohikeitto is a clean soup, not a chowder, so there is no roux and no thickener — the body comes from potato starch and cream alone. The salmon skin and bones simmered in the stock at the start put back the gelatine that a fillet-only soup lacks, and are lifted out before serving.

  • Salmon off the heat, six minutes. Simmering it wastes good fish.
  • Use the skin and bones for the stock. It is the difference between good and very good.
  • Twice as much dill as you think. It is a defining flavour, not a garnish.

item.title: Chicken Lollipop
item.description: Chicken wing drumettes shaped into lollipops, marinated in ginger, garlic and chilli, coated in cornflour and deep fried.
item.content:encoded:
Frenching the wing is what makes it a lollipop and it takes a knife and thirty seconds each: cut through the tendons at the narrow end, then push the meat down the bone into a ball. Do it before you marinate, not after, because the marinade makes the meat slippery. Fry twice — five minutes to cook through, a two-minute rest, then ninety seconds hot for the crust.

  • French the wings before marinating, not after.
  • Two fries: one to cook, one to crisp.
  • Wrap the bone ends in foil if you are serving them by hand.

item.title: Chicken Chettinad
item.description: Tamil chicken curry in a freshly roasted masala of coconut, black pepper, fennel and dried chillies, with curry leaves.
item.content:encoded:
Every spice is roasted dry and ground for the dish, and that is not fussiness — the fennel, pepper and coconut all turn from raw to nutty at different moments, so they go into the pan in stages and come out together. The coconut goes last and needs about ninety seconds; take it past golden and the whole masala turns bitter and there is no rescuing it.

  • Coconut goes in last and comes out pale gold.
  • Grind the masala for this dish, not from a jar.
  • Bone-in chicken — the bones carry the flavour into the gravy.

item.title: Prinsesstårta
item.description: Prinsesstårta — Swedish sponge with jam, pastry cream and a cream dome under green marzipan.
item.content:encoded:
The dome is what makes the marzipan lie smooth: a flat-topped cake gives you folds and cracks at the corners, while a high, evenly rounded mound of firmly whipped cream lets the marzipan stretch over it in one piece. Chilling the assembled dome until firm before covering it is what stops the whole thing slumping.

  • Firm peaks on the cream. Soft cream cannot hold a dome under marzipan.
  • Chill hard before covering. Two hours minimum.
  • Smooth the marzipan from the top down and outwards, never sideways.

item.title: Mutton Curry
item.description: Bone-in mutton or lamb slow-cooked in a browned onion and whole spice gravy with ginger, garlic and garam masala.
item.content:encoded:
Brown the meat in batches and let each batch sit still for two minutes before turning it. Crowded, mutton releases water and boils grey; given room and stillness, it takes a crust that dissolves into the gravy and is most of what makes it dark. The onions want ten minutes of their own, past golden to genuinely brown, and that is where the sweetness comes from.

  • Brown in batches and leave it alone between turns.
  • Onions to brown, not gold — that is ten minutes at least.
  • Rest it off the heat before serving; the gravy settles.

item.title: Egg Curry
item.description: Hard-boiled eggs simmered in a north Indian onion, tomato and ginger gravy, the eggs fried in turmeric first.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the peeled eggs in turmeric and chilli for two minutes before they go into the gravy. It blisters the surface slightly, which gives the sauce something to hold onto — eggs dropped in smooth sit in the gravy rather than taking it up. Add them whole and halve them in the pan at the end, so the yolks stay put.

  • Nine minutes gives a set yolk that still has colour.
  • Blister the eggs in spiced oil before they meet the gravy.
  • Halve them in the pan at the end so the yolks stay whole.

item.title: Egg Bhurji
item.description: Eggs scrambled with onion, tomato, turmeric and green chilli over a brisk heat, finished with coriander.
item.content:encoded:
This is not a French scramble and low slow heat ruins it. The onion needs to catch at the edges and the egg wants to set in curds, not a custard, so keep the pan hot and move the spoon less than you think. Beat the eggs with salt only when the pan is already hot — salted early, they thin and weep.

  • Hot pan, few stirs, curds rather than custard.
  • Salt the eggs as they go in, not before.
  • Off the heat while it still looks underdone.

item.title: Toast Skagen
item.description: Toast Skagen — prawns in dill mayonnaise on butter-fried bread, topped with roe.
item.content:encoded:
The dressing has to be looser and sharper than a standard prawn cocktail, because the fried bread underneath is rich — mayonnaise cut with crème fraîche and a real quantity of lemon is what keeps it from being cloying. Frying the bread in butter rather than toasting it gives an edge that stays crisp under the wet topping for the few minutes it needs to.

  • Dry the prawns properly. It is the single biggest thing.
  • Fry the bread in butter, do not toast it. Different texture entirely.
  • Assemble at the last moment and serve within two minutes.

item.title: Prawn Masala
item.description: Prawns simmered briefly in a south Indian onion, tomato and curry leaf masala with mustard seeds and coconut.
item.content:encoded:
Make the whole gravy before the prawns go anywhere near it. Prawns need three to four minutes and are ruined by six, so the sauce has to be finished and tasted first — then the prawns go in, the pan comes off, and the residual heat does the rest. A prawn that has gone rubbery cannot be brought back.

  • Finish and taste the gravy before the prawns go in.
  • Three minutes for the prawns, then off the heat.
  • Coconut oil rather than vegetable — it is half the flavour.

item.title: Bigos
item.description: Bigos — Polish hunter's stew of sauerkraut, fresh cabbage, mixed pork, dried mushrooms and prunes.
item.content:encoded:
Bigos is a dish that is genuinely better on the third day, because the sauerkraut needs that long to stop tasting sour and start tasting savoury. Using both sauerkraut and fresh cabbage is not padding: the fresh cabbage sweetens as it breaks down and balances the pickle.

  • Make it three days before you want to eat it. This is not an exaggeration.
  • Both cabbages. Sauerkraut alone is too sour, fresh alone is too flat.
  • Reduce it at the end. Bigos should coat, not slosh.

item.title: Khichdi
item.description: Rice and split yellow moong dal cooked together with turmeric, cumin and ghee to a soft, savoury porridge.
item.content:encoded:
Roast the moong dal dry for two minutes before it meets the rice. It is a small step that turns the whole dish from bland to nutty, and it is the difference between khichdi as invalid food and khichdi as something you would choose. The ratio matters too: one part dal to one part rice, and five parts water, gives the soft-set texture. Less water gives you pilaf.

  • Dry-roast the dal. It is two minutes and it changes everything.
  • Five parts water to one of grain, for softness.
  • A spoon of ghee poured over at the table, not stirred in earlier.

item.title: Vegetable Biryani
item.description: Layered vegetable biryani with basmati parboiled to seventy per cent, saffron milk, fried onions and a sealed dum steam.
item.content:encoded:
The rice is boiled to seventy per cent and not a grain more. It finishes in the steam of the sealed pot, and rice that went in fully cooked comes out as paste. Test by pressing a grain: it should break into three with a hard white core still visible. Seal the lid with foil or dough — the steam is the cooking, and a lid that lets it out gives you dry rice on top and wet underneath.

  • Seventy per cent rice: it breaks in three with a white core.
  • Seal with foil under the lid or the steam escapes.
  • Lift to serve, never stir, or the grains break.

item.title: Poha
item.description: Flattened rice rinsed and steamed briefly with mustard seeds, curry leaves, turmeric, onion and roasted peanuts.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse the poha in a sieve under running water for about fifteen seconds and then leave it alone. It carries on absorbing while it stands, so poha that felt right in the sieve is right in the pan five minutes later; poha soaked in a bowl turns to porridge. Use thick poha — the thin sort dissolves whatever you do.

  • Rinse in a sieve, never soak in a bowl.
  • Thick poha only.
  • Fold rather than stir, or it turns to mush.

item.title: Żurek
item.description: Żurek — Polish sour rye soup with white sausage, potato, marjoram and boiled egg.
item.content:encoded:
The soup is defined by zakwas, a rye flour starter fermented for five days — it is what makes żurek sour in a lactic, bready way that vinegar cannot imitate. The starter is stirred in off the boil, because boiling it flattens the sourness and can make it separate.

  • Make the zakwas. Vinegar żurek is a different, lesser soup.
  • Never boil after the starter and cream go in.
  • Crush the dried marjoram between your palms to wake it up.

item.title: Upma
item.description: Roasted coarse semolina cooked with mustard seeds, urad dal, curry leaves and vegetables into a soft savoury porridge.
item.content:encoded:
Roast the semolina dry until it smells like toast and no longer sticks together, then let it cool before it meets the water. Unroasted semolina turns gluey; roasted, the grains stay separate. Pour the semolina into boiling water in a thin stream with the other hand stirring, or you get lumps you will never break up.

  • Roast the semolina and cool it before it meets water.
  • Thin stream in, constant stirring, no lumps.
  • Rest covered for five minutes — it finishes swelling.

item.title: Medu Vada
item.description: Ground urad dal batter beaten until aerated, shaped into rings and deep fried until crisp outside and soft within.
item.content:encoded:
Grind the dal with as little water as you can bear and then beat the batter hard for five minutes, lifting it as you go. The beating is the whole recipe: it whips air into the batter, and a spoonful dropped into water should float. Batter that sinks makes heavy, oily vada no matter how hot the oil is. Wet hands, not floured, for shaping.

  • The float test decides whether they will be light.
  • As little water as possible in the grinding.
  • Wet hands for shaping, and work quickly.

item.title: Svíčková
item.description: Svíčková — Czech beef pot roast with a blended root vegetable cream sauce and bread dumplings.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is the dish: the root vegetables that cooked under the beef are blended into it, which is why it needs no flour and tastes sweet and savoury at once. A splash of vinegar and a spoonful of cranberry at the end are traditional and necessary — the cream and root vegetables are sweet enough to need cutting.

  • Lard the beef. It is the difference between moist and dry after two hours.
  • Blend the vegetables into the sauce — that is the thickener.
  • Balance with vinegar and sugar at the end, tasting as you go.

item.title: Uttapam
item.description: Fermented rice and urad dal batter poured thick and topped with onion, tomato and chilli, cooked on one side then flipped.
item.content:encoded:
Uttapam wants batter a day past its best — slightly sour and slightly thicker than dosa batter, which is exactly what a dosa cook throws away. Put the toppings on the raw upper surface and press them in with the back of a spoon; scattered on loose, they fall off at the flip. One flip only, and thirty seconds on the second side.

  • Day-old batter is better than fresh here.
  • Press the toppings in or they fall off.
  • Thirty seconds on the second side, no more.

item.title: Vegetable Momos
item.description: Nepalese steamed dumplings filled with finely chopped cabbage, carrot and spring onion, pleated and served with tomato achar.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the shredded cabbage and let it stand fifteen minutes, then wring it out in a cloth. Cabbage is mostly water and the filling turns the wrapper to paste from the inside if you skip this — you will be surprised how much comes out. The wrapper is rolled thin at the edge and left thicker in the middle, so the pleats seal and the base does not tear.

  • Wring the cabbage out or the filling floods the wrapper.
  • Thin at the edge, thicker in the middle.
  • Stand a minute after steaming before you lift them.

item.title: Jjajangmyeon
item.description: Korean noodles in a fried black bean sauce with pork belly, onion, courgette and potato, thickened and served with cucumber.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the chunjang paste in oil on its own for two full minutes before anything else goes in. Straight from the tub it is bitter and raw and tastes faintly of ash; fried, it turns sweet, glossy and about two shades darker. Every recipe that skips this makes a sauce people describe as "bitter" without knowing why. Fry it in more oil than feels sensible, then pour the excess off.

  • Fry the chunjang alone for two minutes. It is the whole dish.
  • Dice everything the same size so it cooks together.
  • Serve the sauce on top and let people mix it themselves.

item.title: Trdelník
item.description: Trdelník — Czech spit cake of sweet dough rolled in sugar and walnuts and turned until caramelised.
item.content:encoded:
The sugar coating goes on before cooking, not after: as the dough turns, that sugar melts and then caramelises into a thin glassy shell, which is what gives trdelník its crunch against a soft interior. Overlapping the dough spiral by only a couple of millimetres keeps the shape hollow instead of solid.

  • Sugar before cooking, not after. That caramel shell is the point.
  • Overlap the spiral by millimetres, not centimetres, or the middle stays raw.
  • Roll the wound spit on the worktop to seal the seams.

item.title: Kimchi Fried Rice
item.description: Cold rice stir-fried with aged kimchi, gochujang and sesame oil, topped with a fried egg and seaweed.
item.content:encoded:
Use kimchi that has gone properly sour — the fizzing, three-weeks-open kind that is no longer pleasant to eat raw. Fresh kimchi is crunchy and mild and makes a fried rice that tastes of not much; sour kimchi has developed the acidity and depth the dish is built on. Fry the kimchi in oil for three minutes on its own before the rice, and use its juice too.

  • Sour kimchi, not fresh. Three weeks open is right.
  • Use the juice — it is half the seasoning.
  • Cold rice, pressed and lifted rather than stirred.

item.title: Budae Jjigae
item.description: Korean stew of kimchi, gochujang broth, sausages, tinned luncheon meat, tofu and instant noodles, cooked at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles go in for the last three minutes and not a moment sooner. They are there to be eaten from the pan while still springy, and a block that has sat in the broth for ten minutes turns to sludge and thickens everything around it. Arrange the ingredients in wedges rather than stirring them in, so each person can see what they are taking.

  • Noodles in for the last three minutes only.
  • Arrange in wedges rather than stirring.
  • The cheese is not a joke — it rounds off the chilli.

item.title: Pelmeni
item.description: Pelmeni — small Siberian dumplings with a thin wrapper and raw meat filling, boiled and buttered.
item.content:encoded:
The filling goes in raw with a splash of iced water worked into it, which turns to steam inside the sealed dumpling and gives the juicy interior that cooked-filling dumplings never have. The wrapper is rolled very thin and the dumplings are small, so the meat cooks through in the four minutes the pasta needs.

  • Iced water beaten into the raw filling. It is what makes them juicy.
  • Press every bit of air out before sealing, or they burst.
  • Freeze them on the tray first, then bag. They cook straight from frozen.

item.title: Doenjang Jjigae
item.description: Korean fermented soybean paste stew with courgette, potato, tofu and green chilli in an anchovy and kelp broth.
item.content:encoded:
Dissolve the doenjang in a ladleful of hot broth before it goes into the pot. Spooned in as a lump it never fully disperses — you get salty pockets and a bland broth, and stirring harder only breaks up the tofu. Make the broth with dried anchovy and kelp if you can; it takes ten minutes and is what separates this from a bowl of salty water.

  • Dissolve the paste in broth first, never spoon it in whole.
  • Anchovy and kelp broth takes ten minutes and doubles the dish.
  • Add tofu last and stop stirring once it is in.

item.title: Gyeranjjim
item.description: Korean steamed egg custard whisked with stock and salt, cooked in an earthenware pot until risen and softly set.
item.content:encoded:
The ratio is one and a half parts liquid to one part egg by volume, and it decides everything: less and you get a rubbery omelette, more and it will not set. Strain the mixture — the chalazae, those white cords attached to the yolk, will not break down and show as threads in the finished custard. Cover for the first half so the surface sets before the middle rises.

  • One and a half parts liquid to one of egg.
  • Sieve it, or you will find white threads.
  • Stir for the first three minutes, then leave it entirely alone.

item.title: Bossam
item.description: Whole pork belly simmered with doenjang, ginger and coffee, rested, sliced and served with lettuce, ssamjang and radish salad.
item.content:encoded:
Rest the belly wrapped in foil for fifteen minutes before slicing. Straight from the pot the fat is molten and the slices fall apart under the knife; rested, the collagen firms just enough to hold. A spoonful of instant coffee in the water is a standard Korean trick — it does not taste of coffee, it takes the porkiness off and darkens the meat.

  • Rest wrapped for fifteen minutes or it will not slice.
  • The coffee is for colour and cleanness, not flavour.
  • Slice thin — thick bossam is heavy.

item.title: Chicken Paprikash
item.description: Chicken paprikash — chicken braised with onions and sweet Hungarian paprika, finished with soured cream.
item.content:encoded:
Paprika burns at a surprisingly low temperature and turns bitter, which is why it goes into the pan off the heat, stirred into hot fat and onions with the burner switched off. Tempering the soured cream with hot sauce before it goes back in is what stops it curdling into threads.

  • Heat off before the paprika goes in. Burnt paprika ruins the whole pot.
  • Fifteen minutes on the onions. They are the body of the sauce.
  • Temper the soured cream. Straight from the tub it will split.

item.title: Hotteok
item.description: Yeasted Korean pancakes filled with brown sugar, cinnamon and peanuts, pressed flat and fried until the filling liquefies.
item.content:encoded:
The filling turns to molten syrup at about 150C and will burn a mouth badly, so these want three or four minutes standing before anyone bites one. Press them with an oiled spatula or the bottom of a cup rather than your hand, and press once firmly rather than repeatedly — repeated pressing splits the seam and the syrup escapes into the pan.

  • Seal the parcel completely or the syrup runs out.
  • One firm press, not several.
  • Four minutes standing. The filling is hotter than it looks.

item.title: Lángos
item.description: Lángos — Hungarian deep-fried flatbread rubbed with garlic and topped with soured cream and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
A little mashed potato in the dough is the market-stall trick: it holds moisture, so the lángos stays soft for longer instead of turning leathery within minutes. Stretching the middle thinner than the edges gives the classic shape — a puffed rim around a crisp centre that holds the toppings.

  • Potato in the dough. It is what keeps a lángos soft.
  • Thin middle, thick rim. Stretch, do not roll.
  • Garlic water goes on while it is still hot from the oil.

item.title: Tonkatsu
item.description: Pork loin scored, breaded in flour, egg and panko and deep fried at 170C, rested and sliced, with tonkatsu sauce and shredded cabbage.
item.content:encoded:
Score through the line of fat and sinew that runs round the edge of a pork loin, every two centimetres. Left whole it contracts in the oil and curls the cutlet into a dome, so the middle never touches the fat and cooks unevenly. Fry at 170C, which is lower than instinct says: panko browns fast and pork loin this thick needs six minutes to come through.

  • Score the edge or the cutlet curls.
  • 170C, not hotter — the crust will be ahead of the meat otherwise.
  • Rest on a rack standing on edge, so the underside stays crisp.

item.title: Onigiri
item.description: Seasoned short-grain rice shaped into triangles around salmon or tuna filling and wrapped in toasted nori.
item.content:encoded:
Shape them while the rice is hot enough to be uncomfortable — around 60C. Cool rice has lost the surface starch that makes the grains hold together and an onigiri made from it falls apart in the hand. Wet your palms and salt them; the salt seasons the outside, which is the only part that gets any, and stops the rice sticking.

  • Shape hot, around sixty degrees.
  • Wet, salted palms every single time.
  • Wrap the nori just before eating if you want it crisp.

item.title: Shoyu Ramen
item.description: Clear chicken and kombu broth with a soy tare, rolled chashu pork, marinated egg and thin ramen noodles.
item.content:encoded:
Shoyu ramen is a clear soup and clarity is the whole discipline: it must never boil once the bones are in. A bare shiver at the surface for ninety minutes gives a broth you can see the bottom of; one hard boil emulsifies the fat and it turns cloudy and cannot be brought back. Skim in the first ten minutes, when the grey scum rises.

  • Never let it boil. That is the entire technique.
  • Skim hard in the first ten minutes.
  • Strain without pressing, or you undo the clarity.

item.title: Sarmale
item.description: Sarmale — Romanian cabbage rolls of pork, rice and dill cooked slowly with smoked meat.
item.content:encoded:
Pickled cabbage rather than fresh is what makes these Romanian rather than generic stuffed cabbage — the sourness cuts the fat and seasons the pork from the outside in. Layering smoked ribs or bacon between the rolls sends smoke through the whole pot as it cooks, which no amount of paprika replicates.

  • Pickled cabbage, not fresh. It is the defining ingredient.
  • Roll firmly but leave the rice room to swell.
  • A plate on top keeps the rolls submerged and stops them unravelling.

item.title: Ebi Fry
item.description: King prawns scored along the belly to keep them straight, breaded in panko and deep fried, served with tartare sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Prawns curl in hot oil because the muscle on the belly side contracts more than the back. Three or four shallow cuts across the underside sever that muscle, and then a firm press to straighten before breading — after which they stay straight through the fryer. It is the difference between a prawn that looks like a restaurant made it and one that looks like a comma.

  • Three cuts and a firm press, or they curl.
  • 180C and two and a half minutes — prawns need very little.
  • Tails on, for something to hold.

item.title: Japanese Curry Roux
item.description: A homemade Japanese curry roux of butter, flour, curry powder and garam masala cooked to a nut-brown paste, then made into sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The roux is cooked for twenty minutes over a low heat, which is far longer than a French one, and the colour goes from pale to the shade of peanut butter. That browning is where Japanese curry gets its particular round, almost sweet depth. Take it further and it turns bitter; stop early and the sauce tastes of raw flour, which is the fault of nearly every homemade version.

  • Twenty minutes for the roux. Peanut-butter colour is the target.
  • Loosen the roux with hot stock before it goes into the pan.
  • The grated apple is standard and it is what rounds the edges.

item.title: Mici
item.description: Mici — Romanian skinless grilled sausages of beef and lamb with garlic and a springy texture.
item.content:encoded:
The bounce that defines mici comes from two things: bicarbonate of soda, which raises the pH so the proteins hold more water, and beating cold stock into the mince until it is emulsified and tacky. Both need an overnight rest in the fridge to take effect, which is why same-day mici are always disappointing.

  • Overnight in the fridge. Without it there is no spring.
  • Beat the stock in properly until the mince turns tacky.
  • Very hot coals. Mici want char, not a gentle cook.

item.title: Panang Curry
item.description: Thai panang curry of beef or chicken simmered in a thick coconut and peanut curry paste, finished with kaffir lime leaf.
item.content:encoded:
Crack the coconut cream first: fry the thick top of the tin, without the watery part, until the oil separates and pools. Then fry the paste in that oil for two minutes. Nearly every home version tips paste and liquid in together and produces a thin curry with a flat, raw edge — the separated oil is what carries the spice and gives panang its gloss.

  • Crack the cream before the paste goes in.
  • Panang is thick — do not thin it out with stock.
  • Shredded lime leaf at the end, not cooked in.

item.title: Moo Ping
item.description: Thai grilled pork skewers marinated in coconut milk, garlic, white pepper and palm sugar, basted while grilling.
item.content:encoded:
The coconut milk in the marinade is not for flavour so much as for basting — it keeps the surface from drying while the sugar caramelises, and it is why moo ping comes off the grill glossy rather than leathery. Baste every time you turn them. White pepper rather than black is the Thai signature and tastes distinctly different: floral and hot rather than woody.

  • Baste at every turn — that is what makes them glossy.
  • White pepper, not black. It is a different flavour.
  • Weave the meat so it lies flat and cooks evenly.

item.title: Adjaruli Khachapuri
item.description: Adjaruli khachapuri — a Georgian bread boat of molten cheese finished with an egg yolk and butter.
item.content:encoded:
The cheese blend matters more than the dough: sulguni alone is stringy and mild, so it is cut with a salty brined cheese and a little mozzarella for pull. The yolk goes in during the last two minutes of baking so it stays raw enough to become a sauce when you stir it through the hot cheese.

  • Yolk in for the last two minutes only. It should still run.
  • Salty cheese blend. Mozzarella alone gives you a bread pizza.
  • Very hot oven with a preheated tray, or the base goes pale and soft.

item.title: Crying Tiger Beef
item.description: Thai grilled steak rested and sliced, served with nam jim jaew of toasted rice powder, chilli, lime and fish sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Toasted rice powder is what makes nam jim jaew taste Thai rather than merely hot and sour. Raw sticky rice toasted dry until it is the colour of straw and then pounded gives a nutty, slightly gritty body that thickens the sauce without any fat in it. It takes five minutes and nothing else does the same job.

  • Toast and pound the rice. It is what the sauce is built on.
  • Rest eight minutes, then slice across the grain.
  • Make the sauce first so the flavours have time to meet.

item.title: Khinkali
item.description: Khinkali — large pleated Georgian dumplings with a soupy meat filling and a thick twisted knot.
item.content:encoded:
The soup inside is not stock added as jelly but water beaten into the raw mince, which renders and mixes with the meat juices as the dumpling boils. The thick knot at the top exists so you have somewhere to hold while you bite a hole and drink the broth — it is a handle, and leaving it uneaten is the convention.

  • The filling should look far too wet. That water becomes the broth.
  • Thin rim, thicker centre. It is what makes the pleating possible.
  • Stir the water before they go in, and never let it boil violently.

item.title: Bánh Xèo
item.description: Vietnamese crisp turmeric rice flour crêpes filled with pork, prawn and beansprouts, eaten wrapped in lettuce with nuoc cham.
item.content:encoded:
The batter must be thin as single cream and the pan properly hot, and you pour it in and immediately tilt to spread — hesitate and it sets in a thick patch in the middle. The crispness comes from a generous amount of oil round the edge and from leaving it alone: no poking, no lifting to check, five minutes uncovered and then a lid for one.

  • Batter as thin as single cream, and tilt the moment it goes in.
  • Oil round the rim is what crisps the edge.
  • Do not touch it for five minutes.

item.title: Phở Gà
item.description: Vietnamese chicken noodle soup with a clear broth of charred ginger, onion and toasted spices, poached chicken and rice noodles.
item.content:encoded:
Char the ginger and onion black in patches directly over a flame before they go into the pot. It is not decoration: the burnt sugars give the broth its particular smoky sweetness, and pho made with raw aromatics tastes thin and vegetal in a way people notice without being able to name. Blanch the chicken first and throw that water away — it is where the scum comes from.

  • Blanch and discard the first water — it takes the scum with it.
  • Char the aromatics black in patches.
  • A bare simmer keeps it clear.

item.title: Bún Thịt Nướng
item.description: Vietnamese grilled lemongrass pork served over cold rice vermicelli with herbs, pickled carrot and nuoc cham.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles are dressed with nothing and served at room temperature; all the seasoning arrives as nuoc cham poured over at the table. That is deliberate — the contrast between the hot charred pork, the cool noodles and the sharp dressing is the dish. Rinse the cooked vermicelli under cold water and drain it hard, or the bowl turns into a wet clump.

  • Noodles cold and drained hard.
  • Char the pork properly — the black edges are the flavour.
  • Dress at the table, not in the kitchen.

item.title: Lobio
item.description: Lobio — Georgian kidney bean stew with walnuts, coriander and blue fenugreek, served with cornbread.
item.content:encoded:
Blue fenugreek and dried marigold are what make this taste Georgian rather than generically beany, and both go in at the end because their aroma is volatile. Mashing about a third of the beans thickens the pot without flour and gives the two textures the dish is meant to have.

  • Salt only after the beans are tender.
  • Spices off the heat at the end. Cooking them dulls the whole dish.
  • Mash a third, leave the rest whole. Two textures, one pot.

item.title: Bò Kho
item.description: Vietnamese beef stew of shin simmered two hours with lemongrass, star anise, annatto oil and tomato, with carrots.
item.content:encoded:
Annatto seeds fried in oil for one minute and then strained out give bo kho its red colour without any heat or flavour of their own. It is the reason a proper bowl looks the way it does, and paprika is not a substitute — it muddies the broth. Beef shin, not braising steak: the connective tissue is what makes the sauce sticky rather than watery.

  • Annatto for colour — strain the seeds out after a minute.
  • Beef shin, not braising steak.
  • Carrots in for the last thirty minutes only.

item.title: Chicken Fajitas
item.description: Chicken thigh marinated in lime, cumin and smoked paprika, seared with peppers and onion and served with warm tortillas.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the chicken and the vegetables separately and combine them at the end. Together in one pan they release enough water to stew, and fajitas that have stewed are grey and limp — the whole appeal is char. Get the pan properly hot, work in two batches, and do not stir for the first ninety seconds of either.

  • Two batches. Together they stew.
  • Do not stir for the first ninety seconds.
  • The pan must smoke before anything goes in.

item.title: Greek Lemon Potatoes
item.description: Greek lemon potatoes — roasted in lemon juice, olive oil and stock until the liquid reduces to a glaze.
item.content:encoded:
These are braised before they are roasted: the potatoes sit in liquid for the first forty minutes, absorbing lemon and oregano all the way through, and only crisp once the liquid has boiled away. Cutting them into large wedges gives enough surface for the glaze without them collapsing during the wet stage.

  • One layer, always. Two layers gives you boiled potatoes.
  • Do not skimp on the lemon. It should taste sharp before it goes in the oven.
  • Scrape the tin at the end — that is the best part of the dish.

item.title: Carne Asada
item.description: Skirt steak marinated in lime, orange, garlic and cumin, grilled over high heat, rested and sliced across the grain.
item.content:encoded:
Skirt steak has coarse fibres running in one obvious direction and everything depends on cutting across them. Sliced with the grain it is inedibly chewy no matter how well it was cooked; across, the same steak is tender. Find the direction before you cook, because char makes it harder to see afterwards.

  • Across the grain, always. Nothing else matters as much.
  • One hour in the marinade, not overnight.
  • Rest eight minutes before the knife goes near it.

item.title: Pico de Gallo
item.description: Fresh Mexican salsa of diced tomato, white onion, jalapeño, coriander and lime juice, salted and drained briefly.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the diced tomato on its own for ten minutes and pour off what collects. Tomato is mostly water and unsalted pico turns into a watery bowl within half an hour — drained, it stays a salsa. Rinse the diced onion under cold water too: it takes the raw sulphurous bite off without losing the crunch.

  • Salt and drain the tomato, or it floods.
  • Rinse the onion to take the raw bite off.
  • Season harder than feels right — it dilutes on the plate.

item.title: Salsa Verde
item.description: Mexican green salsa of tomatillos, serrano chillies, onion and garlic charred under a grill and blended with coriander and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Char the tomatillos rather than boiling them. Boiled, they are sour and one-dimensional; blistered black in patches under a hot grill, the sugars caramelise and the whole thing gains a smoky sweetness that balances the acid. Blend it only briefly — a salsa blitzed smooth goes pale and foamy, and it should stay a little coarse and dark green.

  • Char, do not boil.
  • Pulse, do not blend, or it goes pale and foamy.
  • Keep the tray juices — they are concentrated flavour.

item.title: Dolmades
item.description: Dolmades — vine leaves rolled around herbed rice with pine nuts, simmered with lemon and olive oil.
item.content:encoded:
The rice goes in raw and only part-cooked in the pan first, so it swells inside the leaf and packs it tight — pre-cooked rice gives a loose, mushy roll. A plate weighing the dolmades down keeps them submerged and stops them unrolling as the rice expands.

  • Raw rice, part-cooked in the pan. Cooked rice makes mush.
  • Roll firmly, not tightly. The rice has to double.
  • A plate on top is non-negotiable or they will unravel.

item.title: Chile Relleno
item.description: Poblano chillies charred and peeled, stuffed with cheese, coated in whipped egg batter and fried, served in a light tomato broth.
item.content:encoded:
Whip the whites to firm peaks and fold the yolks in rather than beating them together. A whole-egg batter runs off the chilli and fries into a thin skin; a whipped one clings in a thick puffed jacket that is the entire character of the dish. Dust the chilli with cornflour first — the batter needs something to grip on a surface as slippery as a peeled poblano.

  • Whites to firm peaks, yolks folded in after.
  • Cornflour dust or the batter slides off.
  • Spoon hot oil over the top as it fries so the upper side sets.

item.title: Sopa de Fideo
item.description: Mexican soup of fideo noodles toasted in oil and simmered in a blended tomato, onion and garlic broth.
item.content:encoded:
Toast the noodles in oil until they are the colour of a digestive biscuit before any liquid goes near them. It takes about four minutes of constant stirring and it changes the entire flavour from bland to nutty — untoasted fideo makes a soup that tastes of tomato and nothing else. They go from golden to burnt in about twenty seconds, so do not walk away.

  • Toast to biscuit-brown and do not look away.
  • Stand back when the tomato hits the hot oil.
  • Lime at the table is not optional.

item.title: Greek Yoghurt with Honey and Walnuts
item.description: Greek yoghurt with honey and walnuts — strained yoghurt, thyme honey and toasted walnuts.
item.content:encoded:
Straining ordinary Greek yoghurt for a few hours takes it from thick to genuinely dense, which changes how the honey sits on it — it pools instead of sinking. Toasting the walnuts is what removes their tannic edge, and doing it in a dry pan rather than the oven lets you stop at the exact moment they smell right.

  • Strain the yoghurt if you have three hours. It is a different dish.
  • Toast the walnuts and cool them off the pan.
  • A pinch of salt on top makes the honey taste more like honey.

item.title: Arroz con Leche
item.description: Mexican rice pudding simmered on the hob with whole milk, condensed milk, cinnamon and lime peel, served warm or cold.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the rice in water with the cinnamon and lime peel first, until the water has gone, and only then add the milk. Rice started in milk takes twice as long and scorches on the bottom before the grains are through, because milk conducts heat badly and its sugars catch. This way the grain is already soft when the milk arrives and it only has to thicken.

  • Water first, milk second.
  • Scrape the bottom every few minutes or it catches.
  • Take it off looser than you want it — it sets as it cools.

item.title: Menudo
item.description: Mexican tripe and hominy soup in a guajillo and ancho chilli broth, simmered three hours and served with lime, onion and oregano.
item.content:encoded:
Scrub and blanch the tripe twice, discarding the water each time, before it goes anywhere near the chillies. Tripe carries a strong smell that will otherwise dominate everything, and two changes of water takes it out completely. After that it is only time: three hours at a bare simmer turns it from rubber to something that yields between the teeth.

  • Two blanches, both discarded. That is what takes the smell out.
  • Strain the chilli purée or the broth is gritty.
  • The table condiments are part of the dish, not a garnish.

item.title: Pot Roast
item.description: Beef chuck browned and slow-braised with onion, carrot, potato and stock until fork-tender, with a thickened pan gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Chuck, and only chuck. It is the cut with enough connective tissue to turn to gelatin over three hours, which is what makes a pot roast sticky and rich rather than dry — a leaner joint like topside will be stringy at the same temperature for the same time and there is nothing to be done about it. Add the vegetables in the last hour or they dissolve.

  • Chuck. A leaner joint will be stringy however long you give it.
  • Vegetables in for the last hour only.
  • Uncover for the last twenty minutes to reduce the gravy.

item.title: İskender Kebab
item.description: İskender kebab — sliced lamb over pide bread with tomato sauce, browned butter and yoghurt.
item.content:encoded:
The dish is assembled hot and eaten immediately because the bread has a short window between soaking up sauce and disintegrating. The butter is browned separately and poured over at the table for the same reason it is done that way in Bursa: the noise and the smell are part of it, and the butter has to hit while everything is still hot.

  • Sear the lamb hot and fast in batches. Crowded lamb turns grey and tough.
  • Brown the butter properly and pour it at the table while it sizzles.
  • Assemble and serve within a minute. This dish does not wait.

item.title: Sloppy Joe Skillet
item.description: Minced beef simmered with onion, pepper, tomato, brown sugar and Worcestershire into a thick sandwich filling.
item.content:encoded:
Brown the mince properly before any liquid goes in — spread it out, leave it four minutes, and only then break it up. Mince stirred from the moment it hits the pan releases water and simmers grey, and no amount of sauce afterwards puts back the flavour that browning would have made. The sauce wants to be thick enough to sit on a bun, not run off it.

  • Four minutes untouched before you break the mince up.
  • Thick enough to hold on a spoon, or it soaks the bun.
  • Vinegar at the end balances the sugar.

item.title: Potato Salad
item.description: Waxy potatoes boiled, dressed warm with vinegar then mayonnaise, mustard, egg, celery and chives.
item.content:encoded:
Splash the vinegar over the potatoes while they are still hot, before the mayonnaise. Warm potato absorbs it; cold potato does not, and a salad dressed only when cool tastes of mayonnaise sitting on top of bland potato. Use a waxy variety — floury ones break down into a mash the moment you fold them.

  • Vinegar on hot potatoes. That is the step everyone skips.
  • Waxy, not floury.
  • An hour in the fridge — it needs to settle.

item.title: Turkish Lentil Soup
item.description: Turkish lentil soup — red lentils blended smooth with a chilli butter drizzle and plenty of lemon.
item.content:encoded:
The soup itself is deliberately plain — the flavour arrives at the end with the chilli butter and the lemon, which is why a version tasted before those go in always seems disappointing. Blending it completely smooth is not optional in Turkey; texture is what separates mercimek çorbası from a lentil stew.

  • Blend for longer than you think. Silky, not grainy.
  • The chilli butter and the lemon are the recipe, not garnishes.
  • Rinse the lentils until the water is clear or the soup will taste dusty.

item.title: Coleslaw
item.description: Shredded white cabbage and carrot salted and drained, then dressed with mayonnaise, cider vinegar, mustard and sugar.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the shredded cabbage and let it drain for thirty minutes, then squeeze it. Cabbage is about ninety per cent water and undrained coleslaw turns into a pool within the hour — this is why shop-bought slaw sits in liquid. Squeezed, it stays crisp for days and the dressing coats instead of being diluted.

  • Salt, drain and squeeze. That is the whole difference.
  • Sharp before sweet.
  • Chives at the end so they stay green.

item.title: Tuna Salad
item.description: Tinned tuna flaked and mixed with mayonnaise, celery, red onion, lemon and dill for sandwiches or salad.
item.content:encoded:
Drain the tuna thoroughly and press it in the tin lid — every spoonful of oil or brine left in makes the finished salad looser and blander, and you cannot correct it by adding more mayonnaise. Celery diced small is what stops the whole thing being one soft texture, and it is the difference between a good tuna salad and a paste. Tuna tinned in oil gives a richer result than the spring water used here, if you would rather use it — just drain it even more thoroughly, since oil clings harder than brine.

  • Press the tin lid down hard. Every drop matters.
  • Leave some flakes large.
  • Capers do the same job as pickle, with more edge.

item.title: Künefe
item.description: Künefe — shredded kadayif pastry around melting cheese, fried in butter and soaked in cold syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Hot pastry and cold syrup is the rule for every syrup dessert: the temperature difference makes the syrup absorb fast without softening the crust. The cheese has to be unsalted and low-moisture so it stretches rather than releasing water into the pastry, which is why fresh mozzarella is the wrong choice.

  • Hot pastry, cold syrup. Never the other way round.
  • Press it hard, twice. Loose kadayif falls apart when you turn it.
  • Serve within minutes — the cheese stops stretching as it cools.

item.title: Chicken Salad
item.description: Shredded cooked chicken folded with mayonnaise, yoghurt, celery, grapes and toasted pecans, seasoned with lemon and tarragon.
item.content:encoded:
Shred the chicken along the grain rather than dicing it. Shreds hold dressing in their fibres and read as chicken; neat cubes shed it and taste like something from a packet. Half yoghurt and half mayonnaise keeps the dressing light enough that you can still taste the meat, which a full-mayonnaise version buries.

  • Shred along the grain, do not dice.
  • Half yoghurt keeps it light enough to taste the chicken.
  • Pecans in last or they go soft.

item.title: Fudge Brownies
item.description: Fudge brownies made with melted dark chocolate and butter, whisked eggs and sugar for a crackled top, baked until barely set.
item.content:encoded:
The papery crackled top comes from dissolving the sugar into the eggs before the chocolate goes in — whisk them for four minutes until pale and thick, and a thin meringue-like layer forms on top during baking. Take the tin out when the middle still wobbles; brownies carry on cooking in the tin for another ten minutes and one baked until a skewer comes out clean is a chocolate cake.

  • Four minutes of whisking makes the crackled top.
  • Out while the middle wobbles.
  • Cool completely in the tin or they fall apart.

item.title: Shish Taouk
item.description: Shish taouk — Lebanese chicken skewers marinated in yoghurt, garlic and lemon, grilled and served with toum.
item.content:encoded:
Yoghurt marinades tenderise gently because their acid is mild and their calcium activates enzymes in the meat — unlike a lemon-only marinade, which turns the surface chalky if left overnight. The tomato purée is there for colour more than flavour: it is what gives shish taouk its characteristic orange edge under the grill.

  • Thighs, not breast. Breast dries out before it chars.
  • A small gap between cubes on the skewer, or the sides steam.
  • For toum, add the oil painfully slowly at the start. It breaks if you rush.

item.title: Fluffy Pancakes
item.description: Thick American buttermilk pancakes raised with baking powder and soda, rested briefly and cooked on a medium griddle.
item.content:encoded:
Stop mixing while the batter still has lumps in it. Every stir past the point where the flour is just wet develops gluten, and gluten makes pancakes chewy and flat — the lumps hydrate on their own during the rest and disappear in the pan. A rested batter also gives the raising agents a head start, which is where the height comes from.

  • Lumpy batter. Ten folds, then stop.
  • Medium heat — high heat browns them before they rise.
  • One flip only.

item.title: Garlic Bread
