item.description: Baguette split and filled with a garlic, parsley and butter paste, wrapped in foil and baked, then finished uncovered to crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Bake it wrapped in foil first and only uncover for the last five minutes. Wrapped, the butter melts through the crumb and steams the middle soft; uncovered from the start, the outside is dark before the inside has taken up anything. Grate the garlic rather than chopping it — pieces of chopped garlic scorch and turn acrid in the oven, and a paste distributes evenly.

  • Grate the garlic — chopped pieces burn.
  • Foil on for ten minutes, off for five.
  • Cut almost through so it stays one loaf until it reaches the table.

item.title: Pesto Pasta
item.description: Fresh basil pesto with pine nuts, garlic and hard cheese, tossed with hot pasta and starchy cooking water off the heat.
item.content:encoded:
Pesto is never cooked. Add it to the pasta off the heat and loosen it with the starchy cooking water, which emulsifies the oil into a sauce that clings — heat it in the pan and the basil turns khaki and bitter and the cheese goes stringy. Keep a mugful of the cooking water back before you drain; it is the only thing that turns pesto from a paste into a sauce.

  • Never heat the pesto.
  • Keep a mug of pasta water back before draining.
  • Cool the pine nuts or they turn the basil dark.

item.title: Moutabal
item.description: Moutabal — charred aubergine whipped with tahini, lemon and garlic into a smoky dip.
item.content:encoded:
The smoke is the dish, and it only comes from direct flame — an oven-roasted aubergine gives you a sweet purée with no smokiness at all. Draining the flesh in a sieve for twenty minutes is the other essential step: aubergine holds a surprising amount of water, and left in, it makes the dip loose and bland.

  • Open flame or nothing. An oven gives you sweet purée, not moutabal.
  • Drain the flesh for twenty minutes. It is what concentrates the flavour.
  • Chop by hand. A processor makes it gluey.

item.title: Minestrone
item.description: Italian vegetable soup with a soffritto base, borlotti beans, tomato and small pasta, finished with olive oil.
item.content:encoded:
Give the soffritto — onion, carrot and celery — a full twelve minutes over a low heat before anything else goes in. It should collapse and sweeten rather than colour, and it is the whole foundation: rushed for four minutes, the soup tastes of stock and vegetables sitting separately in it rather than of one thing. The pasta goes in for the last eight minutes only.

  • Twelve minutes on the soffritto. It is the foundation.
  • Pasta for the last eight minutes only.
  • A Parmesan rind in the pot is free depth if you have one.

item.title: Spaghetti alla Puttanesca
item.description: Spaghetti in a sauce of anchovies melted in oil with garlic, chilli, olives, capers and tomatoes, cooked fast and finished with parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Melt the anchovies into the warm oil until they disappear completely — two or three minutes over a low heat, pressing them with a spoon. Left as pieces they are salty lumps that people pick out; dissolved, they are invisible and the sauce simply tastes deeper. Do not add salt until the very end: anchovies, olives and capers between them usually make it unnecessary.

  • Start the anchovies in cold oil so they melt rather than fry.
  • No salt until the end.
  • Toss the pasta in the sauce, never sauce on top.

item.title: Maamoul
item.description: Maamoul — semolina shortbread filled with dates or nuts, pressed in carved moulds and baked pale.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is made a day ahead so the coarse semolina can hydrate fully — mixed and baked the same day it stays gritty and the cookies crack. They are baked only until the base colours and the top is still pale, because a browned maamoul has gone from tender to dry.

  • Rest the buttered semolina overnight. There is no way round it.
  • Bake pale. A browned maamoul is a dry maamoul.
  • Cool completely before moving them or they will break.

item.title: Ragù alla Bolognese
item.description: A long-cooked Bolognese ragù of beef and pork with soffritto, milk, white wine and a small amount of tomato, served with tagliatelle.
item.content:encoded:
The milk goes in before the wine and before the tomato, and it must be absorbed completely before anything else joins it. The lactose and the fat tenderise the meat and round off the acidity that comes later — a ragù made without it is sharper and grainier. The tomato is a spoonful of purée and half a tin, not a whole one: this is a meat sauce, not a tomato one.

  • Milk first, and let it go completely before the wine.
  • Very fine dice on the soffritto — it should disappear.
  • Two hours at a bare simmer, uncovered.

item.title: Lamb Kleftiko
item.description: Greek lamb shoulder marinated with lemon, garlic and oregano, sealed in parchment with potatoes and slow-roasted until falling apart.
item.content:encoded:
The parcel must be genuinely sealed, and paper alone will not do it — line it with foil. Everything about kleftiko depends on the steam staying in: it is what cooks the lamb to falling apart without drying, and what makes the potatoes taste of lemon and lamb fat rather than of oven. If steam escapes you have a roast, which is a fine thing but not this.

  • Foil under the parchment. Paper alone leaks.
  • Crimp every edge — steam is the whole method.
  • Open it in front of people. That is the dish.

item.title: Tiropita
item.description: Greek cheese pie of feta, ricotta and egg layered between buttered filo sheets and baked until crisp and golden.
item.content:encoded:
Score the pie into portions before baking, cutting down through the top layers of filo but not into the filling. Baked whole and cut afterwards, the crisp top shatters and slides off in pieces as the knife goes through. Scored first, each portion keeps its lid. Keep the unused filo under a damp cloth: it dries to uselessness in about three minutes uncovered.

  • Score before baking, not after.
  • Damp cloth over the filo at all times.
  • A flick of cold water on top helps it blister.

item.title: Ghormeh Sabzi
item.description: Ghormeh sabzi — Persian herb stew with lamb, kidney beans and dried limes, cooked long and slow.
item.content:encoded:
The herbs have to be fried for a long time — twenty minutes or more, until they darken and the volume collapses by three quarters — because that is where the stew's depth comes from. Dried limes must be pierced before they go in, or they float and never release the sour, slightly fermented note that defines the dish.

  • Twenty-five minutes on the herbs. This is the step that makes the stew.
  • Pierce the dried limes or they will bob about doing nothing.
  • Wait for the oil to rise to the surface. That is when it is done.

item.title: Youvetsi
item.description: Greek beef and orzo baked together in a tomato and cinnamon sauce until the orzo absorbs the liquid, topped with kefalotyri.
item.content:encoded:
The orzo goes in raw and cooks in the sauce, absorbing it, so the liquid has to be measured — about three parts liquid to one part orzo by volume. Boiled separately and stirred in, it tastes of nothing and the sauce stays thin. Stir once at the halfway point and no more, or the starch releases and the dish turns claggy.

  • Orzo raw into the sauce, never boiled first.
  • Stir once, at the halfway point.
  • Rest ten minutes — the orzo keeps absorbing.

item.title: Adana Kebab
item.description: Turkish minced lamb kebab with red pepper flakes and fat, kneaded and pressed onto flat skewers, grilled and served with sumac onions.
item.content:encoded:
The mince needs to be at least twenty per cent fat and it must be kneaded hard for five minutes until it turns sticky and pulls away from the bowl in one mass. That is what makes it cling to a flat skewer over a fire instead of falling into it. Chill the kneaded mixture before shaping — cold fat holds, warm fat slides.

  • Twenty per cent fat, and knead until it is sticky.
  • An hour in the fridge before shaping.
  • Flat skewers, or it rolls and falls off.

item.title: Fesenjan
item.description: Fesenjan — Persian chicken braised in ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses until dark and glossy.
item.content:encoded:
The walnuts must be ground fine and then cooked long enough for their oil to separate and darken the sauce, which takes at least an hour and cannot be hurried. Balancing the pomegranate molasses with sugar at the end is a matter of taste and of brand: molasses varies enormously in sourness, so the recipe has to be adjusted by tasting rather than by measurement.

  • Grind the walnuts fine but stop before they become butter.
  • The long simmer before the chicken goes back is where the colour comes from.
  • Taste and balance at the end. Molasses brands are wildly different.

item.title: Karnıyarık
item.description: Turkish aubergines fried whole, split and stuffed with minced lamb, onion and tomato, then baked with peppers and tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Peel the aubergines in stripes rather than fully or not at all. Left whole-skinned they are tough to cut on the plate; peeled completely they collapse in the pan. Alternating stripes hold the shape together while letting the flesh soften. Salt them for twenty minutes first — it draws water out so they absorb far less oil in the frying.

  • Stripes, not full peeling.
  • Salt for twenty minutes so they drink less oil.
  • Split without cutting through, or the filling escapes.

item.title: Şakşuka
item.description: Turkish meze of fried aubergine, courgette and pepper in a garlic and tomato sauce, served at room temperature.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the vegetables separately and drain them properly on paper before the sauce goes anywhere near. Cooked together they steam and turn to a wet mush, and şakşuka is meant to be distinct pieces sitting in sauce. It is also served at room temperature, not hot — the flavours only come together as it cools, so make it an hour ahead.

  • Fry each vegetable separately and drain each one.
  • Room temperature, never hot.
  • An hour standing is part of the recipe.

item.title: Tahdig
item.description: Tahdig — the golden Persian rice crust, made by steaming parboiled basmati over yoghurt rice or potato.
item.content:encoded:
Parboiling and draining the rice removes surface starch so the grains steam separately, and it is the only way tahdig works — a pot of absorbed-water rice goes gummy against the base rather than crisping. The wrapped lid catches condensation that would otherwise drip back down and soften the crust.

  • Parboil and drain. Absorption-method rice will never make tahdig.
  • The tea towel round the lid keeps the crust dry. Do not skip it.
  • Cold water under the pot for a minute before you turn it out.

item.title: Turkish Pilav
item.description: Turkish rice pilav with orzo toasted in butter, rice soaked and rinsed, cooked with stock and rested under a cloth.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the rice in warm salted water for fifteen minutes and then rinse it until the water runs clear. That removes the surface starch that makes grains stick, which is the entire difference between pilav and a sticky pan of rice. Rest it under a cloth at the end: the cloth absorbs the steam that would otherwise condense on the lid and drip back in.

  • Rinse until the water is clear. That is the whole technique.
  • Toast the orzo brown before the rice goes in.
  • A cloth under the lid for the rest.

item.title: Albóndigas
item.description: Spanish meatballs of pork and beef in a tomato, almond and saffron sauce thickened with fried bread and almonds.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is thickened with a picada — fried bread and almonds pounded together — rather than with flour. It is the classic Spanish method and it does two jobs at once: it gives body and it adds a toasted, nutty flavour that flour cannot. Fry the bread and almonds until properly golden, because that colour is the flavour.

  • The picada, not flour. Fry the bread and nuts properly golden.
  • Small meatballs — this is a tapa, not a main.
  • Chill them before browning so they hold.

item.title: Joojeh Kabab
item.description: Joojeh kabab — Persian saffron chicken skewers marinated overnight and basted with saffron butter.
item.content:encoded:
Grated onion is the workhorse of Persian marinades: its enzymes break down the surface proteins far more gently than acid does, so the chicken stays juicy through a long marinade. Saffron ground with sugar and steeped in hot water gives four times the colour of threads dropped in whole.

  • Grate the onion, do not chop it. The juice is the point.
  • Grind saffron with sugar before steeping — far more colour.
  • Flat skewers. Round ones let the meat spin when you turn them.

item.title: Pollo al Ajillo
item.description: Spanish chicken browned in olive oil with whole garlic cloves and finished with dry sherry, bay and parsley.
item.content:encoded:
The garlic cloves go in whole and unpeeled, fried gently in the oil before the chicken and then returned at the end. Whole, they turn sweet and creamy inside their skins; sliced or crushed at that heat they burn black in ninety seconds and make the whole pan bitter. Squeeze them out of their skins onto the bread at the table.

  • Whole unpeeled cloves. Anything else burns.
  • Fino sherry, not cooking wine.
  • Squeeze the garlic onto bread at the table.

item.title: Tarta de Santiago
item.description: Galician almond cake made with ground almonds, eggs, sugar and citrus zest, baked and dusted through a cross stencil.
item.content:encoded:
Whisk the eggs and sugar for a full five minutes until they hold a ribbon on the surface. There is no flour and no raising agent, so every bit of the cake's lift comes from air beaten into the eggs — undermixed, it bakes into a dense almond slab. Fold the almonds in gently and stop the moment they disappear.

  • Five minutes of whisking. It is the only lift the cake gets.
  • Fold the almonds in, do not beat them.
  • Lift the stencil straight up or you smudge the cross.

item.title: Flapjacks
item.description: British oat flapjacks made with butter, golden syrup and light brown sugar, baked until golden at the edges and cut while warm.
item.content:encoded:
Cut them while they are still warm and leave them in the tin to cool completely. Cut cold, they shatter; lifted out warm, they fall apart. Score them at about ten minutes out of the oven and then do not touch them for an hour. Underbaking by three minutes gives chewy flapjacks and overbaking by three gives crunchy ones — both are correct, so decide which you want.

  • Score warm, lift out cold.
  • Press the mixture down hard or they crumble.
  • Twenty-five minutes chewy, twenty-eight crisp. Pick one.

item.title: Ash Reshteh
item.description: Ash reshteh — thick Persian noodle soup with beans, lentils and greens, topped with mint oil and kashk.
item.content:encoded:
Reshteh noodles are slightly salty and made to break down a little, thickening the soup as they cook — Italian pasta is a poor substitute because it stays separate. The three toppings are not optional garnish: fried mint gives bitterness, crisp onion gives sweetness, and kashk gives sourness, and the soup underneath is deliberately plain so they can do that work.

  • Mint into oil off the heat. Burnt mint is acrid and there is no fixing it.
  • Thick enough for a spoon to leave a trail. Ash is not a broth.
  • All three toppings, every bowl. That is where the flavour is.

item.title: Vegetable Stir-Fry
item.description: Mixed vegetables stir-fried over a high heat in a soy, garlic and ginger sauce thickened with a cornflour slurry.
item.content:encoded:
Cut everything to a thickness that matches how long it takes to cook, not to look tidy: broccoli in thin florets, carrots in matchsticks, peppers in wide strips. Then add them in order of hardness, thirty to sixty seconds apart. A stir-fry that goes in all at once is either raw carrot or grey broccoli, and usually both.

  • Cut to cooking time, not to neatness.
  • Hardest vegetables first, softest last.
  • The slurry goes into a boiling pan, moving.

item.title: Ras Malai
item.description: Homemade chenna kneaded smooth, poached in syrup, flattened and steeped in reduced cardamom and saffron milk with pistachios.
item.content:encoded:
Knead the drained chenna with the heel of your hand for a full eight minutes, until it stops being grainy and goes greasy and smooth. That is the entire difference between ras malai that stays soft and ras malai that sets into rubber. The discs also double in the syrup, so make them half the size you want and leave room in the pan.

  • Eight minutes of kneading. Set a timer.
  • They double in the syrup — leave room.
  • Squeeze the syrup out before they go into the milk.

item.title: Sabich
item.description: Sabich — pitta stuffed with fried aubergine, boiled egg, hummus, salad, amba and tahini.
item.content:encoded:
Salting the aubergine slices before frying draws out water so they brown instead of steaming and soak up less oil. The order of assembly is not arbitrary — hummus first insulates the bread, and the tahini and amba go on last so they run down through the filling rather than sitting on top.

  • Salt and dry the aubergine. Wet slices absorb twice the oil.
  • Hummus against the bread. It stops the pitta going through.
  • Amba is what makes it sabich rather than a vegetable pitta.

item.title: Kulfi
item.description: Whole milk reduced by half with sugar and cardamom, blended with nuts and frozen in moulds without churning.
item.content:encoded:
Kulfi is not churned, so the smoothness has to come from the reduction — boiling the milk down by half concentrates the solids until there is not enough free water left to form large ice crystals. Scrape the skin back into the pan as it forms; that caramelised film is where the flavour is, and left on the surface it becomes rubbery threads in the finished kulfi.

  • Scrape the skin back in as it forms.
  • Reduced by half, not a third — that is what stops ice crystals.
  • Ten seconds in warm water and it slides straight out.

item.title: Gajar ka Halwa
item.description: Grated carrots slow-cooked in whole milk with ghee, sugar and cardamom until reduced and glossy, finished with nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the carrot in the milk until the milk has completely gone before the sugar goes anywhere near it. Sugar added early draws water out of the carrot and stalls the whole thing — you end up simmering in syrup for an hour and it never darkens. Grate on the coarse side of the box grater; fine gratings turn to paste.

  • Milk gone before sugar goes in.
  • Coarse grate, not fine.
  • It is ready when the ghee separates at the edge.

item.title: Falooda
item.description: A layered dessert drink of rose syrup, soaked basil seeds, cooked vermicelli, chilled milk and ice cream.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the basil seeds in plenty of cold water for at least twenty minutes and they swell to eight times their size with a clear jelly around each one. Rushed, they swell in the glass instead and drink like grit. Everything goes into the glass cold — a warm layer melts the ice cream and the whole thing collapses into pink milk.

  • Twenty minutes for the basil seeds, in plenty of water.
  • Everything cold before it meets the ice cream.
  • Pour the milk down the side so the layers stay separate.

item.title: Malabi
item.description: Malabi — rose-scented set milk pudding with red syrup, coconut and crushed pistachios.
item.content:encoded:
Cornflour sets a milk pudding softly and cleanly where gelatine sets it rubbery, and the ratio matters within a tablespoon — too little and it will not stand, too much and it turns to paste. The rose water goes in off the heat because its aroma is driven off by any further boiling.

  • Dissolve the cornflour in cold milk first, thoroughly. Lumps never come out.
  • Rose water off the heat. Boiling it away is the most common mistake.
  • Strain into the glasses for a completely smooth top.

item.title: Shrikhand
item.description: Whole milk yoghurt strained overnight and whisked with icing sugar, saffron and cardamom into a thick set dessert.
item.content:encoded:
Hang the yoghurt overnight and you lose about half its weight in whey — that is not a loss, it is the recipe. Anything less and the shrikhand will not hold a shape on the spoon. Use icing sugar rather than caster: granulated sugar never fully dissolves in something this cold and thick, and you can feel it.

  • Eight hours of hanging, and expect to lose half the weight.
  • Icing sugar, not caster — you can feel caster.
  • One pass through a sieve makes it silky.

item.title: Rasam
item.description: A thin south Indian tamarind and tomato broth spiced with freshly pounded pepper and cumin, tempered with mustard seeds.
item.content:encoded:
Rasam is never boiled once the tamarind and rasam powder are in. Bring it just to the point where a froth rises up the sides and take it off — boiling drives off the volatile aromatics that are the whole point, and turns the pepper harsh and flat. It should be thin enough to drink, not a soup you eat with a spoon.

  • Never boil it after the tamarind goes in.
  • Pound the pepper for this pot; ready-ground tastes flat.
  • Thin enough to drink is correct.

item.title: Israeli Couscous Salad
item.description: Israeli couscous salad — toasted pearl couscous with roast vegetables, herbs, lemon and almonds.
item.content:encoded:
Toasting the pearls in oil before adding liquid keeps them separate and gives a nutty flavour that plain boiling does not — untoasted ptitim clump into a solid mass as they cool. Dressing the couscous while it is still warm means it absorbs the lemon rather than wearing it.

  • Toast the pearls until they smell like popcorn. Untoasted couscous clumps.
  • Dress it hot, then again cold. Two stages, better absorption.
  • Herbs at the very end so they stay green.

item.title: Coconut Chutney
item.description: Fresh grated coconut ground with roasted gram dal, green chilli and ginger, tempered with mustard seeds and curry leaves.
item.content:encoded:
Roasted gram dal is what stops the chutney splitting into water and coconut within the hour. It has no other job and no substitute does it as well — it absorbs the water and holds the emulsion. Grind with ice-cold water: a warm grinder turns coconut oily and the chutney goes greasy and grey.

  • Roasted gram dal is what stops it splitting.
  • Ice-cold water in the grinder.
  • Temper last and pour it over hot.

item.title: Tandoori Roti
item.description: Wholemeal dough rolled thick and cooked on an inverted cast-iron pan until blistered and charred in patches.
item.content:encoded:
A tandoori roti is thicker than a chapati and cooked much harder, so it stays soft inside while the outside chars. Wet one face of the rolled dough before it goes on the metal — the water is what makes it stick to a vertical surface, which is how you get to blister the other side directly over the flame without it falling into the fire.

  • Thicker than a chapati, or it dries out.
  • Wet one face so it sticks to the metal.
  • Char in patches, not evenly — that is what tandoori means here.

item.title: Pani Puri
item.description: Crisp semolina puris filled with spiced mint and tamarind water, potato and chickpeas, assembled and eaten immediately.
item.content:encoded:
The puris puff because the dough is stiff and the oil is hot — a soft dough steams and stays flat, and oil under 190C lets them absorb rather than inflate. Roll thin, cut small, and fry in oil hot enough that they rise within five seconds. Then keep the pani ice cold and assemble one at a time: a filled puri has about twenty seconds before it collapses.

  • Stiff dough and 190C oil, or they will not puff.
  • Cool them completely before storing — warm puris go soft.
  • Fill one at a time. Twenty seconds is all you get.

item.title: Musakhan
item.description: Musakhan — Palestinian roast chicken on olive oil soaked flatbread with sumac onions and pine nuts.
item.content:encoded:
The onions are cooked down slowly with far more sumac than seems reasonable — the sourness has to carry the whole dish, and the volume of onion collapses to about a third. Good olive oil is used at a quantity that looks excessive on paper; the bread is meant to be saturated with it, and that is the texture the dish is built on.

  • More sumac and more olive oil than feels right. That is the dish.
  • Thirty-five minutes on the onions, minimum.
  • Soak the bread with the roasting juices before the onions go on.

item.title: Dhokla
item.description: Gram flour batter soured with lemon, raised with eno and steamed into a light savoury sponge, finished with a mustard and sugar tempering.
item.content:encoded:
The raising agent goes in last and the batter goes straight into the steamer — you have about thirty seconds of usable lift before the bubbles collapse. Have the steamer already boiling and the tin already greased before you add it. The tempering is poured over while the dhokla is still warm so it soaks in rather than sitting on top.

  • Steamer boiling and tin greased before the eno goes in.
  • Cut it in the tin while warm, not after it cools.
  • The sugar tempering is what makes it taste Gujarati.

item.title: Bhel Puri
item.description: Puffed rice tossed with tamarind and mint chutneys, onion, potato, tomato and sev, assembled immediately before eating.
item.content:encoded:
Everything is prepared separately and combined in the last thirty seconds. Half the sev is folded in for flavour in every bite; the other half is saved for on top, so at least some of it is still crisp by the time it is eaten. Puffed rice is hygroscopic to a degree that has to be seen: chutney-dressed bhel is crisp when you toss it and soggy by the time it reaches the table if you dawdle. Toss, plate, hand it over, eat.

  • Everything ready before the chutney touches the rice.
  • Fifteen seconds of tossing, then straight into bowls.
  • Refresh soft puffed rice in a low oven first.

item.title: Harees
item.description: Harees — wheat and meat cooked for hours and beaten smooth, finished with ghee and cinnamon.
item.content:encoded:
Harees is defined by texture: the wheat and meat have to be beaten until neither is identifiable, which only happens after long cooking has broken the wheat down and the meat has fallen into threads. Beating it hot, with a wooden spoon against the side of the pot, develops the wheat starch and gives the stretchy consistency the dish is judged on.

  • Beat it properly. Under-beaten harees is porridge with meat in it.
  • Keep topping up with hot water — cold water stalls the cooking.
  • The ghee at the end is not optional; the dish is deliberately plain without it.

item.title: Grilled Cheese Sandwich
item.description: A grilled cheese sandwich with mayonnaise and butter on the outside, two cheeses inside, cooked slowly over a medium-low heat.
item.content:encoded:
Cook it far more slowly than instinct suggests — medium-low, four minutes a side. High heat browns the bread in ninety seconds and leaves the cheese solid in the middle, which is the single most common failure. Mayonnaise on the outside as well as butter sounds wrong and browns more evenly than butter alone, because it contains egg and oil rather than water.

  • Medium-low and four minutes a side.
  • Mayonnaise as well as butter browns more evenly.
  • Cheese to the edges, so you get some crisped against the pan.

item.title: Perfect Scrambled Eggs
item.description: Eggs cooked over a low heat with butter, stirred constantly into soft curds and taken off the heat while still glossy.
item.content:encoded:
Take the pan off the heat while the eggs still look slightly underdone and glossy. They carry on cooking in their own heat for another thirty seconds, and eggs that looked right in the pan are dry on the plate. Salt at the end, not the beginning: salt added early breaks down the proteins and the eggs weep water as they cook.

  • Low heat, constant stirring, and lift the pan when it runs ahead.
  • Off the heat while still glossy.
  • Salt at the end.

item.title: Banana Pancakes
item.description: American pancakes with mashed ripe banana folded into the batter, cooked on a medium griddle and served with banana slices.
item.content:encoded:
The bananas must be properly overripe — skins going black, flesh almost liquid. An underripe banana is starchy rather than sweet and it makes the batter heavy without adding any flavour, so people end up adding sugar to compensate. Mash it thoroughly before it meets the flour, because lumps of banana in the batter turn to wet pockets in the finished pancake.

  • Blackening bananas, not yellow ones.
  • Mash smooth before the flour goes in.
  • They colour faster than plain pancakes because of the sugar — keep the heat moderate.

item.title: Knafeh Nabulsi
item.description: Knafeh nabulsi — orange semolina dough over fresh white cheese, baked and flooded with syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Nabulsi knafeh uses fine semolina dough rather than shredded kadayif, which bakes into a dense, sandy layer that holds syrup without going soggy. The cheese must be desalted by soaking, because the whole dessert is sweet and a salty layer inside it is jarring rather than balancing.

  • Soak the cheese to desalt it — two hours, three changes of water.
  • Cold syrup on hot knafeh, poured the moment it is turned out.
  • Serve within fifteen minutes. Cold knafeh does not pull.

item.title: Corn Chowder
item.description: A creamy sweetcorn and potato chowder built on a stock made from the stripped corn cobs, finished with cream and chives.
item.content:encoded:
Simmer the stripped cobs in the stock for twenty minutes and then throw them away. The cobs hold a great deal of starch and sweetness that the kernels do not, and it is the single cheapest thing you can do to make a corn chowder taste of corn rather than of cream. Blend a ladleful and stir it back in — that thickens it without flour.

  • The cobs make the stock. Do not skip it.
  • Blend a ladleful back in rather than adding flour.
  • Do not boil once the cream is in.

item.title: Chicken Tagine with Olives
item.description: Chicken tagine with olives — slow cooked with preserved lemon, green olives, ginger and saffron.
item.content:encoded:
Preserved lemon rind and olives are both already salty, so the tagine is barely salted at the start and adjusted only at the end — season early and it becomes inedible. Reducing the sauce hard after the chicken comes out is what turns a thin broth into the sticky glaze the dish is supposed to have.

  • Salt at the end, never at the start. The olives and lemons do that job.
  • Reduce the sauce properly after the chicken comes out.
  • Use the rind of the preserved lemon only — the flesh is bitter and salty.

item.title: Chicken Caesar Wrap
item.description: Griddled chicken, cos lettuce and parmesan in a tortilla wrap with a Caesar dressing of anchovy, garlic, lemon and mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
Dress the lettuce and roll the wrap at the last possible moment. Cos leaves collapse within about ten minutes of meeting a creamy dressing and a wrap made in advance is a wet parcel. The anchovies are not optional and they do not taste of fish in the finished dressing — they are where the savoury depth comes from, and a Caesar without them tastes like mayonnaise.

  • Dress and roll at the last minute.
  • Anchovies are the dressing, not an option.
  • Warm the tortilla or it cracks as you roll.

item.title: Ground Beef Tacos
item.description: Minced beef browned and simmered with cumin, chilli and oregano into a taco filling, served in warm corn tortillas.
item.content:encoded:
Bloom the ground spices in the hot fat for thirty seconds before any liquid goes in. Ground spice added to a wet pan tastes dusty and stays on the surface of the meat; heated in fat first, it dissolves and coats everything. A splash of water at the end and two minutes of simmering makes the difference between dry crumbles and a filling that holds together in the tortilla.

  • Bloom the spices in fat for thirty seconds.
  • Four minutes untouched to brown the mince.
  • A splash of water at the end so the filling holds together.

item.title: Spaghetti and Meatballs
item.description: Beef and pork meatballs bound with a milk-soaked bread panade, browned and simmered in tomato sauce, served with spaghetti.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the breadcrumbs in milk to a paste before they go into the meat. That panade holds water through cooking and is the difference between a tender meatball and a dense one — breadcrumbs added dry absorb the meat's own moisture instead. Brown them for colour only and finish them in the sauce, where they cook gently and give the sauce their fat.

  • A milk-soaked panade, always.
  • Handle the mixture as little as possible.
  • Brown for colour, then finish in the sauce.

item.title: Msemen
item.description: Msemen — Moroccan square laminated flatbread, folded and fried until it separates into flaky layers.
item.content:encoded:
Msemen is laminated the same way puff pastry is, but with oil and dry semolina instead of butter — the semolina keeps the layers physically apart as the dough is folded, which is why they separate rather than fusing. The dough is stretched on a well-oiled surface, never floured, so it can be pulled thin enough to see through.

  • Oil the surface, never flour it. Flour stops the dough stretching.
  • Dry semolina between the layers is what keeps them separate.
  • A dry pan, not an oily one — the dough already carries all the fat it needs.

item.title: Chicken Karahi
item.description: Pakistani chicken karahi cooked fast in a wok with tomato, ginger, garlic and green chilli, finished with ginger julienne.
item.content:encoded:
There is no onion in a real karahi and adding one changes the dish completely — it turns a sharp, tomato-led curry into a sweet, thick gravy. The tomatoes go in whole or halved and are pressed against the side of the pan as they collapse, so the skins can be lifted out. Everything happens over a high heat in about thirty-five minutes; a karahi that has simmered gently is a different, duller thing.

  • No onion. That is what makes it a karahi.
  • Lift the tomato skins out as they loosen.
  • High heat throughout — it is a fried curry, not a stewed one.

item.title: Moroccan Mint Tea
item.description: Moroccan mint tea — gunpowder green tea with spearmint, sweetened and poured from height.
item.content:encoded:
Rinsing the gunpowder leaves with a first pour of boiling water washes away the dust and bitterness that would otherwise dominate — the tea itself is never brewed long. The pour from height is not showmanship: it aerates the tea and builds the foam head that tells you it has been made properly.

  • Rinse the leaves first. It is the difference between smooth and bitter.
  • Mint for four minutes, no longer.
  • Pour from height. Foam is the sign of a well-made glass.

item.title: Pol Sambol
item.description: Sri Lankan coconut sambol of grated coconut pounded with dried chilli flakes, red onion, Maldive fish and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Pound it rather than blending it. A blender chops and aerates and gives you damp pink confetti; a mortar bruises the onion and chilli into the coconut so the oils release and the colour goes right through. If you must use a machine, pulse four times and no more. Add the lime at the very end — early, it starts to cook the onion and the texture softens.

  • Pound, do not blend.
  • Keep going until the colour is even — that is the sign it is done.
  • Lime last.

item.title: Sri Lankan Dhal Curry
item.description: Sri Lankan red lentil curry cooked with coconut milk, turmeric, pandan and curry leaves, finished with a mustard seed tempering.
item.content:encoded:
The tempering goes on at the end and is poured over rather than stirred in during cooking. Mustard seeds, curry leaves, dried chilli and onion fried in oil for thirty seconds carry aromatics that are destroyed by twenty minutes of simmering — added last, they sit on the surface and you get them in the first spoonful. Coconut milk goes in at the end too, and must not boil hard or it splits.

  • Temper last and pour it over.
  • Coconut milk warmed, never boiled.
  • A pandan leaf if you can get one — it is the Sri Lankan note.

item.title: Molokhia
item.description: Molokhia — Egyptian jute leaf stew finished with garlic and coriander fried in ghee, served over rice.
item.content:encoded:
Molokhia must never boil once the leaves are in — boiling breaks the mucilage that gives it its silky body and leaves you with green water and sludge. The taqliya, garlic and coriander fried hard in ghee and poured in at the end, is added off the heat and the pot is covered immediately so the aroma stays in.

  • Never boil the leaves. Below a simmer, always.
  • The taqliya goes in off the heat, and the lid goes straight on.
  • Do not stir it much once the leaves are in — it breaks the texture.

item.title: Kare-Kare
item.description: Filipino oxtail stew in a thick peanut and toasted rice sauce with aubergine and pak choi, served with bagoong.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is unsalted, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight — the bagoong on the side is the seasoning, and each mouthful gets as much as the person wants. Salt the sauce as well and the dish becomes overwhelming. Toasted ground rice thickens it without flour and gives the faint grittiness that tells you it is kare-kare and not a satay sauce.

  • Do not salt the sauce. The bagoong is the seasoning.
  • Toast the rice properly — deep gold, not pale.
  • Strain the annatto seeds out after a minute.

item.title: Lumpiang Shanghai
item.description: Filipino lumpiang Shanghai of minced pork, carrot and water chestnut rolled thin in spring roll wrappers and deep fried.
item.content:encoded:
Roll them thin — no thicker than a finger — and seal with a flour and water paste rather than egg. A thick lumpia has a raw centre by the time the wrapper is golden, and egg-sealed edges pop open in the oil. Freeze them on a tray before frying if you have made a batch: they hold their shape better and the wrapper crisps harder from cold.

  • Pencil-thin. A fat lumpia is raw inside.
  • Flour paste to seal, never egg.
  • Freeze before frying if you are making a lot.

item.title: Tunisian Brik
item.description: Tunisian brik — malsouka pastry folded around tuna, capers and a whole egg, fried with the yolk runny.
item.content:encoded:
The whole point is the runny yolk, which means the brik goes into hot oil the moment the egg is in and comes out in ninety seconds — long enough for the pastry to crisp, not long enough for the yolk to set. Making a small well of filling for the egg to sit in stops it sliding to the edge and leaking during the fold.

  • Ninety seconds total. Any longer and the yolk sets and the point is lost.
  • Build a well of filling for the egg to sit in.
  • Have the oil at temperature before you crack the egg, not after.

item.title: Chicken Inasal
item.description: Bacolod-style grilled chicken marinated in calamansi, vinegar, lemongrass and ginger, basted with annatto and butter oil.
item.content:encoded:
The basting oil is made separately from annatto, margarine and some of the marinade, and it goes on every time you turn the chicken — five or six times over twenty-five minutes. That repeated painting is what builds the deep orange lacquer; brushed on once at the end it just sits there and burns. Use chicken with the bone in and the skin on or it dries out over the fire.

  • Baste at every turn, five or six times.
  • Bone in, skin on.
  • Strain the annatto seeds out or they catch and taste bitter.

item.title: Sisig
item.description: Filipino sisig of pork belly and jowl simmered, grilled and chopped, dressed with calamansi, chilli and onion on a sizzling plate.
item.content:encoded:
Three cooking stages and each does a different job: boiling makes the meat tender, grilling gives it smoke and colour, chopping and frying on the hot plate crisps the edges. Skip the grill and it is a chopped pork stew. The plate must be preheated until it is genuinely dangerous — if it stops sizzling when the meat lands, the plate was not hot enough.

  • Boil, grill, chop. All three.
  • The plate must be smoking before the meat touches it.
  • Chop by hand — a processor gives you paste.

item.title: Ayam Goreng
item.description: Indonesian fried chicken poached in turmeric, lemongrass and galangal, then deep fried and served with the fried aromatic crumbs.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is poached in the spice paste before frying, which seasons it all the way through — battered fried chicken is only seasoned on the surface. Then the leftover poaching liquid, reduced and dropped into the hot oil, sets into the crisp golden crumbs called kremes, which are scattered over. Most recipes throw that liquid away and lose the best part.

  • Poach first — that is how the seasoning gets inside.
  • Dry the chicken on a rack before it goes in the oil.
  • Do not throw the poaching liquid away. It becomes the kremes.

item.title: Merguez Shakshuka
item.description: Merguez shakshuka — eggs poached in a harissa and caraway tomato sauce with browned merguez.
item.content:encoded:
Browning the merguez first and cooking the sauce in its rendered spiced fat is what separates this from a sausage added to shakshuka — the whole pan takes on the harissa and fennel. The sauce needs to be thick enough that the wells you make for the eggs hold their shape, or the whites spread and overcook before the yolks set.

  • Cook the sauce in the merguez fat. That is where the flavour is.
  • Thick sauce before the eggs go in, or they spread and toughen.
  • Cover the pan for the eggs — the steam sets the tops while the yolks stay soft.

item.title: Beef Satay
item.description: Malaysian beef satay marinated in lemongrass, galangal and turmeric, grilled on skewers and served with peanut sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Thread the beef on the skewer in a flat ribbon rather than in cubes, so it grills in three minutes rather than eight. Satay is meant to be charred outside and barely done inside, and cubes cannot do that — by the time the middle is warm the outside is dry. Fry the peanut sauce paste until the oil splits out before the liquid goes in, exactly as with a curry.

  • Flat ribbons, not cubes.
  • Three minutes on the fiercest heat you have.
  • Split the oil out of the sauce paste before the liquid goes in.

item.title: Hokkien Mee
item.description: KL Hokkien mee of thick yellow noodles braised in dark caramel soy with prawns, pork, cabbage and crisp pork lard.
item.content:encoded:
The crisp pork lard is not a garnish and there is no substitute — it is rendered slowly from diced back fat until the pieces are golden and hard, and both the fat and the crackling go into the dish. That fat is what carries the dark soy through the noodles. The wok must be as hot as it will go and the noodles left still for thirty seconds at a time so they catch.

  • Render your own lard. It is the dish.
  • Leave the noodles still so they catch on the metal.
  • Dark soy for colour, light soy for salt — both.

item.title: Jamón Croquetas
item.description: Jamón croquetas — a thick béchamel with cured ham, chilled overnight, crumbed and fried until molten.
item.content:encoded:
The béchamel is cooked far longer than a sauce would be — twenty minutes of stirring — because the flour has to lose its raw taste and the mixture has to be stiff enough to shape when cold. Infusing the milk with the ham trimmings and a bay leaf first puts the flavour into the sauce rather than leaving it in lumps of ham.

  • Twenty minutes of stirring. It is the whole recipe and there is no shortcut.
  • Overnight in the fridge, not two hours.
  • Hot oil, short fry. A cooler pan lets them burst.

item.title: Ghoriba
item.description: Moroccan ghoriba of ground almonds, egg and lemon zest, rolled in icing sugar and baked until the tops crack open.
item.content:encoded:
The cracks are made by the icing sugar, not by the oven. Roll each ball in a thick, unembarrassed coat — far more than looks sensible — and the sugar sets into a dry shell before the almond underneath finishes rising, so the shell has to split. A thin dusting melts into the surface and you get a smooth, pale biscuit that tastes right and looks like nothing.

  • Coat heavily. A dusting will not crack.
  • Pale is done — colour means dry.
  • Chilled dough holds its dome; warm dough spreads flat.

item.title: Kookoo Sabzi
item.description: Persian kookoo sabzi of parsley, coriander, dill and chives bound with egg, walnuts and barberries, cooked slowly in a pan.
item.content:encoded:
The herbs have to be dry and chopped fine, and the pan has to stay low. Wet herbs steam and the kookoo goes grey and weeps; a hot pan scorches the herb next to the metal, which is where the bitterness people complain about comes from. Spin the herbs dry, chop them almost to a paste, and give it the full half hour on the lowest flame the hob will hold.

  • Dry herbs. Wet ones make it grey.
  • Lowest flame you have, the whole way.
  • Barberries need a rinse or they carry grit.

item.title: Placki Ziemniaczane
item.description: Polish potato pancakes of grated potato and onion squeezed dry, bound with egg and flour, fried crisp in oil.
item.content:encoded:
Squeeze the grated potato hard in a cloth and then let the liquid stand for two minutes — a layer of white starch settles at the bottom. Pour the water off and scrape that starch back into the potato. It is the binder, it costs nothing, and it means you need barely any flour, which is what keeps the pancakes light rather than stodgy.

  • Squeeze hard, then reclaim the starch.
  • A rack, not paper, or the underside steams soft.
  • Fry them as you grate — raw potato greys within minutes.

item.title: Crema Catalana
item.description: Crema catalana — lemon and cinnamon custard set with cornflour and burnt under a hot iron.
item.content:encoded:
Unlike crème brûlée, this is thickened on the hob with cornflour rather than baked, so it sets soft and is served cold from the fridge with a warm sugar crust on top. The infusion is done off the heat with lemon peel and cinnamon, because boiling the peel makes the custard bitter.

  • Shallow dishes, not ramekins. The ratio of crust to custard is the point.
  • Blot the surface before sugaring or the crust will not set.
  • Burn it at the table. A crust made ten minutes early has already gone soft.

item.title: Francesinha
item.description: Francesinha — Porto sandwich of steak, sausage and ham under melted cheese in a beer and tomato sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce is what every Porto café argues about, and the version that works at home is built like a light gravy — beer, stock, tomato and a spoonful of piri-piri, thickened just enough to pour rather than sit. The cheese goes on before the sauce so it seals the sandwich, otherwise the bread collapses on the way to the table.

  • Wrap the whole sandwich in cheese, sides included. It is the waterproofing.
  • Sauce hot and poured at the table, over and around.
  • Blend the sauce smooth — a lumpy francesinha sauce is nobody's friend.

item.title: Syrniki
item.description: Russian syrniki of tvorog curd cheese bound with egg and a little flour, shaped into thick discs and pan-fried.
item.content:encoded:
Drain the curd cheese overnight if it is at all wet — wet tvorog needs more flour to hold together and the extra flour is exactly what turns syrniki into rubbery discs. The rule is as little flour as will let you shape them. Shape them thick, about two centimetres, so the outside crisps while the inside stays soft.

  • If you have only wet curd cheese, hang it in muslin overnight before starting.
  • Drain the cheese and sieve it.
  • As little flour as you can get away with.
  • Thick discs, medium heat, patience.

item.title: Brigadeiro
item.description: Brazilian brigadeiro of condensed milk, cocoa and butter cooked to a thick fudge, rolled into balls and coated in sprinkles.
item.content:encoded:
The test is the spoon track: drag a wooden spoon across the base of the pan and the mixture should part and stay parted for a full two seconds before closing. Short of that they will not hold a ball; past it they set hard and crack. It takes about twelve minutes on a low heat and there is no visual shortcut — you have to keep testing.

  • The two-second spoon track is the only reliable test.
  • Cool at room temperature, never in the fridge.
  • Butter your hands or you will fight it.

item.title: Papa a la Huancaína
item.description: Peruvian papa a la huancaína of boiled potatoes under a blended ají amarillo, cheese and cracker sauce with egg and olives.
item.content:encoded:
Cream crackers are the thickener and they are not a substitute for anything — they give the sauce its particular body, somewhere between a dip and a custard, without any flour or cooking. Blend the ají amarillo paste with the oil first so it emulsifies, then add the cheese and crackers. Serve the sauce cold over cold potatoes; warm, it thins and slides off.

  • Cream crackers, and no substitute.
  • Emulsify the chilli paste with the oil before anything else.
  • Everything cold, sauce included.

item.title: Arroz de Marisco
item.description: Arroz de marisco — soupy Portuguese seafood rice with tomato, coriander, prawns, clams and crab.
item.content:encoded:
This rice is malandrinho — deliberately loose — so the ratio is closer to four parts liquid to one of rice, and it is served the moment it is done because it thickens fast in the pot. Making a quick stock from the prawn heads and shells is the step that separates a good version from a red rice with seafood in it.

  • Make the prawn shell stock. Fifteen minutes of work, the whole flavour.
  • It should look too wet when you take it off the heat. It thickens in the bowl.
  • Coriander by the handful, not the sprig. This is a Portuguese dish, not a Spanish one.

item.title: Anticuchos
item.description: Peruvian anticuchos of beef heart marinated in ají panca, garlic, cumin and vinegar, skewered and grilled over high heat.
item.content:encoded:
Beef heart is very lean muscle and it has two states: rare and ruined. Two minutes a side over the fiercest heat you can build, and off. The vinegar in the marinade does the tenderising over several hours, which is why the marinating time is not negotiable, but leaving it overnight makes the surface mushy — four to six hours is the window.

  • Trim all the sinew. It never becomes tender.
  • Two minutes a side, no more.
  • Five hours in the marinade, not overnight.

item.title: Jerk Pork
item.description: Jamaican jerk pork marinated in scotch bonnet, allspice, thyme and spring onion, slow-grilled over pimento wood or charcoal.
item.content:encoded:
Allspice — pimento — is the backbone and it goes in three ways: ground in the marinade, whole berries crushed into the fire, and ideally pimento wood on the coals. Scotch bonnet is not interchangeable with any other chilli either; it is fruity as well as hot and the fruit is half the flavour. Cook it slow and away from the direct flame, or the sugar in the marinade burns before the pork is done.

  • Indirect heat for the hour, direct for the last five minutes.
  • Allspice berries on the coals.
  • Chop it rough through the bark — jerk is not carved.

item.title: Bifana
item.description: Bifana — Portuguese pork sandwich with white wine, garlic and paprika marinade in a crusty roll.
item.content:encoded:
The pork is sliced thin enough to cook in about ninety seconds, which means it never has time to toughen — thickness is doing more work here than any technique. The marinade becomes the sauce: after the meat is lifted out it reduces in the same pan, and the bread is dipped in it before the pork goes back on.

  • Beat the pork properly thin. Thickness is what makes a bifana tough.
  • Reduce the marinade hard before the meat goes back in.
  • Dip the bread in the sauce. That is how it is served in Lisbon.

item.title: Jamaican Beef Patties
item.description: Jamaican beef patties of turmeric and suet shortcrust folded around spiced minced beef with scotch bonnet and thyme.
item.content:encoded:
The filling must be completely cold before it goes into the pastry — warm filling melts the fat in the dough and you lose the flakiness entirely. Make it the day before if you can. The breadcrumbs in the filling are not padding either: they absorb the gravy so it stays inside the patty rather than boiling out through the crimp.

  • Cold filling into cold pastry.
  • Breadcrumbs hold the gravy in.
  • Crimp firmly or they leak.

item.title: Puff Puff
item.description: Nigerian puff puff of yeasted batter with nutmeg, dropped into hot oil and fried into round golden balls, dusted with sugar.
item.content:encoded:
It is a batter, not a dough, and that is the whole thing. It should drop off the spoon in a thick ribbon that takes a second to fall — too stiff and you get bread, too loose and it spreads into a pancake. And the oil wants to be moderate, around 170C: hot enough to seal, cool enough that the middle cooks before the outside browns, which is the failure everyone has the first time.

  • A ribbon off the spoon, not a ball.
  • A dry ice cream scoop gives rounder ones than two spoons.
  • If the first is raw inside, drop the oil 10 degrees.

item.title: Cá Kho Tộ
item.description: Cá kho tộ — Vietnamese fish braised in caramel and fish sauce until the sauce becomes a dark glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Nước màu — sugar cooked to a dark caramel and stopped with water — gives the dish its colour and its bitter edge, and it has to be taken further than looks safe: pale caramel makes a sauce that is only sweet. Braising with the lid off for the last stage is what reduces it to a glaze rather than leaving fish in syrup.

  • Take the caramel darker than feels comfortable. That bitterness is the flavour.
  • Uncover at the end. A covered pot never reduces to a glaze.
  • Coarse black pepper, and a lot of it. It is a defining note, not a seasoning.

item.title: Taiwanese Beef Noodle Soup
item.description: Taiwanese beef noodle soup — shin and tendon braised in a soy and doubanjiang broth over wheat noodles.
item.content:encoded:
The broth is made in two parts: a clean beef stock and a separate braising liquid heavy with doubanjiang and aromatics, combined only at the end. Doing it that way keeps the soup from turning muddy and salty, which is what happens when the fermented bean paste cooks in the whole pot for three hours.

  • Blanch and rinse the beef first. It is the difference between clear and cloudy.
  • Fry the doubanjiang until the oil turns red. Raw bean paste tastes flat.
  • Cook the noodles separately or the broth goes starchy.

item.title: Mandazi
item.description: Kenyan mandazi of cardamom and coconut milk dough cut into triangles and fried until puffed and golden brown.
item.content:encoded:
Roll them thicker than feels right — 5 mm, not 3 — and cut generous triangles. Thin mandazi crisp through and turn into biscuits; the thing you want is a puffed pillow with a hollow inside and a soft crumb, and only a thick piece of dough traps enough steam to blow itself open like that in the first thirty seconds in the oil.

  • Five millimetres. Thinner and they will not puff.
  • Coconut milk, not water — it is what makes the crumb tender.
  • Fry the offcuts first to test the oil.

item.title: Baleadas
item.description: Honduran baleadas of thick homemade flour tortillas folded over refried beans, crema and crumbled salty cheese.
item.content:encoded:
The tortilla is thicker and softer than a Mexican one and it wants to be, because it is folded rather than rolled and has to hold without cracking. Rest the dough for half an hour so the gluten relaxes and it rolls out without springing back, and cook them on a dry pan just until they puff and blister — a second too long and they go crisp, which is the wrong texture entirely.

  • Thick and soft, not thin and crisp.
  • Rest the dough or it fights you.
  • Forty-five seconds a side and into a cloth.

item.title: Lu Rou Fan
item.description: Lu rou fan — Taiwanese braised pork belly over rice, glossy with soy, five spice and fried shallots.
item.content:encoded:
The pork is hand-diced rather than minced, so each piece keeps its layers of fat and meat and renders into the sauce instead of disappearing into it. Fried shallots — made fresh, not from a packet — are the backbone of the flavour, and their oil is used for the braise.

  • Dice by hand. Minced pork gives you a completely different, lesser dish.
  • Make the fried shallots yourself and cook in their oil.
  • Ninety minutes on low. The sauce should be glossy, not watery.

item.title: Tafelspitz
item.description: Austrian tafelspitz of beef rump cap simmered in broth with root vegetables, served in the broth with apple horseradish.
item.content:encoded:
The meat goes into water that is already simmering, not cold water. Started cold, the proteins leach out and you get a superb broth and dull, grey beef — started hot, the outside sets and the meat keeps its flavour, which is the point here since it is the thing being served. Never let it boil after that; a bare shiver for two and a half hours.

  • Into simmering water, not cold.
  • Never boil — that is the whole discipline.
  • Char the onion halves first for colour in the broth.

item.title: Moules Marinière
item.description: Belgian moules marinière of mussels steamed with shallots, garlic, white wine, butter and parsley, served with the cooking liquor.
item.content:encoded:
Cook them in a pan wide enough to hold them no more than three deep and shake rather than stir. Mussels open at slightly different rates, and stirring breaks the ones that opened first while the rest are still shut — shaking redistributes them without damage. Any that stay closed after four minutes should be thrown away, and any open before cooking tapped: if it does not close, discard it.

  • A wide pan, three deep at most.
  • Shake, never stir.
  • Anything still shut goes in the bin.

item.title: Taiwanese Popcorn Chicken
item.description: Taiwanese popcorn chicken — sweet potato starch coated chicken fried twice with basil and white pepper.
item.content:encoded:
Sweet potato starch is coarser than cornflour and fries into a knobbly, glassy crust that stays crisp far longer — it is the single ingredient that makes this taste like a night market rather than a nugget. The basil goes into the oil for eight seconds at the end, which crisps it without turning it black.

  • Sweet potato starch, not cornflour. It is not substitutable here.
  • Squeeze the coating on and rest it 10 minutes before frying.
  • Basil for eight seconds. Bone dry, or it will spit dangerously.

item.title: Stoofvlees
item.description: Flemish beef stew braised in dark Belgian ale with onions, thickened by a slice of mustard-spread bread and sweetened with syrup.
item.content:encoded:
A slice of bread spread thickly with mustard is laid on top of the stew and left to dissolve into it. It thickens the sauce, and the mustard cuts the sweetness of the beer and the syrup — this is the traditional method and it works better than flour, which dulls the flavour. Use a dark abbey-style ale, not a lager and not a stout: lager is thin, stout is bitter.

  • Abbey ale, not lager and not stout.
  • The mustard bread is the thickener.
  • Balance it at the end with more vinegar if it is too sweet.

item.title: Stamppot
item.description: Dutch stamppot of potatoes boiled with kale and mashed with butter and milk, served with smoked sausage and a well of gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Cook the kale with the potatoes rather than separately. It is not about saving a pan — the potato takes up the kale's flavour and colour as they boil together, and stamppot made by folding cooked kale into finished mash is stripey rather than green through. Mash it coarsely too; this is not a purée and the texture should be rough.

  • Kale in with the potatoes, not cooked separately.
  • Steam the pan dry before the butter goes in.
  • Coarse mash, and a real well for the gravy.

item.title: Raggmunk
item.description: Swedish raggmunk of grated potato in a thin milk and flour batter, fried in butter and served with bacon and lingonberry.
item.content:encoded:
Raggmunk is grated potato bound in a thin crêpe batter, which is what separates it from a rösti or a latke — the batter goes into the potato, not the other way round. Do not squeeze the potato: the starch is part of the binding here. Fry in butter rather than oil, and accept that they brown quickly because of it.

  • Grate straight into the batter.
  • Do not squeeze the potato — this is not a rösti.
  • Butter, and fresh butter for every pancake.

item.title: Pineapple Cake
item.description: Pineapple cake — Taiwanese buttery shortbread squares filled with firm, tart pineapple jam.
item.content:encoded:
The filling has to be cooked down until it is genuinely stiff and tacky, well past jam consistency, because anything looser will boil out through the pastry in the oven. Adding a little winter melon or grated apple gives body and tempers the sharpness, which is why traditional versions rarely use pineapple alone.

  • Cook the filling until a spoon leaves a clear channel. Loose filling leaks.
  • Flip them halfway so both faces colour evenly.
  • Cool fully in the moulds — warm cakes fall apart.

item.title: Mansaf
item.description: Jordanian mansaf of lamb simmered in jameed yoghurt sauce, served over turmeric rice with toasted almonds and pine nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Yoghurt splits when it boils unless something holds it, and the something is starch plus one direction. Whisk cornflour into the cold jameed, bring it up slowly, and stir continuously in one direction only until it boils — the traditional instruction, and it is not superstition. Reversing the stir shears the protein network the starch is building, and the sauce curdles in the pan in front of you.

  • One direction, without pause, until it boils.
  • Skim properly at the start or the sauce goes cloudy.
  • Serve the extra sauce hot in a jug; it is meant to be poured on at the table.

item.title: Sfiha
item.description: Lebanese sfiha of yeasted dough rounds topped with minced lamb, tomato, tahini and pomegranate molasses, baked hot.
item.content:encoded:
Salt the onion and tomato and drain them before they go anywhere near the dough. Raw, they release their water in the oven, the topping poaches instead of roasting and the base underneath turns to paste. Ten minutes in a sieve with a teaspoon of salt takes out a surprising amount of liquid and leaves a topping that browns at the edges.

  • Drain the vegetables, then press them again.
  • Thin dough, thick topping — the reverse of a pizza.
  • A preheated tray is what stops the bases going soggy.

item.title: Nihari
item.description: Nihari — beef shank stewed for hours in a spiced gravy thickened with wheat flour, with ginger and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Nihari is one of very few curries thickened with a flour slurry, and it has to be whisked into hot liquid off the boil or it sets into lumps that never disperse. The marrow bones are not garnish: the marrow melting into the gravy is what gives nihari its particular richness, and it is scooped out and stirred in at the end.

  • Whisk the flour slurry into gravy that is off the boil. Lumps are permanent.
  • The overnight cook is traditional and it does show. Four hours is the minimum.
  • Stir the marrow in. It is where a lot of the richness comes from.

item.title: Fattet Hummus
item.description: Lebanese fattet hummus layering crisped pitta, warm chickpeas and garlic tahini yoghurt under browned butter and pine nuts.
item.content:encoded:
Build it at the table and eat it within a minute. The whole point is three temperatures and two textures at once — crisp bread, warm chickpeas, cool yoghurt, hot butter — and the moment it stands, the bread drinks the yoghurt and the dish becomes a bowl of soft beige. Have everything ready, layer it fast, pour the butter over as you carry it.

  • Everything ready before you start layering.
  • Yoghurt at room temperature pours; fridge-cold yoghurt sits in lumps.
  • Save a little chickpea liquid to loosen the yoghurt if it stiffens.

item.title: Shorbat Adas
item.description: Egyptian shorbat adas of red lentils simmered with onion, carrot and cumin, blended smooth and finished with lemon juice.
item.content:encoded:
The lemon is not a garnish, it is the seasoning. Lentils cooked with cumin taste flat and slightly dusty until acid goes in, and then the whole bowl comes into focus — the cumin sharpens, the lentils read as sweet. Squeeze it in at the table rather than in the pan, because the brightness fades within a few minutes of heat.

  • The potato is what makes it velvety, not cream.
  • Blend longer than you think; grainy means unfinished.
  • Lemon at the table, not in the pan.

item.title: Tteok Galbi
item.description: Korean tteok galbi of minced short rib seasoned with soy, pear and sesame, shaped into patties and grilled with a glaze.
item.content:encoded:
Grated pear does two things at once and both matter: its enzymes tenderise the meat and its sugars help the glaze caramelise. Asian pear is traditional, but any hard pear works and apple does not — apple is too acidic and turns the surface of the meat mushy rather than tender. Knead the mixture until sticky so the patties hold on the grill.

  • Pear, not apple.
  • Knead until sticky or they fall apart.
  • Glaze on the last two turns only, or the sugar burns.

item.title: Haleem
item.description: Haleem — wheat, lentils and meat cooked for hours and pounded to a smooth, stringy porridge.
item.content:encoded:
Haleem is judged on whether the meat has disappeared into the grain — you should not be able to find a piece of it, only strands. That only happens with sustained pounding while the pot is hot, which develops the wheat starch and shreds the meat at the same time. Cooking the pulses and the meat separately first means neither is overdone by the time the other is ready.

  • Pound it for at least twenty minutes. That is the entire dish.
  • Cook the grains and the meat separately, then combine.
  • Keep hot water to hand — haleem thickens fast and catches easily.

item.title: Dubu Jorim
item.description: Korean braised tofu, pan-fried until golden then simmered in a soy, gochugaru and garlic sauce with spring onion.
item.content:encoded:
Press the tofu and fry it hard before any liquid goes near it. A golden crust changes both texture and flavour and it stops the slabs disintegrating in the braise — untfried tofu goes to pieces and the dish becomes a soy soup with tofu in it. Fry it dry in a hot pan until it releases on its own; poking it before then tears the surface off.

  • Press it, then fry it dry and hard.
  • Wait until it releases before turning.
  • Sauce around the tofu, not over it, so the crust survives.

item.title: Ojingeo Bokkeum
item.description: Korean spicy stir-fried squid in a gochujang and gochugaru sauce with onion, carrot and courgette over a high heat.
item.content:encoded:
Score the squid on the inside in a diamond pattern before cutting it into pieces. The cuts make it curl decoratively, but more usefully they let heat in fast so it cooks in about three minutes — and squid has two acceptable states, three minutes or forty, with nothing but rubber between them. Have everything else finished before it goes in.

  • Score the inside, not the outside.
  • Three minutes for the squid and not a second more.
  • Vegetables finished before the squid goes in.

item.title: Seekh Kebab
item.description: Seekh kebab — spiced minced lamb moulded on skewers and grilled over coals until charred and juicy.
item.content:encoded:
Minced lamb slides off a skewer unless the mixture is worked until the proteins bind, so it is kneaded rather than stirred and then chilled hard. Raw papaya paste is the traditional tenderiser; it contains papain, which is powerful enough that thirty minutes is plenty and two hours turns the meat to mush.

  • Knead until it is one sticky mass. Stirring will not do it.
  • Squeeze the onion completely dry.
  • Flat skewers and cold mixture. Round skewers let it spin and drop.

item.title: Zosui
item.description: Japanese zosui of cooked rice simmered in dashi with soy and mirin, finished with beaten egg and spring onion.
item.content:encoded:
Rinse the cooked rice under cold water before it goes into the dashi. It sounds odd and it is what stops zosui turning into porridge — washing off the surface starch means the grains stay separate in the broth rather than dissolving into it. The egg goes in off the heat in a thin stream and is stirred once; stirred hard it disappears into cloudiness.

  • Rinse the rice or you get porridge.
  • Egg off the heat, one stir only.
  • Cover for a minute so the ribbons set.

item.title: Hiyayakko
item.description: Japanese chilled silken tofu topped with grated ginger, spring onion, bonito flakes and soy sauce.
item.content:encoded:
There is nothing to hide behind, so buy the best silken tofu you can find and serve it very cold. Drain it on kitchen paper for ten minutes before plating — the water that pools around it otherwise dilutes the soy into something grey and weak. Grate the ginger just before serving; grated ginger loses its aroma within about half an hour.

  • Drain on paper for ten minutes.
  • Chill the plates.
  • Soy at the table so the tofu does not sit in it.

item.title: Chapli Kebab
item.description: Chapli kebab — flat Peshawari beef patties with tomato, coriander seed and pomegranate, fried crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Coarsely crushed coriander seed and dried pomegranate seed are the two flavours that define chapli kebab, and both must be crushed rather than ground so you meet them in bites. The patties are pressed very thin and fried in a shallow pool of fat, which is what makes the outside crusted while the inside is still soft.

  • Crush the seeds coarsely. Powder loses the whole character.
  • Very thin patties. Thick ones steam rather than crust.
  • Shallow fry in fat, not a dry pan. That is where the crust comes from.

item.title: Khai Jiao
item.description: Thai khai jiao omelette beaten with fish sauce and lime, poured into deep hot oil so it puffs, served over rice with chilli sauce.
item.content:encoded:
This is not a French omelette and the oil must be deep and genuinely hot — about 190C, enough that the egg puffs violently the moment it lands. That is what gives the crisp lacy edges and the soufflé middle. A spoonful of rice flour in the beaten egg makes the crust hold, and beating it hard from a height introduces air the puffing depends on.

  • Deep oil at 190C. Shallow oil gives a flat omelette.
  • Pour from a height so it spreads and puffs.
  • Ninety seconds untouched.

item.title: Pad Prik King
item.description: Thai pad prik king of green beans and pork stir-fried in red curry paste with kaffir lime, fish sauce and palm sugar.
item.content:encoded:
No liquid goes into this at all, which is the whole identity of the dish and what makes people think their curry paste has failed. Fry the paste in oil until it darkens and smells cooked — about two minutes — and it will coat the beans as a dry, intensely flavoured crust. A splash of stock turns it into an ordinary red curry.

  • No coconut milk and no stock. It is a dry curry.
  • Dry the blanched beans or the paste slides off.
  • Fry the paste until it darkens before anything else goes in.

item.title: Sri Lankan Fish Curry
item.description: Sri Lankan fish curry — fish in coconut milk with roasted curry powder, goraka and curry leaves.
item.content:encoded:
Sri Lankan roasted curry powder is toasted far darker than Indian garam masala, almost to the edge of burning, and that is where the colour and the smoky depth come from. Goraka — dried garcinia — gives a sourness quite unlike tamarind, and it needs soaking before it will release it.

  • Roast the spices dark. This is the single difference from an Indian curry.
  • Never boil once the coconut milk is in.
  • Shake the pan rather than stirring, or the fish breaks up.

item.title: Bánh Cuốn
item.description: Vietnamese steamed rice rolls filled with minced pork and wood ear mushroom, topped with fried shallots and nuoc cham.
item.content:encoded:
The batter must be thin as milk and rested at least half an hour, and the cloth or pan must be genuinely hot before each pour. The sheet sets in about forty seconds; longer and it toughens, shorter and it tears when you lift it. Oil the work surface rather than the sheet, and lift with a flat blade in one movement — hesitating is what tears them.

  • Batter as thin as milk, rested.
  • Forty seconds and lift in one movement.
  • Oil the surface, not the sheet.

item.title: Bún Riêu
item.description: Vietnamese bún riêu of a tomato and crab paste broth with crab and egg curds, tofu and rice vermicelli.
item.content:encoded:
The crab and egg mixture is poured into simmering broth and then left completely alone for two minutes. It rises and sets into soft clouds on its own; stir it and you get cloudy broth with crab dust in it and nothing to eat. Push it gently to the side once it has set and let the broth clear again before serving.

  • Pour the crab mixture in and do not touch it.
  • A bare simmer — a rolling boil breaks the clouds up.
  • Annatto for the colour, strained out after a minute.

item.title: Egg Hoppers
item.description: Egg hoppers — fermented rice and coconut batter cooked in a bowl pan with an egg in the centre.
item.content:encoded:
The overnight ferment does two things: it produces the sourness that defines a hopper and the gas that gives the lacy, holey edge. The batter must be thin — closer to single cream than pancake batter — because a thick batter cannot be swirled up the sides of the pan into that translucent rim.

  • Thin batter, or you cannot swirl it up the sides.
  • Cover the pan for the egg. It sets the white while the rim crisps.
  • Eat them as they come out. Hoppers go soft within minutes.

item.title: Paneer Tikka Masala
item.description: Paneer marinated in spiced yoghurt and charred under a grill, then simmered in a tomato, cashew and cream gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Grill the marinated paneer and peppers before they go into the sauce, and let them take real colour — black at the corners, not merely warm. That char is the entire difference between paneer tikka masala and paneer butter masala, and it survives the gravy. Paneer added raw makes a perfectly good curry that is simply a different dish.

  • Char it properly. Black corners, not golden.
  • Grill the peppers and onion with the paneer, not separately.
  • Cream off the heat.

item.title: Kottu Roti
item.description: Kottu roti — chopped Sri Lankan flatbread griddled with vegetables, egg and curry gravy.
item.content:encoded:
Kottu is a texture dish: the roti has to be chopped on the hot surface, not before, so the pieces sear as they are cut and stay separate. A ladle of thin curry gravy poured in at the end is what stops the whole thing being dry, and it must be added last so it does not steam the roti soft.

  • Chop it on the heat, not on a board. The searing as you cut is the point.
  • Gravy last, and only a splash. Too much and it turns to porridge.
  • Day-old roti. Fresh roti tears into mush.

item.title: Veg Kolhapuri
item.description: Maharashtrian mixed vegetable curry in a dark roasted masala of dried coconut, sesame and Kashmiri and byadgi chillies.
item.content:encoded:
The masala is dry-roasted almost to the point of burning, and that is deliberate — the darkness is where the colour and the smoky depth come from. Roast the dried coconut last and separately, because it goes from nutty to acrid faster than anything else in the pan. Grind it all while still warm and it comes out as a paste rather than a powder.

  • Roast the coconut separately and last.
  • Grind the masala warm, with a little water.
  • It is meant to be dark and very hot.

item.title: Tawa Pulao
item.description: Mumbai street rice tossed on a hot griddle with pav bhaji masala, butter, peas, peppers and lemon.
item.content:encoded:
Use rice that is cold and slightly dry, and cook it on the widest pan you own over a high flame. The dish is defined by the contact between rice and hot metal — a deep saucepan steams it instead, and the whole point is the slightly scorched grains and the butter catching. Mash a little of the vegetables into the masala so the colour goes through the rice.

  • The widest pan you own, on the highest heat.
  • Mash a third of the vegetables so the colour spreads.
  • Butter twice — some at the start, some at the end.

item.title: Soto Ayam
item.description: Soto ayam — Indonesian turmeric chicken soup with spice paste, noodles, sambal and fried shallots.
item.content:encoded:
The bumbu — the spice paste — must be fried in oil until it darkens and the oil separates out, which takes eight to ten minutes; added raw to the broth it tastes harsh and grassy. The broth itself stays light and clear, and all the richness comes from that fried paste and the toppings.

  • Fry the bumbu until the oil separates. Eight minutes minimum.
  • Keep the broth clear. It is not meant to be a thick soup.
  • Fried shallots and lime at the table are half the dish.

item.title: Dabeli
item.description: Kutchi dabeli of spiced mashed potato in a griddled buttered roll with dabeli masala, pomegranate, peanuts and sev.
item.content:encoded:
The three textures are the dish and each has to stay separate: soft potato, crunchy roasted peanuts and crisp sev. Assemble at the last moment and press the sev on rather than mixing it in — sev folded into the filling is soft within a minute and you have lost a third of the point. The pomegranate is not decoration either; it is the sweet-sharp note against the masala.

  • Sev pressed on at the end, never mixed in.
  • Both chutneys, one on each cut face.
  • Griddle the filled roll — it is not a cold sandwich.

item.title: Martabak Manis
item.description: Martabak manis — thick Indonesian pancake with a honeycomb crumb, filled with butter and condensed milk.
item.content:encoded:
The honeycomb surface comes from a yeasted batter that rests until it is full of gas, plus a pinch of bicarbonate of soda added right before cooking for a second burst. Sprinkling sugar over the surface once the holes have opened is what gives the crisp, caramelised layer under the fillings.

  • Wait for the holes before adding sugar. Too early and they close up.
  • Low heat throughout. A hot pan browns the base before the middle sets.
  • Butter the cut face while it is hot so it soaks in.

item.title: Samosa Chaat
item.description: Crushed samosas topped with chole, yoghurt, tamarind and mint chutneys, onion, sev and chaat masala.
item.content:encoded:
Crush the samosa, do not slice it. The dish depends on ragged edges catching the chole and the chutneys, and a neatly cut samosa keeps its layers sealed so the sauces sit on top and slide off.
