Press down with the back of a spoon until the pastry cracks in several places, then build on top of the wreckage.

  • Crush, never slice.
  • The chole should be thick enough to sit on the samosa, not run off.
  • Assemble one bowl at a time and hand it over.

item.title: Aloo Chaat
item.description: Indian potato chaat of parboiled potato cubes fried crisp and tossed with chaat masala, chilli, lime and coriander.
item.content:encoded:
Parboil the potatoes, then dry them completely and let them cool before frying. Wet or warm potato steams in the oil and comes out soft; dry and cool, the outside dehydrates fast and shatters. Rough the cubes up in the colander after draining — the fluffed surfaces are what crisp, and smooth-cut cubes never get there.

  • Dry and cool before frying.
  • Rough the cubes up in the colander.
  • Season the moment they come out of the pan, while they are hot.

item.title: Dahi Vada
item.description: Urad dal dumplings deep fried, soaked in warm water and squeezed, then dressed in whisked sweetened yoghurt with chutneys.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the fried vada in warm water for twenty minutes and then squeeze each one gently between your palms. It sounds destructive and it is the whole technique: it pushes out the frying oil and leaves the vada able to drink yoghurt instead. Skipped, they stay heavy and greasy and the yoghurt sits around them rather than in them.

  • Soak and squeeze. It is not optional.
  • The float test decides whether they will be light.
  • Two hours in the yoghurt at least; overnight is better.

item.title: Sambal Goreng Tempeh
item.description: Sambal goreng tempeh — crisp fried tempeh tossed in a sweet-hot chilli and palm sugar sambal.
item.content:encoded:
The tempeh has to be fried until genuinely crisp and then cooled before it meets the sauce, or it absorbs moisture and goes soft within minutes. Cooking the palm sugar sambal until it is thick and sticky rather than saucy means it coats the tempeh in a lacquer that keeps the crunch.

  • Thin matchsticks and a proper fry. Soft tempeh will not survive the sambal.
  • Cool the tempeh before it meets the sauce.
  • Sticky sambal, not saucy. Sixty seconds of tossing, then out of the pan.

item.title: Rasgulla
item.description: Bengali rasgulla of homemade chenna kneaded smooth, rolled into balls and boiled in a thin sugar syrup until doubled and spongy.
item.content:encoded:
The syrup must be thin — one part sugar to four parts water — and at a hard rolling boil the whole time. A thick syrup cannot get inside the ball, so the rasgulla stays dense and small; a thin one at a full boil drives in and inflates it. Keep the lid on and do not open it for the first ten minutes, and never let the boil drop.

  • Thin syrup, hard boil, lid on.
  • Rinse the chenna well or the sweet tastes sour.
  • They double — leave room in the pan.

item.title: Mysore Pak
item.description: South Indian mysore pak of gram flour cooked with hot ghee and sugar syrup to a porous set, cut while warm.
item.content:encoded:
The ghee has to be genuinely hot when it goes in, added a ladleful at a time, and it must be absorbed before the next goes in. That repeated absorption is what creates the honeycomb — the texture is aerated fat, not a solid fudge. Once the mixture starts frothing and rising up the pan you have about twenty seconds to pour it out, so have the tin ready and greased before you start.

  • Hot ghee, one ladle at a time, fully absorbed.
  • Tin greased and ready before you start.
  • Cut warm, lift out cold.

item.title: Nasi Lemak
item.description: Nasi lemak — coconut and pandan rice with sambal, fried anchovies, peanuts, cucumber and egg.
item.content:encoded:
The rice is steamed rather than boiled in coconut milk, because coconut fat scorches easily and a boiled pot catches at the base. The sambal is cooked far longer than seems necessary — thirty minutes at least — until it darkens and thickens into a jam, which is what makes it taste of Malaysia rather than of raw chilli.

  • Thirty minutes on the sambal. It should be dark and jammy, not red and wet.
  • Rest the rice off the heat for ten minutes before fluffing.
  • Toast the belacan first — it changes the whole aroma.

item.title: Kaju Katli
item.description: Indian kaju katli of ground cashews cooked with sugar syrup to a dough, rolled thin and cut into diamonds.
item.content:encoded:
Grind the cashews in short pulses and stop the moment they are powder. A few seconds too long and the oil comes out, and oily cashew paste will not set — it stays sticky whatever you do afterwards. Chilling the nuts first buys you a few more seconds of margin. The dough is ready when it comes away from the pan in one mass and holds a fingerprint.

  • Chill the cashews and pulse in bursts.
  • Stop cooking when it leaves the pan in one mass.
  • Knead it warm — that is what makes it smooth.

item.title: Besan Ladoo
item.description: North Indian besan ladoo of gram flour roasted in ghee until nut-brown, mixed with icing sugar and cardamom and rolled into balls.
item.content:encoded:
Roast the gram flour on the lowest heat for a full twenty-five minutes. It changes colour three times — pale, then sandy, then a deep nut brown — and it is only at the third stage that the raw bean flavour has gone. There is no way to hurry it: raised heat scorches the outside while the inside is still raw, and the ladoo tastes bitter and chalky.

  • Twenty-five minutes on the lowest heat. Nothing else works.
  • Cool to warm before the sugar goes in.
  • Press firmly — loose ladoo fall apart.

item.title: Malpua
item.description: Indian malpua of plain flour and milk batter fried in ghee and steeped in cardamom and saffron sugar syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Rest the batter for at least half an hour and fry it in shallow ghee rather than deep oil. The lacy, frilled edge that defines a malpua comes from batter spreading thin in fat that is only about a centimetre deep — in a deep fryer it stays a puffy round and you lose it entirely. Dip them in warm, not hot, syrup or they go soggy.

  • Shallow ghee, about a centimetre.
  • Warm syrup, not hot.
  • Two minutes in the syrup and no longer.

item.title: Roti Canai
item.description: Roti canai — Malaysian flatbread stretched thin, coiled and griddled until it pulls apart in flaky layers.
item.content:encoded:
The overnight rest in oil is what makes the dough stretchable to the point of transparency — gluten needs hours to relax, and the oil keeps the surface from drying. Coiling the stretched sheet into a spiral rather than folding it is what makes the layers separate into ribbons instead of sheets.

  • Overnight in oil. Same-day dough will not stretch thin enough.
  • Coil it, do not fold it. That spiral is what makes the ribbons.
  • Clap it while hot to separate the layers. It is not just for show.

item.title: Thandai
item.description: Indian thandai of almonds, melon seeds, fennel and peppercorns ground to a paste, whisked into cold milk with saffron and rose.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the nuts and seeds for at least four hours and peel the almonds. Unsoaked, they will not grind to a paste and the drink comes out gritty however long you blend it; unpeeled, the skins give a faint bitterness and speckle what should be pale gold. Strain the finished drink through muslin — that last step is the difference between thandai and almond milk with bits in.

  • Four hours of soaking, and peel the almonds.
  • Strain through muslin, not a sieve.
  • Two hours chilling — it tastes different cold.

item.title: Aam Panna
item.description: Indian aam panna of boiled raw green mango pulped with roasted cumin, black salt, mint and sugar, served cold over ice.
item.content:encoded:
Boil the mangoes whole rather than peeling and chopping them first. The skin holds everything in, the flesh steams to a pulp that slips off the stone, and you lose none of the sourness to the water — peeled and cubed, half the flavour ends up in the pan. Black salt is not optional and ordinary salt will not do it: the sulphurous note is what makes this taste like aam panna.

  • Boil them whole and skin them after.
  • Black salt, not table salt.
  • Sour first, salty second, sweet third.

item.title: Ayam Masak Merah
item.description: Ayam masak merah — Malaysian chicken in a red chilli and tomato gravy with coconut milk.
item.content:encoded:
The chicken is fried first, which firms the surface so it does not shred during the simmer and leaves fond in the pan for the gravy. Frying the chilli paste until the oil breaks out on top — pecah minyak — is the standard Malay test for a cooked base, and it takes considerably longer than most recipes suggest.

  • Fry the paste until the oil breaks out. Twelve minutes at least.
  • Fry the chicken first so it holds together in the gravy.
  • Sweeter than a curry, on purpose. Do not under-sugar it.

item.title: Jaljeera
item.description: Indian jaljeera of roasted cumin, mint, coriander, tamarind and black salt blended and served ice cold with boondi.
item.content:encoded:
Roast the cumin seeds and grind them yourself for this. Ready-ground cumin has lost the volatile oils that give jaljeera its whole character and the drink tastes dusty; seeds toasted for ninety seconds and pounded warm are a different ingredient. Black salt again — the sulphur is the point, and this drink is mostly salt, sour and cumin with water behind it.

  • Toast and grind the cumin yourself.
  • Strain the herb paste or it separates in the glass.
  • Boondi goes in at the last second or it dissolves.

item.title: Chaas
item.description: Indian chaas of whisked yoghurt thinned with cold water and seasoned with roasted cumin, ginger, green chilli and curry leaves.
item.content:encoded:
Whisk the yoghurt on its own until it is completely smooth before any water goes in. Water added to lumpy yoghurt keeps it lumpy no matter how hard you work afterwards, because the lumps simply float. And use cold water: warm water splits the drink into curds and whey within a couple of minutes.

  • Whisk the yoghurt smooth first, water after.
  • Ice-cold water or it splits.
  • Twenty minutes standing lets the ginger and curry leaf come through.

item.title: South Indian Filter Coffee
item.description: South Indian filter coffee brewed as decoction in a steel filter, mixed with hot milk and pulled between tumbler and davara.
item.content:encoded:
The pouring between tumbler and davara is not showmanship. It aerates the coffee, cools it to drinking temperature and builds the foam that a good kaapi is judged on — three or four pulls from a good height is right. The decoction itself must drip, not be pressed: pushing the disc down hard extracts bitterness and produces a thin, harsh cup.

  • Never press the disc down.
  • Milk steaming, not boiled.
  • Four pulls from a height for the froth.

item.title: Sinigang na Baboy
item.description: Sinigang na baboy — Filipino pork and vegetable soup soured with tamarind, served with rice.
item.content:encoded:
Sinigang is defined by how sour it is, and the sourness is layered: tamarind for the base, plus the vegetables added in strict order so each is cooked exactly right. Adding the leafy greens in the last minute off the heat keeps them green — they turn grey and slimy within two minutes of boiling.

  • It should be too sour when you taste it. The rice balances it out.
  • Vegetables in order, hardest first. Everything should finish together.
  • Greens off the heat for two minutes. Boiling them ruins the bowl.

item.title: Bombay Sandwich
item.description: Mumbai street sandwich of white bread layered with green chutney, potato, cucumber, tomato and onion, griddled in butter.
item.content:encoded:
Butter one side and green chutney the other on every slice, including the ones in the middle. The butter waterproofs the bread against the wet vegetables and the chutney is the seasoning for everything — a sandwich with chutney only in the middle tastes of bread at the edges. Slice the vegetables thin enough to see through, or the whole thing collapses when you cut it.

  • Butter and chutney on every slice, both faces.
  • Slice the vegetables almost transparent.
  • Sev on top at the very end.

item.title: Lanzhou Beef Noodle Soup
item.description: Lanzhou beef noodle soup with a clear spiced beef broth, white radish, hand-pulled noodles, coriander and chilli oil.
item.content:encoded:
Lanzhou beef noodles are judged on five things and the first is that the broth is clear — the Chinese rule is "one clear, two white, three green, four red, five yellow". Blanch the bones and throw the water away, then never let the pot boil. The white radish is not a garnish either: it goes in for the last forty minutes and sweetens and clarifies the broth.

  • Blanch and discard the first water.
  • A bare simmer, never a boil — clarity is the point.
  • Radish in for the last forty minutes only.

item.title: Lechon Kawali
item.description: Lechon kawali — Filipino pork belly simmered, dried overnight and deep fried until the skin blisters.
item.content:encoded:
Skin only blisters when it is genuinely dry, which is why the overnight uncovered chill matters more than anything that happens in the fryer. Simmering first cooks the meat through so the fry can be short and hot, aimed entirely at the skin rather than at cooking the belly.

  • Twelve hours uncovered in the fridge, minimum. Dry skin is the entire recipe.
  • Prick the skin before frying to let steam out.
  • Rest on a rack, not paper, and chop just before serving.

item.title: Pineapple Bun
item.description: Hong Kong bo lo bao of enriched milk bread dough under a sweet cookie topping that cracks into a pineapple pattern.
item.content:encoded:
The topping is a cookie dough and it must be cold and rolled thin when it goes on the risen bun. It cracks because it sets before the bun finishes rising, and the expanding dough underneath tears it apart — warm topping stretches instead of cracking, and thick topping never sets in time. Chill it hard and roll it thinner than seems sensible.

  • Topping cold and rolled thin.
  • Press it on lightly — pressing hard stops it cracking.
  • Eat warm, split, with a slab of cold butter inside.

item.title: Hong Kong Milk Tea
item.description: Hong Kong silk stocking milk tea of Ceylon tea boiled and strained repeatedly through a cloth bag, mixed with evaporated milk.
item.content:encoded:
The pulling — pouring the tea back and forth through the cloth bag six or seven times — is what makes it smooth. Each pass strains out tannin particles and aerates the liquid, so a tea brewed this strong stops being harsh and becomes velvety. Evaporated milk, not fresh: it has the concentration to stand up to tea this strong without turning the whole thing grey and weak.

  • Pull it at least six times. That is the smoothness.
  • Evaporated milk, not fresh.
  • Brew it stronger than feels right — the milk takes the edge off.

item.title: Pancit Canton
item.description: Pancit canton — Filipino wheat noodles with pork, prawns, chicken and vegetables in a soy broth.
item.content:encoded:
The noodles finish cooking in the sauce rather than in water, absorbing the stock as it reduces, which is why the liquid is measured rather than poured to taste. Everything else is cooked and removed first so the vegetables stay crisp instead of stewing while the noodles soften.

  • Cook everything separately and combine at the end. That is the whole method.
  • Noodles cook in the sauce, not in water.
  • Calamansi at the table. The dish is flat without the acid.

item.title: Shrimp Po Boy
item.description: New Orleans shrimp po boy of cornmeal-battered prawns in French bread with lettuce, tomato, pickle and remoulade.
item.content:encoded:
The bread is the thing people get wrong: it needs a crackly thin crust and a light, almost cottony crumb, so a proper French or Vietnamese baguette works and a dense sourdough does not. Cornmeal in the coating rather than all flour is what gives the prawns their particular sandy crunch, and it stays crisp under the remoulade for longer.

  • Light bread with a thin crust. Not sourdough.
  • Cornmeal in the coating for the crunch.
  • Remoulade on both faces so the bread does not go through.

item.title: French Dip
item.description: American French dip of thinly sliced roast beef in a soft roll with a cup of seasoned beef jus for dipping.
item.content:encoded:
The jus must be seasoned and reduced until it tastes good enough to drink on its own — it is not gravy and it is not stock, and a weak one makes the whole sandwich pointless. Slice the beef as thinly as you physically can: thick slices do not absorb, so you get wet bread and dry meat, which is the failure mode of every bad French dip.

  • Reduce the jus until it tastes good enough to drink.
  • Slice as thinly as your knife allows.
  • Toast the roll or the first dip destroys it.

item.title: Halo-Halo
item.description: Halo-halo — Filipino shaved ice with sweet beans, jellies, fruit, evaporated milk and ube ice cream.
item.content:encoded:
The name means "mix mix", and the order is functional: sweet things go at the bottom so the ice above them stays neutral until you stir, which keeps the dessert from being uniformly sugary. The ice must be shaved rather than crushed — crushed cubes melt into water in a couple of minutes and the glass turns to soup.

  • Shaved ice, not crushed. Crushed ice makes a puddle.
  • Freeze the glasses first. It buys you several minutes.
  • Sweet things at the bottom, ice on top, milk poured through.

item.title: Patty Melt
item.description: American patty melt of a thin beef patty griddled between rye bread with slow-caramelised onions and Swiss cheese.
item.content:encoded:
This is not a burger in bread — it is a grilled sandwich that happens to contain beef, and the differences matter. The patty is thin and cooked through, the onions are caramelised for twenty minutes rather than softened for five, and the whole thing is pressed on a griddle until the bread is dark. Rye bread is not optional: its sourness is what stops the richness becoming cloying.

  • Twenty minutes on the onions. Not five.
  • Thin patty, cooked through.
  • Cheese on both sides of the patty so it seals the bread.

item.title: Cheesy Grits
item.description: Southern cheesy grits cooked slowly in milk and stock with butter and sharp Cheddar, seasoned with white pepper.
item.content:encoded:
Use stone-ground grits and give them the full twenty-five minutes on a low heat, whisking often. Instant grits cook in five and taste of the packet; stone-ground release starch slowly and turn genuinely creamy without any thickener. The liquid ratio is four to one and you may need more — grits absorb far more than seems reasonable, so keep hot liquid to hand.

  • Stone-ground, not instant.
  • Whisk in a thin stream or you get lumps you cannot fix.
  • Keep hot liquid nearby — they drink more than you think.

item.title: Ropa Vieja
item.description: Ropa vieja — Cuban shredded flank steak stewed in a pepper, onion, olive and cumin sofrito.
item.content:encoded:
The beef is cooked twice — boiled until it shreds, then stewed in the sofrito — because shredded meat absorbs a sauce in a way a braised joint never can. Reserving some of the cooking broth and using it as the stewing liquid keeps the beef flavour in the dish instead of pouring it down the sink.

  • Shred along the grain into long strands, not into crumbs.
  • Keep the boiling broth — it is the base of the sauce.
  • Simmer uncovered at the end until the sauce clings. Wet ropa vieja is under-cooked.

item.title: Monkey Bread
item.description: American monkey bread of enriched dough balls rolled in cinnamon sugar, stacked in a bundt tin with butter caramel and baked.
item.content:encoded:
Turn it out within two minutes of it leaving the oven. The caramel sets hard as it cools and monkey bread left in the tin welds itself to the metal — five minutes is already too long. Have the serving plate over the tin ready to go, and do it while it is uncomfortably hot.

  • Turn it out within two minutes or it welds to the tin.
  • Butter every groove of the tin.
  • Stack loosely so the caramel gets between the balls.

item.title: Tattie Scones
item.description: Scottish potato scones of leftover mashed potato worked with flour and butter, rolled thin and griddled dry.
item.content:encoded:
Make them while the mashed potato is still warm and use as little flour as will hold it. Cold mash needs more flour to come together and the extra flour is what makes tattie scones tough and papery — warm potato absorbs it readily and the scones stay soft. Roll them properly thin, about 5 mm, so they cook through in the four minutes a dry griddle gives you.

  • Warm potato and as little flour as possible.
  • Roll to 5 mm, not thicker.
  • A dry griddle, barely greased.

item.title: Bandeja Paisa
item.description: Bandeja paisa — Colombian platter of beans, rice, chicharrón, chorizo, beef, egg, plantain and arepa.
item.content:encoded:
The beans are the anchor and they need a hogao — a slow-cooked tomato and spring onion sofrito — stirred in near the end rather than at the start, so their sweetness stays bright against the long-cooked beans. Everything else is timed backwards from the egg, which has to be the last thing cooked.

  • Hogao goes into the beans late, not at the start.
  • Start the chicharrón with water in the pan — it renders before it fries.
  • Eggs last. Everything else can be kept warm.

item.title: Barmbrack
item.description: Irish barmbrack of dried fruit soaked overnight in strong tea and whiskey, folded into a spiced batter and baked as a loaf.
item.content:encoded:
Soak the fruit in hot tea overnight and it plumps to the point of bursting, which does two things: the loaf stays moist for days, and the fruit stops stealing moisture from the crumb during baking. Fruit added dry gives you a cake that is stale on the second morning. Use tea strong enough to be undrinkable — it is carrying most of the flavour.

  • Overnight soaking, no shortcuts.
  • Tea strong enough to be undrinkable.
  • Slice it thick and butter it heavily.

item.title: Dublin Coddle
item.description: Dublin coddle of pork sausages, streaky bacon, potatoes and onions layered and slow-cooked in stock with parsley.
item.content:encoded:
Brown the sausages and bacon before they go in, even though the traditional recipe does not — the untraditional version is grey and the browning costs six minutes. Everything else stays plain: no herbs beyond parsley, no garlic, no wine. Coddle is meant to taste of pork, potato and onion and nothing else, and cooks who improve it stop making coddle.

  • Brown the meat first, whatever tradition says.
  • Nothing beyond salt, pepper, bay and parsley.
  • Do not stir it. Layers are the dish.

item.title: Rouladen
item.description: German rouladen of thin beef slices rolled around mustard, bacon, onion and gherkin, browned and braised in stock and red wine.
item.content:encoded:
Bat the beef out until you can nearly see through it. Thick slices never become tender in two hours — they stay chewy and the roll is too fat to brown evenly. And spread mustard right to the edges before the filling goes on: it seasons the inside of the roll, which otherwise tastes of nothing, and helps the gravy cling.

  • Bat them genuinely thin.
  • Mustard to the edges.
  • Roll tight and secure, or they unwind in the pot.

item.title: Ajiaco
item.description: Ajiaco — Bogotá chicken and potato soup with guascas, corn, cream and capers.
item.content:encoded:
Three potato varieties are not fussiness: the small yellow criollas dissolve completely and thicken the soup, the sabanera holds its shape, and the pastusa sits in between. Guascas is the herb that makes ajiaco taste like ajiaco and there is no real substitute — it is worth ordering.

  • Three potatoes, three jobs. Using one variety gives a thin soup.
  • Guascas is the flavour. Order it rather than substituting.
  • Cream and capers go in at the table, not the pot.

item.title: Colombian Empanadas
item.description: Colombian empanadas — corn dough shells filled with potato and beef, deep fried until crackly.
item.content:encoded:
The masarepa dough is stiffer and drier than a wheat pastry, so it is rolled between plastic sheets rather than on a floured surface — flour would only make it crack. Sealing them by pressing with a plate or a bowl rim gives a clean, tight edge, and any gap means oil gets in and the empanada bursts.

  • Roll between plastic sheets, never on flour.
  • Cold filling, always. Warm filling steams the dough open.
  • Patch any crack before frying or it will burst in the oil.

item.title: Obatzda
item.description: Bavarian obatzda of ripe Camembert mashed with butter, sweet paprika, onion and a splash of beer, served with pretzels.
item.content:encoded:
Use Camembert that is properly ripe — soft to the point of collapse and smelling strongly. Under-ripe cheese stays in rubbery lumps that no amount of mashing fixes, and it is the ripeness that gives obatzda its depth. Mash it with a fork rather than blending: the texture should be uneven, with some pieces still recognisable.

  • Properly ripe Camembert, rind included.
  • Fork, not blender — the texture should be uneven.
  • Beer a spoonful at a time.

item.title: Pierogi Ruskie
item.description: Polish pierogi ruskie of soft dough filled with mashed potato and twaróg curd cheese, boiled then fried in butter with onion.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is made with hot water rather than cold, which gelatinises some of the starch and makes it far more elastic and forgiving — it rolls thin without springing back and it seals without tearing. Keep it under a bowl the whole time you work, because pierogi dough dries in about four minutes and dry edges will not seal at all.

  • Hot water dough. It changes everything.
  • Keep the dough under a bowl at all times.
  • Boil, then fry. Both.

item.title: Sernik
item.description: Polish sernik baked cheesecake of twaróg curd cheese, eggs and sugar on a shortcrust base, baked low and cooled in the oven.
item.content:encoded:
Twaróg has to be pressed through a sieve or ground twice — it is grainy in a way cream cheese is not, and lumps that look small in the bowl are unpleasant in the finished cake. Bake it low and slow and then leave it in the switched-off oven with the door ajar for an hour: sudden cooling is what cracks the top, and this one cracks readily.

  • Sieve the twaróg twice.
  • Low oven, and cool it in the oven with the door ajar.
  • Four hours in the fridge before it will slice cleanly.

item.title: Causa Limeña
item.description: Causa limeña — cold layered Peruvian potato terrine with ají amarillo, lime and a chicken filling.
item.content:encoded:
The potato is mashed while hot but seasoned and worked until it is smooth and slightly elastic, then chilled — that structure is what lets it be sliced. Ají amarillo paste and lime go in generously because the dish is served cold, and cold food needs more seasoning than hot food to taste the same.

  • Rice the potatoes hot, season hot, chill after. Order matters.
  • Season harder than seems right. Cold mutes everything.
  • Overnight in the fridge gives clean slices.

item.title: Medovik
item.description: Russian medovik of thin honey biscuit layers stacked with a soured cream and condensed milk frosting and rested overnight.
item.content:encoded:
The layers come out of the oven as hard biscuits and that is correct — they are supposed to. The overnight rest is not for flavour but for structure: the moisture in the soured cream frosting migrates into the biscuit and turns the whole stack into something you can cut with a fork. Served the same day it is a stack of biscuits with cream between them.

  • The layers are meant to be hard. They soften overnight.
  • Trim while hot; cold layers shatter.
  • Keep the trimmings — they are the coating.

item.title: Varenyky
item.description: Ukrainian varenyky filled with sour cherries and sugar, boiled and served with soured cream and the cherry syrup.
item.content:encoded:
Drain the cherries and toss them with semolina, not flour or cornflour, half an hour before filling. Semolina absorbs the juice they release without going pasty, so the dumplings do not burst in the water — and any juice that does escape thickens rather than clouding the pan. Seal the edges with damp fingers and pinch twice.

  • Semolina with the cherries, half an hour ahead.
  • A gentle boil, never a rolling one.
  • Pinch the seal twice.

item.title: Pisco Sour
item.description: Pisco sour — pisco, lime, syrup and egg white double shaken to a thick foam, with Angostura bitters.
item.content:encoded:
The dry shake — shaking without ice first — is what emulsifies the egg white into a stable foam; adding ice at the start chills the protein before it can be whipped and the head collapses in a minute. Peruvian pisco is unaged and aromatic, and swapping in a barrel-aged spirit changes the drink completely.

  • Dry shake first, always. Ice first gives you a thin, short-lived head.
  • Double strain so no ice shards break the foam.
  • Fresh lime only. Bottled juice makes the drink taste flat and sweet.

item.title: Dobos Torte
item.description: Hungarian dobos torte of five thin sponge layers with chocolate buttercream, topped with a caramel disc scored into wedges.
item.content:encoded:
The caramel top must be scored into wedges while it is still liquid enough to cut and firm enough to hold the line — about forty seconds after it is poured, and the window is genuinely that short. Oil the knife first. Left to set solid, it shatters when anyone tries to serve it, which is why so many Dobos tortes arrive with a broken lid.

  • Score the caramel at forty seconds. Oil the knife.
  • Keep the flattest sponge for the top.
  • Cool the melted chocolate before it meets the butter.

item.title: Pkhali
item.description: Georgian pkhali of blanched spinach, beetroot and beans separately pounded with a walnut, garlic, coriander and vinegar paste.
item.content:encoded:
The walnut paste is made once and divided between the vegetables, which is what makes a plate of pkhali read as one dish in three colours. Squeeze the blanched vegetables far harder than feels necessary — anything left wet turns the paste to soup. Blue fenugreek and marigold are the authentic seasonings but ground coriander and a pinch of turmeric get close.

  • One walnut paste, divided three ways.
  • Squeeze everything much harder than seems reasonable.
  • Taste and correct each colour separately.

item.title: Jachnun
item.description: Yemenite jachnun of dough stretched paper-thin, spread with butter, rolled and baked slowly with eggs until dark and sweet.
item.content:encoded:
Stretch the dough until you can read through it. Every roll you make is one continuous sheet folded on itself a dozen times, and the layers are what turn to threads over three hours in the oven — thick dough gives you a solid, doughy log instead. Oil the worktop rather than flouring it and pull from the middle outwards with the flat of your hand; the dough is elastic enough to take it.

  • Oil, never flour, or the layers glue together.
  • Roll loosely; a tight roll steams into a dense middle.
  • Foil under the lid matters — it is what keeps the steam in for three hours.

item.title: Provoleta
item.description: Provoleta — a disc of provolone grilled in cast iron until crusted outside and molten inside.
item.content:encoded:
Provolone hilado, the aged Argentinian type, has a low enough moisture content to brown rather than collapse into a puddle — a young provolone dolce will simply melt and run. Drying the cut surface in the fridge for an hour is what lets the crust form before the middle goes.

  • Aged provolone only. The soft kind runs straight out of the pan.
  • Dry the surfaces in the fridge first.
  • Serve in the pan. Off the heat it sets within three or four minutes.

item.title: Sopa de Tortilla
item.description: Mexican tortilla soup of a pasilla and tomato broth topped at the table with fried tortilla strips, avocado, cheese and crema.
item.content:encoded:
The tortilla strips go into the bowl at the table, never into the pot. Cooked in the broth they dissolve into thickener within a couple of minutes and the whole point of the dish — crisp against hot liquid — disappears. Toast and soak the dried chillies rather than using powder; the smoky depth of pasilla is the flavour people remember.

  • Strips at the table, never in the pot.
  • Toast and soak whole dried chillies.
  • Strain the purée or the broth is gritty.

item.title: Camarones a la Diabla
item.description: Mexican camarones a la diabla of prawns in a blended guajillo, arbol and chipotle sauce with garlic, tomato and lime.
item.content:encoded:
Fry the blended chilli sauce for five minutes before the prawns go anywhere near it. Straight from the blender it tastes raw and thin and no amount of simmering with the prawns fixes it, because prawns need three minutes and the sauce needs five on its own. Fry it until it darkens and thickens, then add the prawns and take the pan off almost immediately.

  • Fry the sauce for five minutes on its own.
  • Season the sauce before the prawns arrive.
  • Three minutes for the prawns, then off the heat.

item.title: Milanesa Napolitana
item.description: Milanesa napolitana — breaded beef cutlet topped with ham, tomato sauce and melted cheese.
item.content:encoded:
The cutlet is fried first and topped after, then finished under the grill only long enough to melt the cheese — build it raw and the crumb goes soft under the sauce. Beating the beef to an even 5 mm means it cooks in the three minutes the crust takes to colour.

  • Marinate in the garlic egg. It is what makes a milanesa taste Argentinian.
  • Fry first, top after, grill briefly. Never bake it all together.
  • Rest the coated cutlets 15 minutes before frying.

item.title: Esquites
item.description: Mexican esquites of corn kernels charred in butter with epazote, dressed with mayonnaise, lime, chilli powder and cotija.
item.content:encoded:
Char the kernels properly — leave them still in a hot dry pan until they blacken in patches and start popping. Corn stirred gently in butter is sweet and one-dimensional; charred, it develops the bitter, smoky edge that the lime and chilli play against. Dress it while hot so the mayonnaise loosens and coats rather than sitting in cold blobs.

  • Leave the corn still until it blackens.
  • Dress it hot so the mayonnaise loosens.
  • More chilli powder on top than feels right.

item.title: Dulce de Leche
item.description: Dulce de leche — milk and sugar cooked down slowly to a thick amber caramel spread.
item.content:encoded:
The bicarbonate of soda raises the pH, which speeds up the Maillard browning and gives the deep colour that sugar caramelisation alone would not — without it you get sweetened condensed milk, not dulce de leche. It has to be stirred more and more often as it thickens, because the sugar catches instantly once the water is gone.

  • A wide pan. A narrow one takes twice as long.
  • Stop while it still looks slightly loose. It sets firm when cold.
  • Constant stirring in the last half hour, or it will catch and taste burnt.

item.title: Gorditas
item.description: Mexican gorditas of masa harina griddled thick until they puff, split and filled with beans, cheese and salsa.
item.content:encoded:
They puff because steam builds inside a sealed thick disc, and that only happens if the masa is the right wetness — it should feel like soft modelling clay and not crack at all when you press the edge. If it cracks, wet your hands and knead more water in. A cracked gordita lets the steam out and stays flat, and then there is nothing to split open.

  • Dough that does not crack at the edge. That is the whole test.
  • Dry griddle first, oil at the end.
  • Split them while hot or the pocket seals shut.

item.title: Pastel de Choclo
item.description: Pastel de choclo — Chilean beef and chicken bake under a ground corn and basil topping.
item.content:encoded:
The corn topping is cooked on the hob with milk and basil before it goes on, so it sets to a firm, sliceable layer rather than staying wet — raw ground corn spread over the filling will separate in the oven. The dusting of sugar on top is a Chilean habit that makes a lacquered, slightly bitter crust against the sweet corn.

  • Cook the corn topping on the hob first. Raw corn separates in the oven.
  • Twenty minutes on the onions for the pino. It is the base of the flavour.
  • The sugar on top is not optional — it makes the crust.

item.title: Completo Italiano
item.description: Completo italiano — Chilean hot dog with diced tomato, mashed avocado and mayonnaise.
item.content:encoded:
It is called italiano because the three toppings are the colours of the Italian flag, which means the proportions matter: equal, thick layers of each, not a scatter. Mashing the avocado with lemon and salt rather than slicing it is what lets it sit in a band without sliding off.

  • Drain the tomato. It is the difference between a completo and a soggy roll.
  • Mash the avocado rather than slicing it, so it stays put.
  • Equal bands of all three. That is what makes it an italiano.

item.title: Coxinha
item.description: Coxinha — Brazilian teardrop croquettes of shredded chicken and cream cheese in a stock dough, fried.
item.content:encoded:
The dough is made by cooking flour into hot chicken stock like a choux, which gelatinises the starch so it can be moulded warm without cracking — a cold dough will split every time you shape one. The teardrop shape is traditional because it imitates a chicken drumstick, which is what coxinha means.

  • Shape the dough while it is warm. Cold dough cracks.
  • Cold filling in warm dough, never the other way round.
  • Chill the crumbed coxinhas before frying so they hold their shape.

item.title: Caipirinha
item.description: Caipirinha — lime muddled with sugar, topped with cachaça and crushed ice and stirred until frosted.
item.content:encoded:
The lime is muddled with sugar rather than juiced, so the sugar crystals scrape oil out of the peel — that oil is most of the aroma. Muddling too hard crushes the white pith and turns the drink bitter, which is why the technique is a press and twist, not a pounding.

  • Cut out the white core. It is where the bitterness lives.
  • Press and twist, do not pound. Six or seven presses is enough.
  • Crushed ice, not cubes. It dilutes at the right speed for this drink.

item.title: Rice and Peas
item.description: Jamaican rice and peas — rice cooked in coconut milk with kidney beans, thyme and scotch bonnet.
item.content:encoded:
Cooking dried beans from scratch gives you their cooking liquid, which is what colours the rice and carries most of the flavour — tinned beans make a paler, blander pot. The scotch bonnet goes in whole and unpierced so it perfumes the rice without making it hot, and it must come out before it splits.

  • Cook the beans from dried and keep the liquid. That liquid is the recipe.
  • Whole scotch bonnet, never pierced, out before it splits.
  • Do not lift the lid during the twenty minutes.

item.title: Jamaican Beef Patty
item.description: Jamaican beef patty — turmeric pastry folded around spiced beef and baked until flaky.
item.content:encoded:
The pastry is laminated with cold suet or butter and turmeric, which gives the colour and, more importantly, the flake — patties made with plain shortcrust are a different, duller thing. The filling is bound with breadcrumbs so it stays moist in the oven without leaking through the seam.

  • Cold butter, folded twice. That is where the flake comes from.
  • Breadcrumbs in the filling keep it saucy without leaking.
  • Seal the edge properly with a fork, all the way round.

item.title: Trinidadian Doubles
item.description: Trinidadian doubles — soft fried bara filled with curried chickpeas, tamarind and pepper sauce.
item.content:encoded:
Bara has to stay soft, which means a slack, turmeric-yellow dough proved twice and fried fast at a high temperature so it puffs rather than crisps. The channa is deliberately loose and a little soupy, because the bara has to soak some of it up without falling apart.

  • Twenty seconds a side. Bara should be soft, not crisp.
  • Fry the curry paste until the oil separates before the chickpeas go in.
  • Keep the channa loose. It has to soak into the bara.

item.title: Callaloo
item.description: Callaloo — Trinidadian dasheen leaves cooked with okra and coconut milk into a thick green purée.
item.content:encoded:
Okra is not a vegetable in this dish so much as a thickener — its mucilage is what gives callaloo its particular smooth, slightly viscous body. The leaves have to be cooked far past the point where they look done, until they lose all structure, which is the difference between callaloo and creamed greens.

  • Cook it well past the point where the leaves look done.
  • Okra is the thickener. Do not leave it out.
  • Scotch bonnet whole and out before it bursts, unless you want real heat.

item.title: Moin Moin
item.description: Moin moin — Nigerian steamed bean pudding of peeled black-eyed beans, peppers and onion.
item.content:encoded:
The beans must be peeled — soaked and rubbed until the skins float off — because the skins make the finished pudding grainy and grey rather than smooth and orange. The batter needs to be thinner than seems right, closer to double cream, since it sets firm as the bean starch cooks.

  • Peel the beans properly. Skins make it grey and grainy.
  • Batter like double cream. Too thick and it sets solid and dry.
  • Beat air in for three minutes before steaming.

item.title: Nigerian Pepper Soup
item.description: Nigerian pepper soup — a thin, fiery broth of West African spices with goat, fish or chicken.
item.content:encoded:
Pepper soup spice is a specific blend — ehuru, uda, uziza and grains of paradise — and its aroma is volatile, so half goes in early for depth and half at the end for perfume. The broth is deliberately thin: it is a soup to drink, and thickening it changes what the dish is for.

  • Half the spice early, half at the end. The aroma does not survive a long simmer.
  • Keep it thin. Pepper soup is drunk, not spooned through.
  • Fish goes in last and is never stirred.

item.title: Waakye
item.description: Waakye — Ghanaian rice and beans coloured with sorghum leaves, served with shito and sides.
item.content:encoded:
The colour and the faint earthy flavour come from dried sorghum leaves, and a pinch of bicarbonate of soda in the water is what releases the pigment — without it the leaves give very little. The beans are part-cooked before the rice goes in so both finish at the same time.

  • The bicarbonate of soda is what draws the colour out of the leaves.
  • Part-cook the beans first so they finish with the rice.
  • Lid stays on for the full 25 minutes and the 10-minute rest.

item.title: Kelewele
item.description: Kelewele — Ghanaian spiced fried plantain with ginger, chilli, cloves and anise.
item.content:encoded:
The plantain must be properly ripe — black-skinned, not yellow — because its sugar is what caramelises in the oil into the almost-burnt edges the dish is about. Marinating in a wet spice paste rather than a dry rub means the seasoning sticks through the frying instead of falling to the bottom of the pot.

  • Black-skinned plantain only. Yellow ones will not caramelise.
  • A wet paste, not a dry rub. It stays on in the oil.
  • Take them darker than feels safe. That is where the flavour is.

item.title: Nyama Choma
item.description: Nyama choma — Kenyan goat or beef grilled slowly over coals and served with kachumbari and ugali.
item.content:encoded:
Nyama choma is grilled low and slow rather than seared, over coals that have burned down, so the connective tissue in cheaper cuts has time to soften while the outside dries into a crust. Salt is genuinely the only seasoning in the traditional version — everything else happens on the plate with kachumbari.

  • Coals burned down, not flaming. This is an hour of cooking, not fifteen minutes.
  • Salt only. The kachumbari does the rest.
  • Chop it on the board at the table — that is part of the meal.

item.title: Ugali and Sukuma Wiki
item.description: Ugali and sukuma wiki — stiff maize meal with collard greens fried with onion and tomato.
item.content:encoded:
Ugali is cooked far past the point where it looks done — pressed and turned against the side of the pot for a full ten minutes — because that is what develops the smooth, firm texture you can tear and dip with. Sukuma is cooked briefly and stays green; long-cooked greens go grey and lose the point of the dish.

  • Turn and press the ugali for ten minutes. Undercooked, it tastes raw and grainy.
  • Greens for eight minutes only. They should stay green.
  • A heavy pan and a strong wooden spoon. This takes real effort.

item.title: Bunny Chow
item.description: Bunny chow — a hollowed quarter loaf filled with Durban mutton curry, with the bread to dip.
item.content:encoded:
Durban curry is defined by its chilli-forward masala and the fact that it is thickened by potato rather than by a paste, so it is loose enough to soak into the bread but not so thin it runs straight through. The loaf must be a dense white bread with a strong crust, which is the only thing holding the whole construction together.

  • Fry the masala until the oil separates. It is the base of a Durban curry.
  • Potato is the thickener, added late so it holds some shape.
  • Unsliced white bread with a firm crust. Anything softer collapses.

item.title: Malva Pudding
item.description: Malva pudding — South African apricot jam sponge soaked in a hot cream and butter sauce.
item.content:encoded:
The sauce goes over the sponge while both are hot, which is the only way it gets absorbed rather than pooling underneath — a cooled cake sheds it. A tablespoon of vinegar in the batter reacts with the bicarbonate of soda for lift and, more usefully, keeps the very sweet sponge from being cloying.

  • Hot sauce onto hot sponge, straight out of the oven.
  • Prick it all over first so the sauce has a way in.
  • It will look like too much sauce. It is not.

item.title: Lamingtons
item.description: Lamingtons — squares of butter sponge dipped in chocolate icing and rolled in desiccated coconut.
item.content:encoded:
The sponge has to be a day old and preferably chilled, because fresh cake falls apart the moment it meets the thin icing. The icing itself is deliberately runny — closer to a glaze than a frosting — so it soaks a millimetre into the crumb rather than sitting on the surface in a shell.

  • Day-old, chilled sponge. Fresh cake disintegrates in the icing.
  • Thin icing, not thick. It should run off the fork.
  • Two forks and a rack. It is a messy job however you do it.

item.title: Pavlova
item.description: Pavlova — crisp-shelled meringue with a marshmallow centre, topped with cream and fresh fruit.
item.content:encoded:
Cornflour and vinegar are what create the marshmallow interior: the acid stabilises the foam and the starch keeps the centre from drying out into plain meringue. Cooling the pavlova in the switched-off oven with the door shut is the single best defence against the cracking that comes from a sudden temperature drop.

  • Sugar in slowly, a spoonful at a time. Rushing gives a weeping meringue.
  • Rub a little between your fingers — no grit means it is ready.
  • Cool in the closed oven. Cracks come from sudden cooling.

item.title: Anzac Biscuits
item.description: Anzac biscuits — oat and coconut biscuits bound with golden syrup and bicarbonate of soda.
item.content:encoded:
The bicarbonate of soda is dissolved in boiling water and stirred into the melted butter and syrup, where it reacts immediately and aerates the mixture — added dry with the flour it does far less. There are no eggs, which is why the originals kept for the length of a sea voyage and why the texture depends entirely on baking time.

  • Dissolve the bicarbonate of soda in boiling water first. It has to foam.
  • Twelve minutes chewy, sixteen crisp. Pick your side.
  • Leave them on the tray for five minutes or they will fall apart.

item.title: Kalua Pork
item.description: Kalua pork — Hawaiian salted pork shoulder wrapped in banana leaf and slow cooked until it shreds.
item.content:encoded:
Kalua pork traditionally cooks in an imu, an underground oven, and the whole flavour is smoke, salt and pork with nothing else — which means the salt has to be coarse and generous, and any extra seasoning takes it away from what it should be. Banana leaf keeps the meat moist and adds a faint grassy note that foil alone cannot.

  • Salt, smoke, pork. Adding anything else makes it a different dish.
  • Wrap tightly. All the moisture has to stay in the parcel.
  • Toss the shredded meat through the juices, every drop of them.

item.title: Loco Moco
item.description: Loco moco — rice topped with a hamburger patty, brown gravy and a fried egg.
item.content:encoded:
The gravy is built in the pan the patties cooked in, so all the browned fond ends up in it — made separately it tastes like packet gravy on a burger. The egg has to be fried in hot fat with a runny yolk, because the yolk running into the gravy and rice is the point of the assembly.

  • Build the gravy in the patty pan. That fond is the flavour.
  • Runny yolks, always. They finish the dish at the table.
  • Dimple the patties so they stay flat under the egg.

item.title: Breakfast Hash
item.description: Breakfast hash — crisp fried potatoes with peppers and onions, finished with eggs under the grill.
item.content:encoded:
Par-boiling the potatoes and then drying them gives a floury surface that crisps in the pan, which raw diced potato never does in the time available. Leaving the pan alone for five minutes at a time is the other half — the crust forms in contact with hot metal, and stirring resets the clock every time.

  • Par-boil and steam dry. Raw potato will not crisp in the time you have.
  • Leave the pan alone for five minutes at a stretch. Stirring stops the crust.
  • Grill the eggs rather than covering the pan, so the tops set but the yolks do not.

item.title: Ribollita
item.description: Ribollita — Tuscan bean and cavolo nero soup thickened with stale bread and reboiled the next day.
item.content:encoded:
The name means "reboiled", and it is not romanticism: the soup is made one day, left overnight for the bread to dissolve completely into it, and reheated the next, which is when it becomes a single thick mass rather than soup with bread in it. Puréeing a third of the beans gives body without cream or stock.

  • Make it a day ahead. Reboiled is the recipe, not a suggestion.
  • Twenty minutes on the soffritto. Everything else depends on it.
  • Finish with far more raw olive oil than seems polite.

item.title: Roasted Vegetable Buddha Bowl
item.description: Roasted vegetable buddha bowl — roast vegetables, grains and chickpeas with a tahini dressing.
item.content:encoded:
A bowl like this fails when everything is the same texture, so the components are cooked separately and deliberately differently: vegetables roasted hard, chickpeas crisped, grains dressed while warm, greens raw. Whisking iced water into tahini makes it seize and then loosen into a pale, creamy dressing, which is the only reliable way to get the consistency right.

  • Iced water into the tahini. It seizes first, then loosens — keep going.
  • Dress the grains warm so they take the acid.
  • Sections, not a mix. The contrast is the whole appeal.

item.title: Affogato
item.description: Affogato — vanilla gelato with a shot of hot espresso poured over it at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The whole dish is a temperature contrast that lasts about ninety seconds, so the glass is chilled, the ice cream is hard-frozen and the espresso is pulled at the last moment. A single shot to one scoop is the ratio that keeps it a dessert rather than a coffee with cream in it.

  • Chill the glasses. It buys another thirty seconds of contrast.
  • One shot per scoop. More and it becomes a coffee float.
  • Pour the espresso the moment it is made, at the table.

item.title: Berry Smoothie Bowl
item.description: Berry smoothie bowl — frozen fruit blended thick enough to spoon, topped with fruit, seeds and granola.
item.content:encoded:
The difference between a smoothie and a smoothie bowl is liquid, and specifically how little of it: the fruit must be frozen solid and the liquid added a tablespoon at a time, using the tamper rather than more milk to keep the blades moving. Any more and it becomes a drink and the toppings sink.

  • Frozen fruit and almost no liquid. Add milk by the tablespoon.
  • Use the tamper, not more milk, to keep the blades turning.
  • Chill the bowls and eat it straight away.

item.title: Cold Brew Coffee
item.description: Cold brew coffee — coarse coffee steeped in cold water for 18 hours to a smooth, low acid concentrate.
item.content:encoded:
Cold water never extracts the bitter and sour compounds that hot water pulls out in seconds, which is why cold brew tastes smooth and sweet without being weaker — the trade is time, roughly eighteen hours for what hot water does in four minutes. Grinding coarse is essential: fine grounds over-extract even cold and clog every filter you own.

  • Coarse grind. Fine grounds turn cold brew bitter and cloudy.
  • Do not stir during the steep.
  • Filter twice, and be patient with the second pass.

item.title: Chicken Milanese
item.description: Chicken Milanese — chicken breast beaten thin, breaded and fried in butter until deep gold and crisp.
item.content:encoded:
Pounding to an even 5 mm means the cutlet cooks through in the three minutes the crust needs to brown — any thicker and you choose between a pale crust and dry meat. Clarified butter takes the heat without the milk solids burning, which whole butter would do in a shallow fry.

  • Even thickness beats thinness. A cutlet thin at one end and thick at the other cooks two different ways.
  • Rest after breading. Fifteen minutes is the difference between a crust that stays on and one that peels.
  • A rack, not kitchen paper — paper traps steam and softens the underside immediately.

item.title: Pasta Puttanesca
item.description: Pasta puttanesca — tomatoes, anchovies, olives, capers and chilli, made in the time the pasta boils.
item.content:encoded:
The anchovies are melted into warm oil rather than added to a hot pan, so they dissolve completely instead of frying — done properly the sauce tastes savoury and deep rather than of fish. No salt is added at any stage: anchovies, olives and capers between them bring more than enough.

  • Start the anchovies in cold oil. Dropped into a hot pan they seize and stay in lumps.
  • No Parmesan. Cheese on a puttanesca is a genuine offence in Naples and it does not need it.
  • Do not salt the sauce until you have tasted it at the end.

item.title: Pots de Crème
item.description: Pots de crème au chocolat — dark chocolate baked custards, set in a bain-marie and served chilled.
item.content:encoded:
Custard sets by coagulating egg protein, which happens around 80°C and curdles above 85°C — the bain-marie holds the pots below that ceiling so they set smooth rather than grainy. Pouring the hot cream onto the chocolate rather than melting them together avoids seizing.

  • Strain the custard. It takes ten seconds and is the difference between silky and slightly grainy.
  • They should wobble when they come out. A firm pot in the oven is an overcooked pot on the plate.
  • Use chocolate you would eat on its own — there are only three other ingredients.

item.title: Salade de Chèvre Chaud
item.description: Salade de chèvre chaud — grilled goat cheese toasts on dressed leaves with walnuts and honey.
item.content:encoded:
A log-shaped goat cheese with a rind holds its shape under the grill where a soft, rindless cheese collapses through the toast. Dressing the leaves before the toasts land keeps them crisp — hot cheese on undressed leaves steams them flat.

  • Use a rinded log. Rindless goat cheese slides off the toast and through the grill rack.
  • Dress the leaves first, then add the toasts. The other way round gives you a warm, wilted salad.
  • Stand and watch it. Three minutes is right and five is a puddle.

item.title: Pork Shogayaki
item.description: Pork shogayaki — thin pork loin in a ginger, soy and mirin glaze, with shredded cabbage. Ready in 25 minutes.
item.content:encoded:
Grated ginger is added twice — some in the marinade for penetration, the rest at the end for aroma, since gingerol degrades quickly over heat and a single early addition tastes flat. Dusting the pork in a little flour gives the glaze something to cling to instead of pooling in the pan.

  • Score the fat edge. Unscored pork loin curls into a cup and cooks unevenly.
  • Half the ginger goes in at the end. That late hit is where the aroma comes from.
  • The iced cabbage is not garnish — the cold crunch against the hot glaze is the point of the plate.

item.title: Buta no Kakuni
item.description: Buta no kakuni — Japanese braised pork belly, simmered until a chopstick passes through, with egg and mustard.
item.content:encoded:
The belly is boiled in plain water with rice or leek tops first, then discarded — that pre-boil removes both scum and a great deal of fat, which is why kakuni tastes rich rather than greasy despite the cut. Cooling in the braising liquid overnight lets the seasoning penetrate and makes the surface fat easy to lift off.

  • The hour-long pre-boil is what makes this rich instead of greasy. Do not skip it.
  • Overnight in the liquid, then skim. Both the flavour and the texture depend on that rest.
  • A chopstick, not a knife, is the doneness test — it should meet nothing at all.

item.title: Shui Zhu Fish
item.description: Shui zhu fish — Sichuan poached fish in chilli broth, finished with smoking oil poured over at the table.
item.content:encoded:
The fish is velveted in egg white and cornflour and poached for barely two minutes, so it stays silky in a dish that looks aggressive. The smoking oil poured over the aromatics at the end blooms them instantly — done in the pan instead, the chillies would burn long before the dish reached the table.

  • The oil must be smoking. Anything cooler and the chillies steam rather than bloom.
  • Slide the fish in one slice at a time and leave it alone — stirring breaks it apart.
  • Most of the chillies are there for aroma, not to be eaten. Push them aside as you go.

item.title: Lo Bak Go
item.description: Lo bak go — steamed daikon and rice flour cake with dried shrimp and lap cheong, pan-fried crisp in slices.
item.content:encoded:
The daikon is cooked down first and its liquid kept, because that liquid is what hydrates the rice flour — using water instead loses most of the flavour. The cake must chill overnight before slicing: warm, it is too soft to cut and falls apart in the pan.

  • Keep the daikon cooking liquid. It carries the flavour and hydrates the flour.
  • Overnight in the fridge, without exception. A warm cake cannot be sliced.
  • Fry it properly — the contrast between crisp exterior and soft interior is the whole pleasure.

item.title: Bhindi Masala
item.description: Bhindi masala — okra fried dry with onion and spices, kept crisp rather than slimy. A 40-minute dry curry.
item.content:encoded:
Okra releases mucilage when cut wet, so it is washed and dried completely hours ahead and never covered while cooking — trapped steam is what makes it slimy. Adding acid only at the very end matters too: acid early in the cook draws the mucilage out.

  • Dry the okra hours ahead. This is the single most important step.
  • Never cover the pan, at any stage. Trapped steam is what causes slime.
  • Amchur goes in at the end. Acid early in the cook makes the problem worse.

item.title: Shahi Paneer
item.description: Shahi paneer — paneer in a pale cashew and cream gravy with cardamom and rose. Mild Mughlai cooking.
item.content:encoded:
The gravy is built on blanched cashews and melon seeds rather than tomato, which is why it stays pale — the onions are boiled rather than browned for the same reason. Sieving the blended paste is what gives the glassy restaurant texture that no amount of blending alone achieves.

  • Boil the onions, do not brown them. Colour in the base means it is no longer shahi paneer.
  • Sieve the paste. It takes two minutes and transforms the texture.
  • Rose water is powerful — a teaspoon perfumes, a tablespoon ruins.

item.title: Beef Barbacoa
item.description: Beef barbacoa — chuck braised for hours with dried chillies, cloves and bay until it shreds.
item.content:encoded:
Toasting the dried chillies before soaking wakes the oils in their skins, which is where their fruit and smoke live; soaking them straight from the packet gives a flat, tannic sauce. Chuck and cheek both carry enough collagen that four hours turns them silky rather than dry.

  • Toast the chillies briefly — 30 seconds a side. Burnt chilli makes the whole pot bitter.
  • Cheek is the better cut if your butcher has it: more collagen, more silk.
  • Cook it the day before. Barbacoa is better on day two, every time.

item.title: Tinga Tostadas
item.description: Tinga tostadas — crisp tortillas topped with smoky chipotle chicken, beans, crema and cheese.
item.content:encoded:
Tinga is defined by the ratio of chipotle to tomato: enough chipotle to smoke the sauce, enough tomato to keep it from being just heat. A smear of refried beans on the tostada before the chicken is structural — it glues the toppings down so the first bite does not shed everything onto the plate.

  • Beans first, always. They are the glue that holds a tostada together.
  • Build them at the table. A dressed tostada goes soft in about four minutes.
  • Chipotles in adobo vary in heat. Start with two and add the third after tasting.

item.title: Buttermilk Biscuits
item.description: Buttermilk biscuits — tall, flaky Southern biscuits made with cold butter and a folded dough.
item.content:encoded:
Layers come from sheets of cold butter trapped between sheets of dough: in the oven the butter steams, pushing the layers apart. Folding the dough over itself three or four times builds those sheets, and a straight-down cut with a sharp cutter keeps the edges free to rise rather than sealing them shut.

  • Cold butter, cold buttermilk, warm oven. Any warm butter and you get scones, not biscuits.
  • Never twist the cutter. Twisting seals the edge and the biscuit rises lopsided.
  • Sides touching on the tray gives you height; spaced apart gives you spread.

item.title: Chicken and Waffles
item.description: Chicken and waffles — buttermilk-brined fried chicken on yeasted waffles with hot sauce and maple syrup.
item.content:encoded:
A yeasted waffle batter, rested overnight, sets up crisper and tastes savoury enough to stand next to fried chicken — a baking-powder batter goes soggy under the syrup within a minute. The buttermilk brine does two jobs: its acid tenderises and its salt seasons past the surface.

  • 165C, not hotter. Thighs on the bone need time, and a hot pan burns the crust first.
  • Rest the coated chicken 15 minutes before frying so the crust bonds.
  • Yeasted waffle batter overnight. It is a different food from the quick version.

item.title: Maryland Crab Cakes
item.description: Maryland crab cakes — jumbo lump crab with minimal binder, Old Bay, and a hot grill.
item.content:encoded:
The measure of a crab cake is how little is in it besides crab, which means the binder has to be a barely-set custard rather than breadcrumb bulk. Chilling the shaped cakes for an hour lets that binder firm up so they hold together under the grill without being packed tight.

  • Fold, do not mix. Every extra turn breaks the lumps you paid for.
  • Tall mounds, not flat discs. Flat means dry.
  • Chill an hour before cooking or they slump on the tray.

item.title: Bread and Butter Pudding
item.description: Bread and butter pudding — buttered bread and raisins baked in vanilla custard until crisp on top.
item.content:encoded:
The soak is the recipe: thirty minutes lets the custard get into the crumb so the pudding sets as one thing rather than as bread sitting in scrambled egg. Leaving the top layer proud of the custard is what gives you the crisp, almost caramelised peaks that make the dish worth eating.

  • Day-old bread, not fresh. Fresh bread turns to paste.
  • The 30-minute soak is the difference between pudding and bread in custard.
  • Leave the top points dry so they crisp instead of steaming.

item.title: Scotch Eggs
item.description: Scotch eggs — soft-boiled eggs wrapped in sausage meat, breadcrumbed and fried with the yolk still soft.
item.content:encoded:
Everything depends on the egg being cooked to six minutes and then chilled hard: any longer and the yolk sets, any warmer and the shell will not come off cleanly. The sausage layer is thin and even, so the meat cooks through in the same four minutes it takes the crumb to brown, which is the whole trick.

  • Six and a half minutes, then straight into ice. This is the only timing that matters.
  • Double crumb them. A single coat cracks and lets the fat in.
  • Even meat thickness all the way round, or you get raw patches.
